olor coordinate is treated as an important parameter for phosphors for the application of white LED.The CIE chromaticity coordinates of Ca2-xGa2GeO7; x Dy3+( x=0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.09 ) are shown in Fig.3(b) and Table 1.In addition, the PL intensity ratio of blue/yellow (B/Y) is also listed in Table 1.Obviously, with increasing Dy3+ concentration (x), B/Y decreases when x≤0.07 and then increases when x reaches 0.09.Correspondingly, the emission colors can be tuned with the chromaticity coordinates varying from (0.283, 0.305) to (0.339, 0.368).At last, the white-emitting phosphor Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+ with the appropriate CIE coordinates (0.322, 0.348) is obtained.When the sites of Ca2+ ions are occupied by Dy3+ ions, the charge cannot be balanced in Ca2Ga2GeO7.Then defects Dyca may occur, which could result in the non-radiative processes and deteriorate the luminescence properties.In order to improve the luminescent efficiency, charge compensators are necessary to be introduced, which may reduce the number of defect in the phosphor.Therefore, the samples with electric neutrality of Ca1.94Ga2Ge O7.0.03Dy3+, 0.03R + ( R=Li, Na, K ) and Ca1.97Ga2.03Ge0.97O7: 0.03Dy3+ were prepared.The influ ence of charge compensations on the PL intensity of Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7.0.03Dy3+ is shown in Fig.4.Evidently, Li+, Na+, K+ and Ga3+ ions can significantly enhance the PL intensity of Dy3+ by varying degrees: K+ > Li+ > Ga3+> Na+.Considering that the incorporation of Li+, Na+, K+ and Ga3+ ions may create the Rca (R=Li, Na, K) and GaG defects, which will help to compensate the unbal anced charge in Ca2Ga2GeO7: Dy3+ [ 28 ].With charge compensations, the number of defects may decrease, which could reduce the probability of non-radiative processes and lead to the enhancement of Dy3+ emission[29].

e probability of non-radiative processes and lead to the enhancement of Dy3+ emission[29].Moreover, the possible reason of different improvement level by Li+, Na+, K+ and Ga3+ is that they can induce asymmetry in the host lattice on different levels: rk (0.38) > r Li (0.24) > r Ga (0.21) > r Na (0.02).The asymmetry in the host lattice can be estimated as r R=(rR-rCa) / r Ca (R=Li, Na, K) and r Ga=(rGa-rGe) / r Ge.Maybe, inducing asymmetry in the host lattice to a certain extent is beneficial to improvement of the PL intensity of Dy3+.Besides, the changing of blue-yellow ratio of Dy3+ may also be caused by the changing of symmetry in the host.The CIE chromaticity coordinates and view pictures of the optimized specimen Ca1.94Ga2Ge O7.0.03Dy3+, 0.03K + comparing with Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+ are shown in the inset of Fig.4 and Table 2.With 0.03K+ co-doped as charge compensation in Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+ the emission colors can be tuned with the chromaticity coordinates varying from (0.322, 0.348) to (0.333, 0.353), which is more close to the ideal white light.Furthermore, the quantum efficiency of Dy3+( ex=347 nm, em=574 nm) can be improved from 17.24% (Ca2Ga2GeO7: Dy3+) to 19.77% ( Ca2Ga2GeO7: Dy3+, K+ ).

rom 17.24% (Ca2Ga2GeO7: Dy3+) to 19.77% ( Ca2Ga2GeO7: Dy3+, K+ ).Table 1Comparison of CIE chromaticity coordinates and the PL intensity ratio of blue/yellow (B/Y) for Ca2-xGa2GeO7: x Dy3+( ex=347 nm) No.CompositionCIE xCIE yB/Y1Ca1.99Ga2GeO7:0.01Dy3+0.2830.3050.9672Ca1.98Ga2GeO7:0.02Dy3+0.31:0.03Dy3+0.3220.3480.8694Ca1.95Ga2GeO7:0.05Dy3+0.3290.3550.8525Ca1.93Ga2GeO7:0.07Dy3+0.3390.3680.8476Ca1.91Ga2GeO7:0.09Dy3+0.3340.3630.977 The decay curves of Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+ and Ca1.94Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+, 0.03K+ phosphors are depicted in Fig.5(a) ( ex=347 nm, em=574 nm) and Fig.5 (b) (ex)=347 nm, em=478 nm ).All the decay curves of Dy3+ can be well-fitted via the double-exponential equation I (t)=A1exp (-t/1) + A2exp (-t/2) [ 30 ], where I is the PL intensity of Dy3+; A1 and A2 are constants; t is time; and 1 and 2 are the luminescence lifetimes.Moreover, the average lifetime * can be estimated as *=( A112+A222 ) / ( A22+A22 ) [ 31 ] ].On the basis of equations above, the average lifetimes for Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7.0.03Dy3+ and Ca1.94Ga2Ge O70.03Dy3+, 0.03K + are determined to be 0.013 and 0.472 ms when excited at 347 nm and monitored at 574 nm.When excited at 347 nm and monitored at 478 nm, the average lifetimes are calculated to be 0.027 and 0.165 ms Fig.4PL spectra of Ca1.97Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+, Ca1.94Ga2Ge O7: 0.03Dy3+, 0.

of a blue InGaNLED and the yellow-emitting phosphor ( 3Al5012: Ce3+) [5].However, this method has to face an unavoidable problem of low color rendering index (CRI) and high correlated color temperature (CCT), leading to the fact that the w-LEDs has a poor white color quality due to the lack of sufficient red emission.Accordingly, another approach to obtain white light is generated by means of near-ultraviolet (n-UV) chip LED assigned with the mixture of tricolor (blue, green and red) phosphors.This type also faces some disadvantages such as high cost and poor luminous efficiency due to self-adsorption occurring among the phosphor particles, which limits the popularization of RGBemitting phosphor [6–8].Therefore, an alternative and favorable approach to generate efficient white-light sources is to use a single-component phosphor to widespread use in w-LEDs application, which can have unprecedented advantages such as better stability and reproducibility, and simpler fabrication processes [9].Recently, as an important family of trivalent rare earth ions, dysprosium (Dy3+) ions with 4 f9 electronic configuration and two principal emissions in the blue and yellow regions corresponding to the 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions are being developed intensively research interests and widely used in luminescence materials for w-.E Ds [ 10-12 ].Customarily, the 1.Introduction Asa burgeoning technology, solid state lighting is rapidly developing and emerging as a greener candidate to replace the existing technology in the lighting industry.Especially, white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs) which made a major breakthrough in solid state lighting technology, are considered as a candidate for superseding conventional incandescent and fluorescent lamps owing to their advantages of long lifetime, low power consumption, high energy efficiency, good reliability, compactness, and environmental-friendly characteristics [1–5].The correlated color temperature (CCT) rating for lamps is a general ‘warmth’ or ‘coolness’ measure of its appearance.Usually, WLEDs can be generally categorized as warm WLEDs (<4000K) and cool WLEDs (≥4000K) [6,7].A rating of 3000K is considered a more ideal CCT value for warm WLEDs with higher luminous efficacy of radiation and more energy efficiency [8].Compared with the cool WLEDs, warm WLEDs have lower CCT and are closer to sunlight color, which is beneficial for keeping natural circadian rhythms in humans and offering more visibility.Commercial WLEDs are assembled by combining a chip with powder phosphors, which are usually embedded in epoxy resins.This structure is unsuitable for fabricating high power WLEDs due to many drawbacks.The poor heat resistance of the epoxy resins cause the WLEDs to age more rapidly and the temperature increase of the chip results in lower luminous efficiency.Compared with powder phosphors, single crystals possess good anti-light irradiation, as well as good thermal, mechanical, and chemical stability.The rigid cyclic symmetric structure of single crystals results in high luminous efficiency of active ions.These are helpful for producing high power warm WLEDs to obtain high stability, long lifetime, high luminous efficiency, and excellent color [9,10].

WLEDs to obtain high stability, long lifetime, high luminous efficiency, and excellent color [9,10].Some reports have focused on yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG)-based fluorescent crystals for WLEDs, but its high melt point (1950C) results in a high cost and some difficulties in crystal growth [11,12].Comparatively speaking, bismuth silicate ( Bi4Si3O12, BSO) crystal which is an important scintillation material has a comparatively lower melt point (1030C), as well as other superior properties—large specific heat, small thermal expansion, high optical damage threshold, high optical transmittance, and high hardness—render it more suitable for serving as a fluorescent host for high power LEDs [10,13–15].In recent years, as an important lanthanide ion, trivalent dysprosium ions (Dy3+) were doped in various fluorescent hosts and have been widely studied for WLEDs.Because the visible luminescence of Dy3+(4f9) excited by UV light mainly consists of three bands in blue (470–500 nm), yellow (570–590 nm), and red (655–670 nm) regions, which results in white light emission.However, the CCT values of many fluorescent materials—such as some fluoride, tungstate, borate and silicate—are close to or even higher than 4000K [16–26].Our group has investigated the growth and properties of BSO crystals for several years [10,14,15,27–31].According to our previous work, the yellow bands in Dy3+ doped BSO crystals are more intense than the blue bands [10], and when combined with the red bands they may deduce lower CCT relative to other Dy3+ doped materials.Meanwhile, crystallization quality is crucial for single crystal.However, due to the great difference of the melt point and density between Bi2O3 and SiO, there is always precipitated phase at the top of BSO crystals.It was reported that doping germanium ions (Ge4+) in BSO crystals could effectively modify the crystallization behavior and improve the quality [29].

Synthesis, spectral and surface investigation of novel CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ nanophosphor for UV based white LEDsVinay Kumara,b,*, M.Manhasa, A.K.Bedyalb, H.C.Swartb a Department of Physics, Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University, Katra, 182320, J&K, India b Department of Physics, University of the Free State, P.O.Box 339, Bloemfontein, ZA9300, South Africa ARTICLEINFOArticle history: Received 7March 2017Accepted 20March 2017Available online 22March 2017Keywords: Nanophosphors XPSPhotoluminescence (PL) UV–vis spectroscopy UVLEDsABSTRACTThis paper reports the surface, spectral and luminescent properties of Dy3+ doped CaMgB205 phosphor synthesized by combustion method.X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to characterize the phase structure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to investigate the surface elemental composition and chemical states of the synthesized phosphor.The luminescent properties of CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor was investigated by using photoluminescence emission, excitation and reflectance spectra.The excitation spectra under 576 nm emission consist of charge transfer band (CTB) and a series of 4f-4f transition states of Dy3+ ion.The emission spectra o CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor recorded at 349 nm excitation shows sharp peaks at 485 nm, 576 nm and 665 nm assigned t4F9/26H J / 2: ( J=15, 13, and 11) transitions of Dy3+ ion.The CIE chromaticity color coordinates ( 0.38, 0.40 ) of CaMgB205Dy3+ phosphor falls in the yellowish white region of the horse shoe plot ofcolor gamut.The band gap of the material was calculated to be 5 eV.The phosphor decay curve was also determined.The results show that CaMgBO: Dy3+ phosphor might be potential phosphors for n-UV-based white light-emitting diodes.

content: that CaMgBO: Dy3+ phosphor might be potential phosphors for n-UV-based white light-emitting diodes. 1.Introduction The first commercial white emitting LED was developed in 1997 [1] after the fabrication ofa blue-emitting GaN light emitting diode LED in 1993 by Nakamura et al.[2] after that more and more interest was focused on GaN-based white-emitting LEDs (W-LED).The white light can be obtained by a variety of methods such as by combining blue InGaNLED with a broadband yellow-emitting phosphor, e.g., YAG: Ce3+[3].In addition to this, white light can also be produced by the combination of UV-LED with blue, green and red phosphor and by the combination of blue, green and red LED’s.Among them for white light the use oftricolor (red, green and blue) LEDs has potential high efficiencies and flexible user controlled color.It is well known that photoluminescent (PL) properties of Dy3+ doped phosphors have been widely studied because of the different optical energy levels of Dy3+ which shows light emitted in the white regions because of the existence of two intense emission band in, blue (4F9/26H15/2) ) and yellow (4F9/26H13/2) region and a weak red ( 4F9/2→6H13/2 ) region.The yellow 4F9/26H13/2 transition is a hypersensitive forced electric dipole transition DJ2 and is very sensitive to the coordination environment of the host.However blue (4F9/26H15/2) transition is a host insensitive magnetic dipole transition ( J=3 ) [ 4, 5 ].Thus we can obtain white light with doping of Dy3+ ion into the host materials by changing the yellow to blue (Y/B) ratio.The borate based phosphor materials show excellent lumines cent properties as host matrix due to their large band gap, low synthesizing temperature and high chemical and physical stability [6].A large verity of borate phosphors doped with rare earth ions has been reported in the literature for their applications in solid state lighting, TL personal dosimetry, field emission display panels (FDP) etc.[7–9].

tions in solid state lighting, TL personal dosimetry, field emission display panels (FDP) etc.[7–9].Among these borate materials, alkaline earth borates are good candidates as a host structure due to their low synthetic temperature, easy preparation, and high luminescent brightness [10].In this family the luminescence properties of Sr2B2O5 doped with different rare earth ions has been reported as good host material for LEDs [11–13].The luminescent properties of mixed alkaline borate phosphors doped with different rare earth/ transition metal ions such as Ba2Ca (BO3) 2: Ce3+, Ba2Mg (BO3) 2: Eu2+Mn2+ and M2Mg (BO3) 2Sm3+( M: Sr and Ba) have been reported for the applications of LED [ 14-16 ].The crystal structure of CaMgB205 host was reported by Yakubovich et al.(1976) and Simonov et al.(1980) [17] which show two stable phases; orthorhombic below 400C and monoclinic above 400C.To best our knowledge, no report is available on the photoluminescence and optical studies of Dy3+ doped CaMgB205 phosphor.In the present work, a noble yellowish-white emitting CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphors have been synthesized by the combustion method and its optical and photoluminescence (PL) properties have been investigated.In PL studies, the effects of Dy3+ concentration on luminescent properties and the mechanism for concentration quenching have been reported.In addition, the decay curve and optical energy band gap of CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphors also have been investigated. 2.Experiment The CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphors were synthesized by combustion method using urea as fuel.Calcium nitrate [ Ca (NO3) 2.4H2O ] magnesium nitrate [ Mg (NO3) 26H2O ], boric acid [ H3BO3 ], urea [ CH4N20 ] and dysprosium oxide [ Dy2O3 ] of (AR) grade from Merck chemical were used as starting materials.The samples were synthesized by varying the concentration of dopant Dy3+ from 0.5 to 3.0 mol% according to the complete chemical reactions shown below:- (1-x) Ca (NO3) 24H2O + Mg (NO3) 26H2O + 2H3BO3+ 3.34CH4N2O + 0.5 xDy2O3→Ca (1-x) MgDyxB2O5+ 11.67H2O + 3.34CO2+ 5.

+ Mg (NO3) 26H2O + 2H3BO3+ 3.34CH4N2O + 0.5 xDy2O3→Ca (1-x) MgDyxB2O5+ 11.67H2O + 3.34CO2+ 5.34N2 (1) For complete combustion, the oxidizer/fuel ratio should be equal to unity in order to have the maximum energy release [18].All the reactants were taken according to the balanced Eq.(1) and mixed together according to the stoichiometric ratio in an agate mortar pastel up to 40 min, until the mixture turns into a thick viscous paste.The thick paste was then transferred to a beaker and then introduced into a preheated muffle furnace at 600 -C to produce the phosphors by undergoing a flaming combustion.The whole process was completed within 4 min.The mixture experienced rapid dehydration and foaming followed by decomposition and evolution of combustible gasses.After some time a volumetric combustion occurs, with a yellow flame yielding a white porous solid foamy product with the evolution of the large amount of gases such as CO2, N2 and H2O.The final foamy product was cooled to room temperature and was ground to obtain a fine powder.The fine powder was then annealed at 900C temperature for three hours to improve crystallinity.The phosphors were characterized by using X- ray powder diffractometer of Rikagu-Miniflex, operated at 45 kV and 100 mA and using CuK radiation (=1.5406A ).The XRD patterns were recorded in the range of 10260 with step size of 0.02- (2u).The lattice parameters of the phosphor were calculated by using the UnitCellWin program [19].The photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra were recorded by using a Cary–Eclipse Spectrofluorometer equipped with a150W Xenon lamp as an excitation source with slit width of 5 nm.The decay curve for this phosphor is recorded by using excitation at 349 nm and emission at 578 nm with slit width of 5 nm.The diffuse reflectance spectra of the powder samples were recorded on a Shimadzu UV–VIS2600 double beam spectrophotometer attached to the ISR (IntegratingSphereAssembly) using BaSO4 as a standard powder Fig.3.Concentration quenching spectrum o CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor.The PL emission spectra of CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor at different Dy3+ ion concentration is shown in Fig.3.With increase in Dy3+ ion concentration in CaMgB205 host material, the emission intensity increase with an increase in the Dy3+ concentration and reaches the maximum value of 1.5 mol%.After this, a decrease in emission intensity is observed with increase in Dy3+ concentration.This decrease of PL emission intensity for Dy3+ concentration may be caused by the well knows concentration quenching phenomena [25].As the concentration increases, the distance between Dy3+ ions becomes smaller, leading to a higher probability of energy transfer among Dy3+ ions.The effect of Dy3+ concentration on the PL emission intensity of CaMgB205 phosphor is shown in the inset of Fig.3.The concentration quenching is mainly caused by the nonradiative energy transfer among Dy3+ ions, which occurs as a result of an exchange interaction, radiation re-absorption, or a multipole – multipole interaction.The type of the interaction mechanism can be understood by obtaining the critical distance (R) between the neighboring Dy3+ ions.

echanism can be understood by obtaining the critical distance (R) between the neighboring Dy3+ ions.According to Blasse theory, the critical distance (R) can be obtained by using the Eq.(2):- Rc = 2(3V/(4πXCZ))^(1/3)Where V is the volume ofone unit cell, Z is the number ofcations in the unit cell and X is the critical concentration of the activator ion.By taking the values of V=771.85A3, Z=8 and Xc=0.015 respectively, the calculated value of critical distance (R) between Dy3+ – Dy3+ ions is 23.0 Å.If the value of Dy3+- Dy3+ distance is greater than 5A, the exchange interaction become ineffective and only the multipole – multipole interaction is the major cause of concentration quenching of Dy3+ in the phosphors.In the present study the value of Rc for CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor is calculated to be 23.0 Å, which represent that the multipole interaction plays an important role in the concentration quenching mechanism of Dy3+ in the CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor.There are several types of interactions, such as dipole–dipole (d–d), dipole – quadrupole (d–q), quadrupole – quadrupole (q–q) which are responsible for interaction between the same activators.According to the theory of Dexter [26] the multipole interaction can be calculated from the equation 1x=K [ 1+(x) Q / 3 ] - 13Where, K and are constants for the same excitation condition for the given host, x is the activator concentration which is greater than the critical concentration, Q is the series of multipole interaction for dipole–dipole (d–d), dipole–quadrupole (d–q) and quadrupole–quadrupole (q-q) interactions when the values of Q are 6, 8 and 10, respectively.The value of Q can be obtained from the slope (Q/3) of the linear line of the plot log (I/x) vs log(x).The relation between log (I/x) and log(x) in CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor is shown in Fig.4.The slope of the curve was obtained as 1.984.

Fig.6.The CIE1931 chromaticity diagram fo CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphors under 349 nm excitation.To calculate the color correlated temperature (CCT) for CaMgB2O5: Dy3+(1.5 mol%) phosphor, the McCamy empirical formula [29] is used CCT=- 473 n3+ 3601 n2-6861 n + 5514.32, and n=(x-xe) / (y-ye)6 where, x and y are the color coordinates, Xe=0.3320 and ye=0.1858 are the chromaticity epicenters, respectively.Generally, it is considered that if the value of CCT is greater than 5000K indicates the cold white light used for commercial lighting purpose and if the value of CCT is less than 5000K, indicates the warm white light used for home appliances.For the color coordinates ( x=0.38 and y=0.41 ), CCT value was obtained to be 4206K indicating that CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor can be used as a warm white light (4206K) phosphor for home appliances applications.The schematic energy level diagram of Dy3+ ions in rl CaMgB205; & Dy3+ phosphor, under CT band and different excitation wavelengths is shown in Fig.7.When CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor is excited at 200 nm, the electrons first excited to the conduction band from the valance band and then the energy is moderately transferred to the Dy3+ ions, populating the 4F3/2 energy level as shown in Fig.7.Then, this excitation energy transferred from the conduction band by 02 to Dy3+ ions through the resonance process.

citation energy transferred from the conduction band by 02 to Dy3+ ions through the resonance process.Similarly, under different excitation wavelengths such as 293, 323, 349, 364, 384 and 427 nm, the electron get excited to 4L3/2, 4L19/2, 6P7/2, 6P5/2, 4I13/2, and 4G11/2 higher energy levels from 6H15/2 ground state energy level of Dy3+ ion.From these energy levels the electrons relaxes to 4F9/2 level through non radiative relaxations (NR) processes because of the small energy difference between the excited levels higher than the 4F9/2 energy level.Due to these non radiative relaxation processes the electrons from the higher level populates the 4F9/2 level.Finally, from the 4F9/2 energy level of Dy3+ ion through the radiative transitions the blue (480nm), yellow (578nm) and a weak red (667nm) emissions correspond to the 4F9/26H15/2, 4F9/26H13/2 and 4F5/26H11/2 energy levels were observed. 3.5.Diffuse reflectance spectroscopy and band gap of CaMgB2O5: Dy3+ phosphor Fig.8 shows the diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) of rl CaMgB205: & Dy3+( 1.5 mol % ) phosphor.It is seen from Fig.8 that the strong absorption band at about 200 nm is due to the charge transfer (CT) from the oxygen to the Dy3+ ion in the host matrix which is consistent with the excitation spectrum of Dy3+ ion in Fig.2.This shows that light having this particular wavelength has observed and corresponds to the band gap of the material.The weak absorption peaks at 350 nm (6H15/24I11/2), 365 nm (6H15/24P7/2) and 385 (6H15/24I13/2) correspond to the f-f transition of Dy3+ in CaMgB2O5: Di y3+ phosphor [30].Also the peaks at higher wavelengths at 799 nm, 892 nm, 1077 and 1260 nm can assign to the transitions from the ground state of 6H15/2 to 6F5/2, 6F7/2, 6F9/ 2+ 6H7/2, 6F11/2+ 6H9/2 states of the Dy3+ ion [ 31 ] Fig.7.Schematic energy level diagram of Dy3+ doped CaMgB205 phosphor.

content: TL materials.Different types of sulfates have been synthesized to examine their TL characteristics.Ca SO4, MgSO4 and BaSO4 are the most familiar kinds of these materials.Ca SO4: Dy was known as a suitable dosimeter because of its high TL sensitivity and simple preparation methods.It has been employed extensively for environmental radiation measurements and personal monitoring (Yamashita et al., 1968, 1971).Also it has been found that CaSO4: Dy with high temperature TL peaks can be used in reactor or hot waste dosimetry (Mathur et al., 1999).Along with calcium sulfate, other types of sulfates like SrSO4 and BaSO4 (Dixon and Ekstrand, 1974) and also MgSO4 have been studied.It has been found that pure magnesium sulfates does not show good TL properties (Luo et al., 1999a).So, this material was synthesized with different impurities (Luo et al., 2006; Manam and Das, 2010; Zhang et al., 2002).Dysprosium due to its desirable properties was used as dopant more and more (Upadhyay et al., 2011).Zhang et al.(2000) synthesized MgSO4: Dy ( 0.1 mol%) with hot sulfuric acid.TL glow curve of irradiated MgSO4: Dy was deconvoluted into four glow peaks at about 135, 196, 262 and 361C based on Gaussian function fitting.In another investigation, Zhang et al.(2001) synthesized MgSO4: Dy with above mentioned method.TL spectra of this material following 10 kGy gamma irradiation had four glow peaks at 140, 190, 260, 360 C.Kher et al.(2008) also studied the luminescence behavior of MgSO4: Dy.First this substance was synthesized by solid state diffusion method and then TL glow curve of gamma irradiated MgSO4: Dy was recorded and two peaks at 110, 220C were identified.The amount ofdysprosium was optimized at 0.1 mol% for this phosphor.Mg SO4: Dy nano-rods was also synthesized and TL glow curve of this material following gamma irradiation was deconvouluted by using general order (GO) model.The main glow curve was decomposed into four peak components at 416, 436, 489, 550K.

order (GO) model.The main glow curve was decomposed into four peak components at 416, 436, 489, 550K.Dose response of MgSO4: Dy nano-rods was linear up to absorbed dose of 104Gy (Zahedifar et al., 2016).In this work, MgSO4: Dy was synthesized by solid state method.This technique is much safer than hot sulfuric acid method and TL sensitivity of the produced phosphor is much higher than those of all pre-mentioned methods. 2.Experimental The precursors used in this work are Mg (NO3) 26H2O ( 99..99% purity), (NH4) 2S04 ( 99.99 % purity) and Dy (NO3) 3, all prepared from Merk Chemicals.For synthesizing MgSO4: Dy, 0.8.g.of Mg (NO3) 2.6H2O ( 99.99% purity), 0.4 g of (NH4) 2S O4 ( 99.99% purity) and 0.007 g ( 0.5 mol%) of Dy (NO3) 3 were rubbed in a mortar and mixed together very well.Then the mixture was put in a crucible and placed in a furnace at 600C for 50 min.Then the produced white powder was rubbed until a uniform white powder of MgSO4: Dy was obtained.Structure of the synthesized MgSO4 was confirmed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern using a Rigaku D-max III diffractometer (BrukerD8Advance) with CuK (=1.54 A ) radiation under the conditions of 40 kV and 30 mA, at a step size of 2=0.02.The shape of the produced MgSO4 phosphor and elemental concentrations were recognized by a scanning electron microscope model Philips XL-30ESEM equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS).The mass of samples was fixed a0.0040.0001 g during all the experiments by using a SHIMADZUAx120 (ma rx=120 g, d=0.1 mg).Irradiations were performed using a60Co gamma source.The TL readouts were carried out in a Harshaw model 4500 computer-based TL reader using a contact heating with a precision of 1 C..The temperature of the heater strip was recorded as indicator of temperature of the sample.The heating rate for readout was 2C / s (withpreheatof50C) to a maximum temperature of 350C.

ample.The heating rate for readout was 2C / s (withpreheatof50C) to a maximum temperature of 350C.All the samples were heated and annealed in a programmable oven with temperature precision of 1C and then were cooled rapidly to room temperature ( 75C / * min ) 3.Results and discussion Impurities are of crucial importance in creating trapping centers or acting as activators in the host material.Therefore a proper dopant with optimum concentration can fundamentally improve the TL sensitivity.Here, dysprosium was chosen as dopant.Mg SO4 phosphor was produced with different amount of this impurity and the TL responses were recorded for the same conditions of annealing, reading conditions and the same absorbed dose of 500 mGy.Shown in Fig.1 (a) are the TL responses (theareaunderneaththeglowcurve) of MgSO4: Dy for different amounts of Dy which indicates that the most sensitivity yields for 0.3 mol% of impurity.For each impurity concentration, the sample preparation was repeated for three times.The average TL responses along with uncertainties for different impurity concentrations are shown in Fig.1(a).For better comparison, TL glow curves of MgSO4: Dy phosphor for different amount of dysprosium dopant after 500 mGy gamma irradiation are shown in Fig.1(b).This figure also reveals that the optimum concentration is achieved at 0.3 mol% of Dy.Presented in Fig.2 is the XRD pattern of MgSO4 microcrystalline confirming an orthorhombic structure that is in correspondence with ICSD collection code no 74-1364.The shape and size of the synthesized MgSO4 powder particles are shown in SEM image of Fig.3.Since the XRD pattern cannot reveal the presence of impurity with low concentration, EDS analysis was carried out to estimate the elemental concentration in produced MgSO4: Dy phosphor.The result is shown in Fig.4 and the percentages of elements are shown in the inset of the figure.EDS analysis was used to investigate the chemical composition and purity of products.

of the figure.EDS analysis was used to investigate the chemical composition and purity of products.The EDS spectrum of MgSO4: Dy sample shows characteristic signals of Mg, S, O and Dy (asdopant) elements as is shown in Fig.4.In this figure, there is no trace signals related to other elements, as indication of proper sample.The weight percent of elements detected by EDS analysis and calculated are: Mg (EDS:15%, cal:20%), S (EDS:34.95%, cal:27%), O (EDS:44.82%, cal:53%).EDS is most often used for qualitative elemental analysis, in other words it is used to simply determine which elements are present in the sample and what is their relative abundance, furthermore only the main Ka lines of Mg, S and O are present in EDS spectrum.So differences between theoretical and calculated values is due to EDS limitations.Fig.5 shows TL glow curves of MgSO4: Dy phosphor and LiF:Mg,Ti (TLD-100) after 500 mGy gamma ray irradiation.Inserted in top right of Fig.5 is a comparison between TL sensitivities of LiF:Mg,Ti (TLD-100) and MgSO4: Dy phosphor synthesized by hot sulfuric acid (Luo et al., 1999b).which exhibits that TL intensity of MgSO4: Dy phosphor is about 8 times less than TLD-100.MgSO:Dy phosphor produced in this work is about 8.5 times more sensitive than TLD-100.This is the highest TL sensitivity observed in MgSO4 phosphor.As mentioned above, all samples had the same weight and comparison of TL response was carried out considering corrections due to different masses.To study TL properties ofa certain material, it is necessary to find a thermal regime that optimizes the TL response.Proper annealing regime, in addition to empty the traps remained occupied in preceding irradiations, causes restoration of centers or clusters responsible for a trapping state which in turn improves TL sensitivity of the material.An annealing program of 900C - 30 min.Fig.7 shows the dose response of MgSO4: Dy phosphor in a loglog scale.In a log-log scale, a straight line with slop 1 corresponds to linear dose response.It is seen that the dose response is linear up to absorbed dose of 10Gy and then becomes sublinear.Saturation at low amounts of absorbed dose is a common behavior of high sensitive TL materials.In another work on TL dose response of MgSO4: Dy phosphor following gamma irradiation, a linear dose response up to absorbed dose of 930Gy was reported and in higher doses saturation was occurred (Upadhyay et al., 2011).TL dose response for MgSO4: Dy nano-rods with very low TL sensitivity is linear until the absorbed dose reaches 104Gy (Zahedifar et al., 2016).For testing the reusability of MgSO4: Dy material, seven sample of magnesium sulfate with the same weight were prepared, then they were subjected to annealing, 10Gy irradiation followed by readout and these cycles were repeated for 10 times.The results is depicted in Fig.8.As is observed, within a low uncertainty, the TL response remains unchanged upon 10 above cycles.TL signal stored in a phosphor by irradiation with ionizing radiation fades with storing the sample at room temperature.This phenomenon is more significant for low temperature peaks and depends upon kinetic parameters such as activation energy and frequency factor.For dosimetry purposes, it is required that the stored TL signals to be stable during irradiation and readout the sample, so fading is an undesirable property.The plots that show fading of MgSO4: Dy microcrystalline are depicted in Fig.9 (a, b).In part (a) it is obvious that the intensity of first peak at about 407K is declined around 19.7% after one month, while intensities of second and third peaks remain almost unchanged after 20 days storage at room temperature.Shown in Fig.

Fig.8.Reusability of MgSO:Dy phosphor after 10Gy gamma irradiation.Tm - Tstop is an efficient method to identify the number of glow peaks accommodated in the main glow curve.In this method, firstly the irradiated sample (here the samples were irradiated to 5Gy dose from 60 (co) is heated in TL reader with a constant heating rate (here5C/s) to a certain temperature known as Tstop, then is cooled to room temperature in TL reader without removing the sample and is heated again with a constant heating rate (here2C/s) for recording the TL glow curve.The maximum temperature in TL glow curve is recorded as Tm.This procedure was repeated in this work for increased Tstop in temperature interval between 90 and 350C with steps of 10C for Tstop and different Tm values related to each Tstop were obtained.The plot of Tm against Tstop is presented in Fig.10 for MgSO4: Dy phosphor.As is seen in this Figure, by raising Tstop, the peak temperature Tm is also increased, however this increment is not smooth and several jumps are observed.In Tm-Tstop plot, each single glow peak is characterized by a plateau region.

- group exhibits very strong absorption.The phosphors emit warm-white luminescence under vacuum ultraviolet excitation of147 nm, which consists of three main emission peaks located at475 , , 570 and662 nm, respectively.According to the luminescence and color chromaticity of the optimal sample K Sr P O4 : 1 mol%Dy<sup>3</sup>þ, 1.3 mol%Liþ, it can be a potential candidate for mercury-free fluorescent lamps.© 2018Chinese Society of Rare Earths.Published by Elsevier B.V.All rights reserved ## 1.Introduction The driving forces of the recent developments for lighting are climate change, energy saving, and energy efficiency.There is even political support for alternative solutions in the form of light-bulb bans and climate-saving emissions targets.

content: pport for alternative solutions in the form of light-bulb bans and climate-saving emissions targets.White-light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), organic light-emitting diode (OLEDs) and mercury-free fluorescent lamp are all possible candidates.But the present WLED is a point light source that is not the most suitable candidate for lighting.The OLEDs is a flat panel lighting that is suitable for interior lighting, however, it has a limited lifetime for practical application.Therefore there is an increasing demand for white light based mercury-free fluorescent lamp as a flat light source because of their long lifetime, higher energy efficiency, and environmental friendly characteristics.1e4 Recently, phosphate compounds have emerged as an important family of luminescent materials accommodating rare earth (RE) ions.Their merits are the host absorption edge at rather short wavelengths, excellent thermal stability and the tetrahedral rigid three dimensional matrix of phosphate which is thought to be ideal for charge stabilization.5-7Because of the different size of the two cations A and B, the ABPO4 (A)=monovalent cation and B=divalent cation) monophosphate family can crystallize as various structure types.8,9 Adjusting the ABPO4 family structures can optimize their physical property for developing new useful materials.Another advantage is its nonlinear optical property, which makes them attractive for several important applications on optical technology researches.10 The current researches about phosphate phosphors are focused on the development of novel host materials to improve the luminescence properties of phosphors, for example, (Eu,Tb,Tm)-doped AZ2 (PO4) 3 phosphor and NaGdFPO4: Ln3+ are explored as excellent VUV phosphor, Eu2+.

-doped AZ2 (PO4) 3 phosphor and NaGdFPO4: Ln3+ are explored as excellent VUV phosphor, Eu2+.activated KSrPO4 phosphor emitting strong blue light with excellent thermal stabilities, blue phosphate phosphor LiSrPO4: Eu2+ red-emitting phosphor Sr8ZnSc (PO4) 7: Eu3+, Li+, white-emitting phosphor SrZnScPO4 ) 7: Dy3+ and white-emitting Sr8CaSc (PO4) 7: Eu2+, Ce3+, Mn2+ phosphor with tunable color chromaticity.8,11e16 Hence there is an increasing interest in the investigation of new efficient phosphate materials.Usually, the white light is obtained by the blend of red, green, and blue-emitting phosphors, and it could exhibit an excellent color rendering.However, this method leads to the increase in manufacturing cost and decrease in luminous efficiency.Recent studies have found that it is probable to generate white light by doping single activator in one matrix.For instance, Dy3+ is widely used as a potential activator for white-emitting phosphors due to its yellow (4F9/26H13/2) and blue (4F9/26H15/2) emissions, whose luminescent properties have been investigated in SrB4O7 and ZnNb2O6 host matrix under UV (ultraviolet) and VUV (vacuumultraviolet) excitation in our previously work.15-19To the best of our knowledge, there are very few reports on the VUV luminescence properties of Dy3+ doped KSrPO4 for directly white emission.Therefore the present investigation aims at exploring the mechanism on the VUV luminescence properties of white emitting phosphor KSrPO4: Dy3+ 2.Experimental The series of KSrPO4: Dy3+ phosphors were prepared by solid state reactions.The raw materials (NH4) 2H PO4, K2CO3, Sr (NO3) 2 and Li2CO3 are all A.R., and the purity of Dy2O3 are 99.99%.The amount of Dy3+ and Li+ dopants were adjusted in the regions of 0-3 mol% and 0-1.5 mol%, respectively.The starting reagents (NH4) 2H PO4.Sr (NO3) 2, Dy2O3, Li2CO3 and K2CO3 were weighed as stoichiometric amounts and ground together.The final mixtures were obtained by the heat treatment at 1200C for 7 h.

K2S04 structure with Pnma space group.20 The PO43- tetrahedra network creates cavities in which the K and Sr cations are inserted.The K and Sr atoms are coordinated with ten or nine oxygens, which form a three-dimensional atomic arrangement.Along b axis, the structure of KSrPO4 is observed as the layers of phosphate tetrahedral being separated by potassium and strontium ions.The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of k SrP04: x Dy3+( 0 x3 mol%) together with the Joint Committee on Powder Diffraction Standards (JCPDS) card No.33-1045 are shown in Fig.1.From the comparison between them, the position and intensity of the diffraction peaks are matched very well.No impurity lines were observed, so the entire diffraction patterns are well indexed as the KSrPO4 single phase. 3.2.PL spectra of KSrPO4: x Dy3+ phosphors The VUV excitation spectrum of KSrPO4: 1 mol% Dy3+ is shown in Fig.2 (a).There are three main absorption bands in VUV excitation spectra.In Table 1, the absorption positions of PO4 group in different materials are listed.15, 16According to these reports, the excitation band peaking at 125-153 nm can be attributed to the absorption of the PO4 group.Theoretical calculation showed that the lowest intramolecular 2 t2→2 a, 3t transition energy of the tetrahedral PO43- molecule was around 7-10 e V.20That calculated result coincided with the energy position by us observed.

S1.Powder X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy The single-phase character of the final products was checked by powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) on a Shimadzu MAXimaX XRD–7000 diffractometer using CuKα radiation in the 2θ range from 10 to 80 with a step of 0.03.The absence of possible impurity phases was proved by comparing the XRD patterns with those in the ICSD-Web database (2017).Rietveld refinement of crystal structure was carried out with the GSAS program suite [1, 2].The crystal structure of Ca2GeO4 [3] was used as a starting model for the full profile refinement of Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 ( x=0.

[3] was used as a starting model for the full profile refinement of Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 ( x=0.00, 0.01, 0.025, 0.04 ).The peak profiles were fitted with a pseudo–Voigt function, I (2)=x L (2) + (1-x) G (2), where L and G are the Lorentzian and Gaussian parts, respectively.The angular dependence of the halfwidths of the diffraction peaks was described by (FWHM) 2=U2+V+W, where FWHM is the full line width at half maximum.The background level was described by a36-order Chebyshev polynomial (Figs.S2–S5).The olivine-type lattice contains two distinct octahedrally coordinated Ca2+ sites and one isolated GeO4 tetrahedron (4c).The dominant feature of the olivine structure is a stretched infinite chain of edge-sharing Ca(1) octahedrons parallel to the b axis (Fig.S6).At the same z height, the Ca (2) octahedrons are attached to this chain on opposite sides of a central Ca(1) octahedron by common edges; Color temperature tunable of Dy3+-doped LaPO4 nanorods prepared via hydrothermal method for white LEDs applications K.Hamraoui, M.Ferhi∗, K.Horchani-Naifer, M.Ferid Physico-Chemistry Laboratory of Mineral Materials and their Applications, National Center for Research in Materials Sciences, Technopole de Borj Cedria, BP73, 8027, Soliman, Tunisia ARTICLEINFOKeywords: LaPO:Dy3+ Nanorods Hydrothermal method White LEDColor temperature ABSTRACTNano-powders of La (1-x) DyxPO4 with rod-like morphology have been synthesized via hydrothermal method and characterized by X-ray difraction, TEM, FTIR and Raman spectroscopy.The X-ray difraction patterns collected for the prepared materials indicated the high purity of crystalline phase with a monoclinic structure.Photoluminescence properties have been investigated based on excitation and emission spectra, decay curves and chromatic coordinates.The emission spectra show a broad blue band ascribed to the transitions from the excited levels 4I11/2, 4I13/2, 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 to the fundamental levels 6H15/2. A yellow band related to the 4F9 / 26H13/2 transition has been observed at 573 nm.The luminescence intensities ratio and lifetimes have been found to be dependent on the concentration of Dy3+ ion and the excitation wavelength.The decay curves present double exponential shape for all concentration o Dy3+.The yellow-to-blue emission intensity ratios and CIE chromaticity coordinates have been used to estimate the color of the emitted light.A high-quality of white light with three-color temperature (Warm, Natural or Daylight, Cool) has been obtained from a single emitting phosphor, LaPO4: Dy3+.

content: (Warm, Natural or Daylight, Cool) has been obtained from a single emitting phosphor, LaPO4: Dy3+.The improved emission lifetimes and color temperature are suitable for application in the white light LED devices. 1.Introduction In recent years, white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs) have got large attention in new lighting sources for general illumination.For instance, WLEDs are considered as an ideal background illumination for colored displays.These diodes can replace conventional fluorescent and in candescent lamps due to their eficiency, long working lifetime, energysaving capability, high reliability and lower energy consumption [1,2].Actually, two approaches were presented for creating white light.The first was the mixed-color white light which is based on mixing the light from several colored LEDs to create a spectral power distribution that appears white.It is similar to the tri-phosphor fluorescent lamps using three phosphors.Each phosphor emits a relatively narrow spectrum of blue, green or red light upon receiving ultraviolet radiation from the mercury arc in the lamp tube.By locating red, green and blue LEDs adjacent to one another, and properly mixing the amount of their output, the resulting light is white in appearance [3].The second approach is the Phosphor-converted white light.In this case, the generation of white light is by use of yellow phosphors together with a short-wavelength or blue LED.The white light was obtained by mixing the blue LED emission and the yellow emission upon excitation with the short-wavelength or blue LED.Nowadays, the color temperature of a room lighting (measured in degrees of Kelvin (K)) becomes very interesting and gives a special mood to a room or booth [4].In this context, several phosphors for white LED were used based on their multicolor emissions.

[4].In this context, several phosphors for white LED were used based on their multicolor emissions.These emissions have been obtained by varying lanthanide ions with diferent contents and the up conversion phenomena, such as GdVO4: Ln3+/ Yb3+( Ln3+=Ho3+, Er3+, Tm3+, Ho3+/ Er3+/ Tm3+) nanorods [5] and Ba2Gd2Si4O13: Ce3+, Eu2+, Sm3+[ 6 ], Perfect phosphors with good ef-ficiency should have an ideal morphology of particles with several attractive features such as narrow size distribution and good dispersion [7,8].Lanthanides monophosphates LnPO4 are very interesting lumi nescent materials due to their exceptional properties such as; excellent chemical and mechanical stability, ability to accommodate a brilliant white emission, sharp ultraviolet absorption, wide visible emission, long decay time, high quantum yield and large Stock shifts [ 9, 10 ].Since a half century ago, macro- and nanosized lanthanum monophosphates were used as a lattice for lanthanide ions to produce phosphors that emit in a broad range of colors [11].Recently, the synthesis and investigation of LaPO4 nanoparticles doped by diferent rare-earth ions find a considerable attention that reliably lead to well-defined and homogenous products with the desired particle size, morphology and phase [12,13].These monophosphates were presented in diferent shape such as nanocrystals [14–17] nanorods [18], nanofibers [19] etc.Nanoparticles of LaPO4 present an eficient host for rare earths emitting lights with diferent colors under UV excitation. Fig.1.Difractograms of La (1-x) DyxPO4 (0%,1%, 2%, 5%, 10%) powders.Of the many rare-earth ions, Dy3+ has drawn much interest as an activator dopant for many diferent inorganic lattices.

Dy3+ has drawn much interest as an activator dopant for many diferent inorganic lattices.Generally, Dy3+ exhibits two dominant blue and yellow emission bands corresponding to the magnetic dipole 4F9/26H15/2 transition and the hypersensitive electric dipole 4F9/26H13/2 transition [20,21].The adjustment of yellow-to-blue intensity ratio (Y/B) value provides a mechanism producing white light which were recently applied in the solid state lighting technology [22].In last decades, several research were developed on Dy3++-doped NaSrPO [23], NaCaPO [24], LiSrPO [25] and LiBaPO [26] and shown their ability to emit white light.Choi et al.have studied Dy3+ containing glasses for fibre-optic amplifiers and yellow–green up conversion applications [27].The Dy3+- doped alkal fluoro tungsten tellurite glasses was studied by Annapurna Devi et al.for LASER and white LED applications [28].Lithium yttrium borate glass doped with Dy3+ for laser medium, W-LEDs and scintillation materials applications was developed by Kaewnuam et al.[29].In this paper the synthesis of doped LaPO4: Dy3+ at diferent concentrations by the hydrothermal method was presented.The excitation, emission spectra and decay times were measured for diferent con centrations of Dy3+ ions.The influence of dopant concentration on the fluorescent intensity, lifetimes and chromatic coordinates were investigated.These results indicate that the LaPO4: Dy3+ phosphors can be used for blue, yellow emission and essentially white light LED devices with the three color temperature of the white lighting using a single phosphor. 2.Experimental 2.1.Sample preparation LaPO (x mol % Dy3+) ( x=0, 1, 2, 5 and 10) powders were synthesized by hydrothermal method.La2O3 and Dy2O3 were firstly dis solved into 5 mL of concentrated phosphoric acid (85%) with a molar ratio around 1.5% and a transparent ionic solution was obtained.

d phosphoric acid (85%) with a molar ratio around 1.5% and a transparent ionic solution was obtained.After stirring, the solution was poured into Teflon-lined autoclave and subsequently 20 mL of deionized water was added.The autoclave was closed well and maintained for 24 h at 200C.In the last step and after cooling the autoclave a white suspension was obtained which is filtered, washed with deionized water and finally dried at 80C in air.The samples in the form of white powders are referenced as follows; LP0, LP1, LP2, LP5 and LP10 for 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10%, respectively. 2.2.Measurements The crystallinity of all samples were checked by X-ray powder dif fraction (XRD) with a PANalytical powder difractometer (X'Pert PRO) using CuKα (1.5418 Å) radiation.TEM pictures were recorded with a JEOL1200EX microscope.For this purpose, the particles were dispersed in ethanol and then dropped onto copper grids coated with porous carbon films.Infrared (IR) spectra were performed by a Perkin Elmer spectrometer FTIR2000 using KBr pellets in the region of 4000-400 cm - 1.Raman scattering is recorded through HORIBAScientific spectrometer (labRAMHR) using a laser source (632nm) and a CCD detector.Photoluminescence (PL), photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectra as well as decay time curves were performed at room temperature by a Perkin-Elmer spectrophotometer (LS55) with Xenon lamp (200–700 nm).The emission spectra registered under excitation with a laser source at a wavelength of 325 nm were recorded using a HORIBAScientific spectrofluorometer (labRAMHR). 3.Results and discussion 3.1.Sample characterization Hydrothermal method is a wet-chemistry strategy widely adopted for preparing a high quality of phosphor powders with good crystal linity, specific particle size and shape.The difractograms of all the obtained powders are shown in Fig.1.The indexing of these dif fractograms is carried out using an X'Pert High Score Plus program.

Fig.1.The indexing of these dif fractograms is carried out using an X'Pert High Score Plus program.These difractograms show that all samples are well crystallized and adopt the monoclinic structure of the monazite type (Space group P21 / n (N°14)) with lattice parameters: a=6.836A; b=7.076A; c=6.509;=90.00;=103.23; Y=90.00; V=306.583 and Z=4..All the difraction peaks are in agreement with the standard PDF sheet ICDD-PDFN°: 032–0493 of LaPO4 [ 30 ].This result confirms the substitution and the incorporation of Dy3+ in the LaPO4 lattice.In the structure of LaPO4, the rare earth element (La) is coordinated with 9 oxygen atoms forming a LaO9 polyhedron bound to the PO4 phosphate group by pooling two oxygen atoms [31].The ionic radius of Dy3+(1.02 Å) is less than La3+(1.18 Å) on basis of 9 co-ordination numbers, which indicates that La3+ ion was successfully substituted by the Dy3+ in the LaPO lattice [32].The (120) reflection peaks show low shifts to higher angles with increasing Dy3+ ion concentrations indicating that Dy3+ with smaller ionic radius was incorporated at the La3+ ion site.The Scherrer equation was used in the analysis of X-ray difraction lines to estimate the average size of nanocrystallites [33].D=Kco s1Where K is the Scherrer constant and is generally taken to have the value 0.9, λ is the wavelength of light used for the difraction, β is the “full width at half maximum” of the sharp peaks, and θ is the angle measured.The crystallite size of the prepared samples, calculated based on Scherrer equation (1), reveal small variation with increasing Dy3+ ion and it is found to be in the range of 200 nm.High resolution TEM observation reveals that the synthesized LaPO4: Dy3+ products have rod-shape morphology with a narrow size distribution with thickness in the range of 30 nm and lengths ranging from 50 to 400 nm (Fig.2).Similar morphology are observed for CePO4 [ 34 ], Ce3+ co-doped LaPO4Tb3+, Ce3+ co-doped LaPO4Sm3+[35] and GdPO4Yb3+[ 36 ].

section: Towards a new group of olivine-type afterglow phosphors: the case of Ca2Ge O4 : Dy3+Larisa V.Ermakova, Ivan I.Leonidov ⇑ ![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-08-11/e2303e60-65ee-4192-b36e-c6e3be351ff8/45472c6bbc77e5420d8fac75274526e4edac0c34d88216d9a69b0ec4180a3a3b.jpg) Institute of Solid State Chemistry, UB RAS, 620990Ekaterinburg, Russia ## a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received11May2018Received in revised form13August2018Accepted22August2018Available online23August2018Keywords: Crystal structure Ceramics Optical materials and properties Luminescence Raman ## a b s t r a c t Powder XRD confirms that Ca2 - 3 x Dy2 x Ge O4 ( x = 0 .00 , 0 .01 , 0 .025 , 0 .04 ) synthesized by ceramic route crys tallize with the olivine-type unit cell (space group Pnma, Z = 4 ) ..The trivalent dysprosium ions occupy two crystallographically nonequivalent sites (4a) and (4c) with the Ci and Cs symmetry, respectively.Raman spectroscopy corroborates the crystal structure features of orthorhombic Dy3+, -doped Ca2Ge O4 with the maximum phonon energy of760 c m - 1 .The phosphors with optimal dopant concentration of1 at% exhibit yellow emission under349 nm excitation and white afterglow for more than1 h after240 nm excitation for5 min. 2018Elsevier B.V.All rights reserved.## 1.Introduction While germanates doped with lanthanide and transition metal ions continue attracting much attention for potential use in efficient laser systems [1], optical glass fibers [2,3], and promising phosphors for up- and downconversion [4,5], development of germanate-based multifunctional optical hosts for various applications in optical engineering and light conversion remains problematic.Orthogermanates with olivine-type crystal structure favorably stand out from many other compounds of the germanate class.

content: olivine-type crystal structure favorably stand out from many other compounds of the germanate class.Superior chemical, mechanical and thermal stability, lack of moisture sensitivity, relatively simple and easy processing are the advantages offered by this group of compounds [6].In its turn, Ca2GeO4 has shown to be an important oxide host material for a variety of optical and laser applications.In particular, Cr4+-doped Ca2GeO4 single crystals are known as laser media [7].Given that lanthanide ions play an important role in modern lighting technologies due to the abundant emission colors based on their 4f–4f or 4f–5d optical transitions [8,9], some of them have been already utilized for the rational design and synthesis of multifunctional optical materials based on the Ca2GeO4 host [10,11].Whereas Ca2+ can be relatively easy substituted by appropriate divalent and trivalent lanthanide ions ( Ln2+/ 3+), the crystal structure of Ca2-3xLn2xGeO4 should not be completely free of lattice defects which may lead to persistent luminescence.The present study aims at elucidating the crystal structure and optical properties of Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 for further development of a new group of olivine-type afterglow phosphors. 2.Materials and methods The Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 ( x=0.00, 0.01, 0.025, 0.04 ) powders were prepared by the solid state reaction between the calculated amounts of the initial reagents CaCO3 (99.9%) and Ge02 (96.5%), and Dy2O3 (99.999%) for the doped samples.The ground mixture was previously calcined at 900C for 7 h to achieve decarbonization.Afterwards, a stepwise heat treatment was applied in the temperature range from 1000C to 1200 C for 8 h with subsequent additional annealing at 1200 C for 8 h.The details of the synthesis procedure, powder X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Raman microscopy and optical spectroscopy employed in the present study can be found in the Supplementary Material. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.

in the present study can be found in the Supplementary Material. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.Structural chemistry The diffraction peaks on the room temperature powder XRD patterns of Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 ( x=0.00, 0.01, 0.025, 0.04 ) match well with the orthorhombic olivine-type phase (Fig.S1), ICSD card 173459; space group Pnma (No.62), Z=4 [ 12 ].Rietveld refinement of the crystal structures shows that lattice parameters decrease slightly in the doped samples (Fig.1; S2–S5) since the crystal radius of Dy3+( 1.048: A ) in 6-fold coordination (4aand4csites) is smaller than that of Ca2+(1.140) [ 13 ].The Ca2-xLi2xGeO4 solid solution demonstrates a similar dependence of cell parameters on the dopant concentration [6].No phase transformation or impurity is observed in the current range of doping concentration.Raman spectroscopy confirms the crystal structure features of orthorhombic Dy3+-doped Ca2GeO4 with the maximum phonon energy of 760 cm - 1 ( Fig.2 ).The Raman spectrum of a germanate olivine is characterized by 36 active modes at k=0 (=11Ag + 7-B1g+11B2 g + 7B3 g ) in the range of 50-800 cm - 1 [ 14 ]..Slight broadening and shift of two lines at 139–142 cm 1 assigned to translational motions of Ca2+ cations reveal insignificant disorder in calcium sublattice of the Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 oxides (Fig.2(inset)).There is no evident structural change in the sublattice of GeO4 units.The Supplementary Material comprises more discussion on factor group analysis for olivine-type crystals and vibrational properties of Ca2-3xDy2xGeO4 ( x=0.00, 0.01, 0.025, 0.04 ). 3.2.Optical spectroscopy Whereas many germanate hosts exhibit a broad band, which is due to the presence of intrinsic defects, in the visible spectral range under UV excitation [15,16], this has not been observed in the photoluminescence (PL) spectrum of Ca2GeO4 featured the optical band gap of 5.65 eV (Fig.S8).The host under consideration has no afterglow after being irradiated by UV light.

of 5.65 eV (Fig.S8).The host under consideration has no afterglow after being irradiated by UV light.Photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectra of Ca2GeO4: Dy3+ clearly demonstrate typical intense and sharp lines in the range of 300–500 nm which are assigned to the 4 f - 4 f transitions of Dy3+( Fig. 3 (a) ).The excitation peaks are located at 324, 349 and 385 nm and correspond to the groups of highly mixed transitions from the 6H15/2 ground state [17].Under 349 nm excitation ( 6H15/2→4I11/2++ 4I9/2 ), the PL spectra are characterized by blue and yellow emission lines peaked at 485 nm and 574 nm, respectively, and weak red and infrared emissions at 662 nm and 758 nm which are associated with the transitions from the 4F9/2 state to 6H J ( J=15/2, 13/2, 11/2 ) and (6H9/2+6F11/2) in Dy3+.The 4F9/26H13/2 transition belongs to the forced electric dipole transition type, its intensity depends on the dopant environment and is most pronounced when the Dy3+ ion is located at a low symmetry site without an inversion center [18].The profile of the PL spectrum confirms the presence of Dy3+ ions in the crystallographical position 4c without a center of symmetry (C) and local deviation of inversion center in the site 4a (C) in the crystal structure of Dy3+-doped Ca2GeO4 [12].The strongest emission signal is attained in the sample with 1 at% dysprosium content that is well compared to the optimal lanthanide concentrations of 0.5–3.0 at% in olivine-type phosphors [10,11,19].The CIE chromaticity coordinates of Ca1.97Dy0.02Ge O4 are found to be x=0.451 and y=0.468, and the internal quantum efficiency of this sample has been determined to be 17%. Fig.2.Raman spectra of CaDyGeO (x=0.00, 0.01, 0.025, 0.04).The white afterglow of Ca1.97Dy0.02Ge O4 is only ascribed to Dy3+ emission with the CIE chromaticity coordinates x=0.402 and y=0.419 ( Fig.3 ( b, f ) )..Generally, persistent luminescence is attributed to the capture of charge carriers by traps in the host lattice under UV/vis excitation and then the releasing of trapped charge carriers under the thermal activation at room temperature.Here, thermoluminescence (TL) technique can be used to provide information on depth of the trapping centers in a host lattice [20].The TL curve of Ca2GeO4: Dy3+(1 at%) recorded at the delay time of 3 min after the removal of 240 nm excitation (for5min) features a dominated broad band with a weak shoulder band at higher temperature (Fig.3(d)).This indicates that at least two different trap centers are generated by the incorporation of Dy3+ ions into the Ca2GeO4 host lattice.The trap depths can be determined from the TL peaks using the empirical Urbach’s relation ET=Tm / 500 ( ET.stands for the trap depth, Tm is the TL curve temperature maximum) at a constant slow heating rate of 5K * min - 1 [ 21 ].The most intense peak at 436K and its shoulder at 485K correspond to the presence of deep electron traps at 0.87 eV and 0.97 eV below the conduction band.The decay curve is well fitted by hyperbolic function ( I (t)=I0 / (1-t) with the I0 and k constants) that allows estimation of the afterglow decay time to be about 70±1 min (Fig.3 (c)).The role of doping Dy3+ ions should be considered to introduce different types of traps or to increase the concentration of traps responsible for afterglow (Fig.3(e)).Under UV excitation, electrons are promoted to the conduction band followed by subsequent trapping of them in the shallow traps.

ns are promoted to the conduction band followed by subsequent trapping of them in the shallow traps.During thermal disturbance at room temperature, captured electrons are released from shallow traps and backtracked to the Dy3++ energy levels via a conduction band.Finally, the electrons recombine with emission centers to generate persistent luminescence.The above process is consistent with a generally accepted long-lasting luminescence mechanism [20].The trap filling process may also occur directly through tunneling from the activating ions, which does not require short wavelength excitation, but is clearly less efficient.(a) (b) (e) (f) Fig.3.(a) PL ( ex=349 nm) and PLE ( em=574 nm) spectra of Ca2GeO4: Dy3+; (b) persistent luminescence spectrum, (c) afterglow decay profile and (d) TL glow curve of Ca1.97Dy0.02Ge O4; (e) possible scheme of the electron trapping and persistent luminescence mechanism for Ca2GeO4Dy3+; (f) CIE chromaticity diagram. 4.

trapping and persistent luminescence mechanism for Ca2GeO4Dy3+; (f) CIE chromaticity diagram. 4.Conclusions Persistent luminescence of dysprosium-doped olivine-type germanates includes a combination of the yellow and blue emission components which originate from the 4 f - 4 f transitions of the doping Dy3+ ions.The white afterglow of Ca1.97Dy0.02Ge O4 can last for more than 1 h after 5 min UV excitation suggesting promising candidates for development of a new group of phosphors. content: zing radiations.A good linear dose response was also shown by the phosphor for photon beam exposure.However, in case of ion beams exposure, dose response of the phosphor was good only for low energy oxygen ion beam.Also the phosphor showed good photoluminescence (PL) property with sharp peaks present in the PL emission and excitation spectra corresponding to the characteristic peaks of the dopant Dy.The Commission International de l’E clairage (CIE) was also used to calculate chromaticity coordinates and color temperature in order to investigate the phosphor's application in white LEDs.All these good characteristics make this phosphor a suitable candidate for radiation dosimetry and solid state lighting. 1.Introduction Inorganic luminescent materials have been popular for their variety of applications in diferent areas such as radiation dosimetry, medicine, solid state lighting, persistence luminescence and up and down conversion [1–5].In order to improve optical properties for eficient use in various applications, search for new luminescent materials is always warranted.Most of the inorganic phosphors are easily prepared through inexpensive techniques and are non-toxic in nature.Inorganic solid state materials doped with rare earth elements are capable of emitting light in the visible region.And the present paper also focuses on studying one such material.Most of the phosphors are made up of an inert host material with a wide band gap and dopant ions present in small amounts acting as luminescent centres.Phosphors’ features and their suitability for diferent applications depend mainly on the nature of the dopants and their concentrations.Usually, it is the rare earth and transition elements that are used as dopants in the host material.In the present work, potassium calcium borate (KCaBO3) is the host material, having a wide band gap, and the rare earth material dysprosium (Dy) is the dopant.

he host material, having a wide band gap, and the rare earth material dysprosium (Dy) is the dopant.Rare earth elements have good luminescent properties as a result of their incompletely filled 4f orbitals, Dy3+ is used as a dopant due to its good luminescence properties and potential for application in the field of white light emission [ 6, 7 ] Thermoluminescence (TL) phenomenon is one of the important luminescence phenomena used in a variety of diferent applications [1].It is majorly used in the dose assessment of ionizing radiations for personal, environmental and clinical dosimetry.Moreover, it has plenty of other applications such as studying of defects in crystals, dating of ancient objects in archaeology, measuring the eficiency of surface catalysts and determining of impurities in rocks [8–10].In addition to the above applications, the TL technique, is also useful in standardizing food preservation [11].TL is basically the emission of stored energy in the form of light from a material on its subsequent heating post exposure from an ionizing radiation [1].Borates are considered as good hosts for many optoelectronics and dosimetric applications [12–14].The presence of isolated planer [ BO3 ] 3-group in the borate compounds makes the borate host good in optical and birefringent characteristics [ 12-14 ].Moreover, these compounds also attract attention of researchers because of their low cost, easy preparation, high sensitivity to irradiation and good chemical stability [ 15, 16 ].A lot of work has been done on borate based compounds in TL based dosimetry, especially in medical dosimetry [15–17].Borates are usually of low efective atomic number (Z), which makes them tissue equivalent.Li2B4O7 doped with copper, manganese and rare earth elements is the lowest Z value phosphor suitable for low dose medical dosimetry [15–17].Also, magnesium borate (MgB4O7) doped with various dopants is nearly a tissue equivalent phosphor with good TL properties [17–19].

) doped with various dopants is nearly a tissue equivalent phosphor with good TL properties [17–19].However, these TL phosphors have low sensitivities and the dose response is also not good for higher doses.Several mixed borates have also been studied for their TL properties, such as LiMgBO3, LiCaBO3 and NaSrB5O9, doped with various dopants [ 10, 14, 20-23 ].In the present work, a mixed borate, potassium calcium borate, doped with Dy (KCaBO3Dy) has been studied for its TL properties for the first time.This phosphor has shown good TL sensitivity and dose response towards gamma and UV rays.Borate compounds not only show good TL properties but also show good PL properties.The most common borate phosphors used in solid state lighting are Na2Y2B2O7: Eu3+[24], Sr2Mg (BO3) 2: Ce3+[25], Na2Gd2B2O7: Ce3+, Tb3+ [ 26 ], Sr2Mg (BO3) 2; Ce3+ [ 27 ], NsrBO3: Ce3+[28] and NaSr4 (BO3) 3Ce3+, Mn2+[29].All these phosphors emit just single colors, which makes them unsuited for white light emission.However, a lot of work has been done in developing white light emitting phosphors such as LiSr4 (BO3) 3: Dy [30], 3 a2Li B5O10: Dy3+[31] and NaSrB5O9: Dy [23].In the present work also, the phosphor KCaBO3 doped with dysprosium has been studied for its white-light emitting properties.The host material (KCaBO3) doped with other dopants has also been studied in the recent past for its luminescence properties [32–35].Subrata Das et al.studied the strong green up-conversion property of the phosphor KCaBO3 co-doped with Er3+ and Yt3+[32].Another paper by Subrata Das et al.reported the white-light emission property of the phosphor KCaBO3 co-doped with Dy3+ and Eu3+[33].The phosphor KCaBO3 doped with Eu has also been studied by Reddy et al.for its PL properties [34].Further, the same host material doped with Tb3+ has been investigated for its luminescence, optical and surface properties by Bedyal et al.[35].

Tb3+ has been investigated for its luminescence, optical and surface properties by Bedyal et al.[35].For the phosphor under study ( KCaBO3: Dy ) the commission international de I'Eclairage CIE (1931) has been used to obtain CIE chromaticity coordinates and color corre lation temperature (CCT) value.The present phosphor (KCaBO3Dy) has also been studied for ion beam dosimetry, which has become quite popular nowadays due to its application in the field of radiation therapy [36].Ion beams are being preferred over conventional photon beams such as the x-rays and gamma rays in radiotherapy, because their efective radiation dose deposition profiles which allow for confining nearly the entire doses in the tumor region (byaccuratelypositioningtheBraggpeakwithinthetumor) thereby sparing the surrounding healthy tissues from any unwanted radiation exposure and providing maximum radiation killing of the malignant cells [36,37].Further, it is important to measure the radiation dose that is delivered to the afected areas accurately.This assessment of dose can be done by TL dosimeters.This further drove us to additionally investigate the reliability of the current phosphor (KCaBO3Dy) for ion beams dosimetry.This phosphor was irradiated with carbon ion (C6+) and oxygen ion (06+) beams of diferent en ergies to study its TL properties.To the best of our knowledge, reporting of TL and PL properties of the prepared phosphor KCaBO3: Dy is being done for the first time, through this paper. 2.Experimental Potassium calcium borate with 0.1 mol% of dopant dysprosium (KCaBO3Dy) was prepared by solid state difusion method [32–34].Chloride salts of potassium (KCl) and calcium (CaCl), boric acid (H3BO3) and dysprosium chloride (DyCl3) were used as preparatory salts for the synthesis of KCaBO3: Dy.All the salts used for the preparation of the phosphor were of Analytical Reagent (AR) grade.

: Dy.All the salts used for the preparation of the phosphor were of Analytical Reagent (AR) grade.All the salts with the stoichiometric ratio (as per equation (1)) were taken in a mortar and mixed properly with a pestle.After mixing the salts uniformly, the mixture was taken in an alumina ceramic boat and heated for 1 h at 450C in air atmosphere.After being cooled down the mixture was further grinded using the mortar pestle in order to convert it into a fine powder.This powder was further heated at 950C for 21 h to carry out the difusion process.The compound was thus formed by placing the hot alumina ceramic boat containing the difused powder straight from the furnace to the surface of a metal block kept at room temperature resulting in the quenching of the phosphor.KCl + CaCl2+H3BO3DyCl3→KCaBO3+ 3HCl1X-ray difraction (XRD) pattern of the phosphor KCaBO3: Dy was taken on Bruker AXSDS advance difractometer with graphite monochromatic Cu-K ( 1.5406A ), operating at 40 kV voltage and 30 mA current.The ultra plus 55 field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) operating at 20 kV was used to take image of the phosphor for its surface morphological characterization.For the functional group ( BO33.−) identification present in the compound Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was done using PerkinElmer Fourier transform spectrometer.In order to prepare the sample for FTIR recording, KBr was used for mixing with the given sample.FTIR spectrum of the sample was recorded in the range 400 cm−1 to 4000 cm - 1..The presence of dopant (Dy) was confirmed by PL emission and excitation spectra of the phosphor.These spectra were recorded on Horiba Canada PTIQM – 8450 – 11 – C fluorometer.Band gap of the given phosphor was determined using the ultraviolet–visible difuse reflectance spectroscopy (UV–Vis DRS).The DRS spectrum was recorded on Shimadzu UV.2450UV–Vis spectrophotometer in the range of 200 nm–800 nm wavelength.

hor KCaBO3: Dy, FE-SEMEDS elemental mapping was conducted.The ele mental mapping shown in Fig.4 clearly shows uniform distribution of all elements within the selected area of FE-SEM image.It can be seen in figure (e) that the dopant Dy, which is present in small concentration, is also uniformly distributed with in the material.The FTIR spectrum given in Fig.5 shows various vibrational bands of the functional group BO3-3.And also a few due to presence of moisture content in the given phosphor.The broad bands near 3334 cm - 1 and 1630 cm - 1 are due to stretching vibrations of O–H bond.The peaks near 2147 cm - 1 are due to symmetric hydrogen bonds.The vibrational bands corresponding to important structural entities related to asymmetric and symmetric stretching appear in the region 4741463 cm - 1 [ 38 ].Generally borates show IR bands in the spectral range from 400 cm - 1 to 1600 cm - 1 38.Peak values obtained in the FTIR spectrum were compared with the characteristic values of the – functional group BO3-3.For the planar triangular group BO3-3, the wave numbers are in the region 1000-1400 cm - 1 (resultinginstrongandbroadpeak) corresponding to asymmetric stretching of B–O bonds [39,40].And the peak observed in the present FTIR spectrum also is a strong and broad one in the same region.The weak spectral peaks obtained in the region 900-1000 cm - 1 correspond to the symmetric stretching of B–O bonds [39,40].Peaks in the wavenumber range 650-800 cm - 1 can be attributed to the out-of plane bending of BO3-3 unit [ 39, 40 ].The peaks observed in this spectral region are normally sharp and strong.Peaks present in wavenumber range 450-650 cm - 1 correspond to in-plane bending of BO3-3 unit [39,40].So the present FTIR spectrum confirms the presence of basic structural units of BO3-3 in the crystal system of KCaBO3Fig.2.

d to determine band gaps of KCaBO3: Dy4.TL glow curve analysis 4.1.Gamma irradiation Fig.8 shows TL glow curves of KCaBO3: Dy exposed to diferent doses (10Gy-7kGy) of gamma radiation.It is seen in general that the shape of all glow curves is similar but the peak temperature shifts towards low temperatures on increasing the dose from mostly beyond 2 kGy.This behaviour of the given phosphor indicates that electrons which are trapped in shallower traps contribute more towards the TL intensity on increasing the gamma ray dose.Also the TL glow curves show three peaks at diferent temperatures.The main dosimetric peak is around 150C and the other two peaks are around 180C and 369C.Fig.9(a) shows the dose response of KCaBO3: Dy in the dose range of 10Gy to 2 kGy and it clearly shows a linear increase in the TL intensity on increasing the radiation dose.Fig.9(b) shows the complete dose response from 10Gy to 7 kGy.It can be seen in Fig.9(b) that the phosphor after showing a linear dose response to up to 2 k Gy, shows a supra-linear behaviour on further increasing the dose from 2 kGy to 5 k Gy.After 5 k Gy on further increasing the dose to 7 k Gy., the phosphor shows saturation in its TL peak intensity.Linearity obtained in the TL response curve from 10Gy to 2 k Gy is for obvious reasons: TL intensity being proportional to the dose dependent number of trapped electrons.The unwanted supralinearity with its onset at 2 k Gy is largely dependent on the phosphor configuration and the method of TL read-out [46].Moreover, it also appears to us that the shifting of the dosimetric peak to lower temperatures on increasing the radiation dose beyond 2 kGy could be responsible for causing this supralinearity as more shallow traps are filled beyond this dose to up to 5 kGy.Finally the saturation obtained in the TL response curve beyond 5 kGy is because of the combined efect of traps getting exhausted and damage induced by radiation.

content: ally been made to realize solid-state lighting devices based on white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs).WLEDs are important candidates for solid-state lighting because of its high luminous efficiency, compactness, long-lifetime, diversity design, fast switching good material stability and environmental friendly [1,2].The most commercially available w-LEDs are fabricated by combination ofInGaN LED chips with Y3Al5012: Ce3+ yellow-emitting phosphor [3,4].But the above method infers some major disadvantages in the red spectral region, including high correlated color temperatures (CCTsN4500K) and low color rendering indices (CRIsb80).Another effective method is to utilize near-UVLEDs chips coupled with multi-phosphors of red, green and blue phosphor [5,6].Dy3+ as the activator can be doped into suitable hosts to obtain white light emission in a single phase.It can present two characteristic emission bands in luminescence spectrum, including blue emission band derived from 4F9/26H15/2 (488nm) and yellow emission band derived from 4F9/26H13/2 (580nm) [7–12].The ratio ofthe blue light to the yellow light can be adjusted to generate white light.Recently, tellurate compounds doped with lanthanide ions have been studied.Considering the phonon energy of tellurate about 800–900 cm−1, it can overcome competitive nonradiative decay of lanthanide ions [13].Some tellurates as luminescence materials were reported, such as Li3Gd3Te2012: Sm3+[14], NaMgGdTeO6: Mn4+[15], rl (Gd1-xEux) 6 (Te1-yMoy) O12: Eu3+& [ 16 ], Sr2MgTeO6: Eu3+[ 17 ] LiSrBiTeO:Eu3+ [18], YAG:Ce phosphor-in-tellurate-glass [19], etc.The perovskite-type compounds are potential hosts for luminescent materials due to their excellent optical properties and diversity of their structure and composition [20–26].But to our knowledge, Dy3+ doped tellurate phosphor is rarely studied.In this paper, the yellowemitting Ca3TeO6Dy3+ phosphors were firstly synthesized.
