synthesis [1e6].Biosynthetic routes can provide improved defined size and morphology of the nanostructures compared to those of physicochemical methods of production and there is no need to use high energy, high temperature, and high pressure for the synthesis procedure.Furthermore, this method can also be scaled up for large-scale synthesis [7,8].For the past few years, metals and metal oxides doped with trivalent lanthanide ions have been widely investigated due to the utility of these materials in numerous significant applications, such as in optoelectronic devices, laser materials, ions, such as in optoelectronic devices, laser materials, displays, medical diagnostics, etc.[9e11].The luminescence properties of the weakly emitting particles in the host material can be enhanced by doping with suitable elements which can emit by themselves upon excitation in the UV-visible region.Among the inorganic nanophosphors (NPs), ZnONPs have entered into the scientific attention for their semiconducting, piezoelectric, antibacterial, and UV filtering properties, as well as their photochemical activity etc.[12e14].Nanophosphors with the incorporation of rare earth activators having Structural and luminescence properties of thermally stable coolwhite light emitting NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphor Govind B.Naira,*, Sumedha Tambolib, S.J.Dhobleb,*, H.C.Swarta,* a Department of Physics, University of the Free State, P.O.Box 339, Bloemfontein 9300, South Africa b Department of Physics, R.T.M.Nagpur University, Nagpur, 440033, India ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Phosphate LEDPhosphor Photoluminescence Thermal stability ABSTRACTThe photoluminescence (PL) properties of NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphor synthesized by sol-gel method forms the main focus of this report.The structural, morphological and luminescence properties of the NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphors were examined using X-ray difraction, scanning electron microscopy and PL.The structure of the phosphor with the optimum Dy3+-concentration was refined using the Rietveld method.The PL spectra under 350 nm excitation revealed three peaks in the blue, yellow and red region.Stark splitting was observed for the blue emission peak.The thermal quenching behavior of the PL emission of the phosphor was analyzed to de termine its thermal stability. 1.Introduction Phosphor-converted light emitting diodes (pc-LEDs) have evolved over the years to remain as the dominant leader in the lighting industry [1].Inorganic phosphors doped with Dy3+ ions have been extensively studied for their white-light emitting properties [ 2, 3 ] These jons produce a blue and a vellow band when excited at around 350 nm.Their emission bands are narrow and blend to form a white light whose color temperatures can be tuned depending on the yellow to blue (Y/B) intensity ratio.

content: e light whose color temperatures can be tuned depending on the yellow to blue (Y/B) intensity ratio.The blue and the yellow emission bands arise due to the magnetic dipole and electric dipole transitions, respectively.Hence.the former is insensitive to the crystal environment while the latter is highly sensitive to even the slightest change in the crystal environment.Thus.it is possible to tune the Y/B ratio by modifying the crystal environment around the Dy3+ ion [4].Although their emission transitions are strictly forbidden by the selection rules, they can still be utilized if the selection rules can be relaxed for these transitions, This can be achieved if the Dy3+ ions succeed in locating themselves in those sites of the host which are non-centrosymmetric.Phosphates form a special class of inorganic materials which have exceptional importance in the field of lighting applications.Among them, ABPO4 ( A.=monovalent metal ion, B=divalent metal ion) has the simplest chemical formula and has been studied vigorously by choosing diferent metal ion combination for their structural, magnetic, optical and electrical properties [ 5, 6 ].These host lattices provide suitable sites to comfortably accommodate the rare-earth dopants and therefore, show excellent luminescent properties.Na CaPO4 belongs to the family of glaserites with a general formula AxBy (XO4) (x+y) / 2 [7].Na CaPO4 is a suitable host matrix for luminescence materials owing to its excellent physical and chemical stability [8].These orthophosphates show low phonon energies and large optical band gap that provide favourable conditions for a rare-earth ion to luminesce [9,10].In this work, the photoluminescence properties of NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphor has been explored.The luminescence-stability with varying temperatures was also analyzed and reported here. ig.1 depicts the powder XRD patterns of NaCa1-xPO4; x Dy3+( x=0.0005, 0.005, 0.01, 0.03 and 0.05) phosphor together with the standard XRD pattern of the NaCaPO4 (JCPDSFile No.29-1193).All the difraction peaks of the samples match well with the standard JCPDS data, thereby, indicating the formation of pure phase samples.There were no traces of impurities or additional phase formation due to the doping of Dy3+ ions in the host samples.This confirms that the Dy3+ ions did not form any other impurity phase and have incorporated well into the NaCaPO4 host lattice.The shifting of the peak-position due to the Dy-doping can be inspected from Fig.2The magnified view of the XRD profiles from 20 to 25 and from 30 to 35 shows that the peaks shifted towards the higher 2θ angle with increasing Dy3+-concentration.The probability of Dy3+ ions occupying the Ca2+ site is higher, owing to their compatible ionic radii.However, there is a marginal diference in their ionic radii ( Ca2+=1A and Dy3+=0.912: A ) that has led to the shifting of the peak positions with increasing Dy3+-concentration.Based on the resemblance of the XRD pattern with the standard JCPDS data, the Rietveld refinement of the experimental data o the NaCaPO4: 0.01Dy3+ phosphor was carried out using the structural model of NaCaPO4 (orthorhombic, space group Pna 21) in the FullProf program [12].The Pseudo-Voigt peak profile function was employed and the background was approximated using linear interpolation.Fig.3(a) shows the Observed (crosses), calculated (solidline), and diference (bottom) XRD profiles for the Rietveld refinement of the NaCaPO4: 0.01Dy3+ phosphor.The Bragg reflections of the calculated pattern are shown by short vertical lines.The crystallographic data for the NaCifO4: Dy3+ phosphors, obtained after the Rietveld refinement, are listed in Table 1.The refinement converged with the factors Rwp=25.4, Rp=25.5, Rexp=13.

candidate for white light-emitting diode applications. 1.Introduction Recently, white light-emitting diodes (W-LEDs) have drawn much attention in the fields of displays and general lightings due to their superior advantages, such as environmentally friendly, energy saving capabilities, high brightness, long serving lifetime, high material sta bility and well energy eficiency on its applications in replacing the daily-used incandescent and traditional fluorescent lamps [1–3].Thus, W-LEDs may become the potential candidates for the next generation solid-state lighting source [4–7].Nowadays, commercial white emitting LEDs were fabricated by combining a GaN- LED (Bluechip) with a broad band yellow-emission phosphor of cerium (III)-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Yellowphosphor) to generate white light [8–10].However, this approach sufers from some unavoidable problems, such as high correlated color temperature of 7750K and lower color rendering index of <80 owing to the lack of a suficient red component [11–13].In order to solve these problems, one of the approaches is to obtain W-LEDs by combining near-ultraviolet (n-UV, 350–410 nm) LED chips with red/green/blue tricolor phosphors [14–16].Nevertheless, the white light emission generated from this method have some disadvantages of low luminous eficacy due to the reabsorption of the emission and diferent aging rate for multi-phosphors [17–19].In order to overcome those problems.

he emission and diferent aging rate for multi-phosphors [17–19].In order to overcome those problems.One of the best strategy is by using UVLEDs and UV-excitable white light emitting phosphors.The solution not only improve the luminescence reproducibility but also enhance color stability [20,21].Thus, it is urgent to develop a single phase white emitting phosphor for UV-pumped W-LEDsUnder UV excitation, the trivalent Dy3+ ion doped-phosphors shows white-emitting because of two dominant and one weak emission bands: the blue band around (460–500 nm) corresponding to the 4F9/26H15/2 transition, the yellow band around (560–590 nm) corresponding to the 4F9/26H13/2 transition, and one weak red band around (650–670 nm) corresponding to the 4F9/26H11/2 transition [22–24].Meanwhile, the blue (4F9/26H15/2) transition is the magnetic transition, which hardly varies with the local environment, while the yellow (4F9/26H13/2) transition is the electric dipole transition and its intensity is very sensitive by the surrounding chemical environment around Dy3+ ions.Therefore, we can obtain white light emission in Dy3+ ions doped materials by tuning the yellow-to-blue emissions intensity ratio (Y/B) [25–30].Until now, there are a lots of Dy3+ doped phosphors have been reported, such as molybdates ( Y2 (MoO4) 3: Dy3+) [31], vanadates ( YVO4: Dy3+) [32], phosphates ( LiSrPO4; nderstand the changes to the electronic structure with the presence of Dy3+ 2.Experimental 2.1.Synthesis of LaSBSi2O13: Dy3+The (La1-xDyx) 5B Si2O13 (where x=0.01, 0.03, 0.05 and 0.07) phosphors were prepared by a conventional solid state reaction.La2O3 (A.R.99.9%), HBO (A.R.99.99%), SiO (A.R.99.99%), DyO (A.R.99.99%) were used as raw materials directly without further purifica tion.All the reactants were weighted and ground together according to the stoichiometric ratio in an agate mortar.After homogeneously mixed, the powders were transferred to an alumina crucible and cal cined in air at 1350 °C for 8 h, and then the obtained products were cooled down to room temperature.Then, the final products were reground into white powders for further measurements. 2.2.Characterizations The crystalline structures of the phosphor were characterized by Xray powder difraction (XRD) patterns using a Bruker D8ADVANCE powder difractometer equipped with a Cu-Kα (=1.5418 ) radiation and linear VANTEC detector.The 2θ ranges of all the data sets are from 10 to 80° with a step size of 0.016°, and the counting time was 2 s per step.The photoluminescence excitation (PLE) and photoluminescence (PL) spectra of Dy3+ doped La5BSi2O13 phosphors were measured by a Spex Fluorolog-3Spectrofluorometer equipped with a450W Xe lamp as excitation source.Thermal stability measurements were investigated on the same Jobin-Yvon Spex, Model FluoroMax-3 spectrophotometer in combination with a.heating apparatus (THMS-600). 2.3.Theoretical calculations Density functional theory calculations were performed at the Generalized-Gradient-Approximation and Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof level of theory [47] using the plane-wave basis set method implemented in CASTEP [48].An800 eV cut-of energy was used with ultrasoft pseudopotentials and 222Monkhorst-Pack grid size [49] for geometry optimization and band structure calculations.

tials and 222Monkhorst-Pack grid size [49] for geometry optimization and band structure calculations.Atomic positions for La5Si2BO13 and its lattice parameters were provided by experimental work [50], with a total of 42 atoms in the cell P63/m space group, while the phosphor with Dy3+ doping was simulated with the virtual crystal approximation method using mixed occupancies to achieve one dysprosium atom present for every four lanthanum atoms and an overall chemical formula of La4DyBSi2O13.This lowers the symmetry in the structure which presents as P21/m space group.Calculation on both these models allows for comparison of the efect of Dy3+ doping.Convergence tolerance for geometry optimization include 510-6 eV/atom for energy of the system, 0.01 eV/Å for maximum ionic force, 0.510-3A for maximum ionic displacement, and 0.02GPa for maximum stress component. 3.Results and discussion For the purpose of examining the phase purity, crystallinity and composition of the final products, XRD patterns were discussed.Fig.1(a) depicts the XRD patterns of the (La1-xDyx) 5B Si2O13 ( x=0.01.0.03, 0.05 and 0.07) phosphors which were calcined at 1350 °C in air for 8 h.It demonstrated that all the observed difraction peaks of the as synthesized samples coincide well with the standard data of La5BSi2O13 phase (ICSD file no.91318) and no other secondary phases or any im purity were observed.Therefore, the results indicated that the as synthesized samples were single-phased and the doping Dy3+ ions do not cause significant changes on the structure of the host.Besides, the main difraction peaks position of the as synthesized samples slightly shifted to higher angle with increasing Dy3+ concentration, but the overall phase maintains unchanged.The difraction peaks slightly shifted to the larger angle due to the ionic radius of La3+ was a little larger than that of Dy3+.

Synthesis and photoluminescence characteristics of Dy incorporated MoO3 phosphor: Suppression concentration quenching M.Ayvacikli a, Ümit H.Kaynar b, Y.Karabulut c, A.Canimoglu d, M.Bakr e, S.Akca f, N.Can c,e,* a Manisa Celal Bayar University, Hasan Ferdi Turgutlu Technology Faculty, Mechatronics Engineering, Turgutlu-Manisa, Turkey b Bakırcay University, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Department of Fundamental Sciences, Menemen, Izmir, Turkey c Department of Physics, Manisa Celal Bayar University, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Muradiye-Manisa, 45010, Turkey d Nigde Omer Halisdemir University, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Physics Department, Nigde, Turkey e Jazan University, Physics Department, P.O.Box 114, 45142, Jazan, Saudi Arabia f Physics Department, Cukurova University, Arts-Sciences Faculty, 01330, Adana, Turkey ARTICLEINFOKeywords: MoO3XRDGel-combustion method Photoluminescence Quenching ABSTRACTA series of MoO3: Dy3+ phosphors have been synthesized via the gel-combustion method.The X-ray and pho toluminescence (PL) emission spectra were employed to characterize the obtained phosphors.The prepared samples were characterized through XRD measurements and exhibited that Dy3+ ions can be successfully incorporated into the host material.The PL emission bands of Dy3+ doped MoO3 were observed at 486 nm, 574 nm and 666 nm which are assigned to the transitions of 4F9/2→6H15/2,: 4F9/2→6H13/2 and 4F9/26H11/2, respectively.Concentration quenching were largely taken into consideration as one of the crucial aspects limiting the application range of phosphors in today’s modern world.

content: n as one of the crucial aspects limiting the application range of phosphors in today’s modern world.An abnormal thermal quenching dependence was reported when Dy3+ ions were incorporated into MoO host matrix.In order to understand the origin of this beneficial behaviour, energy transfer processes occurring via radiative and nonradiative mechanisms were investigated to elucidate this suppression of the concentration quenching. 1.Introduction Wide-gap metal oxides semiconductors like SnO, MoO, TiO, Nb2O5, and In2O3 have attracted much attention due to their technological and scientific importance in many areas of chemistry, physics, and materials science such as light emitting diodes, gas sensors, optoelectronic circuits, batteries, piezoelectric devices etc.(Fernandez Garcia et al., 2004; Ghrib et al., 2019; Ana de Betttencourt-Dias, 2007; Hwang et al., 2013; Eliseeva and Bunzli, 2010; Zhang et al., 2014).The physical and chemical properties displayed by means of metal oxide semiconductors are more advantages over any other class of materials.Molybdenum trioxide (MoO), which is seen as one of the important n-type semiconductors, is a fascinating class of materials that exhibit rich physical properties that may be useful in optical devices (Dwivedi et al., 2018), medicine and agriculture (He and Yao, 2006), and smart windows (Salman et al., 2011).In this manner, MoO3 is attracting growing attention.Literature reviewers have indicated that a numerous method such a sol-gel method (Layegh et al., 2018a), chemical vapor deposition (Wang et al., 2016), spin coating (Balaji et al., 2016), sol-gel spin coating (Layegh et al., 2018b), hydrothermal (Yogananda et al., 2018a), and sonochemical techniques (Yogananda et al., 2018b) were suggested to tune the structure and morphology of the MoO product.However, there is no study present regarding a gel combustion method.Among the existing synthesis techniques, gel combustion method may be considered to be an effective and simple procedure.

nthesis techniques, gel combustion method may be considered to be an effective and simple procedure.The method has advantages of relatively rapid synthesis of metal and mixed metal oxides because it contains fast heating and cooling steps.Incorporation of appropriate lanthanide ions into semiconductors with a wide band gap, which MoO3 is one of the wide band gap (2.9–3.15 eV) transition-metal oxides, can often give rise to dramatic changes in its optical and luminescence properties.More recently, Kumar et al.described structure and luminescence properties of MoO3 doped with Tb3+ ions (Sanal Kumar et al., 2017).They indicated that the intensity of the luminescent emission peak augmented with increasing in Tb doping concentration.Yogananda et al.reported that Sm doped MoO3 phosphors exhibited orange-red light and were promising material for the fabrication model of white light emitting diodes (WLEDs) (Yogananda et al., 2018a).Dysprosium (Dy) is considered as the third most luminescent lanthanide (III) ions with abundant energy levels, good-colour purity, and high conversion and light efficiency for the development of new luminescence phosphors (Liu et al., 2014).However, to the best of our knowledge, no report has been found so far using Dy ions for MoO3.In this work, Dy doped MoO3 phosphors were prepared through the gel-combustion approach.The samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction.Photoluminescence behaviour of Dy activated MoO3 phosphors are discussed.To examine the impact of concentration quenching phenomenon, we tested the effect of Dy3+ contents on the PL emission intensities varied from 0 to 7 mol% 2.Experimental sections 2.1.Materials The doped MoO3 materials have been prepared by the gelcombustion method.High purity Ammonium Heptamolybdate Tetrahydrate ( (NH4) 6Mo7O24 * 4H2O, Merck> 99%), Ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3) and urea (NH2CONH2) were used in the study.All items were weighed at a stoichiometric ratio ( 0, 1; 2 and 1).

0.50%; 0.75%; 1%; 2%; 3%; 5% and 7%.For synthesis, the nitrate salts of the host and additive element were dissolved in 10 ml distilled water in a quartz beaker.Ammonium nitrate and urea were added to this solution in the beaker, and the beaker was kept on the magnetic stirrer for 1 h at 80C.Then, the beaker is opened and the mixing process is done to evaporate excess water at the same temperature until the gel becomes a consistency.The gel-like solution is placed in a muffle furnace heated at 500C..As soon as water in the solution evaporates, the combustion reaction takes place and MoO3 nanoparticle materials are obtained in the form of fly ash.Synthesis of the samples kept at 500C in the muffle furnace for 2 h are accomplished without additional processes such as washing or annealing. 2.2.Measurement XRD experiments of the prepared phosphors doped with Dy ions with variable concentration (0.25–7 mol%) were performed via a Philips PW-1710/00 diffractometer using Cu-Kα (1.5418 �A) radiation.These data were collected at room temperature and over an angular range of 20-70.Luminescence was excited by the 349 nm line of a Nd:YLF pulse laser.All the optical arrangements were designed to collect the luminescence which was dispersed with a monochromator with focal length of 500 mm spectrometer using 1200 line/mm grating and detected by a liquid nitrogen cooled charge-coupled device (ICCD). 3.Results and discussion 3.1.XRD Undoped MoO3 and Dy3+ doped MoO3 powder samples have been exposed to X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the phase purity in the current samples.XRD patterns are in good agreement with that of the α-orthorhombic structure according to the JCPDS card No.98-064-4058.The unit cell volume lattice parameters are a=13.82A, b=3.69A, c=3.95 �A and V=201.

other words, the crystalline size shown in Fig.2 does not increase beyond 1 mol% Dy3+ concentration.The findings from these data suggest that the Dy3 doping enhances the crystallinity of the prepared samples. 3.2.Photoluminescence (PL) studies The photoluminescence emission spectra of pure MoO3 and MoO3 doped with Dy3+ at different concentrations were recorded at excitation wavelength at 349.The PL spectrum of pure MoO3 are displayed in Fig.3.It is seen that host MoO3 exhibits very broad band at low intensity.With excitation of 349 nm laser light, the effects of the Dy3+ concentration on emission PL intensity of MoO3: Dy3+(from 0.25 mol% to 7 mol %) are displayed in Fig.4.All the samples at different concentration follow a similar pattern.With the Dy3+ doping concentration increasing, the emission intensity presents an upward inclination.As it is known, for low excitation rates (i.e.photoluminescence), we can expect concentration quenching process (Benz and Strunk, 2012).In contrast, concentration quenching mechanism did not occur in cathodoluminescence experiments.As the dopant distance (i.e.increasing concentration) decreases the energy transfer probability increases.Therefore, at high concentrations concentration quenching may take place.Unlike the above-mentioned explanations, we did not observe a quenching effect at this host material and the concentration quenching has been suppressed.The data shown in Fig.5 appears to suggest that increasing trend of the main emission peak (547nm) is sharp at first up to 0.5 mol% and then slows down up to 1 mol%.The slowing down observed in emission intensity in the dopant concentrations between 0.5 mol% and 1 mol% of Dy3+ can be contributed to the occurrence of energy transfer from Dy3+ ion to Dy3+ ion at a low rate.Blasse (1969) pointed out that critical distance (Rc) of energy transfer can be given by Fig.1.XRD patterns of undoped MoO3 and Dy doped MoO3.

7 mol%.This can be explained by the energy transfer occurred via radiative or non-radiative centers.This anomalous behaviour suggests that the energy transfer process from excited ions to the non-radiative recombination centers should be suppressed or limited by some mechanism in the Dy3+ doped MoO3 phosphors.As already reported in the literature (Polikarpov et al., 2015; Kucuk et al., 2018), the distance between the activator ions declines with increasing concentration of activator ions ( i.e.in our case Dy3+).This will give rise to enhance the energy transfer between activator ions.At high doping concentrations, a high rate of non-radiative transitions is usually called as ‘‘concentration quenching’‘.In contrary, in our case, PL emission data was not quenched at even high Dy3+ concentrations.It is generally difficult to control the energy transfer processes.However, as long as the energy transfer rate is high enough the nonradiative transition rate is proportionally affected through concentration of non-radiative centers.This can be evaluated from crystallinity of the phosphor samples.It can be concluded that higher crystallinity should increase the emission intensity by means of reduced concentration of non-radiative centers like crystal defects (Yilmaz and Erdogmus, 2020). is related to the symmetry of the crystal field around the Dy ion (Hou et al., 2020).In this study, PL intensity at 574 nm is much stronger than that of 486 nm.Therefore, Dy3+ ions are in low symmetric positions with no inversion centers because the emission peak located at 574 nm (4F9/26H13/2) is dominant in our study.In contrast, blue emission located at 486 nm (4F9/26H15/2) is dominant if Dy3+ ions are in low symmetric positions.Related luminescent mechanism which is responsible from those emissions can be explained as follows.Under the excitation of 349 nm laser light, the electrons in the ground state 6H15/2 of Dy3+ is excited into the 6P5/2 level and then relaxes to 4F9/2 level via non-radiative transition.The Dy3+ ions will be depopulated from excited 4F9/2 level to the levels 6H15/2, 6H13/2 and 6H11/2 via radiative transition, producing blue, yellow and red emissions at located 486 nm, 574 nm and 666 nm, respectively. 4.Conclusions Dy incorporated MoO3 crystalline powder phosphors were success fully produced via a gel-combustion method.XRD data indicates that the prepared samples exhibit α-orthorhombic structure.The average crystallite sizes were calculated by Scherer formula and seen to augment with increasing dopant concentration of Dy3+.The PL emission spectra shows a series of peaks at 486, 574 and 666 nm which are assigned to the transitions 4F9/2→6H J ( J=15/2,.13/2 and 11/2) of Dy3+, respectively.Importantly, the PL emission spectra reveal that the intensity of the main emission peak located at 574 nm increase with increasing Dy concentration without concentration quenching phenomenon.Our finding also reveals that the concentration quenching is supressed.These findings enhance our understanding of the luminescence properties and thermal quenching mechanism.This enables us original views for designing and synthesizing novel rare earth doped phosphors.

content: PAPERView Article Online View Journal Check for updates Cite this: DOI: Thermally robust and valence-variation-induced white-light emission of a novel stannate phosphor Sr3Al10SnO20Dy3+: crystal structure, luminescence property, and mechanism investigation† Shuangyu Xin,a,b Miao Gao,a,b Jialing Ma,b Heng Daia,b and GeZhu *a,b The development of novel white-light-emission phosphors is of great importance for applications in lighting and display fields.Trivalent Dy3+ is widely used as a potential luminescence center for white-light emission.However, Dy3+-doped phosphors often sufer a poor yellow to blue ratio due to the deficiency of its 4F9/2→6H15/2 transition, low luminescence eficiency, and unsatisfactory thermal stability.The importance of the present research work is that we have achieved a tunable white light in a single phased stannate phosphor S3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ with robust thermal stability.The crystal structure, phase purity, and chemical composition were investigated via X-ray difraction Rietveld structure refinement, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive spectrometry.The luminescence spectra indicated that Sr3Al10SnO20; Dy3+ not only exhibited characteristic 4F9/2→6H I / 2 ( I=11, inherent transition emissions of Dy3+, but also showed an abnormal blue band emission, which was identified through X-ray photoelectric spectroscopy as the T1→S0 transitions of Sn2+, resulting from the valence variation of Sn4+The eficient energy transfer from Sn2+ to Dy3+ was also confirmed and the transfer eficiency was calculated.Owing to the valence-variation-induced emission of Sn2+, a tunable white light could be realized from a cool to warm white light region, with Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage coordinates and a correlative color temperature varying from (0.277, 0.333) and 8634K to (0.353, 0.404) and 4913K, respectively.

ive color temperature varying from (0.277, 0.333) and 8634K to (0.353, 0.404) and 4913K, respectively.The luminescent and defects formation mechanism as well as the luminescence kinetics were further investigated.Moreover, Sr3Al10SnO20; Dy3+ had a high quantum eficiency (∼34.6%) and a super-stable thermal stability behavior (82.5% at 240C of the initial integral emission intensity at 30C ) with a large activation energy (ΔE ∼ 0.1654 eV).Finally, a charge-compensation test was performed to further verify the efect of defects on the luminescence property and the related mechanism was discussed.The current work provides a novel method to achieve tunable white-light emission in Dy3+ single-doped phosphors and the related mechanism is efectual for other rare earths for potential applications in lighting and display fields.Received 18th August 2020, Accepted 21st October 2020DOI: rsc.li/dalton 1.Introduction To date, rare earth- and transition metal-activated luminescence materials have attracted significant attention owing to their various applications in light-emitting diodes (LEDs), plasma display panels (PDPs), field-emission displays (FEDs), lasing, bio-imaging, and scintillators.1–5 Among these, the study of phosphor-converted white LEDs has blossomed since Nakamura invented the GaN/InGaN blue LED chip in 1993.6–8 Currently, white LEDs are usually acquired through two methods: one is by using a yellow phosphor spread on a blue LED chip 9,10 and the other is fabricated by ultraviolet (UV) or near-ultraviolet (n-UV) LEDs chips coated with tri- or multicolor phosphors.11,12 However, both methods sufer from a high correlative color temperature (CCT), inferior color rendering index (CRI), strong re-absorption, and complex bending process.

ture (CCT), inferior color rendering index (CRI), strong re-absorption, and complex bending process.Therefore, much efort is devoted to realize whitelight emission in a single-component host material via incorporating some appropriate rare earth ions or ion pairs, typically Eu2+–Mn2+ or Ce3+–Mn2+ ion pairs or single Eu3+ or Dy3+ ions.13–16 Among all the rare earth, trivalent Dy3+ ions exhibit two intense fluorescence transitions; that is, the blue one of the 4F9/26H15/2 transition and the yellow-orange one of the 4F9/26H13/2 transition.17 The 4F9/26H13/2 transition is hypersensitive and easily afected by the environment around the lattice.Thus it is theoretically possible that Dy3+ could emit white light in a suitable host with a proper yellow to blue (Y/B) ratio.18,19 Till now, many Dy3+-doped white-light-emission phosphors have been developed, such as phosphates Ba3Bi (PO4) 3: Dy3+, LiAP4O12: Dy3+, 20, 21 aluminates YAlO3: Dy3+, Mg2Al4Si5O18: Dy3+, 22, 23 and niobates NaSr2Nb5O15: Dy3+ and BaNb2O6: Dy3+.Compared to Eu2+- Mn2+ or Ce3+- Mn2+ activated white-light-emission phosphors, trivalent Dy3+.-doped phosphors can not only avoid the energy loss during the energy-transfer (ET) process between diferent luminescent centers, but also can simplify the later preparation process of a white LED.In addition, ion pairs consisting of diferent luminescent centers usually sufer diverse thermal quenching behaviors, resulting in an unstable color-rendering property.However, Dy3+-doped white-light-emitting phosphors have their own problems.For example, the hypersensitive 4F9/2 6H13/2 transition of Dy3+ belongs to a forced electric dipole transition, which is unfavorable to the lattice environment and is only allowed when Dy3+ occupies a non-inversion center symmetry.Thus, to acquire standard and desired white-light emission, it is necessary to adjust the Y/B ratio for Dy3+-doped phosphors through co-doping other impurity ions.

is necessary to adjust the Y/B ratio for Dy3+-doped phosphors through co-doping other impurity ions.For instance, x – Sr2P2O7: Dy3+, Li+, K2Y (WO4) (PO4): Tm3+, Dy3+ and CaZr4 (PO4) 6; Dy3+, Ce3+.26-28Moreover, the quantum yields and thermal stability of the above phosphors still need to be improved, especially for application in high-power photo-electric devices.For example, the quantum eficiency is only 4% in zirconate Y2Zr2O7: Dy3+ 21.6% in silicate phosphor MgY4Si3O13: Dy3+(thermal quenching 51.3% @ 250 °C), 18.1% in aluminosilicate phosphor Mg2Si5Al4O18: Dy3+(thermal quenching 70% 2250 C ), and 25% in borate phosphor LiCaBO3: Dy3+(thermal quenching about 41% @ 205 °C).29–32 In recent years, stannates have attracted much attention for their various advantages, including low toxicity, deficiency of radioactive elements, and good thermal and chemical stability.33In1979, W.L.Konunenduk et al.reported the X-ray characterization of the space group information of ( Sr, Ba ) 3Al10 ( Si, Sn ) O20.34However, the detailed structural information is not given, even though the crystallographic structural information of the phosphor is vital to its luminescence properties.In this work, we successfully synthesize a novel white-light-emission phosphor Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ with robust thermal stability and analyze its crystal structure, phase purity, and chemical composition.The valence-variation-induced tunable-emission property, luminescence dynamics, charge-compensation efect, and the related mechanism are also systematically studied. 2.Experiment 2.1.Materials and synthesis The samples Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ and Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+, M+ ( M=Li+, Na+, and K+) were prepared through a high-temperature sintering.The starting materials were SrCO3 ( 99.9 % ), Al2O3 (99.9%), SnO (99.9%), DyO (99.9%), LiCO (99.9%), K2CO3 (99.9%), and Na2CO3 (99.9%).The stoichiometric mixtures were carefully weighed and soaked with ethanol in an agate mortar.

9.9%).The stoichiometric mixtures were carefully weighed and soaked with ethanol in an agate mortar.Then the mixtures were moved to a crucible and sintered at 1550 °C for 3 h to get the target phosphors. 2.2.Characterization The structure and morphology of Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ were tested by X-ray difractometry (XRD, Rigaku Ultima IV) and a scanning electron microscopy (SEM, S-4800) system with an attached energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS) unit.The room temperature quantum yields as well as the decay curves were tested on an FS5-MCS fluorescence spectrophotometer.The temperature-dependent photoluminescence spectra were assessed using a FLS1000 fluorescence spectrophotometer.The chemical valence of Sn was confirmed via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (Kratos, Axis Ultra DLD) with AlKα ( h=1486.6 eV) as the radiation source. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.Phase identification and crystal structure of Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+To investigate the phase purity and crystal structure of the Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ powder samples, Rietveld analysis is used to refine the structural parameters based on the GSAS program, using the structural parameters of Sr3Al10SiO20 as the starting model, as illustrated in Fig.1 (a).35In that figure, 6699 represents the experimental difraction peaks, while the red solid lines indicate the theoretical difraction peaks, and the green vertical lines and blue solid line show the positions of the simulated difraction patterns and the deviation of the measured and calculated values, respectively.The calculated data and the experimental patterns correspond well, with Rp=9.36 % and Rwp=13.77 %, demonstrating the successful synthesis of the Sr3Al10SnO20 powder sample.The obtained crystallographic structural parameters and detailed crystal structural information of Sr3Al10SnO20 are shown in Tables 1 and 2.The results confirm that Sr3Al10SnO20 is crystallized in a monoclinic space of C2/m with the cell lattice parameters a=15.193 Å, b=11.241 Å, and c=4.916A..

%.The inset of Fig.2(d) clearly shows a simple schematic diagram of the ET process from Sn2+ to Dy3+.Due to the ET process, the emission color of Sr3Al10SnO20: Dy3+ can move from the cool white light region with Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.277, 0.333) and a correlated color temperature (CCT) of 8634K to the warm white light region with CIE coordinates of (0.353, 0.404) and a CCT of 4913K, as shown in Fig.2(e).Fig.2(b) and (c) also show that the content quench ing point of Dy3+ ions in Sr3Al10SnO20 is 0.02, above which the emission intensity of 4F9/26H13/2 transitions of Dy3+ suddenly decreases with the increasing content of x.Generally, the content quenching is primarily due to the non-radiative energy migration among luminescent centers, which is related to the structural feature of the host materials.When the critical distance (Rc) between luminescent center ions is less than or equal to 5, the exchange interaction mechanism dominates the energy migration process.Otherwise, the energy migration process will be realized through the electric multipolar interaction.39 Fig.2(f) shows the local atomic distribution along the (001) crystal plane of the Sr3Al10SnO20 host, which clearly indicates that the distance between neighboring Sr2+ ions is refined to be 4.0825, 6.2669, and 6.8023A, respectively.In consideration of the low content of Dy3+ in the current host (themaximalvalueis0.04), then Rc will be much bigger than 5 A, indicating that the energy migration process between Dy3+ ions in Sr3Al10SnO20 follows the electric multipolar interaction rather than the exchange interaction mechanism.The critical distance Rc can also be calculated according to Blass’s theory,40 Rc = 2(3V/(4πXcZ))^(1/3) where xc represents the optimal doping content of Dy3+, V is the volume of the unit cell, and Z indicates the number of formula units per unit cell.Here Z=2, xc=0.02, and V=797.610A3.

also be reduced to divalent Sn2+ and give a broad emission band due to the T1S0 transitions of Sn2+.51, 52In this case, to clarify the intrinsic ascription of the blue emission band, XPS is utilized to confirm the valence state of Sn in the presence and absence of Dy3+ and the results are shown in Fig.3(a).For the Sr3Al10SnO20 host, the XPS spectrum shows strong signals at 486.46 and 494.85 eV, corresponding to the 3 d5/2 and 3 d3/2 orbit binding energy of Sn4+.However, the XPS spectrum is found to be obviously broadened after introducing Dy3+ ions.As presented in Fig.3(b), the XPS spectrum of Sr3Al10SnO20Dy3+ can be well divided into two separate signal peaks and the newly generated small peaks are located at higher binding energies of 487.48 and 496.61 ev, respectively, attributed to 3 d5/2 and 3 d3/2 orbit binding energies of Sn2+ 53, 54The XPS results further identifies that a valence variation of Sn4+ to Sn2+ occurred when Dy3+ enter Sr3Al10SnO20 and the broad blue emission band can be attributed to the triplet to singlet (T1S0) transitions of Sn2+ ions. lity, corrosion resistant, thermal insulation, shock resistance and good mechanical stability [1–9].All the aforementioned studies motivated us to prepare a novel glassy system having relative less phonon energies and suitable for white-light generation as well as visible laser devices.Therefore, the great amount of investigation has been carried out and studied through absorption and luminescence properties which strongly depend on the glass composition influenced by the ligand field ofthe surrounding rare-earths (RE3+) ions.Among all glass matrix, borate having their unique properties such as good optical quality, good thermal and mechanical stability, high gain, high energy storage capacity, low optical losses, good rare earth ion solubility, large emission cross-section and narrow emission bandwidth [10,11].The only drawback with borate glasses are its higher phonon energy leads to nonradiative emission by the multi-phonon relaxation.Addition ofmodifier ions such as TeO2 and BaF to borate glass causes to reduce the phonon energy ofglass host.Furthermore, tellurite based glasses acquires significant importance because of their high dielectric constant, high refractive index, low melting point, and low phonon energy (346cm-1) [12,13].Hence, mixing of tellurite to the present glass system leads to increase the stability against devitrification.On the other hand, addition offluorides leads to observe the OH groups present in the glass network and improves the quantum efficiency of the glass host material [14].However, fluoride glass technology has some common negative features, such as the chemical reactivity offluoride melts, tendency ofcrystallization and sensitivity to water.To minimize the negative effects of fluorides, ZnO is added to the glass network which further increases the glass forming tendency and radiative rates of Dy3+ ions [14,15].

488 cm - 1, 2365 cm - 1, and 3458 cm−1 and their assignments are presented in Table 1.The band observed around 566 cm - 1 is attributed to the vibrations of the Bi-O bending vibrations in BiO6 and/or BiO3 units in the Bi2O3-B2O3 glass system [16].The band centered at around 764 cm - 1 confirms the combined vibrations of B-0-B linkages [17,18] and also the stretching vibrations of Bi-O in [ BiO3 ] units and TeO bond in TeO3 and TeO6 [ 19 ].The band at 1132 cm - 1 is ascribed to the fundamental stretching vibrations of B bonds in BO4 tetrahedral units from tri-, tetra-, penta-borate groups [20].The intense band located at 1488 cm−1 is due to the stretching of BO bond vibrations containing planar six member borate groups [21].The sharp peak at 2365 cm - 1 reveals the presence of - OH group in the title glasses [22].The broad band around 3458 cm - 1 is the characteristic of the fundamental stretching of O group in the prepared glasses [23]. content: RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYStructural and photoluminescence properties of Dy3+-activated NaCaPO phosphor derived from solution combustion Yatish Ratn Parauha | Sanjay Janaraoji Dhoble Department of Physics, R.T.M.Nagpur University, Nagpur, India Correspondence Sanjay Janaraoji Dhoble, Department of Physics, R.T.M.Nagpur University, Nagpur, 440033, India.Email: sjdhoble@rediffmail.com Funding information Department of Science and Technology (Ministry of Science and Technology, India), Grant/Award Number: IF180284Abstract In the current investigation, a series of NaCa1-PO4; x Dy3+( x=0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0,.1.5 and 2 mol%) phosphors were synthesized using a solution combustion method and citric acid as fuel.The investigated results from the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern showed phase purity of the synthesized material and orthorhombic crystal structure with space group Pna 21.Photoluminescence properties of the synthesized phosphors were investigated.The synthesized Dy3+-activated phosphor displayed blue (482nm) and yellow (576nm) emission under near-ultraviolet or blue excitations.These emission bands were ascribed due to the 4F9/2→6H15/2 and 4F9/2→6H13/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions.Commission International de l'Eclairage chromaticity coordinates showed emission in the near-white region for the proposed phosphors under different excitations.In addition, the current–voltage (I–V) characteristics of the NaCa1-PO4xDy3+ ( x=1.5 mol%) phosphor-coated silicon solar cell and an uncoated solar cell were investigated under a solar simulator.The I–V characteristics of the proposed phosphor-coated silicon solar cell showed enhancement in solar cell efficiency by 7.92%.The entire studies and their outcomes showed that synthesized phosphors have potential as white light emitting diodes and for solar applications.

section: K E Y W O R D S crystal structure, photoluminescence, silicon solar cell, solution combustion method, WLEDs ## 1 | INTRODUCTION In the past few years, lanthanide-activated phosphors have attracted much attention from research groups.These phosphors show excellent luminescence behaviour and spectroscopic properties with various host materials.The demand for efficient luminescence inorganic materials has attracted more researchers and has motivated the development of lanthanide-activated phosphors.Generally, most inorganic phosphors absorb light in the ultraviolet (UV), blue or near infrared (NIR) region and emit visible (V) light.These materials have been widely used in various application fields such as in display devices and thermoluminescence dosimeters (TLD), for bio imaging and latent fingerprinting, or in WLEDs, solar cells and scintillators.<sup>[1–3]</sup> In the present scenario, lanthanide-activated phosphors have been widely studied for phosphor-converted white light emitting diodes (PC-WLEDs).Blue GaInN chip-excited Y A G Ce3+and Eu2+-doped SiAlON phosphors have gained popularity as commercial materials for PC-WLEDs.<sup>[4–6]</sup> It is clear that light is an important part of life in the21st century, we cannot imagine a comfortable life without light.Light-based technologies have played a very important part in science and technology development.As such, the discovery of WLEDs in the energy field has been an important part of energy-saving applications.

content: the discovery of WLEDs in the energy field has been an important part of energy-saving applications.WLEDs are considered to be the next-generation lighting sources in the field of lighting because they have shown their usefulness through outstanding features such as high efficiency and brightness, energysaving, eco-friendly behaviour, longer operational lifetime, low cost, and lack of mercury pollution.[7–10] The emphasis on phosphor materials with improved luminescence properties in multidisciplinary fields has focused research efforts in this area towards achieving better material properties.Oxides, silicates, nitrides, sulphates, phosphates, vanadate, tungstate, halides and mixed ligand systems have been used as host materials for the growth of various colour emitting phosphors.[11] Over the past two decades, progress has been observed in the synthesis and characterization of lanthanide-activated phosphate-based phosphors, largely due to the suitability and adaptability of phosphate-based phosphor materials in solid-state lighting.[12,13] As published previously, phosphate-based luminescent materials have excellent chemical and thermal stabilities In particular, ABPO4 ( A=K, Li, Na; and B=Ca, Mg, Sr)-based phosphors have been widely studied for WLED applications exhibiting superior luminescence properties.[14] In the past few years, several lanthanide-activated phosphate-based phosphors have been investigated that are useful for WLED applications.Apart from hos materials, lanthanide ions also play an important role.Among all the lanthanide ions, Dy3+ is the most commonly used activator.Dy3+ activated phosphors exhibit sharp emission in the visible blue and yellow regions under UV excitation.[15–18] Some Dy3+-activated phosphate-based phosphors have been described previously and are available, which shows their applicability for WLEDs.Recently, Ramteke and colleagues[19] investigated Dy3+-activated Ca3 (PO4) phosphors using a wet chemical synthesis method.

[19] investigated Dy3+-activated Ca3 (PO4) phosphors using a wet chemical synthesis method.They reported that synthesized phosphors have the potential for lighting applications Jayachandiran and colleagues[20] studied Ba3Bi2 (PO4) 4: Dy3+ phosphors for WLEDs.They showed emission bands in the blue, yellow, and red emission region under UV excitation.In addition, Commission International de l'Eclairage (CIE) chromaticity coordinates of the prepared phosphor were found to be located in the near-white region ( x=0.329, y=0.349 ).Mukesh Sahu and co-workers[21] reported Ca3Bi3 (PO4) 3Dy3+ phosphors for solid-state lighting, samples were prepared using a co-precipitation method.Yali Chen and colleagues[22] investigated Dy3+-doped K2Sr (PO4) phosphors and reported photo luminescence (PL) properties under VUV excitation (147nm).Nair and colleagues[23] reported NaCa (PO4): Dy3+ phosphors that were synthesized using a sol–gel method.Manju Dahiya and Dinesh Kuma investigated Ca9Al (PO4) 7: Dy3+ phosphors for cool white LEDs unde near-UV light excitation.[24] In the present work, solution combustion-assisted NaCaPO4.Dy3+ phosphors were synthesized and their structural, morphological, and vibrational features, thermal stability, luminescence properties, and I–V characteristics were measured.The PL emission spectra revealed blue and yellow emission under near-UV excitations.This investigation revealed that synthesized phosphors have the potential for WLEDs applications. 2 | EXPERIMENTAL2.1 | Synthesis of NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphors The solution combustion method was used to synthesize NaCaPO4: Dy3+ phosphors with different concentrations of Dy3+ ions.The Dy3+ ion concentration was varied according to the value of x ( x=00.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mol%).Sodium nitrate (NaNO3), calcium nitrate tetrahydrate extrapure [ Ca (NO3) 2.

, 2.0 mol%).Sodium nitrate (NaNO3), calcium nitrate tetrahydrate extrapure [ Ca (NO3) 2.x H2O ], di-ammonium hydrogen orthophosphate anhydrous [ (NH4) HPO4 ], and dysprosium oxide (Dy2O3) were used as starting raw materials and citric acid was used as a fuel.All mentioned raw materials were purchased from Loba Chemie (AR/ACSgrade) and had 95–99.99% purity.In the initial stage, all the raw materials were combined in the designed ratio and the weighed Dy2O3 was dissolved with nitric acid to convert it to its nitrate form.Thereafter, all reagents were mixed one by one in distilled water with stirring to prepare an homogeneous solution.The converted dysprosium nitrate was added to the obtained solution.Finally, citric acid was mixed with the solution as fuel with stirring.After stirring, the aqueous solution was converted to a transparent gel.This gel was then transferred to a china dish and heated at 525C for 10 min in an open furnace.Due to heating, a flame (gas) was released and an exothermic, oxidation reaction occurred.Furthermore, the obtained powder was ground through an agate mortar and heated for 15 h at 700C in a muffle furnace in an air atmosphere.After completion of heating, the furnace was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature.The final products were grounded and used for further characterization.Coating of the synthesized phosphor on the surface of silicon solar cell was carried out using the doctor blade method.Ethanol, terpineol, ethyl cellulose, and acetic acid were used with the synthesized phosphor to coat the solar cell.The coating process and detailed information have been reported previously by Kadam and Dhoble.[25] 2.2 | Characterization techniques Phase formation is characterized on a Rigaku miniflex d600X-ray diffractometer, with CuKα radiation (=0.154056 nm ).Morphological behaviour was studied using a JSM-6360LV scanning electron microscope (JEOL, USA).

).Morphological behaviour was studied using a JSM-6360LV scanning electron microscope (JEOL, USA).Vibrational bonds, stretching, and thermal stability, thermogravimetry and differential thermal analysis (TG/DTA) were analyzed on a Brucker Alpha FT-IR spectrometer and Shimadzu DTG-60 simultaneous DTATG apparatus.The PL properties of the synthesized samples were measured using a Shimadzu RF5301PC spectrofluorophotometer with a xenon flash lamp (150W).CIE chromaticity coordinates and other photometric characterizations were carried out using a OSRAMSYLVANIA colour calculator.I–V characteristics of the proposed phosphor-coated silicon-based solar cells were measured in the presence of direct sunlight and a JETSPIN solar simulator.The JETSPIN solar simulator provided light equivalent to 1 sunlight. 3 | RESULTSANDDISCUSSION3.1 | Phase purity and Rietveld refinement The XRD pattern of the synthesized NaCa1-xPO4: x Dy3+( x=1.5.mol %) phosphor was recorded with a0.02 step size in the range 15–60.Figure 1 shows the XRD pattern of the synthesized sample and displays a comparison with the standard XRD pattern of NaCaPO4 (JCPDS file no.29-1193).The recorded XRD patterns matched well with the standard data, no impurity phase was detected.This shows the formation of pure phase samples and also confirmed that Dy3+ ions were successfully doped into the host lattice without additional phase formation.In this investigation, it was assumed that the Dy3+ ions replaced the Ca2+ sites, due to their favourable ionic radii.It is known that ionic radii of Ca2+ and Dy3+ are 1 Å and 0.912 Å, respectively.Therefore, doping of Dy3+ ions did not change the XRD pattern.Figure 2 reveals the XRD pattern of the NaCa1-xPO4: x Dy3+( x=1.5 mol%) phosphor obtained from the Rietveld refinement.The refinements were carried out using the FullProf program and pseudo-Voigt peak profile function.

.The refinements were carried out using the FullProf program and pseudo-Voigt peak profile function.The obtained Rietveld refinement profile showed four lines (the black cross line, the red solid line, the blue solid line, and the short vertical line), which represent the observed, calculated, difference between observed and calculated data, and Bragg positions, respectively.Figure 2 displays the fit parameters of the Rietveld refinement such that R-pattern (RP)=18.8, R-weighted profile residual r (RWP)=17.6, experimental value of R-pattern (Rexp)=13.04 i, goodness of fit indicator (2)=2.27..The lattice parameters obtained from the refinement are displayed in Table 1.The results obtained from the Rietveld refinement indicated that the data were reliable and confirmed the single-phase formation without any extra phases. sup>1 to 500 cm - 1, as shown in Figure 5.FT-IR spectra exhibited several vibrational modes.The vibrational band at 3800–3600 cm 1 corresponded to water molecules or O–H stretching vibrations.[27] The absorption bands at 1650 cm - 1 and 1408 cm - 1 were attributed to the vibrational modes of C=O.[ 28, 29 ] In addition, absorption bands at 1020 cm - 1 and 860 cm - 1 corresponded to the symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibrations (v1andv3), respectively, of the PO4 [30] vibrational band centred at 565 cm - 1 was due to the bending vibrations of 0 mathsf P-O.[ 31 ] 3.5 | Thermal stability Figure 6 shows the TG–DTA curves of the synthesized NaCaPO4 phosphor for analysis of thermal stability.The TG–DTA curves were recorded from room temperature to 800C.The DTA curve showed an endothermic peak at 180C due to the removal of water molecules.Then, the TG curve showed excellent thermal stability up t o600C, after that the curve showed the weight loss due to the removal of residual amounts of citric acid, which was incorporated as a fuel during synthesis.Furthermore, the TG curve showed the stability of the proposed sample.Heating from room temperature to 800C resulted in a total weight loss of 3-4 %..This confirmed that the synthesized phosphor had good thermal stability, indicating that this phosphor was suitable for the proposed applications. nescence properties of Dy3+-activated NaCa (PO4) phosphors were investigated using PL techniques.Figure 7(a, b) shows the PL excitation spectra of NaCaPO4; x Dy3+( x=0.1, 0.3, 0.5,.0.7, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mol%) phosphors under 482 nm and 576 nm emission wavelengths.The inset images in Figure 7(a, b) show the variation in excitation intensity with different concentrations of Dy3+ ions.The nature of the excitation bands under 482 nm and 576 nm emission wavelengths was similar.Both excitation bands exhibited the same absorption bands at 325 nm, 350 nm, 365 nm, 388 nm, FIGURE73DPL excitation spectrum of the NaCa1-PO4; Dy3+( x=0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0,.1.5 and 2 mol%) phosphors under (a) 482 nm and (b) 576 nm emission wavelengths (inset image: variation of the excitation intensity at different excitation peaks with the variation in concentration) 425 nm, and 454 nm.These excitation bands were attributed to the 6H16P3/2, 6H16P7/2, 6H16P5/2, 6H14 l13/2, 6H14G11/2, and 6Hj→4I15/2 (where, j=15/2 and 13/2) transitions of Dy3+ ions, respectively.The excitation bands (350 nm, 365 nm and 388 nm) matched well with the emission of NUVLED chips and the 454 nm excitation band matched well with the emission of the blue LED chips.Therefore, all these excitation bands provided suitability according to WLED applications.Under 325 nm, 350 nm, 365 nm, 388 nm, and 454 nm excitations, the PL emission spectra were measured for NaCa1-PO4: x Dy3+(x=0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5 and 2 mol%) phosphors, as shown in Figure 8(a–e).The nature of the emission bands was found to be similar under different excitations, except for the 454 nm excitation.

emission bands was found to be similar under different excitations, except for the 454 nm excitation.The measured emission bands exhibited two strong emission bands at 482 nm (blue) and 576 nm (yellow), which were ascribed to 4F9/26H15/2, and 4F9/2→6H13/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions.The emission spectrum depicted that maximum emission intensity was observed for the 482 nm (blue) emission band.Previous studies on Dy3+-activated phosphors have suggested that 4F9/2→6H15/2 (482nm) is a magnetic dipole (MD) transition, while the 4F9/2→6H13/2 (571nm) transition is an electric dipole (ED) transition together (hypersensitivetransition) with L=2; J=2.It is clear from previous studies, if the MD transition is dominant compared with ED transition then Dv3+ ions are present in high symmetry sites with inversion centres.But, if the ED transition is dominant then the Dy3+ ions are present in low symmetry sites without inversion centres.[32–34] In this investigation, we found that the MD transition was dominant, therefore Dy3+ ions were situated in high symmetry sites with the inversion centre of the host matrix.The inset images in Figure 8(a–e) show the relationship between emission intensity and concentration of Dy3+ ions.It was noted that emission intensity initially increased and then decreased with increasing concentrations of Dy3+ ions.From the plotted graphs, it was observed that emission intensity reached maximum for a1.5 mol% concentration of Dy3+ ions.After this, emission intensity decreased due to concentration quenching of luminescence.As described in previous publications, two reasons are possible behind the drop in emission intensity.First, the distance between the dopant ions decreases due to the high amounts of doping, so dopants are unable to add additional luminescence, therefore emission intensity decreased.Second, when Dy3+ ions enter the site of Ca2+ ions, their charges are unbalanced, which will inevitably bring about vacancies, therefore resulting in a decrease in emission intensity.

Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; Dy3+, M+ ( M=Li2., Na, K) white-emitting phosphors: Charge compensation effect of M+ on the photoluminescence enhancement Teshen Wang, Wentao Zhang *, Xiaomeng Wang, Xue Huang, Peicong Zhang College of Materials and Chemistry & Chemical Engineering, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu, 610059, China ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Ca19Zn2(PO4)14 Rare earth White-emitting phosphor Charge compensation Luminescence enhancement ABSTRACTA series of - Ca3 (PO4) 2 type single-component Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; Dy3++, M+ (M=Li, Na and K) white-emitting phosphors were synthesized via a high-temperature solid-state reaction method, where alkali metal ions (M+) co-doped as charge compensator into the Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+ phosphor was aimed at improving the overall luminescence.The influences of synthesis temperature and the M+ introduction on both structure and luminescence property were thoroughly studied.X-ray diffraction patterns verify that the as-prepared phosphors attain the standard Ca19Zn2(PO4)14 phase without impurities.Photoluminescence peaks at 484 nm and 575 nm (originatingfromthe4F9/26H15/2and4F9/26H13/2electrontransitionsofDy3+ions) were produced for all samples with an excitation of 386 nm, which then combined to emit white light.The luminescence intensities of Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; Dy3-+ were dramatically improved through co-doping with M+ into the phosphor structure.These results demonstrate the promising application prospects of Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14.Dy3+, M+ white-emitting phosphors in white light-emitting diodes. 1.

content: 19Zn2 (PO4) 14.Dy3+, M+ white-emitting phosphors in white light-emitting diodes. 1.Introduction Because of their long lifetime, low energy consumption and envi ronmental friendliness, white light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs) are regarded as alternatives to traditional lighting equipment for many applications [1,2].Due to the imminent energy crisis and environmental protection issues, it is expected that there will be greater potential for w-LEDs for various applications and future development [3–5].Until now, commercial w-LEDs are fabricated by combining blue InGaN chips and yellow-emitting phosphors ( Y3Al5O12; Ce3+) [6–8].The lack of red-light component within these w-LEDs, however, leads to a high correlated colour temperature ( CCT > 5500K ) and low colour rendering index ( CRI < 82 ), which effectively impede their potential applications [9,10].To solve this issue, many researchers have studied white-light production through near-ultraviolet (n-UV) chips coated with tricolour (RGB) phosphors [11,12].However, the white light emitted in this way has been found to be unstable due to the different degradation rates of the RGB light output and reabsorption between tricolour phosphors [13].As a result, the way that the single-component white-emitting phosphor excited by n-UV chips is considered to be the most effective type of w-LED [14,15].Currently, a variety of single-component phosphors have been studied to obtain white light by means of energy transfer mechanisms between activators, for example, Eu2+/ Mn2+ [ 16, 17 ], Eu3+/ Tb3+[ 18 ], Ce3+/ Tb3+/ Mn2+[ 19, 20 ], Tb3+/ Mn+ [ 21 ], which have been shown to undergo some energy loss during the energy transfer process.The search for a single-component phosphor achieving white light efficiently has thus become of huge research interest.Among the rare-earth ions, Dysprosium ions (Dy3+) are employed extensively as activators in various inorganic compounds like borate, silicate, molybdate and phosphate to form phosphors for w-LEDs [22–25].

ganic compounds like borate, silicate, molybdate and phosphate to form phosphors for w-LEDs [22–25].The emitted white light can be composed of two main emissions of Dy3+ ions; one at 480 nm results from the 4F9/26H15/2 electron transition and the other at 570 nm originates from the 4F9/2→6H13/2 electron transition [26,27].Phosphates with a mineral structure have been shown to possess both excellent biosafety and thermal stability as well as provide a good crystal environment for luminescence centres [28].Many researchers have designed and reported white-emitting phosphate phosphors for w-LEDs via doping with Dy3+ ions, such as CagBi (PO4) 7: Dy3+ [ 29 ], 3 a3Lu (PO4) 3: Dy-3+[30], Ba3Y (PO4) 3: Dy3+[31], Ca3Bi (PO4) 3: Dy3+[32], YPO4: Dy3+[33], and Ba3Bi2 (PO4) 4; Dy3+[34].Among the phosphate compounds, the Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 phase with the R3c space group has an isostructural structure of - Ca3 (PO4) 2 [35] that is appropriate for display and lighting applications as a phosphor host.However, Dy3++-doped Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 Fig.1.(a) The XRD patterns for Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; 2 / 0Dy3+ phosphors with different synthesis temperatures and (b) the Rietveld refinement for the Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; 2 / 0Dy3+ sample prepared at 1400C.Lattice parameters and volumes for the standard Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 structure and Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; 2 / 0Dy3+ phosphors with different synthesis temperatures.

4 ) 14 structure and Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14; 2 / 0Dy3+ phosphors with different synthesis temperatures.Samplea (Å)b (Å)c (Å)V (Å3)standard °C °C °C °C phosphors for white light production has been seldom researched.Additionally, the luminescence intensity of rare-earth ion-doped alkaline earth metal phosphors can be enhanced via charge compensation of alkali metal ions [36,37].Thus, the single-component Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+, M+ phosphors with excellent luminescence properties have shown great significance for w-LEDs application.In this study, the designed Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+, M+ white-emitting phosphors were synthesized using a high-temperature solid-state method.In particular, the luminescence intensity enhancement was achieved via the addition of alkali metal ions M+ charge compensator in Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+, M+ phosphors.Furthermore, the impacts of the preparation temperature and co-doping alkali metal ions M+ on the phosphors’ luminescence property and structure were systematically analyzed. 2.Experimenta All Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+, M+ ( M=Li, Na and K) samples were synthesized through a high-temperature solid-state reaction.Aspurchased ZnO (99%), CaCO3 (99%), NH4H2PO4 (99%), Dy2O3 (99.9%) and Li2CO3 / Na2CO3 / K2CO3 (99%) were weighed based on stoichiometric ratios (0.005 mol Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 ) and ground completely in an agate mortar to obtain powdered mixtures.The mixtures were subsequently calcined at temperatures ranging from 1100 ◦C to 1500C for 2 h in a muffle furnace.

s were subsequently calcined at temperatures ranging from 1100 ◦C to 1500C for 2 h in a muffle furnace.Finally, samples were furnace cooled to room temperature and ground for further measurement.The phase of the obtained phosphors was identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using an X-ray diffractometer (Ultima IV, Rigaku, Japan) with CuKα radiation (=1.5406 ) in the 2θ range from 5 to 70◦.Absorption spectra of as-prepared samples were performed on a UV–Vis–NIR diffuse reflectance spectrophotometer (Cary 5000, Agilent Inc, USA).Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Phenom ProX, FEI, The Netherlands) together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was utilized to analyze phosphors’ morphologies and chemical compositions.Excitation spectra, emission spectra and decay curves for all samples were achieved by a fluorophotometer (F-4600, Hitachi, Japan).The thermal quenching and quantum efficiency characteristics of the synthesized samples were measured via a photoluminescence spectrometer (FLS1000, Edinburgh, England) in the range of 20 – 170C with a heating rate of 30C / min 3.Results and discussion The crystal structure of the phosphor host acts as an important role in the luminescence property of the phosphor.To understand the crystal structure of Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14: Dy3+ phosphors calcined at temperatures between 1100C and 1500C, XRD was performed as shown in Fig.1 and compared to the pattern of the Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 (PDF48–1196) standard crystal.All XRD peaks of the phosphor samples coincide with the reference Ca19Zn2 (PO4) 14 crystal pattern, which crystallized in a trigonal geometry with space group of R3c (161) and lattice parameters of a=b=Å, c=37.173 Å, V=3453A3 and==90,=120◦.No diffraction peaks of impurity phases are observed, indicating that the exchange of Ca2+ with Dy3+ does not transform the structure.

Combustion assisted spectroscopic investigation of Dy3+ activated SrYAl307 phosphor for LED and TLD applications Abhijeet R.Kadama,b, Samiksha B.Dhoblea, Girish C.Mishrab, A.D.Deshmukha, S.J.Dhoble a,∗ a Department of Physics, R.T.M.Nagpur University, Nagpur 440033, India b Department of Applied Physics O.P.Jindal University, Punjipathra, Raigarh 496109, India articleinfo Article history: Received 20August 2020Revised 27January 2021Accepted 13February 2021Available online 24February 2021Keywords: Combustion synthesis Aluminate phosphors Thermoluminescence LEDsPhotoluminescence Lamp phosphor abstract Long-persistent inorganic phosphors are widely studied materials owing to their high routine energystoring ability.In the present study we were interested in Dy3+ ion-doped inorganic phosphors for near ultraviolet (UV) excited light-emitting diode (LED) applications.Dy3+ ion-activated SrYAl307 phosphors were prepared using a solution combustion route at 550C.Photoluminescence characterization of SrYAl307: Dy3+ phosphors showed a482 and 573 nm emission peak in the blue and yellow region of the spectrum due to the 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transition of Dy3+ ions under excitation at 325, 350, 366 and 388 nm in the near-UV region.These emissions are supported for white light generation for LED lighting.Crystal structure of the proposed phosphor was determined by Reitveld refinement.Morphology of the sample was analysed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), which showed that the samples were crystallized in a well known structure.As prepared sample was irradiated with a 60Co - (gamma) source at a dose rate of 7.2 kGy/h.

Research paper Cool white light emanation and photo physical features of combustion derived Dy3+ doped ternary yttrate oxide based nanophosphors for down converted WLEDsMonika Sheoran a, Priyanka Sehrawat a, Neelam Kumari b, S.P.Khatkar a, R.K.Malik a,* a Department of Chemistry, Maharshi Dayanand University, Rohtak 124001, India b Department of Chemistry, Meerut College, Ch.Charan Singh University, Meerut 250001, India ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Combustion Rietveld refinement White emission BaSrY4O8Nanophosphors ABSTRACTNovel orthorhombic symmetry type BaSrY4 (1-x) Dy4xO8 (x=1, 3, 5, 7, 10 mol %) cool white light emitting nanocrystals was synthesized by low temperature based solution combustion approach.Information related to crystallographic analysis was made by utilizing X-ray diffraction and Rietveld-refinement technique.The manufactured nanoparticles exhibit cool white emission corresponding to 4F9/26H15/2 (at 480 nm, blue color), 4F9/26H13/2 (at 572 nm, yellow color) and 4F9/26H11/2 (at 673 nm, a weak red color emission).CIE coordinates and CCT values of optimized nanocrystals were found resemblance with white-coordinates of commercial LEDs and NTSC which prove them a potential candidate for outdoor lightning purpose i.e.in WLEDs. 1.Introduction With the development of SSL (solidstatelighting) technology, WLEDs have been expected as the potential candidate to replace ordi nary light sources like incandescent lamps, gas lamps and florescent bulb due to their diverse superior application such as optical sensors, display devices etc [1,2].

t bulb due to their diverse superior application such as optical sensors, display devices etc [1,2].Currently, the WLEDs are prepared via either pumping monochromatic tricolor (blue/green/red) phosphors with NUV chips in an appropriate manner.But, resentfully, stronger reabsorption and irregularity in luminance are some limitations for their successful utilization.Consequently, it admires the material researchers to investigate some advanced, economical and ecological single-phased phosphors that are solution of all the above mentioned snags [3,4].However, blending of the near-UVLED chips with single phased phosphors has been considered as a novel approach to fabricate the energy saving WLEDs.Therefore, the lanthanide doped nanocrystals due to their promising credits like minimal energy consumption, prolonged lifetime and enhanced luminance have been considered of central importance in the solid state lighting technology [5–7].Among various dopants of lanthanide family, Dy3+ ion is of vital importance and in the present research, authors selected Dy3+ as an activator ion due to its white light emitting property for the doping in the host matrix.Being an fruitful activator ion, Dy3+ exhibit emanation of white light because of three emission band occurs at 480 nm, 572 nm and 673 nm which laying in the blue (B), yellow (Y) and red (R) region.Therefore, by adjusting the blue/yellow color light intensities ratio, white light emission can be obtained [8–13].Now, the selection of a worthy host matrix is vital need for the fabrication of nano-crystalline phosphors, as activator ion only replaces the proper host ion.In the present work, a novel ternary yttrate host lattice BaSrY4O8 due to its high stability, excellent thermodynamics, dielectric, superconducting and optical properties, inertness, eco-friendliness, better lumen output, low toxicity has selected as the proper host lattice for the doping of Dy3+ ions.

tter lumen output, low toxicity has selected as the proper host lattice for the doping of Dy3+ ions.Although as per the author’s knowledge is concerned there is not a single report is present on the opto-electronics and crystallographic studies of the RE3+ doped BaSrY4O8 lattice up to a recent date, which thus indicates the novelty of the present work.The objectives of the undertaken work are to investigate all the optoelectronics and crystallographic properties of the BaSrY4O8: Dy3+ host lattice in an elaborate manner.There are various methods are available for the fabrication of rare earth doped nanomaterials like hydrothermal, sol–gel, solid state reaction approach but fabrication of nanomaterials via these conventional method have some disadvantages in form of sturdy mechanism of preparation, very high calcinations temperature, heterogeneous product, long duration of time and sometimes decrease in luminescence properties by virtue of grinding process.Thus, considering Fig.1.XRD profile of BaS4 (1-x) Dy4xO8 ( x=1, 3, 5, 7, 10 mol %) nanophosphors along with standard data of BaSrY4O8 host.these facts fabrication of the Dy3+ activated BaSrY4O8 nano-structured phosphors was done by using fast, non hazardous, low temperature, eco-friendly and self-ignition solution combustion route which was assisted by a nitrogen containing fuel i.e.urea.In this work, the organized investigations about morphological, photometric, spectroscopic and crystallographic properties are carried out in elaborate manner.Surface morphological and crystal size of the fabricated phosphors was determined by using SEM and TEM.Elemental composition and nanocrystalline nature of the nanosample was investigated by utilizing EDAX mapping and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern respectively.Diffuse reflectance (DR) spectrum revealed Egap as well as refractive index values.

n respectively.Diffuse reflectance (DR) spectrum revealed Egap as well as refractive index values.The analysis related to the ample crystal struc ture of the resulted nano-crystalline powders was done by PXRD study.Further, excellent white light emission of the synthesized nanopowder was revealed by PL (Photoluminescence) analysis, which was further confirmed by chromaticity diagram.At the last cool white light emission of synthesized nanophosphors was proved by correlation color temperature (CCT) investigation which strongly revealed usage of the prepared phosphors as a promising candidate in single-phased phosphor converted WLEDs. 2.Experimental 2.1.Phosphor synthesis BaSrY4 (1-x) O8; 4 x Dy3+( x=1, 3, 5, 7,.10 mol %) nanophosphors were fabricated in situ by the low temperature based eco-friendly, fast and non-hazardous solution combustion approach in which all the desired starting element are highly pure (99.999%) collected from sigma Aldrich i.e.Ba (NO3) 2, Sr (NO3) 2, Y (NO3) 3.6H2O, Dy (NO3) 3.6H2O and urea (NH2CONH2).The method was initialized by mixing of analytical grade metal nitrates (Oxidizer) and urea (reducer) in their stoichiometric ratio in deionized water and to obtained homogenous mixture the precursors obtained was warmed on hot plate for 10–15 min [14].And then, it was delivered into a muffle furnace and fired at 500 ◦C temperature for about 15–20 min, where self-restricted combustion reaction took place which results into removal of impurity like N2, CO2 and moisture.A fizzy powder was obtained after this heat treatment, which was granulate later on and sintered at 1100C for span of 3 h [15,16].Thereafter, the targeted nanocrystalline material possess uniform, crystallinity were synthesized with a great success.The general chemical reaction took place in the muffle furnace is given below: Fig.2.
