KEYWORDS activation energy, dosimetry, frequency factor, kinetic parameter, thermoluminescence 1 | INTRODUCTIONRecently, high performance thermoluminescence (TL) materials have received more attention in technology fields due to an increasing demand for TL dosimeters (TLD), which have wide application in industrial, environmental, personal, and clinical ionization radiation protection.[1] Thermoluminescence is a phenomenon of crystalline materials that absorbed energy from electromagnetic radiation or other ionizing radiation that is then re-emitted as light upon heating and which can be utilized for radiation dosimetry.[2,3] The emission intensity of light revealed by phosphors on heating gives an idea of the irradiation dose given to it.A theoretical model for TL analysis was first proposed by Randall and Wilkins.[4] According to this model, electrons are trapped during excitation in some lattice sites.When crystals are heated, electrons are released thermally into the conduction band and are finally recombined with holes at the recombination sites, resulting in TL emission, which is represented by the TL glow curve.Thermoluminescence does not refer to thermal excitation, but to stimulation of luminescence in a sample that has been excited in a different way.The TL material cannot emit light again by simply cooling the sample and reheating it another time.It should first be reexposed to ionizing radiation to again produce light.Generally, TL phosphors useful for dosimetry application must satisfy some important characteristics such as high TL dose sensitivity and accuracy, show linearity of dose–response over a wide range.
section: K E Y W O R D S activation energy, dosimetry, frequency factor, kinetic parameter, thermoluminescence ## 1 | INTRODUCTION Recently, high performance thermoluminescence (TL) materials have received more attention in technology fields due to an increasing demand for TL dosimeters (TLD), which have wide application in industrial, environmental, personal, and clinical ionization radiation protection.<sup>[1]</sup> Thermoluminescence is a phenomenon of crystalline materials that absorbed energy from electromagnetic radiation or other ionizing radiation that is then re-emitted as light upon heating and which can be utilized for radiation dosimetry.<sup>[2,3]</sup> The emission intensity of light revealed by phosphors on heating gives an idea of the irradiation dose given to it.A theoretical model for TL analysis was first proposed by Randall and Wilkins.<sup>[4]</sup> According to this model, electrons are trapped during excitation in some lattice sites.When crystals are heated, electrons are released thermally into the conduction band and are finally recombined with holes at the recombination sites, resulting in TL emission, which is represented by the TL glow curve.Thermoluminescence does not refer to thermal excitation, but to stimulation of luminescence in a sample that has been excited in a different way.The TL material cannot emit light again by simply cooling the sample and reheating it another time.It should first be reexposed to ionizing radiation to again produce light.Generally, TL phosphors useful for dosimetry application must satisfy some important characteristics such as high TL dose sensitivity and accuracy, show linearity of dose–response over a wide range.

content: cs such as high TL dose sensitivity and accuracy, show linearity of dose–response over a wide range.Also they should not exhibit any thermal quenching, be inexpensive, free from hygroscopic and toxicity properties, show negligible UV light response, be reusability, and be easy to process.[5,6] Dosimetric characteristics of a TL phosphor are mainly influenced by their trapping parameters such as activation energy (E), frequency factor (s) and order of kinetics (b), which describe the defect centres responsible for TL emission.Mixed sulphate-based phosphors have excellent TL characteristics due to their high sensitivity, low fading over long duration, and be cost effective and reproducible; this have generated promising attention in the environmental TLD field.[7–11] One important factor that affects the dosimetric characteristics of many TL materials is the heating rate, which reveals change in location as well as shape and size of the glow curve.[12] Various rare earth-activated sulphate-based phosphors such as KCaSO4Cl: Ce, Dy, [ 13 ] Na6 (SO4) 2F Cl: Dy, [ 14 ] K2Ca2 (SO4) 3: Eu, [ 15 ] K3Na7K4K4K5K6K7rlrlr (SO4) 2: Eu, [ 16 ] & & K2Mg (SO4) 2: Dy, [ 17 ] & & Ca2Mg2 (SO4) 3: Dy, [ 18 ] and Ka3Ca2 (SO4) 3F: Eu, Ce [ 19 ] have been studied extensively to improve their TL properties and to obtain reasonable responses for TL characteristics.In principle, irradiation of sulphate materials leads to the formation of 504-502 -, 03 -, or 000 radicals that combine with holes/ electrons on heating, resulting in the emission of light.[20] The present study describes the synthesis of a Dy3+-activated K3Ca2 (SO4) 3F phosphor using a solid-state reaction method and illustrates its TL characteristics.Trapping parameters, including activation energy and frequency factor, were evaluated using the initial rise method and Ilich’s method. 2 | EXPERIMENTAL2.1 | Synthesis A fluoride sulphate-based K3Ca2 (SO4) 3Fx Dy3+ ( x=0.05, 0.1, 0.

2.1 | Synthesis A fluoride sulphate-based K3Ca2 (SO4) 3Fx Dy3+ ( x=0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 mol%) phosphor was synthesized using a two-step hightemperature solid-state reaction method.In the present study, analytical grade starting materials such as potassium sulphate (K2SO4), calcium sulphate (CaSO4), ammonium fluoride (NH4F) and rare earth dysprosium oxide (Dy2O3) were used to prepare the phosphor material.The starting materials for each chemical were weighed and prepared at the correct stoichiometric ratio and then mixed thoroughly in a pestle and mortar for 1 h.The mixture was then kept in an alumina crucible and heated at 400C for 2 h for calcination and then at 800C for 24 h for sintering in a muffle furnace.Finally, the sample was cooled to room temperature in the furnace and ground again to obtain a fine powder and then used for further characterization. 2.2 | Characterization The phase purity and structural analysis of the prepared phosphor was studied using the powder X-ray method and a Bruker Advance D8 diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation (X-ray tube operated at 40 kV and 40 mA) scanning in 2θ with a step size 0.021 and 0.5 s per step.Particle size and surface morphology were analyzed using a scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and a JEOLJSM-58 scanning microscope.The prepared samples at different concentrations were irradiated using gamma (γ)-rays generated from the 60Co source at IUAC, New Delhi.After γ-irradiation, TL glow curve measurements were recorded using a Nucleonix TL1009ITL reader.All characterizations were performed at room temperature. 3 | RESULTSANDDISCUSSION3.1 | X-ray diffraction The phase purity and crystalline nature of the as-prepared K3Ca2 (SO4) 3F Dy3+ phosphor was characterized using X-ray diffraction analysis.Figure 1 shows the experimental XRD pattern of prepared phosphor material monitor in the range 20–80o, and revealed that the diffraction peaks matched well with the standard ICSD data file (reference code no.

evealed that the diffraction peaks matched well with the standard ICSD data file (reference code no.98-020-2,165), which confirmed that the for mation of the compound belonged to an orthorhombic structure with space group Pn21a (33).[ 21 ] The ionic radius of Dy3+( 1.027A ) was much closer to that of Ca2+ (1.12A), therefore it was expected that trivalent Dy3+ ions replaced the divalent Ca2+ ions.Therefore there was no significant change in crystal structure when adding 1 mole% Dy3+ ions into the K3Ca2 (SO4) 3F phosphor.The crystal structure was refined using the Rietveld refinement method.The standard CIF file for the K3Ca2 (SO4) 3F compound (file no.9001046) for Rietveld refine ment of the XRD data was used and the corresponding refinement analysis of the XRD pattern was performed using the Full Prof suite software program with the Pseudo-Voigt profile function, as shown in Figure 2.There was a good match between the observed and calcu lated patterns with nearly uniform residues.Some of the important refinement and lattice parameters obtained after Rietveld analysis are summarized in Table 1.The position of atoms along with their respective occupancies is depicted in Table 2.Figure 3 shows the crysta structure of the K3Ca2 (SO4) 3F phosphor obtained from the Rietveld refinement. 3.2 | Scanning electron microscopy The surface morphology of the prepared phosphor was studied using SEM analysis and is shown in Figure 4.The micrograph shows that the particle size of synthesized phosphor was in the submicron range at around 50-100 μm, with a spherical shape.

Thermoluminescence study and evaluation of trapping parameters CaTiO: RE ( RE=Eu3+, Dy3+) phosphor for TLD applications A.R.Kadam a,b, Girish C.Mishra b, S.J.Dhoble a,∗ a Department of Physics, R.T.M.Nagpur University, Nagpur- 440033, India b Department of Applied Physics O.P.Jindal University, Punjipathra, Raigarh - 496109, India articleinfo Article history: Received 2July 2020Revised 3August 2020Accepted 20August 2020Available online 20August 2020Keywords: Radiation dosimetry Thermoluminescence Trapping parameters RE3+ ions Solution combustion abstract Thermoluminescence study of RE3+( RE3+=Eu3+.and Dy3+) activated CaTiO3 phosphors and determination of trapping parameters are the main focus of this work.Here, CaTiO3X mol % RE3+ phosphors were synthesized by low temperature solution combustion method at 500200C using citric acid as a fuel.Structure, bonding between each element of the sample and morphology of the sample were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), which showed that the samples were crystallized in a well known structure.Both the samples were irradiated with 60Co - (gamma) source and thermoluminescence studies of both samples were done by Nucleonix TL1009I thermoluminescence (TL) reader.Chen’s peak shape method, Initial rise method and Ilich method are used to determine trapping parameters of both samples like activation energy (E), order of kinetics (b) and frequency factor (s).This all results indicate that both the phosphors are potential candidate for the thermoluminescence dosimetry. 1.

sensor technology [2] and photocatalysis [3].Inorganic phosphor materials with differed morphology and surface, controlled crystallography, and micro scale or nano-scale structures are required in view of their one of kind chemical, physical and optical properties [4].Many rare earth doped inorganic phosphors like aluminates, silicates, borates, titanates, oxides with different morphology has been synthesized using different methods like, solid state synthesis, combustion, sol-gel, co-precipitation etc [5–11].These materials discover their applications in solid state lighting system, display devices and optoelectronics innovation.Nonetheless, due to the ionicity and simple cubic structure, they comprise an interesting model for optical examinations on insulating metal oxides [12].Among the alkaline earth oxides, calcium oxide is pulled in numerous researchers because of its unrivaled properties, bounty and wide scope of uses [13,14].Phosphors which are exposed by some ionizing radiations then it absorb energy in the form of trapped electrons and holes pairs in the band gap.These trapped electrons are then emitted by thermal energy commencing external source with constant heating rate [15,16].Typical defects are made by the dislocation of a negative ion that goes about as an electron trap.These Defects in the lattice structure are liable for these traps.When trapped, an electron will at last be removed by thermal vibrations of the lattice as the temperature raised these vibrations get more grounded and the trapped electrons are immediately liberated.Thermoluminescence is nothing but the thermally stimulated luminescence which is the method of stimulation by means of thermal energy, the emission of luminescence from a substance subsequent the absorption of energy from an external source by that substance [17].

from a substance subsequent the absorption of energy from an external source by that substance [17].Thermoluminescent materials exhibit a wide range of applications like personal dosimetry, environmental dosimetry, medical research field etc.Thermoluminescence dosimetry (TLD) is one of the most significant procedures used to evaluate the consumed portion, notwithstanding different strategies dependent on solidstate dosimetry, for example, radiation-induced absorbance [18,19].TLD badges are used for different radiation monitoring applications.Many phosphors like oxides, fluorides and sulphates based phosphors are available in the form of thermoluminescent badges.Nonetheless each of the badges are not applicable for low or high dosimetric application, for this reason scientists all over the world are still searching for more authentic novel materials and to develop the dosimetric properties of existing materials to be used as eficient TLD materials over a wide range of radiation doses.Table 1Structural parameters of CaTiO3 phosphor obtained from the Rietveld refinement.Sr.

RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYWhite light emission and thermoluminescence studies of Dy3+-activated hardystonite (Ca2ZnSi2O7) phosphor Siteshwari Chandraker 1 | Jagjeet Kaur 1 | Ruby Priya 3 | Vikas Dubey 2 | Neha Dubey 1 1Department of Physics, Govt.V.Y.T.Post Graduate Autonomous College Durg, Chhattisgarh, India 2Department of Physics, Bhilai Institute of Technology Raipur, Kendri, Raipur, India 3Department of Physics, University Institute of Sciences, Chandigarh University, Mohali, India Correspondence Vikas Dubey, Department of Physics, Bhila Institute of Technology Raipur, C.G., 493661, India.Email: jsvikasdubey@gmail.com Abstract Here, we report the photoluminescence and thermoluminescent properties of Dy-activated Ca2ZnSi2O7 phosphors synthesized using the solid-state method.The synthesized phosphors showed hardystonite type structure, and had micron-sized particles.Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) showed the existence of the functional groups and confirmed the formation of phosphor and photoluminescence techniques.The phosphors under excitation at 239 nm exhibited green-yellow emission spectra in the region 481–575 nm corresponding to the 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/2→6H13/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions.The Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) coordinates were achieved to be (0.25, 0.27), which was narrowly close to the white region.Thermoluminescence (TL) glow curve analysis of prepared Dy3+-activated Ca2ZnSi2O7 phosphors were recorded for different ultraviolet (UV) light exposure times and found to have a linear response with dose.The TL glow curves, recorded with various UV exposure times ranging from 5 to 25 min, showed a linear response with dosage.The corresponding kinetic parameters were also calculated using a computerized glow curve deconvolution (CGCD) technique.

etic parameters were also calculated using a computerized glow curve deconvolution (CGCD) technique.Activation energy was observed to enhance the increase in the peak temperature and its value was substantially higher for the third peak fitted using CGCD.The obtained results indicated that the synthesized pristine phosphors could be potentially used for lighting, displays, and dosimetric applications. KEYWORDS dysprosium, hardystonite, phosphors, solid-state method, TL glow curve 1 | INTRODUCTIONRare-earth-doped white light-emitting phosphors find vast applications in various optoelectronic and display devices.[1–4] This is due to the ff transitions in the rare-earth elements that lead to the sharp, narrow, and distinct emission spectra.To exhibit white light emission phenomena, Dy3+-doped phosphors are generally used due to their transitions.However, the host material plays a significant role in achieving white light.Among the various host lattices, silicates are promising candidates due to their low phonon energy, water resistant property, high thermal and mechanical durability, effective cost fabrication, and wide band gap structure.[5–8] To date, many silicates such as Ca2MgSi2O7, Sr2SiO4, and SrSiO3 are doped with Dy3+ ions to generate white light emission.[9–12] In the silicate family, compounds with the general structure X2MY2O7: ( X=Ca, Sr, Na; M=Mg, Zn; Y=Si, Al, B) form a melities group with a tetragonal crystal structure.[13–22] In the present study, we synthesized Dy3+-doped Ca2ZnSi2O7 phosphors using a solid-state method and studied their photoluminescence and thermoluminescent properties in detail.The concentration of Dy3+ ions was varied from 0.1 to 2 mol% in the host lattice.All the structural, morphological, and optical properties were studied in detail.

content: deposition etc.Among wet chemical methods, ‘solution combustion synthesis’ has different advantages.It requires simple apparatus and the materials used are more economical [8].It requires low energy, short time and this technique may also be employed to turn out standardized, high-purity, crystalline oxides.The nature of crystalline, surface area and agglomeration of the synthesized products are primarily governed by flame temperature during combustion which itself dependents on the nature of the fuel and the fuel to oxidizer ratio [9].It is known that, a good fuel should react nonviolently without producing venomous gasses and act as a complexing agent for metal ions.While the solid state reaction method has several shortcomings such as prolonged reaction time, larger size grain growth and poor homogeneity.The combustion synthesis process is to dissolve metal nitrate and fuel in water, and then to heat the solution in a microwave oven.The fuel and metal nitrate decomposing and give flammable gases such as NH3 and NO2, respectively.After the solution reaches the point of spontaneous combustion, it begins burning and becomes a solid, which burns at high temperature.The combustion is not finished until all the flammable substances are all burned out and it turns out to be a loose substances which show voids, pores, and high friable formed by the escaping gases during the combustion reaction.Thermoluminescence (TL) has been a dynamic field of research in the present decade because of its broad function potential [10,11].Its most remarkable application has been in its utilization in radiation dosimetry.Ionizing radiation dosimeters, which depend on the thermoluminescence properties of materials, have helped in the arrangements of numerous dosimetric issues due to their long time stockpiling limits, autonomy of portion with radiation forces, ease with which estimations are done and light weight [12].Thermoluminescence is the production of light (generallyinthevisibleregion) when a TL phosphor already exposed to ionizing radiation (c, b, X) is heated.

in the visible region) when a TL phosphor already exposed to ionizing radiation (c, b, X) is heated.The plot of light production with time at dissimilar temperatures is known the glow curve and the area below the glow curve can be associated to the dose of radiation.The glow curve not only supports accurate estimation of the dose, it can also assist in maintaining the superiority of dose estimation in addition to maintaining the superiority of phosphor preparation.The overall TL dosimetry set up includes the TL instrumentation and TL detector, and many factors can cause spurious signals there by leading to errors in dose estimation.Further, it is very difficult to assess or foretell some of the spurious signals whereas others can be minimized by proper design, operation, and maintenance of TL instruments and by using new computational techniques, for example computerized glow curve deconvolution (CGCD) [13].In the present work, Dy3+ doped Na14Al12Si13O51 phosphor is synthesized via combustion technique at 600C by using urea as a fuel.The synthesized sample was characterized by XRD verify their phase composition; SEM analyzed their size and morphology.Reliable dosimetric studies of TL material additionally include a good knowledge of kinetic parameter.These kinetic parameters are vital for the mechanism of responsible TL emission of the material.Dosimetric properties are also depending on the kinetic parameter of its glow curve.TL parameters are activation energy (E), frequency factor (s), kinetic order (b).These trapping parameters are calculated by differential methods together with peak shape (PS), initial rise (IR) Chen’s technique.The kinetic order (b) is usually calculated by peak shape methodology from peak form parameter. 2.Materials and experimental The following materials used for the synthesis of Na14Al12Si13-O51Dy3+ phosphor, which are highly purified A.R.grade chemicals with purity 99.23% of nitrate group as NaNO3, Al (NO3) 3, SiO2, NH2-CO-NH2, Dy2O3 are used.

rity 99.23% of nitrate group as NaNO3, Al (NO3) 3, SiO2, NH2-CO-NH2, Dy2O3 are used.A series of Dy3+ doped sodium aluminum silicate hydrate is prepared by simple combustion method at 55020C using urea as a fuel.The systematic ratio 1:1:2 are maintain and collected all samples in a Petri dish.Rare earth element dysprosium oxide and europium dioxide are used as doping agent, dissolved in A.R grade Nitric Acid to form Dysprosium nitrate.Then all materials are mixed and crush together by using pestle mortar to form homogeneous material.These compound materials are heated in muffle furnace at 55020 C using and liberated NO2 and S02 gases converting the compound state to floppy ash.The complete reaction is completed in specific time of 10 min and form white powder material.Here urea is used as a fuel.This prepared material is characterized by XRD, FT-IR, TL and SEM.The sophisticated instrument is used at the lab provided by a Nucleonix (model-1009I) for the thermo luminescence measurement of prepared phosphate material and heating rate 5 C/sec.The TL reading measurement with the range of 50-400C..Fig.1 shows schematic presentation of material synthesis. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.XRD analysis The XRD pattern of synthesized Na14Al12Si13O51 phosphor were recorded by X-ray Diffractometer and this recorded pattern is shown in Fig.2.The XRD pattern of synthesized Na14Al12Si13O51 phosphor shows good crystalline nature of the samples.The obtained spectra were compared with standard JCPDS card no.1036.The XRD patterns of synthesized material is confirmed by using Rigaku miniflex d600X-ray diffractometer with CuKa radiation (=0.154056 nm ) operated at 40 kV, 15 mA.The XRD pattern was recorded in the range of 20 to 80 with step size 0.02. 3.2.SEM Morphology of Na14Al12Si13O51 phosphor was studied by scanning electron microscope.The SEM images reveals non-uniform plate like structure as can be seen in Fig.3 (c) & (d).Fig.

scope.The SEM images reveals non-uniform plate like structure as can be seen in Fig.3 (c) & (d).Fig.2 (a) and (b) shows that cracks and voids in particles which are due to non-uniform allocation of temperatures and accumulation flow during synthesis.The particle size in range of sub-micrometers to few micrometers; the non-consistency in particle size is due to non-uniformity of temperature during the synthesis.The cracks and voids in the particle are probably created due to emission of glass molecule during synthesis of sample by simple combustion process. Additional Notes: Differences between PL lifetime and afterglow duration The afterglow duration of 115 min indicates that, after the extinction of the ultraviolet excitation, the sample emits light for the duration of 115 min with decayed intensity to 0.32 mcd/m2.The time-resolved PL spectrum of CaAl2O4: Dy3++ (0.8 mol%) shows that lifetime of Dy3+ emission at 574 nm is in the order of millisecond.Such a large difference between the afterglow duration and the PL lifetime can be accounted by the fact the PL and the afterglow are two distinctly different processes.The PL decay measures the electron depopulation of excited states, and PL lifetime is the time a fluorophore spends in the excited state before emitting a photon and returning to the ground state.As discussed before, the PL lifetime equals to the inverse of summation of the radiative and non-radiative rates.Generally, PL lifetime varies from picoseconds to hundreds of nanoseconds depending on the fluorophore.The afterglow measure the carrier depopulation from traps, and the afterglow duration of a material is governed by the reaps in the material.In the case of the characteristic emissions of Dy3+ in the lattice of CaAl2O4, the long PL lifetime in the order of millisecond is caused by the spin-forbidden transitions (i.e., the 4 f - 4 f transition).As a contrast, the long afterglow duration is caused by the storage of energy in traps that are slowly promoted to the luminescence center of afterglow.In afterglow materials, the energy is stored by trapping charged carriers ( i.e., electrons and holes) in traps, which are slowly released from the traps upon thermal stimulation.

., electrons and holes) in traps, which are slowly released from the traps upon thermal stimulation.Thus, afterglow is a particular case of thermostimulated luminescence and is a defect dependent phenomenon.Detailed discussions can be found in relevant reviews. Research Article Effect of partial substituting 3+ with Ln3+( Ln=La, Gd ) on photoluminescence enhancement in high-performance Na5Y (MoO4) 4: Dy3+ white-emitting phosphors Yunhang Du, Xiaomeng Wang, Zeliang Qiu⁎, Zhou Zhao, Xue Huang, Haiying Du, Wentao Zhang College of Materials and Chemistry & Chemical Engineering, Chengdu University of Technology, Chengdu 610059, China articleinfo Article history: Received 21September 2021Received in revised form 15December 2021Accepted 21December 2021Available online 23December 2021Keywords: NaY(MoO) Rare earth White-emitting Luminescence enhancement Partial substitution White light-emitting diode abstract White-emitting Na5Y1-yLny (MoO4) 4Dy3+( Ln=La, Gd ) phosphors were synthesized by a sol-combustion method.The effects of Ln3+ partial introduction on the structure and photoluminescence of Na5Y1-yLny (MoO4) 4; Dy3+( Ln=La, Gd) phosphors were studied.The X-ray diffraction and chemical composition results verified the successful introduction of Dy3+, La3+ and Gd3+ into the Na5Y (MoO4) 4 lattice.Under the excitation of ultraviolet at 352 nm, the as-prepared phosphors showed a white emission with characteristic emission peaks at 577 nm (yellow) and 485 nm (blue), corresponding to the 4F9/26H13/2 and 4F9/26H15/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions, respectively.By substituting 3+ ion with La3+ and Gd3+, the photoluminescence intensity of Na5Y (MoO4) 4: Dy3+ sample was obviously enhanced due to the crystal field effect surrounding the luminescence center Dy3+.The chromaticity coordinates of all phosphors were located at the white light region, and the substitution of La3+ or Gd3+ could realize a higher color rendering index of white emission.Therefore, the as-prepared white-emitting Na5Y0.90La0.06 (MoO4) 4; 0.

index of white emission.Therefore, the as-prepared white-emitting Na5Y0.90La0.06 (MoO4) 4; 0.04Dy3+ and Na5Y0.88Gd0.08 (MoO4) 40.04Dy3+ phosphors could be used as single-component phosphor for w-LEDs application. 1.Introduction Recently, the phosphor-converted white light-emitting diodes (pc w-LEDs), with the advantages of long life, high eficiency and environmental friendliness, have been widely used in solid-state lighting, display and information fields [1–3].Nowadays, there are two alternative approaches for realizing the w-LEDs: the commercial way is combining blue InGaN chip with Y3Al5012: Ce3+ yellow phosphor, but the white light lacks red light component, resulting in high correlated color temperature ( CCT > 5500K ) and low color rendering index (CRI, Ra < 82) [4,5].And another way is using an ultraviolet (UV) chip to excite tri color phosphors, in which multi-phosphors have very serious reabsorption and different attenuation of emission, leading to low luminous eficiency and light change [6–9].Therefore, the single-component white-emitting phosphor is very promising to avoid the above problems for w-LEDs, the white emission can be achieved by introducing multi-lanthanides ions in structure, such as Nelli et al.[10] reported the Gd dioxycarbonate phosphor activated with Sm3+, Eu3+, Tb3+, Dy3+ and Tm3+, and Wang et al.[11] synthesized the complexes of terephthalic acid (H2BDC) with Ce3+, Eu3+ and Tb3+.Among rare earth ions, the character istic white emission of Dy3+ ions include yellow (4F9/26H13/2) and blue (4F9/26H15/2) peaks [12,13], and the white light with different chromaticity parameters would be realized by adjusting the proportion of blue and yellow light.Hence, a novel singlecomponent white-emitting phosphor with Dy3+ doping could be studied for w-LEDs application.

vel singlecomponent white-emitting phosphor with Dy3+ doping could be studied for w-LEDs application.Molybdate with mineral structure is widely studied as an excellent phosphor host for rare earth doping, due to its low synthesis temperature, stable physical and chemical properties and strong energy absorption ability of tetrahedral MoO42- groups [14–22].Among molybdate structures, A5M (Mo004) 4: ( A=Li, Na, K; M=Y, La, Gd, Dy, Er, Yb) with scheelite structure has been used as a suitable phosphor host.For example, Dhanya et al.[23] synthesized Na5M (MoO4) 4 ( M=Y, Yb ) ceramics via solid state ceramic route and confirmed the existence of regular MoO42- tetrahedral ions in the unit cells; Chiu et al.[24] confirmed the potential application of M5Eu (WO4) 4-x (M004) x ( M=Li, Na, K) for w-LED; Guo et al.[25] reported Na5Ln (MoO4) 4: Eu3+( Ln=La, Gd, Y ) and their luminescence properties under near-ultraviolet light; Liu et al.[26] synthesize Na5RE (MoO4) 4 ( RE=La, Gd, Dy, Er ) by solid-state reaction method, and Jin et al.[27] studied the luminescence property of NaLa (MoO4) 4; Tb3+, Eu3+, Tm3+ phosphor, but there are few studies have been reported on Dy3+.-doped Na5Y (MoO4) 4 phosphors [28].In addition, the luminescence performance of phosphors especially intensity must be further improved to meet the aim of practical w-LEDs application [29].Always, partial substitution of cations in structure can increase the luminescence properties of phosphors based on the environmental effect of crystal field around luminescence center.Ba2, 94-2 x LaxNaxP4O13; 0.06Eu2+[ 30 ], Ca3-xMx (PO4) 2Eu2+( M=Sr, Ba ) [ 31 ], Ca1-xYxTi1-xAlxO3Dy3+[ 32 ], rl r2-x GdxO3Eu3+& [ 33 ], & 2-x MxO3Eu3+( M &=- Gd, Bi) [34] and Ca2BO3Cl: Eu2+, M2+ ( M=Sr, Ba) [35] were researched and the luminescence properties were enhanced through partial cation substitution.

Fig.1.(a) XRD patterns of Na5Y0.96-yLay(MoO4)4:0.04Dy3+ (0 ≤ y ≤ 0.10) and (b) XRD patterns of Na5Y0.96-yGdy(MoO4)4:0.04Dy3+ (0 ≤ y ≤ 0.12) samples.In this study, the Na5Y1-yLny (MoO4) 4: Dy3+( Ln=La, Gd ) phosphors were synthesized by a sol-combustion method with simple process.By substituting 3+ ion with cations La3+ and Gd3+, the luminescence intensity of phosphors could be enhanced due to the crystal field around Dy3+ ions changed.The influences of partial 3+ substitution with La3+ and Gd3+ on the crystal structure and photoluminescence properties of Na5Y (MoO4) 4: Dy3+ powders were researched.The as-prepared Na5Y1-yLny (MoO4) 4Dy3+( Ln=La, Gd) white-emitting phosphor powder was used in w-LEDs to explore its practical application. 2.Experimental The Na5Y1-yLny (MoO4) 4: Dy3+ ( Ln=La, Gd ) phosphor samples were synthesized by sol-combustion method.Dy2O3 (99.95%), 4O3 (99.8%), YO (99.5%), La2O3 (99.95%), Gd2O3 (99.99%), citric acid (AR) and (NH4) 6Mo7O244H2O (99%) were used as the starting materials.The doping concentration of Dy3+ in the structure was controlled at 0.04 of 3+, while the contents of La3+ and Gd3+ were varied in the range of 0-0.12 of 3+.Stoichiometric Dy203, Na2CO3, 203, La203 and Gd2O3 were dissolved in a certain diluted HNO (1mol/L), and citric acid and (NH4) 6Mo70244H20 were successively added to the above solution.

ofthe host phosphor via co-doping oftransition metal ions.In this paper, we report a significant improvement in the white light emission of Dy3+ doped CaMoO4 by co-doping Zn2+ ions.The x-ray diffraction pattern confirms the tetragonal phase ofpure and doped CaMoO phosphor.The peak broadening and a red-shift in the absorption peak are observed by UV–vis absorption analysis of Zn2+/ Dy3+ doped CaMoO4..From Photoluminescence studies, we have observed that in Dy3+ doped CaMoO4, the 4 % Dy3+ doped CaMoO4 exhibits maximum emission.The Zn2+ ions are co-doped to further increase the luminescence intensity o CaMoO4: 4 % Dy3+ and the maximum luminescence is obtained for 0.25% Zn2+ concentration.Two intense emission peaks centered at 484 nm and 574 nm related to transitions 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 of Dy3+ ion are observed for Dy3+ doped phosphor.The 4F9/26H13/2 transition is the forced electric dipole transition which is affected by its chemical environment.After Zn2+ co-doping, the 4F9/26H13/2 transition is affected due to a change in asymmetricity around the Dy3+ ions.The 0.25% co-doping of Zn2+ gives 34% enhancement in luminescence emission of 4% Dy3+ doped CaMoO4..As a result, the CIE coordinates ofchromaticity diagram and the color purity ofthe 0.25% Zn2+ co-doped CaMoO4: 4Dy3+ show improvement in the overall white light emission.We have shown that with Zn2+ co-doping, the non-radiative relaxations are reduced which results in improved white light emission o Dy3- ions. 1.Introduction For the past two decades, White Light Emitting Diodes (w-LEDs) have been increasingly preferred over traditional light sources due to their unique properties such as environmental friendliness, longer operating lifetime, electric energy saving, enhanced optical power, and higher luminous efficacy [1–3].

phosphor onto InGaN blue chips to emit white light [4, 5].White light emission can also be realized by the combination of red, blue, and green multiphase phosphors.However, Several drawbacks in this technique due to multistage phosphors such as adjustment of color ratio, color reabsorption, emission efficiency, etc [6, 7].Therefore, the solution to these shortcomings is a single component phosphor that gives excellent white light emission with near Ultraviolet (UV) absorption.Various phosphors have been studied as the host for white-light-emitting phosphors.Many of these previously published host phosphors have several drawbacks such as Ca2SiO4, CaF2, which are prepared by complex synthesis processes whereas, hosts such as SrWO4, CaSrAl2SiO7 have limited thermal and chemical stability, making them difficult to produce on a large scale [8–11].Therefore, importance has been given to the quest to develop thermally and chemically stable phosphors that can be prepared via environment-friendly and cost-effective technology.Molybdates such as CaMoO4 have gained special attention in the research fraternity due to their potentiating properties.The CaMoO4 shows a tetragonal crystal structure with self-activated broadband emission lying in the visible light region [8].The advantages of CaMoO4 host phosphor over other phosphors are that CaMoO4 possesses good chemical and thermal stability, a longer average decay lifetime (14ms), and a higher melting point (1435C-1480C) [9].The CaMoO4 phosphor can be prepared through various synthesis processes such as auto-combustion, solid-state technique, solgel, solvothermal/hydrothermal, and one-step spray pyrolysis, etc [8, 10–14], among which the auto-combustion process (urea fuel-based) is advantageous over others because CaMoO4 phosphors have become increasingly important owing to their remarkable optical properties.These materials are being widely investigated in the fields of optoelectronics and medical devices such as display devices, white-light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs), optical fiber, semiconductor laser, photo-catalysis, temperature sensors, photodynamic therapy, bio-imaging, biosensors, etc [4, 15–21].The RE3+ doped CaMoO4 phosphors are significantly better than other traditional phosphors due to their sharp spectral emissions covering UV to Near Infrared (IR) region and also depict color tunability due to the different arrangements of the 4 f electrons.Among all RE3+ ions, the Dy3+ ion is studied with various spectroscopy techniques because its spectroscopic properties are very sensitive to its local environment in the host matrix.The Dy3+ ion is used as a dopant in various host materials for different applications, some of which are listed in table 1.The Dy3++ ions present two predominant luminescence bands lying in the blue and yellow spectral regions, correspond to the 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 electronic transitions, respectively [26].White light emission may be easily obtained due to adjustment ofratio ofblue and yellow spectral bands of the Dy3+ ions.Thus, Dy3+ doped luminescent material emits white light in the form of a single-ingredient phosphor, addressing the shortfalls of commercial w-LEDs.As a result, the possibility of obtaining white light with high luminous efficiency increases.There are some reports on Dy3+ doped materials such as NaSr2Nb5O15 [ 26 ] Ba5CaAl4O12 [ 27 ] LiSr4 (BO3) 3 [ 29 ], and Ca2MgSi2O7 [ 36 ] ] for white light emission, but these phosphors have several shortcomings such as weak selfactivated emission and synthesized via high-temperature solid-state processes.However, there are no such drawbacks in Dy3+ doped CaMoO4 phosphor.In this article, the increase in the emission intensity of Dy3+ doped CaMoO4 phosphor via Zn2+ codoping is reported.The phosphors were synthesized via a lucrative auto-combustion method.

via Zn2+ codoping is reported.The phosphors were synthesized via a lucrative auto-combustion method.The PL spectra of all samples were studied and observed that the PL emission intensity ofthe Dy3+ transitions enhances up to 34 percent by 0.25% co-doping of Zn2+ ion.The CIE coordinates ( x, y ) for the 0.25% Zn2+ co-doped phosphor are (0.319, 0.381), which is very close to proper white emission, and the color purity is very low around ∼10%.Our results show that improved white emission may be obtained by optimum Zn2+ co-doping.Thus, Zn2+/ Dy3+ doped CaMoO4 as a singleingredient phosphor might be a potential candidate for white light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs). 2.Synthesis method and characterization The un-doped CaMoO4, Dy3+(2%, 3%, 4%, 5%) doped CaMoO4 and Zn2+(0.1%, 0.25%, 0.5%, 1%) co-doped 4%Dy+3 dopedCaMoO phosphorshavebeendescribed with code names CMO, Dy2, Dy3, Dy4, Dy5, Z0.1, Z0.25, Z0.5, and Z1 respectively.The required materials for synthesis were calcium carbonate ( CaCO3, 99.5%, Alfa Aesar), Dy (COOCH3) 3 * 4H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9%), Zinc acetate dihydrate ( Zn (COOCH3) 2 * 2H2O, > 98 % Alfa Aesar), and ammonium molybdate (Para) tetrahydrate ( (NH4) 6Mo7O24 * x H2O3, 99.99%, Alfa Aesar).For the Z0.25 sample, the required quantities of CaCO3, Dy (COOCH3) 3 * 4H2O, and Zn (COOCH3) 2 * 2H2O were collected in a beaker and concentrated nitric acid was poured dropwise for 2-3 h.The stoichiometric amount of Zn(COOCH)*2H O was 0.0053 gm, 0.0134 gm, 0.0268 gm, 0.0534 gm for preparation of 5 gm sample of Z0.1, Z0.25, Z0.5, and Z1, respectively.Metal nitrates transparent gel solution was obtained and heated continually to remove extra nitric acid.In a second beaker filled with DI water, a required amount of (NH4) 6Mo7O24 * 4H2O was taken and stirred at room temperature for 2 h.A stoichiometric amount ofurea was mixed to the solution for the auto-combustion process.The solution was further stirred at a constant rate for the next 1 h to form a homogeneous solution.

.The solution was further stirred at a constant rate for the next 1 h to form a homogeneous solution.This homogeneous solution was added with the first transparent gel solution at 120C..The obtained final solution was placed in an oven preset at 250C for auto-combustion for 4 h.The obtained powder after combustion was annealed in a closed furnace at 1000C for 4 h.The obtained final powder from the furnace was used for characterizations [8].All samples were prepared by the same synthesis procedure. content: atterns represent the pure phase of synthesized materials that was formed with monoclinic structure.The metal–ligand bonding nature and electronic band structure have been examined optical absorption spectra.The luminescence emission curves of the silicate phosphors display an intense vellow emission peak at 579 nm and a blue emission peak at 491 nm.Among the emission bands, the band observed in the yellow region due to 4F9/26H13/2 transition was found to be higher intensity.The radiative parameters like transition probabilities (AR), branching ratios (b) and stimulated emission cross-section (PE) values were calculated using Judd– Ofelt parameters and refractive index values for the observed transitions in emission spectra.The life time measurements were made for 4F9/26H13/2 transition of all the studied samples by keeping an excitation at 350 nm and emission at 579 nm and decay curves were fitted to bi-exponential fitting method.The CCT values obtained from the color coordinates suggested that present xDyKBS phosphors can emit warm and neutral white light depending upon the dopant concentration under near-UV excitation.Our results demonstrated that the optimum concentration 0.05DyKBS phosphor can be successfully utilized as a promising and potential candidate for various innovative photonic applications like warm white LEDs.solar cells, optical sensors and lasers 2021Elsevier B.V.All rights reserved. 1.Introduction Nowadays, rare earth (RE) ions doped optical materials have attracted great research interests owing to their wide range of applications in plasma display panels, white LEDs, traffic signals; full-color displays cellular phone illumination and biomarkers etc.[1-5].Further, rare earth doped phosphors are also useful for fabricating optoelectronic devices like lasers, display monitors, sensors and optical fiber amplifiers.

ricating optoelectronic devices like lasers, display monitors, sensors and optical fiber amplifiers.Although commercial White-LEDs were fabricated by making use of a blue jean- LED chip coated with trivalent cerium activated yttrium aluminum garnet yellow phosphors, which undergo few weakness for instance, low stability of color temperature, poor color rendering index, lower lifetime and poor luminescence intensity [6].These drawbacks bound the application of light emitting diodes in certain areas.RE- activated phosphors were considered as an alternative approach that can be used as blue/green/red tri-color emitting source to fabricate near-UV based W-LEDs.Such kind of W-LEDs have drawn much importance in the fields of displays and general lightings owing to their advantages such as, high luminous efficiency, compactness, energy saving capabilities, high brightness, long serving lifetime, fast switching, good material stability, diversity in design and environmental friendliness [7-9].Among all RE ions, Dy3+ is the most significant lanthanide ions for the fabrication of visible lasers and white light emitting phosphors.Dy3+ ion is capable of emitting several interesting wavelengths between its f–f transitions, that have potential applications in diverse fields.Dy3+ ions have been exhibited two emission bands, one in blue ( 470–500 nm) and another one in yellow ( 570– 600 nm) region attributed to the transitions 4F9/2→6H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 [10-12].A suitable combination of these blue and yellow luminescence leads to generation of white light that can be tuned in phosphors.The white light emission can be attained in Dy3+ activated phosphors by tuning appropriate Y/B intensity ratio, and the same was influenced by RE ion concentration, composition and excitation wavelength [13].The selection of host is crucial the design and development of good lasing materials and optoelectronic devices.

n of host is crucial the design and development of good lasing materials and optoelectronic devices.For the past few years, RE3+ ions doped metal oxide based phosphors play a major role in the fabrication of photonic devices such as infrared lasers, compact microchip lasers, flat-panel displays, fiber amplifiers, biomedical diagnostics, sensors, infrared detectors, optical data storage devices and up-conversion lasers.The Dy3+ ions were doped in many hosts for luminescence activities such as silicate [14], gallates [15], molybdate [16], phosphates [17] and aluminates [18].Silicate based materials are attractive class of inorganic phosphors used for a wide range of applications owing to its properties like, easy synthesis process, chemical resistance, high physicochemical stability, and visible light transparency, etc,.Furthermore, alkaline earth based silicate such as (Mg, Ca, Ba, Sr) silicates are generally used as host for long lasting luminescent material.The present work is to explore the spectroscopic properties of Dy3+ activated KBaScSi3O9 phosphors.The Judd–Ofelt (J–O) theory [19-22] has been used to investigate the intensity and radiative properties of synthesized silicate phosphors.CIE color coordinates were estimated to find the emission color of the title phosphors.The luminescence decay curve analysis was made to obtain excited state lifetime.Finally, the obtained results were analyzed, interpreted, discussed and compared with previously reported articles. 2.Experimental 2.1.Synthesis The various concentrations of Dy3+ doped KBaScSiO (1 mol %, 3 mol %, 5 mol %, 7 mol % and 9 mol %) phosphors were prepared by using solid-state reaction technique in air atmosphere.The prepared phosphor samples were named as 0.01DyKBS, 0.03DyKBS, 0.05DyKBS, 0.07DyKBS and 0.09DyKBS based on the concentration of Dy3+ ions.Raw materials contain Potassium Carbonate (K2CO3), Barium Carbonate (BaCO3), Scandium (III) Oxide (Sc203), Silicon Dioxide (SiO2) and Dysprosium Oxide (Dy2O3) ware used as the starting materials.

), Silicon Dioxide (SiO2) and Dysprosium Oxide (Dy2O3) ware used as the starting materials.The chemicals were homogeneously mixed according to their stoichiometric amount and ground systematically by using agate mortar.The combination of chemicals was transferred to platinum crucible and preheated at 600 C for 2 h.Then, the chemicals were reground and sintered at 1100C for 12 h.Finally, all the xDyKBS samples were slowly cooled to room temperature and grounded well into fine powders for further characterization. 2.2.Material characterization X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Dy3+ activated KBaScSi3O9 samples were recorded for various Dy3+ concentrations using a RIGAKUBruker D8 advance X-ray diffractometer with Cu-Ka radiation (1.54178 Å).The surface morphology and phosphor components were analyzed by field emission scanning electron microscope (SU6600Hitachi High-Technologies Corporation) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (EDS).UV–Vis–NIR absorption spectra were recorded for prepared powders on Perkin Elmer Lambda 750 spectrophotometer.Hitachi F-7000 fluorescence spectrophotometer equipped with 150W xenon lamp as excitation lamp was used to record the photoluminescence spectra.Horiba Jobin Yvon Fluorolog - FL3-11 instrument has been used for decay measurements.All these measurements were carried out at room temperature only. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.Powder-XRD analysis In order to study the structural effects of dysprosium doping into KBaScSi3O9 host matrix, the crystal structure of phosphors have been studied (presented in Fig.1) with the help of powder-XRD technique.The XRD patterns illustrated that fine-resolved diffraction peaks matching well with the previously reported articles by Takeshi et al.[23,24].As-synthesized silicate phosphors were crystallized in monoclinic structure with P21 / n space group on comparing with standard data as per ICSD no.166999.

monoclinic structure with P21 / n space group on comparing with standard data as per ICSD no.166999.No other phase or impurity peaks are observed, which indicates high crystalline purity of Dy3+ activated silicate phosphors Fig.1.PXRD spectra of the xDyKBS phosphors.In the KBaScSi3O9 matrix, effective ionic radii for Ba2+ is 1.38 Å ( CN=6 ) and Dy3+ ion is 0.97A ( CN=6 )..In Dy3+ doped silicate phosphors, it is assumed that Dy3+ ions occupied the Ba2+ in the crystal structure.The tolerable percentage difference in ionic radii between activator and host ions should not reach above the 30%.The radius percentage difference (Dr) between the doped ions (Dy3+) and the possible substituted Ba2+ ions in KBaScSi3O9 host was calculated by using the following formula [25], Dr=100Rm (CN) - Rd (CN)Rm (CN)1In this expression, Dr stands for the radius percentage difference, Rs (1.38) and Rd (0.97) are corresponds to the ionic radii of host cation and doped ions and, CN refers to the coordination number respectively.D value was calculated to be about 29%, which is smaller than 30%.Hence, the Ba2+ ions would be willingly substituted by Dy3+ ions and thus formed the xDyKBS silicate phosphors.The morphology of the xDyKBS phosphors are investigated by field emission-SEM and the results were shown in Fig.2.The micrographs display that the phosphor material is well agglomer ated having irregular and non-uniform structures.EDS profile in Fig.2 confirmed the presence of elements like, Dysprosium (Dy), potassium (K), Barium (Ba), Scandium (Sc), Silicon (Si) and Oxygen (O) in 0.05DyKBS phosphor. 3.2.Optical studies 3.2.1.Absorption spectra and bonding parameter The study of optical absorption is a useful method for investigating the optically induced transitions.The UV–Vis-NIR absorption spectrum of one of the prepared phosphors (0.09DyKBS) recorded in the wavelength region 260–1700 nm was shown in Fig.3.

the prepared phosphors (0.09DyKBS) recorded in the wavelength region 260–1700 nm was shown in Fig.3.The spectrum exhibits six absorption bands centered around 451, 471, 748, 882, 1064 and 1265 nm, attributed to the transitions originating from the 6H15/2 ground state to the various excited states are 4I15/2, 0.3 em 0 ex 4F9/2, 0.3 em 0 ex 6F5/2, 0.3 em 0 ex 6F7/2, 0.3 em 0 ex 6F9/2, and 6F11/2+ 6H9/2 respectively [26].It is observed from Fig.3 that the band centered at 1265 nm corresponding to 6H15/26F11/2 transition was found to be higher in intensity compared to all other absorption peaks.The intensity of the absorption bands observed in NIR region is found to be stronger than those observed in the visible region.Also, some of the absorption peaks of Dy3+ ions in the visible region are not well resolved and some peaks in the ultraviolet region are vanishing due to the strong absorption of phosphor host.From the observed energy level positions, the nephelauxetic ratio (b) and bonding parameter (d) have been calculated to explore the binding nature of Dy3+- ligand bond in the prepared phosphors [27].The nephelauxetic ratio (b) can be defined as the ratio between the wave number (incm-1) of a particular RE-ion transition in the host matrix (vc) to that of the corresponding aqua-ion transition (a) and the same is given by the equation,=v cv a2From the mean values of b (termedas), the bonding parame ter (d) values can be calculated as follows,=(1-)1003The observed band positions (cm-1), band d values are pre- sented in Table 1.The bonding nature of metal–ligand bond may be ionic or covalent depending upon the positive or negative sign of d values.In the present work, d values of all the silicate phosphors possess the negative sign indicate the ionic nature of Dy3+.O bonds in xDyKBS phosphors. 3.2.2.Optical band gap and refractive index The investigation of absorption spectra is relatively useful in calculating the band gap of silicate phosphors.

gation of absorption spectra is relatively useful in calculating the band gap of silicate phosphors.In the present work, there is no confirmation for sharp absorption edges in absorption profiles that demonstrates the crystalline nature.According to Mott and Davis theory [28], the relation between absorption coefficient and band gap can be expressed as, h=B (h-Eopt) n4 where, n is the index number that can have values as 1⁄2 and 2 are depends upon direct and indirect allowed transitions [29].The band gap of prepared phosphors was determined by extrapo lating the linear region of the curve in Tauc’s plot ((ahm)n vs.hm) at (ahv) n=0 as shown in Fig.4.The calculated Eopt values are found to be 3.939, 3.933, 3.904, 3.817 and 3.716 eV corresponds to xDyKBS ( x=0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 & 0.09 ) phosphors, respectively.It is noticed that band gap values decreases with the increase in Dy3+-ion content in prepared silicate phosphors.The decrement in the bandgap values is mainly attributed to the presence of non bridging oxygen’s (NBO’s) which created due to the replacement of metal cations by Dy3+ ions in the investigated phosphors.The NBO’s are generally linked with the valence band maximum (VBM) thus the increasing NBO’s then shifts VBM towards the conduction band which in turn leads to have a drop in the bandgap values.The refractive index (n) of prepared Dy3+ activated phosphors were calculated using the relation given by [30,31], (n2-1n2+2)=1-Eg205 were n symbolize the refractive index and Eg signify the band gab.Refractive index values are found to be 2.182, 2.183, 2.189, 2.206 and 2.227 corresponds to 0.01DyKBS, 0.03DyKBS, 0.05DyKBS, 0.07DyKBS and 0.09DyKBS silicate phosphors, respectively. 3.2.3.Oscillator strengths and Judd–Ofelt intensity parameters The experimental oscillator strengths (fexp) can be obtained by measuring the integrated areas of observed absorption bands and it is expressed as, fexp=2.303 m c2N Ae2 (v) dv=4.31810-9 (v) d v6 where ‘m’ and e.

and it is expressed as, fexp=2.303 m c2N Ae2 (v) dv=4.31810-9 (v) d v6 where ‘m’ and e.are the mass and charge of the electron, (v) is the molar extinction coefficient of a band at m (cm1), c represents the light velocity and N is Avogadro’s number.The J–O theory has been used to evaluate the theoretical oscillator strengths (fcal).The fcal values of the absorption transitions from ground state (WJ) to the excited state (W0J0) depends on three J–O intensity parameters ( 2, 4 and 6 ) were calculated using the following equation [32], fcal=82 mc v3 h (2J+1) (n2+2) 29 n=2, 4, 6 (NJ | | U | | NJ ) 27In this equation, n stands for refractive index and h is the plank’s constant.J represents total angular momentum and (U) 2 symbolizes the doubly reduced squared matrix of unit ten- sor operators with rank 2, 4 and 6.These values were taken from the literature reported by Carnall et al [26] because they are nearly independent of host matrix.The parameters were determined Fig.2.SEM image of the silicate phosphors.by taking least square fitting between fexp and fcal values.Table 2 shows the f, f and root mean square (rms) values of present Dy3+ activated silicate phosphors.It is observed that the fexp and fcal values of 6H15/26F11/2+ 6H9/2 transition is found to be higher when compared to all other transitions..The lower root mean square values indicate better quality fit between fexp and fcal values and also the validity of J-O theory [33].

thermometers has become a research interest.Direct contact with the object is required for the conventional strategy of measuring temperatures.Moreover, they cannot be used for microscopic samples [1,2].Additionally, it has serious limitations such as slow response rate, low resolution, interference with the electromagnetic field, and inability to measure in harsh environments like high spatial resolution [7e9].Optical temperature sensing is based on the temperature-dependent luminescence properties of the phosphors, and such phosphors are termed thermographic phosphors.Generally, temperature-dependent photoluminescence parameters such as FIR-fluorescence intensity ratio, emission color, spectral shift, and luminescence decay time are selected [10e13].The FIR method offers superior qualities like self-referencing and negligible drift through which better sensitivity and accuracy can be achieved [14,15].

tised Gd2Ge2O7Dy3+ for thermometry applications in which sensitivity of 2029.5 / T2 is achieved [25].On the other hand, Li et al.utilized timeresolved fluorescence in calcium tungstate host for thermometric studies [26].As an essential member of the phosphor family, garnets have been extensively studied for lighting and temperature sensing applications due to their unique structural framework, strongly interlinked luminescence properties [27e31].Based on the general stoichiometry of the typical garnet structure- A3 [ B2 ] (C3) O12, dodecahedral site, octahedral and tetrahedral sites are occupied by A, B, and C cations with D2, C3i, and S4 symmetries, respectively.Garnet crystallizes in space group Ia3d ( 230, 0 h l0 ) and is stable due to the strong polyhedral network, and the possibility ofcationic substitution increases the tunability ofproperties.Apart from this, tellurate-based phosphor materials are widely reported as a host material for the luminescence centers owing to their advantages, such as low phonon energy, which inhibits non-radiative transitions [32e40].Also, Li3Y3Te2O12 is reported for enhanced luminescence properties [39].Considering the full advantage of the host and the peculiarities of Dy3+, tellurate garnet type Li3Y3Te2O12 are selected as matrix and Dy3 as the activator.Consequently, we demonstrated the phosphor Li3Y3Te2O12Dy3+ with garnet structure in the field of optical thermometry for the first time.The temperature-dependent luminescence properties are investigated in detail by analysing temperature-dependent photoluminescence spectra and determining the temperature sensitivity. 2.Experimental 2.1.Synthesis methods Polycrystalline samples of phosphors, Li3Y3Te2O12xDy3+( x=0 – 15 % ) were synthesised via solidestate reaction route.The selected precursors - Li2CO3 ( 99.0 %, Sigma Aldrich) 203, (99.999%, Alfa Aesar), TeO ( 99%, Sigma Aldrich), Dy2O3 (99.999%, Alfa Aesar), were weighed in a stoichiometric ratio; their riveting and unique optical and electronic properties.

hold an outstanding position because of their riveting and unique optical and electronic properties.The convoluted spectroscopic characteristics are enabled owing to the parity forbidden intra-configurational 4f–4f transitions of lanthanides, and the 4f orbitals are quite well protected by filled 5 s2 and 5 p6 orbitals.13 In contrast to their conventional counterparts as organic fluorophores, the lanthanide-activated phosphors offer remarkable photoluminescent properties that include sharp and narrow emission spectra with full-width half maxima of around B10 nm, long luminescence lifetimes (intherangeofafewmilliseconds), least sensitive to chemical environment, emissive transitions in UV, visible and nearinfrared spectral window, large Stokes and anti-Stokes shift (morethanornearto200nm) etc.11,12 These also exhibit better photostability, low intermittency and minimized background and auto-fluorescence leading to high signal-to-noise ratio, higher monochromatic (color) purity leading to improved color performance and optical tunability.12,14,15 In spite of the beneficial luminescence properties, lanthanide ions often suffer from the limitation of relatively low molar absorption coefficient;=1-10M - 1 cm - 1.16Hence, to adequately make use of the proficient luminescence properties of lanthanide ions, the choice of an appropriate host matrix is of utmost importance.

nce properties of lanthanide ions, the choice of an appropriate host matrix is of utmost importance.Among the studied rare-earth compound host materials such as oxides, hydroxides, vanadates, phosphates, sulphates etc., the sodium rare-earth fluorides (NaREF), particularly NaYF provide some distinct advantages.17,18 NaYF4 exhibits low phonon energy (350cm-1), high refractive index and wide band gap (8eV), and thus is regarded as the most competent host material for both down-conversion as well as up-conversion phosphor systems.19,20 Most commonly, the NaYF4 crystal structure exhibits two phases, cubic (zNaYF4) and hexagonal phases (NaYF4), the formation of which usually depends upon the synthesis condition and methods.18 Additionally, by modulating the dopants and dopant combinations in the host system, a broad spectrum of lanthanide-doped phosphors possessing multicolor emission or tunable emission can be obtained.Thus, the dopants and their concentration also play a vital role in developing an efficient phosphor system.Wide band gap materials (inorganic, semiconductor, or insulators) phosphors are expected to show valuable thermoluminescence properties.Thermoluminescence dosimetric studies are highly useful for understanding the electronic trapped states and processes of energy transfer mechanisms involved in the emission of light upon heating an already irradiated crystalline lattice.21 The electron trapping process relies on numerous factors such as the inherent properties of the crystalline material, type and dose of ionizing radiation, and exposure time intervals.The lattice defects, vacancies, etc.act as trapping centers/trapping sites for the trapping of charges, electrons and holes.These trapping sites are generated within the energy bandgap of TL phosphor because of the existence of impurity, dislocations and defects.

in the energy bandgap of TL phosphor because of the existence of impurity, dislocations and defects.Thus, when the phosphor material, pre-irradiated by ionizing radiation, is stimulated by heat, the ejection of trapped electrons from the trap centers takes place and then it recombines radiatively and non-radiatively leading to the generation of photons (lightemission) and phonons, respectively.22 Henceforth, thermoluminescence (TL) is a defectassociated process induced by radiation, wherein, the light emission occurs via stimulation by heat to the phosphor material upon energy absorption from ionizing radiation.A plot of emission light intensity as a function of the heating temperature is represented as a thermoluminescence glow peak.Thermolumi nescence is a potent technique utilized for dose assessment as the amount of emitted light is proportional to the absorbed radiation dose.23 The obtained TL glow curve structures, such as the shape, position, and intensity of the glow curve, provide valuable information about the kinetic parameters, which helps in understanding the luminescence mechanism.The important kinetic parameters include the activation energy, also called trap depth or the eficacy of a trap, order of kinetics and frequency factor that can be estimated by the analysis of the thermoluminescence glow peak.

of the advantages of sapphire is its high transparency.It is hard to reach similar transparency in polycrystalline alumina (PCA) due to its birefringence, resulting in a strong dependence of light transmission on grain size [2].High values of real in-line transmission are obtained only in materials with very fine-grained pore-free microstructures, possibly with mean grain size (MGS) well below 500 nm.On the other hand, PCA offers significant benefits over single crystals, such as the possibility of pre paring more complex shapes [3], better mechanical properties [4–6], etc.In addition, if transparent ceramic with added functionalities is desired, the introduction of various doping agents is indispensable.The solubility of such dopants in the alumina matrix is usually rather low [7].However, the high grain boundary (GB) area of submicron PCA represents a disordered structure that admits dopant ions in a much higher concentration than their solubility in Al2O3 crystals.Functional properties such as photoluminescence can be thus achieved at a relatively low overall concentration of dopants [6,8].In terms of transparency, the effect of dopants depends strongly on their concentration.Up to a certain level, especially in the case of rareearth elements, which hinder the growth of alumina grains, its effect is positive.At higher concentrations, the real in-line transmittance (RIT) decreases significantly, presumably because of exceeding the solubility limit at GBs and creating inclusions of secondary phases [9,10].The combination of several dopants can lead to higher RIT values due to more effective grain growth inhibition compared to a single doping strategy [7].

trix, Dy with its limited solubility [7,20] in alumina occupied the grain boundaries preferentially.The kinetics of dissolution of precursors of dopants Advanced thermodynamic modelling can effectively treat the diffusion of dilute dopants in ultra-fine-grained ceramics and significantly contribute to optimisation of their processing ensuring homogeneous distribution of dopants and their equilibration at GBs.Such models combine classical diffusion theory with the trapping concept, which assumes that there are several sorts of traps with different energy depths in the system, where the species can be captured.In a system where dopant segregation at GBs occurs, the GBs can be considered as such traps of this kind with a rather wide spectrum of trapping energies.In the case of co-doping, the individual species compete for traps, and significant nonlinear effects may occur.(nanograinsofdopantoxideshomogeneouslydispersedintheinitialaluminapowder) as well as homogenisation of the dopants and their eventual segregation at GBs are controlled by diffusion.In this case, however, only Fick laws in their classical mathematical form cannot be applied, as they do not account for the trapping of the dopants and their mutual interactions.It should be noted that the linear relation between the fluxes and driving forces, as it is assumed by the first Fick Law, remains unchanged.However, in the case of trapping, the mass conservation law must be significantly modified, which leads to a significant difference in the mathematical formulation of the second Fick law.A combined diffusion and trapping theory was published first by McNabb and Foster in their pioneering work [41] in 1963.They treated diffusion in a system with a single diffusing species and a single sort of traps and introduced capture and release rates describing the interaction of atomic species with the trap.

KEYWORDS colour coordinates, gel combustion, LaAlO3: Dy3++, nanophosphors, photoluminescence 1 | INTRODUCTIONOver a few decades, investigations on luminescent materials have gathered great interest for the design of efficient phosphors with good luminescence efficacy and appropriate stability towards thermal and chemical conditions.Extensive applications are associated with these materials such as fluorescence lamps, solid-state lighting, displays, cathode ray tubes, white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), sensors, and biological labelling.[1–6] WLEDs are advantageous over conventional light sources due to their various characteristics such as longer lifetime, improved brightness, and low power consumption.[7,8] Phosphor materials proficiently emit light, i.e.show luminescence upon excitation of either particles or electromagnetic radiation.The confined structure and composition of the host material affect the photoluminescence (PL) properties of the rare-earth-doped compounds.[9] The current research in this field has been focused on the luminescence of lanthanides (Ln) in various hosts based on molybdate, tungstates, borates, phosphates, silicates, and aluminates.[10,11] Among these, Ln-activated aluminates are superior phosphors due to their easy synthesis, high luminescence efficacy, feasible structural properties, and brilliant thermal as well as chemical strength.

scence efficacy, feasible structural properties, and brilliant thermal as well as chemical strength.The high colour purity of the rare-earth-doped compounds is due to their sharp 4f intrashell transitions.[12,13] Due to their variety in structure and composition, ABO3 perovskite-type compounds (possessinghighchemicalandphysicalstabilities) are excellent host materials for WLEDs.Their wide band gap and considerably low photon energy present the potential applications of LaAlO3 (LAO) as host materials for phosphors, substrates for superconductors, colossal magnetoresistive materials, and magnetic thin films.[14,15] LaAlO3: Dy3+ nanophosphors have attracted much attention because of their white light emission.The Dy3+ ion evinces two intense emission bands in the yellow ( 4F9/26H13/2, 574 nm) and blue ( 4F9/26H15/2, 482 nm) regions of the visible spectra.[16,17] The combination of these two colour, i.e.yellow and blue colours, results in the emission of bright white light that is utilized in various applications such as LEDs, paints, optoelectronic devices, and modern displays.[18,19] Numerous synthetic techniques used for the preparation of the phosphors are coprecipitation, solid-state methods, aerosol furnace methods, spray-pyrolysis processes, precursor decomposition approaches, and sol–gel and gel-combustion methods, etc.120 –24] Among these, the gel-combustion method has many advantages such as low synthesis temperature, good control of stoichiometry, uniform morphology, uniform mixing of the starting materials at the molecular level, and adequate particle size.[25,26] This paper deals with the synthesis and characterization of a single-phase perovskite LaAlO3: Dy3+ phosphor.To the best of our knowledge, no significant report is available on the synthesis of the selected phosphor using a combustion technique.

nificant report is available on the synthesis of the selected phosphor using a combustion technique.Detailed luminescence and structural features of the materials were examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR), energydispersive X-ray (EDX), and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy to support their applications in WLEDS. 2 | EXPERIMENTAL2.1 | Synthesis Dy3+- doped LaAlO3 nanomaterials were synthesized using a gelcombustion process and C6H12N4 [hexamethylenetetramine (HMT)] as a fuel.Nitrates of the metal were used as raw chemicals for the synthesis of nanophosphors due to their lower disintegration temperature.Here, lanthanum nitrate hexahydrate, dysprosium nitrate hexahydrate, aluminium nitrate nonahydrate, and HMT are cast off as raw materials and H2O behaves as a solvent.The solution combustion process is superior because of its uniform dissolution of ingredients in the solvent and its low decomposition temperature.[27] Metal nitrates when dissolved in deionized water provided active oxygen that behaves as an oxidizing agent.Additionally, HMT acts as a reducer in the chemical reaction.A series of phosphors La1-AlO3: x Dy3+( x=0.01-0.07 ) was synthesized by varying the composition of the dysprosium ions in a lattice.In silica crucibles, considerable amounts of all metal nitrates have been involved in the preparation of a uniform aqueous solution that underwent further heating action (at80C).The vaporization of free water molecules occurred on heating the aqueous solution that resulted in a viscous material.[28] A specific quantity of HMT fuel along with some distilled water was added and heated on a hot plate with a magnetic stirrer until the solution turned into a gel.The added HMT was utilized to frame a metal compound by dissolving it consistently in the reactive solution.For combustion, the reaction solution was positioned in furnace kept at 600C for 12 min.

Short communication New Dy3+-activated KCa2Nb3O10 yellow-emitting phosphors for w-LEDs application: Preparation and optical properties Bin Deng a,b,d,1,*, Jianhong Jiang b,d,1, Wensheng Chen a, Anlin Zhang b,d, Zhikai Liang b,d Feng Lib,d, Fanhua Zeng b,d, Gongguo Zhang c, a Hunan Nonferrous Chenzhou Fluoride Chemical Co., Ltd., Chenzhou, Hunan 423000, P.R.China b School of Chemistry and Environmental Science, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou, Hunan, 423043, P.R.China c Department of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Jining University, Qufu, Shandong 273155, P.R.China d Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Xiangnan Rare-Precious Metals Compounds Research and Application, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou, Hunan 423043, P.R.China ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Phosphor Niobate KCaNbO:Dy3+ Thermal stability w-LEDsABSTRACTA series of Dy3+ doped KCa2Nb3O10 niobate phosphors that generated yellow emission was prepared using the molten-salt method.The crystal structure, X-ray diffraction (XRD), optimal concentration, photoluminescence excitation/emission (PLE/PL), and luminescent stability of the prepared phosphors were exhaustively studied.The KCa2Nb3O10 lattice has a perovskite-like structure, which possesses the Cmcm (No.63) space group.The KCa2Nb3O10: Dy3+ phosphors can be efficiently excited by n-ultraviolet (n-UV) excitation of 388 nm.Besides, KCa2Nb3O10: Dy3+ phosphors can emit three dominant peaks centered at 486, 577, and 662 nm, which are ascribed to the 6H J / 2 ( J=15/2, 13/2,., and 11/2) transitions, respectively.The optimum doping concentrations of Dy3+ ions in the KCaNbO host are determined to be 0.02 mol.

ely.The optimum doping concentrations of Dy3+ ions in the KCaNbO host are determined to be 0.02 mol.The thermal-quenching temperature ( T0.5 ) for the KCa2Nb3O10; 0.20Dy3+ sample is estimated to be above 500K, and the calculated activation energy (Ea) is 0.29 eV.Furthermore, the Commission International de IEclairage (CIE) color coordinates of prepared KCa2Nb3O10; Dy3+ phosphors change slightly.K Ca2Nb3O10; Dy3+ phosphors possess good color purity, color stability, and low correlated color temperature (CCT).All results indicate that the KCa2Nb3O10; Dy3+ phosphors are suitable for white light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs) applications. 1.Introduction The white light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs), particularly the phosphorconverted w-LEDs possess a longer working lifetime, better ecofriendliness, higher energy efficiency, and faster response time, compared with the traditional solid-state lighting sources (incandescent light, halogen tungsten lamp, fluorescent lamp, and so on) [1–6].Therefore, w-LEDs are rapidly emerging as the next-generation solidstate lighting.The main strategy to achieve white light emission is to combine a blue InGaN chip and yellow phosphor Y3Al5O12: Ce3+(YAG: Ce3+).Due to the lack of red-light components, the color rendering index (Ra) is too low and the CCT is too high [7–9].To overcome these problems, a new method is proposed to generate white light emission by combining the blue LED chip with multicolor phosphors (blue, green, and red) phosphors [10–14].As blue and green phosphors have been commercialized, thus, designing the red phosphors for the high-quality w-LEDs field is extremely important.Dysprosium trivalent (Dy3+) ions with 4 f9 electronic configuration are regarded as excellent dopant candidates, which produce efficient yellow emission in many different matrixes under UV excitation [15,16].Dy3+ ions possess two primary emissions in the blue and yellow regions ascribing to 4F9/26H13/2 and 4F9/26H15/2 transitions, respectively.

ons in the blue and yellow regions ascribing to 4F9/26H13/2 and 4F9/26H15/2 transitions, respectively.The magnetic dipole transition o4F9/26H15/2 is hardly affected by the local environment of the Dy3+ activated host.However, the electric dipole transition of 4F9/26H13/2 is easily affected by the local environment [8,17].A series of Dy3+-activated phosphors have been reported in recent years, such as Ca2Al2SiO7: Dy3+, S3MgSi2O8: Dy3+, and Ba3Bi2 (PO4) 4: Dy3+ phosphors [18–20].The matrix is a vital factor for the properties of prepared phosphors.Niobate is an excellent host matrix for the doping of rare-earth ions and possesses excellent luminescent properties, great chemical stability, and good thermal stability.Therefore, niobate-structured phosphors like Y3NbO7: Ln3+( Ln=Pr,., Sm), Ca2GdNbO6: Eu3+, LaNbO4: Er3+/ Yb3+, and Sr3NaNbO6: Mn4+ have been proposed by researches [ 21-24 ].In2000, Bizeto et al.[25] researched the luminescence characteristic of layered perovskite KCa2Nb3O10 niobate phosphors doped with Eu3+ and L3+.In2022, Che et al.[26] explored the luminescent properties of KCa2Nb3O10: Sm3+ phosphors.They discovered that s m3+ doped KCa2Nb3O10 samples could match well with the NUV chips and emit orange-red emissions for w-LEDs application.However, to our knowl edge, Dy3+-doped KCa2Nb3O10 phosphors have not been reported yet.Herein, we had firstly investigated the luminescence properties of a series of KCa2Nb3O10: x Dy3+( x=0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.25,., and 0.30 mol) samples.The crystal structure, the phase purity, and lumi nescent behaviors of the pure KCa2Nb3O10; Dy3+ phosphors were also studied in detail.Moreover, The CIE color coordinates, color purity, and CCT were analyzed. 2.Experimental 2.1.Sample and the synthesis The yellow-emitting KCa2Nb3O10: x Dy3+( x=0.01-0.30 mol ) samples were firstly synthesized via molten-salt method.The starting materials were as follows: K2CO3 ( 99.0 % ) CaCO3 ( A.R.), Nb2O5 ( 99.5 % ), and Dy2O3 ( 99.9 % ).

and regulating the production of nano- and microcrystalline materials of various sizes and shapes has become increasingly pop ular in recent years.It is commonly known that the size, form, and morphology of a material have a strong and substantial association with its quality.

size, form, and morphology of a material have a strong and substantial association with its quality.Thus, manipulating these parameters is critical for scientific and industrial utilization of materials.Several distinc approaches have been used to synthesize nano- and micro crystalline materials including solid-state methods [6] and we chemical methods, such as sol–gel [7], hydrothermal [8], coprecipitation [9], microwave [10], and ultrasonication [11].Solidstate synthesis is the most frequently used and preferable method because of its low cost, potential for large-scale manufacturing, and eco-friendly preparation conditions.Rare earth tungstate oxide-based nanocrystalline phosphor materials have gained pop ularity in innovation owing to their distinct properties, such as small particle size, good thermal as well as optical stability, chem ical durability, strong covalence, weak polarizability, low toxicity, and low moisture sensitivity compared to their fluoride, sulfide, and nitride-based counterparts [12].In the recent past, lanthanum oxide-based nanocrystalline phosphors have been considered a leading class of research materials due to their remarkably high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), narrow and intense emission and/or absorption bands.They are used for numerous practical applications in various fields such as solid-state lighting, photovoltaic and flat-display devices, sensors, bioimaging, anticounterfeitingtelecommunication.scintillators and lightemitting diodes (LEDs) owing to their self-sensitization and strong UV absorption [13].Recently, there has been a surge in interest in producing white light in a cost-effective and eco-friendly manner with high efficiency and a long lifetime.Although white light can be produced using various techniques, such as incorporating a3Al5O12: Ce3+ phosphor into blue color-emitting InGaNLEDs, and combining a UVLED with blue, green, and red emitting components.
