energy separation (7000cm-1) between the 4F9/2 excited level and the next low lying energy level of Dy3+.This in turn will provide a markedly good quantum efficiency of the 4F9/2 level for most of the Dy3+ activated phosphors [15].Another significant step is the selection of an appropriate host to disperse these Dy3+ ions, since the crystal structure, morphology etc are also having a great significance on the performance of a luminescent material [16].The environmental impact of the proposed materials is also a factor to be taken care of.For instance, if we consider the case of commercially available WLEDs made of YAG: Ce3+ phosphor along with Y2O2SEu3+ phosphor, the luminescence efficiency is excellent, but are having some negative impact on the environment as well as on human health due to the release of CS2 and HS during the synthesis process of the Y2O2SEu3+[ 17 ].In this perspective, phosphate which is an oxysalt host material has gained immense research interest as luminescent material for its non-toxic nature, moderate preparation conditions, low production cost, environment friendliness, low annealing temperature, strong absorption in the NUV and UV region, high luminous intensity, exemplary charge stabilization, high thermal, chemical and hydrolytic stability [18–20].In addition to that, phosphate hosts with alkali or alkaline earth elements are prominent compounds as they could provide a suitable ligand field environment for the rare earth ions to overcome the limitation of low intensity of 4f- 4f transitions in free lanthanides.Moreover, the PO4 tetrahedron with which the phosphates are made of being flexible, it is possible to dwell in various coordination environments by modulating the P-O bond lengths [21].In this regard materials scientist are trying for novel phosphate-based matrices that could meet the various criteria mentioned above.

are trying for novel phosphate-based matrices that could meet the various criteria mentioned above.In this work a batch of newly designed Dy3+ doped Na6CaP2O9 phosphors were synthesized by a general solid state phase method and characterized through several means to realize its applications in various optoelectronic devices.It is very interesting to note that when compared to the previously reported Dy3+ doped plant habitat conscious phosphors [8,9], the sintering temperature required for Dy3+ doped Na6CaP2O9 is appreciably low and the thermal stability is also promising. 2.Materials and methods The powder samples of pure and Dy3+ doped Na6CaP2O9 phosphors were synthesized by conventional high temperature solid state reaction method.The starting materials used are Na2CO3 (AR), CaCO3 (AR) NH4H2PO4 (AR) and Dy2O3 (AR).The stoichiometric proportions of these materials are weighed and ground in an agate mortar to get fine mixtures.Then the homogenous mixture is transferred to an alumina crucible and sintered at 1000 ◦C for 4 h in a muffle furnace.The obtained product was then furnace cooled to room temperature and then ground again to fine powders for further characterizations.XRD analysis of the phosphors were performed using Rigaku D/max-IIB diffractometer with CuK radiation (=1.5418 ) at 40 kV and 26 mA.The TEM and EDS analyses were performed using JEOLJEM2100.The diffused reflectance spectra were recorded using Varian Carry 5000UV–Vis–NIR spectrophotometer with an integrating sphere arrangement.The photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra were characterized by a spectro fluorophotometer (Horiba fluorolog-3 with an integrating sphere attachment).The temperature dependent photoluminescence spectra were recorded using Hitachi 650–40 fluorescence spectrophotometer, along with the help of a home-made mini-heater.Decay analyses were carried out by Perkin Elmer LS50 spectrometer. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.XRD analysis The phase purity of the prepared samples was confirmed using the Xray diffraction analysis.

analysis The phase purity of the prepared samples was confirmed using the Xray diffraction analysis.All the diffraction peaks of the Na6Ca (1-X) P2O9: XDy3+( X=0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10 ) phosphors were well indexed to the hexagonal structured Na6CaP2O9 (PDF21–1108) as illustrated in Fig.1.Dy3+( rd=102.7.p.m., CN=8 ) ions are easily incorporated into the Ca2+( rs=112 p.m., CN=8 ) sites for their ionic radii being comparable.To recognize the feasibility of getting a solid solution compound, the percentage difference in ionic radii was determined and was found to be Dr=8.30 %, which is much less than the maximum allowed value of 30% for Dr [ 22, 23 ] The lattice constants of virgin Na6CaP2O9 lattice along with Dy3+ doped lattices are tabulated in Table 1.It is interesting to note that the value of the lattice constants doesn’t show a large deviation from that of the virgin lattice on doping with Dy3+ ions.When Dy3+ ions replace Ca2+ ions, there will be shrinkage of lattice and a small reduction in the lattice parameters, especially volume, as the radius of Dy3+ being smaller than Ca2+ sites, thus making some distortions in the lattice [when compared to the virgin lattice ( X=0.00 ) ].Still, it is clear from Table.1 that the lattice volumes of all the doped samples are smaller than that of the virgin sample indicating a contraction of the host lattice on incorporation of the comparatively smaller Dy3+ ions into the larger Ca2+ sites.The lattice parameters and crystallite size of the r Na6Ca (1-X) P2O9; XDy3+ phosphor.

Fig.1.XRD patterns of Na6Ca (1-X) P2O9: XDy3+ phosphor. 3.3.Diffused reflectance spectra and Tauc plot Diffused reflectance spectra of the powdered samples for various concentrations of Dy3+ in the UV–Visible range are given in Fig.4(a).The spectra consist of several bands corresponding to the f-f transitions of Dy3+ ions.The spectra of the undoped host material do not show any distinct peaks.The region of spectrum from 300 nm to 800 nm consists of several peaks corresponding to f-f transitions of Dysprosium from the 6H5/2 ground state to various excited states 4M17/2 (324nm), 6P7/2 (352nm), 6P5/2 (364nm), 4I13/2 (386nm), 4G11/2 (425nm), 4I15/2 (454nm) and 6F3/2 (744nm) [27].The optical band gap energies of the samples were determined by the method put forth by Kubelka and Munk.The band gap energy was determined using the expression, [ F (R) h ] 2=A (h-Eg)1 where hν is the energy of incident photon, A is a proportionality constant, Eg is the band gap energy and F (R) is the Kubelka – Munk function [28].On extrapolating the line for [ F (R) h ] 2=0, the values of Eg were estimated for various concentrations of Dy3+ and found to vary in the range 4.69–5.00 eV as illustrated in Fig.4 (b).Initially there observed to have a slight increase in band gap from 4.69 eV to 5.00 eV with the increase in Dy3+ concentration (X=0.02–0.04) due to Burstein-Moss effect which arises when the carrier concentration of electrons go beyond the density of states in the conduction band.

when the carrier concentration of electrons go beyond the density of states in the conduction band.Since all the levels below Fermi level are occupied, the Fermi level will then lie in the conduction band.Moreover, it is interesting to note that in nanocrystalline materials, due to its large surface to volume ratios, band bending may occur at grain boundaries [29,30].After a concentration of X=0.04 the band gap renormalization occurs resulting in the narrowing of the intrinsic band gap for the samples with concentrations X=0.06 ( Eg=4.91 e V ), X=0.08 (4.84eV), X=0.10 (4.78eV), where a lowering of conduction band minimum occurs due to the drastic modifications of various levels in conduction band [22]. 3.4.Excitation and emission spectra To have a better understanding regarding the excitation energy to be given to get an efficient emission from the prepared phosphor, the excitation spectrum is to be recorded by monitoring the emission wavelength at 574 nm as shown in Fig.5.The excitation spectra consists of four characteristic excitation peaks of Dy3+ ions at 325 nm (6H15/26P3/2), 350 nm (6H15/26P7/2), 364 nm (6H15/26P5/2) and 388 nm (6H15/24K17/2) [31].It is evident from the spectrum that the excitation transition, 6H15/26P7/2 at 350 nm is having the highest intensity and chosen as the excitation wavelength.Moreover, since most of the intense bands are observed in the NUV regions of the spectrum, the present phosphor can assume to be excellent in developing white LEDs using commercially available NUV chips (340–410 nm) [32].Just as observed in Fig.6, the emission spectra consist of two prominent bands at 480 nm (blue) and 574 nm (yellow) corresponding to the transitions 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 respectively.The 4F9/26H15/2 transition representing the blue emission is attributed to magneting dipole transition and hardly depends on the surroundings.

e blue emission is attributed to magneting dipole transition and hardly depends on the surroundings.But, for the forced electric dipole transition 4F9/26H13/2, the transition being a hypersensitive transition is subjected to the chemical environment surrounding the Dy3+ ions in the host matrix and is allowed when Dy3+ ions occupy local sites with inversion symmetry.When Dy3+ ions occupy low symmetry sites, yellow emission will dominate the blue and if they occupy sites with inversion symmetry (highsymmetrysites) blue emission will be stronger [33–36].As is observed from Fig.6, yellow emission at 574 nm is prominent compared to blue emission at 480 nm indicating the Dy3+ ions to be occupying low symmetry sites in the present host matrix.It is clear that Dy3+ ions exhibit relatively narrow emission and can provide white or near white Fig.2.(a) TEM image and (b) SAED pattern of Na6Ca0.96P2O9; 0.04 Dy3+ Fig.3.EDS of Na6Ca0.96P2O9: 0.04 Dy3+(a) (b) Fig.4.(a) Diffused reflectance spectra and inset shows magnification from 300 to 750 of representative sample, (b) Tauc plots of Na6Ca (1-X) P2O9: XDy3+ phosphor.emission when they are incorporated in a suitable host to get an emission with proper Y / B ratio.

r.emission when they are incorporated in a suitable host to get an emission with proper Y / B ratio.Here, the Y/B ratio is observed to be very close to unity and hence the material can be considered as aproming candidate for white light emitting devices [37].The corresponding Y/B ratio values are tabulated in Table.2.Just as mentioned in the intro duction part the lack of any red-near IR emission makes this phosphor a potential candidate in fabricating PHC-WLEDs.Eventhough a red component in lighting units are of great significance to improve the color rendering of the device, it is not compatible for PHC-WLEDs as they are meant to inhibit the night time photosynthesis [9].Moreover, it is evident from the previous literatures that the blue and yellow emissions of Dy3+ ions positioned at 480 nm and 574 nm does not match with the absorption range of any of the major plant pigments Chlorophyll A or Chlorophyll B.The red-near IR emissions derived from the 4F9/26H11/2 and 4F9/26H9/2 transitions being very feeble in the prepared phosphor, the integrated intensity of red illuminance may considered to be very weak.This will further help in inhibiting photosynthesis as this would reduce the absorption of red or NIR light by phytochromes [9,38].Thus the development of PHC-WLEDs using the Na6Ca (1-X) P2O9: XDy3+ phosphor may be a promising approach to mitigate the effect of lighting on night time photosynthesis. Tunable luminescence and energy transfer mechanism of Ca2Sb2O7: Dy3+ host sensitized single phase cool white light emitting phosphor Anns George a,b, Adon Jose a, T.Krishnapriya a, Tony Francis c, Cyriac Joseph a, P.R.Biju a,* a School of Pure & Applied Physics, Mahatma Gandhi University, Kottayam, Kerala, 686560, India b Assumption College Autonomous, Changanacherry, Kottayam, Kerala, 686103, India c St.Mary’s College, Manarcaud, Kottayam, Kerala, 686019, India ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Calcium antimonate Energy transfer Concentration quenching White light emission ABSTRACTTunable white light-emitting Ca (2-x) Sb2O7: x Dy3+ phosphors were synthesized via high temperature solid-state reaction method.The crystal structure, morphology, luminescence characteristics, and energy transfer mechanism of the phosphors were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM), UV–Visible spectroscopy, photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, and Fluorescence lifetime analysis.The XRD, EDS, and TEM analysis confirmed the phase purity and orthorhombic weberite structure of the samples with an average particle size in the range of 0.2 to 0.3 μm.Under ultraviolet (UV) excitation of 330/351 nm, the prepared phosphors exhibit characteristic emission bands of Dy3+ ions along with the blue emission band of the host.

content: ors exhibit characteristic emission bands of Dy3+ ions along with the blue emission band of the host.The broad band peaking at 440 nm corresponds to Sb5+02-transition of host and the peaks at 477, 575, and 670 nm originates from 4F9/26H15/2, 4F9/26H13/2 and 4F9/26H11/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions respectively.There exists efficient energy transfer from Ca2Sb2O7 host to Dy3+ ions and the energy transfer efficiency increases with an increase in Dy3+ ion concentration.Using Dexter’s theory, the mechanism of energy transfer was found to be dipole-quadrupole interaction and the energy transfer process is explained in detail.The decay lifetime of Dy3+ ions was estimated to be in the microsecond range.The critical distance for concentration quenching is determined to be 13.807 Å and the dominant mechanism is dipole-dipole interaction.The calculated Commission International de L’Eclairng (CIE) coordinates and correlated color temperature (CCT) values imply that the emission color can be tuned from blue (0.144, 0.097) to near-white (0.296, 0.292) in the cool CCT region.The results suggest that Dy3+ doped CaSbO phosphor is a potential candidate for solid-state lighting and display fields 1.Introduction The development of white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs) based on solid-state lighting technology (SSL) is emerging as an interesting field of research and a highly sustainable alternative to conventional lighting technologies [1,2].Phosphor-converted WLEDs (pc-WLEDs) have gained a significant amount of attention in this context with eco-friendly and energy-saving methods in lighting technology [3–5].Phosphors have significant chemical, electronic and optical properties which makes them suitable for application in pc-WLEDs, display devices, lighting gadgets, solid-state lasers, medical devices, ionization radiation, and so on [6,7].

vices, lighting gadgets, solid-state lasers, medical devices, ionization radiation, and so on [6,7].Rare-earth ions are widely used as activators for these phosphors due to their characteristic 4f-4f and 5d-4f transitions, which produce abundant emission colors in the visible region when doped into a suitable host matrix [8,9].Even though a large number of phosphor-converted white lightemitting diodes are available, they have so many shortcomings that limit their extensive applications [10,11].The commercial WLEDs use YAG:Ce3þ yellow emitting phosphor in combination with InGaN blue LED chip.However, due to the lack of red components, these LEDs have serious drawbacks like high correlated color temperature and low color rendering index.An alternative approach is to use ultraviolet (UV) or near-UV (NUV) LED chips in combination with tricolor phosphors.But due to the re-absorption of emitted radiations by adjacent phosphors and different degradation rates of individual phosphors, these WLEDs also possess serious shortcomings.These limitations can be reduced by using UV/NUV excited single-phase phosphors which can simultaneously emit different colors whose combination constitutes white light [12–14].Moreover, white light emitted from single-phase phosphors is expected to have high luminous efficiency, good color stability, improved color rendering index, and relatively low production cost [15,16].Currently, there are many reports on white light generation from a single-phase host lattice, but none of them has reached a commercial scale [3].Hence, it becomes inevitable and essential to explore novel multi-color emitting single-phase phosphors for UV/NUV light pumped w-LED’s.One of the most commonly used approaches in this regard is a host matrix doped with single activator ions.Trivalent dysprosium ion (Dy3+) is one of the most commonly used activators for white light generation.Also, phosphors doped with Dy3+ ions have a longer lifespan with better efficiency [17].

n.Also, phosphors doped with Dy3+ ions have a longer lifespan with better efficiency [17].Dysprosium ions are characterized with intense blue and yellow emissions, which corresponds to 4F9/26H15/2, and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions respectively, and a weak emission from 4F9/26H11/2 transition in the red region.The ratio of these two dominant emissions is strongly influenced by the crystal field surrounding the Dy3+ ions.Therefore, by adjusting the intensity of yellow and blue emission through crystal field engineering, white light emission can be obtained in Dy3+ activated phosphors [18–20].However, due to forbidden parity selection rules, the f-f transitions of Dy3+ ions have low oscillator strength 10-6 ).Also, the 4f-5d absorption bands of the Dy3+ ions are located in the vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) region below 200 nm and hence, it is very difficult to excite Dy3+ ions by UV light [21].Nevertheless, one can overcome these problems either by adding impurity ions as sensitizers or by host sensitization [22,23].In general host excitation is more efficient than rare-earth excitation since, f-f transitions of rare-earth ions are parity forbidden, whereas charge transfer (CT) transitions are allowed.Hence, host sensitization through energy transfer between excited host and activator ion is an effective route to improve the emission intensity of activator ions and the generation of white light [24].The luminescence properties of materials not only depend on the nature and type of activator ion but also on the composition of the host matrix.Hence it is important to find a suitable host matrix capable of transferring its excitation energy, to enhance luminescence efficiency and to have an efficient white light emission.As the luminescence of Dy3+ ion depends strongly on the local environment of the host lattice, it is necessary to search for appropriate host materials that give intense emission.

compositions.Although the luminescence characteristics of antimony-based compounds were reported since ancient times [25], there are only a few reports on antimonate phosphors.Ca SbO is a ternary content: 文章编号: 1000-7032(2022)05-0676-08 热稳定性优异的单一基质白光 Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6: Dy3+荧光粉发光性能 王一航1, 连雪珠1, 徐华伟2∗, 康晓娇1, 吕 伟1∗(1.东莞理工学院 电子工程与智能化学院, 广东 东莞 523808;2.工业和信息化部电子第五研究所, 广东 广州 510006) 摘要: 通过高温固相法合成了一系列单基质白光荧光材料 Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+,并对其结构特性、浓度猝灭机理 发光特性 温度特性 荧光寿命进行了测试与讨论 研究结果表明 该样品的发射峰主要位于nm 和 577 nm,且能在近紫外光/紫外光激发下产生单一白光。对比发现该样品在 Dy3+掺杂浓度为 7% 时荧光强度最强 且通过计算得出该样品的浓度猝灭机理是由于偶极 偶极相互作用 热稳定性分析结果表明该样品的热稳定性优异,在 150 °C下的荧光强度可达初始室温强度的 97% 。因此, Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+是一种热稳定性优异的潜在的单一基质发白光材料 关 键 词: 单基质; Dy3+; LED; 荧光粉 中图分类号: O482.31 文献标识码: ADOI: Single-phase White Light-emitting Phosphor Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6: Dy3+ with Excellent Thermal Stability WANGYi-hang 1, LIANXue-zhu 1, XUHua-wei 2∗, KANGXiao-jiao 1, LYUWei 1∗ (1.School of Electrical Engineering and Intelligentization, Dongguan University of Technology, Dongguan 523808, China; 2.The Fifth Research Institute of Ministry of Industry and Information Technology(MIIT), Guangzhou 510006, China) ∗Corresponding Authors, E-mail: xuhuawei 2018@ 163.com; lvweiluwei@ 163.com Abstract: In this paper, a series of single-phase white light-emitting Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+ phosphor were synthesized by high-temperature solid-phase method.Their structure characteristics, photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra, lifetime and temperature-dependent emission spectra have been discussed.The results show that the emission peaks of the sample are mainly located at 490 nm and 577 nm, and can produce uniform white light under the excitation of near-ultraviolet light / ultraviolet light.The concentration quenching mechanism has been investigated and demonstrated to be a dipole-dipole interaction.The thermal stability based on the temperature-dependent PL spectra of Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+ demonstrated that this phosphor showed superior thermal behavior.

content: ectra of Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+ demonstrated that this phosphor showed superior thermal behavior.Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 6Dy3+ is a potential single white light-emitting material with excellent thermal stability.Key words: single-phase; Dy3+; white light-emitting; phosphor 1 引 言 白光 LED 由于具有绿色环保、高效节能、寿命长等特点被广泛应用于照明显示中[1] 但目前的商用 都存在许多不足 比如商用白光LED 就是将黄色荧光粉 YAGCe3+与蓝光 LED芯片组合从而实现白光,但这种黄色荧光粉由于红色成分不足 存在色温较低的问题[2] 还有广泛应用的一种使用红、绿、蓝三基色荧光粉与近紫外或者紫外 芯片相结合的形式来实现发白光,但这种方式存在着三色荧光粉比例难以控制的问题[3]。而且,荧光粉热稳定性不好、合成条件复杂等 这些都限制了其应用[4] 因而荧光粉还有很大的进步空间。因此,研发一种具有高热稳定性 合成条件简单的单基质实现白光的荧光粉具有重要意义。稀土离子是如今被广泛用作激活剂的离子其中, Dy3+在可见光波段主要有两个发射带,分别为位于 400500 nm (4F9/26H15/2) 的蓝光区域和位于 500600 nm (4F9/26H13/2) 的黄光区域,且可被近紫外/紫外芯片激发,通过调整蓝光和黄光比就可以实现白光发射[5-7] 因此 Dy3 是潜在的单一发白光离子而被广泛应用为激活剂 近年来 稀土离子 Dy3+激活的磷酸盐 钒酸盐、硅酸盐和硼磷酸盐 荧光 粉得到 了广泛研究[8-13] 。Patnam 在 2018 年 合 成 了 在 150 ‰ 下仍有 77% 初 始 温 度 发 光 强 度 的 优 异 热 稳 定 性 Ba3La6 (SiO4) 6Dy3+黄 色 荧 光 粉[14], Yu 在 2020年探究了 p H 值对 Ca3 (PO4) 2Dy3+白色荧光粉的性能影响[15] Priya 在 年研发出了具有95% 高量子效率的 Ca9Bi (VO4) 7Dy3+荧光材料[16] 但它们都存在烧结温度较高 合成条件复杂等情况 而硼磷酸盐由于其合成材料易获得 合成温度较低且稳定性良好而被广泛用作荧光粉的基质材料[17-21]。近期,我们合成了一种烧结温度较低的 Cs2Li3Sr2B3 (PO4) 硼磷酸盐,且目前尚未见其作为荧光粉基质的相关报道 本文利用 Dy3+作为激活剂 硼磷酸盐作为基质材料 采用高温固相法合成了一种 Cs2Li3Sr2B3- (P04) 6Dy3+荧光粉 并测试分析了其晶体结构物相特性 浓度猝灭机理 热稳定性及荧光寿命 获得了一种热稳定性优异的单一基质白光荧光材料 2 实 验 2.1 实验原料及制备方法 实验采用高温固相法合成了 Cs2Li3Sr2B3- (PO4) 6: x Dy3+( x=0.005, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07.0.09,0.11, 0.13, 0.15 ) 荧 光 粉。实 验 原 料 为:LiCO ( 99% ) 、 Cs2CO3 ( 99% ), SrCO ( 99% ) 、BO (98% )、NHHPO (99% ) 和 Dy2O3 ( 99.99 % ) 以上原料均从上海阿拉丁公司购入 首先按照目标化合物的化学计量比称取原材料 然后将称量好的各原材料放入玛瑙研钵中 充分研磨混合均匀 再把研磨后的材料装入氧化铝坩埚内 最后放入马弗炉中升温至750 °C并煅烧4 h,待冷却至室温后取出并研磨成粉末状,依次装入真空储物袋中密封保存待检测。 2.2 样品性能测试 射线衍射测试采用日本 公司的 MiniFle x600 型 射线衍射仪进行分析表征 其辐射源为 Cu 靶 Kα 射线 (=0.15405 nm ),扫描范围 2θ 为 1090,扫 描 速 度 为 15 ( °)/min,工作电压为 40 k V,电流为15 mA。

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: RSCAdv., 2023, 13, 11557 Lumino-structural properties of Dy3+ activated Na3Ba2LaNb10O30 phosphors with enhanced internal quantum yield for w-LEDsKanishk Poria, a Ravina Lohan,b Sanjana Bhatia,a Amit Kumar,b Rajwinder Singh,a Nisha Deopa, *b Rajesh Punia,c Jangvir Singh Shahi*a and A.S.Raod With an intend to develop white light emitting phosphor, for w-LED application, a series of dysprosium (Dy3+) doped novel NaBaLaNbO phosphors were prepared using solid state reaction technique at 1300 °C.Their structural, morphological and vibrational spectroscopic analysis was performed.We illustrate the luminescence characteristics of the prepared phosphors for various Dy3+ ion doping concentration.The XRD analysis demonstrates that the prepared phosphors were in single phase, and of tetragonal tungsten bronze structure of the P4bm space group.The FE-SEM image reveals that the prepared phosphors contained irregular shaped both nano and micro particles.Under near-ultraviolet (n-UV) irradiation at 387 nm, the photoluminescence (PL) emission spectra shows three characteristic bands at 481 nm (blue), 575 nm (vellow) and 666 nm (red) Obtained optimized Dy3+ ion concentration for the prepared sample is 7.0 mol%, beyond which the concentration quenching begins.Bonding between Dy-O is covalent in nature as confirmed by bonding parameters and the Dexter theory revealed that the energy transfer among Dy3+ ions is dipole–diploe interaction.CIE chromaticity coordinates, CCT and color purity confirms the formation of warm white light emitting phosphors.Lifetime analysis demonstrates the longer decay time in the phosphors.The Internal Quantum Yield (IQE) and brightness (B) for the optimised phosphor is calculated as 45.35% and 11.41% respectively, which makes it a suitable phosphor for w-LED.

hosphor is calculated as 45.35% and 11.41% respectively, which makes it a suitable phosphor for w-LED.Received 24th February 2023Accepted 24th March 2023DOI: rsc.li/rsc-advances 1Introduction Phosphor is any material that exhibits the phenomenon of luminescence when subjected to UV radiation, X-rays, electron bombardment, friction or any other form of excitation.A phosphor primarily comprises of a host matrix and an activator ion in its lattice.1 These activators act as the luminescent centres, i.e.the electron relaxes radiatively at this activator site, within the host matrix.Rare earth elements such as Eu3+, Eu2+Dy3+, Pr3+ are few example of activators.Phosphors are used, in the creation of several optoelectronic devices, including light converters, solid state lasers, solid state lighting, optical thermometer and optical ampliers, etc.2-7In the last decade, phosphor-converted white light emitting diodes (pc-wleds) have been studied signicantly owing to their key characteristic, such as eficient light output, low power consumption, longer operational lifetime (>100000 hours), sturdiness and environmentally safer as compared to their predecessors, uorescent and incandescent lamp.8–12 Nowadays, w-LEDs are widely used in plant cultivation (including vegetables, owers, herbs, etc.), display, medical lighting, and outdoor lighting.13–15 White light emission can be obtained in three ways from solid state lighting sources.16,17 The rst way is to setup an array of multiple LED chips emitting light at diferent frequencies.Multiple LED setup has excellent colour rendering index and the white point can be easily controlled.However, there is no control on correlated colour temperature, since each LED needs an independent output power control and has its own diferent lifetime.The second way is to use a single UVLED chip coated with a combination of red, green and blue down-converting phosphors.

use a single UVLED chip coated with a combination of red, green and blue down-converting phosphors.This setup is quite cost eficient than LED matrix, as it gives excellent colour rendering and a control over white light-CCT.Because of stokes conversion, this approach becomes less energy eficient, and it is dificult to manage the homogeneity of the phosphor coating.Another demerit is that phosphors deteriorate faster than LEDs.The third way is utilizing a single LED (blue) with a coating of yellow downconverting phosphor.The blue light bleeds through the phos phor to give white light.This setup is small, light-weight, easy to operate and has a long lifetime.Demerit of this setup is that it is less eficient because of stokes shi and has a very poor colour rendering.Since niobates have better chemical and physical stability, they make excellent luminous matrixes.Some rare-earth ion doped niobates, such as Sr2LaNbO6: Eu3+, Sm3+; LaNbO4: Bi3+/ Dy3+ and Ca2LaNbO6: Sm3+, have been shown to exhibit outstanding luminous characteristics along with high thermal stability.18–20 It is important to note that the tungsten bronze structure (TTB) exhibits chemical and magnetic stability with excellent crystal structure.Niobates having TTB structures are excellent candidates for ferroelectric and piezoelectric materials.The decient perovskite TTB niobates consist of cornersharing NbO6 octahedra arrays and three diferent tunnels for cation lling, leading to large spontaneous polarization and high dielectric constants.21 In deformed metal–oxygen polyhedra, they likewise show dominating electron–hole separation and transport through static electric elds between structureinduced dipole moments.As a result, a little structural change such as changing the cation-site occupancy has a huge inuence on charge mobility.Utilising this property, we have opted to use niobate based TTB structure to investigate its photoluminescence properties.

y, we have opted to use niobate based TTB structure to investigate its photoluminescence properties.Moreover, the tungsten bronze phosphors such as Sr5YTi3Nb7O30, NaSr2Nb5O15 and Ba-LaTiNb9O30 have been reported to have potential applications in photonics, especially in W-LED.22-24The tetragonal tungsten bronze structure has been shown to readily accept lanthanides or transition metals as constituents or dopants because of its tetragonal crystal structure, which enables the manufacture of high-quality doped single crystals.25 The general practice to prepare niobate-based phosphors is the solid state reaction method, which has the benet of producing samples with excellent morphology and luminosity, over other methods.26 In search of a suitable host lattice, scientists have been conducting research in order to prepare phosphor-converted white light emitting diode (pc-wled).27 In our present study, we focus towards the generation of white light from dysprosium doped Na3Ba2LaNb10O30 phosphors via solid state reaction technique.We examine the structure parameter, surface morphology and elemental analysis of the as prepared phosphors using the X-ray difraction (XRD), eld emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), respectively.Further, optical properties were examined employing the steady-state and time resolved photoluminescence.Generally, Dy3+ ions exhibit three emission bands in the visible spectra, the blue emission (450–490 nm) corresponds to 4F9/26H15/2 transition, yellow emission (550–590 nm) corresponds to 4F9/26F13/2 hypersensitive transition and the red emission (640–680 nm) corresponds to 4F9/26H11/2 transition, latter being a feeble transition.28–30 2Experimental procedure 2.1Phosphor preparation The samples of dysprosium doped niobate-based Na3Ba2-LaNb10O30: x Dy3+( x=0, 1, 3, 5, 7.and 10 mol%) phosphors have been synthesized via high-temperature solid-state reaction technique.

Short communication A novel yellow-emitting CaGdSbWO8: Dy3+ single-phase phosphor with high thermal stability and application in w-LEDsLiZhou a,1, LuLiu a,1, Ruiqi Yang a, Jiayun Kong a, Yuxin Lia, Yixuan Zhao a, Yufeng Dua, Changlin Lia, Zhequan Zou a, Bin Deng b,c,*, Ruijin Yua,* a College of Chemistry & Pharmacy, Northwest A&FUniversity, Yangling, Shaanxi 712100, PRChina b School of Chemistry and Environmental Science, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou, Hunan 423043, PRChina c Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Xiangnan Rare-Precious Metals Compounds Research and Application, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou, Hunan 423043, PRChina ARTICLEINFOKeywords: CaGdSbWO8:Dy3+ W-LEDThermal stability Phosphor ABSTRACTDy3+ doped tungstate CaGdSbWO (CGSW) phosphors have been synthesized following a conventional high temperature solid-state reaction at 1300 ◦C.Their phase purity, surface morphology, optical characteristics, thermal stability, and the Commission International de L’Eclairage (CIE) chromaticity were systematically studied.The results show that the CGSW: Dy3+ can be excited over a broad range from 250 nm to 470 nm.Four monitored emission peaks at 487 (bluelight), 575 (yellowlight), 667, and 754 nm are attributed to the 4F9/2-6H15/2, 4F9/26H13/2, 4F9/26H11/2, and 4F9/2-6H9/2 energy level transition of Dy3+ ions, respectively.The critical quenching concentration of Dy3+ in CGSW:Dy3+ phosphor was 5 mol%, and the concentration quenching mechanism is due to the dipole-dipole interaction.

osphor was 5 mol%, and the concentration quenching mechanism is due to the dipole-dipole interaction.Most notably, the prepared phosphors demonstrate the excellent thermal stability with a high activation energy (0.250eV).The emission intensity of the concentration optimized (5 mol%) phosphor remained 93.0% at the typical operating temperature (420K) of light-emitting diode (LED).The fabricated w-LED achieved a high R (89), low correlated color temperature (CCT) of 5096K, and the CIE coordinates of (0.341, 0.334), which fell in the white region and were very near the standard National Television System Committee (NTSC) white point (0.333, 0.333).The results indicated that the CGSW: Dy3+ phosphors could participate in fabricating the w-LEDs as the yellow component. 1.Introduction Thus far, luminescent materials in rare-earth doped states have attracted a lot of interest for their potential application in a wide range of fields, including display devices, latent fingerprints, pesticides detection, and w-LEDs [1–3].Specifically, w-LEDs, as the latest generation of the light source, have become a hot topic in research owing to their long life, high luminous efficiency, environmental friendliness, low energy consumption, and so on [4–6].In commercial w-LEDs, blue GaN chips are typically combined with yellow-emitting Y3Al5O12: Ce3+(YAG: Ce3+) phosphors [7].However, the w-LEDs made in this manner are deficient in the red region, resulting in a high CCT and a poor color rendering index (Ra) [8,9].To overcome these shortcomings, scientists have fabricated the w-LEDs with tricolor (red, green, and blue) phosphors excited by near-ultraviolet (n-UV) chips [10].Hence, it is necessary to prepare new phosphors with a simple synthesis and high performance in the manufacturing process of w-LEDs.Dy3+ ions have been widely studied for their use in white-emitting phosphors in the large family of rare-earth ions.Nakajima et al.

ied for their use in white-emitting phosphors in the large family of rare-earth ions.Nakajima et al.[11] researched the effect of the w-LEDs composed of Dy3+-doped phosphors on plant photosynthesis, and found that these w-LEDs reduced the nearinfrared emissions and inhibition of bloom impediment.It is further demonstrated that Dy3+ ions can be used to design suitable phosphors.Blue, yellow and red emission peaks can be generated in the photoluminescence emission spectra (PL) due to the 4f-4f transitions of Dy3+[12].The sharp peaks at 485 (blue), 580 (yellow), and 675 nm (red) are attributed to 4F9/2-6H15/2, 4F9/2-6H13/2, and 4F9/2-6H11/2 energy level transition of Dy3+, respectively [12,13].There have been reports that the coordination environment of Dy3+ ions can greatly influence the luminous intensity ratio of 4F9/2-6H13/2 to 4F9/2 – 6H15/2 [ 14 ].Therefore, it is possible to obtain white light by doping Dy3+ with a suitable host material.The tungstate compounds could be an excellent matrix material thanks to their superb luminescence performance, great thermal and chemical stability [ 15 ].Additionally, due to the charge transfer transition from the ligand of (WO4) 2 and (WO6) 6 complexes to metal, a wide range of excitation and emission spectra can be observed in tungstatebased phosphors.Hence, many tungstate phosphors doped with rareearth ions have been studied to explore novel luminescent materials.For example, K0.5La0.5Sr MgWO6Mn4+ [ 16 ], CaGd2 (WO4) 4Eu3+ [ 17 ].Li Gd (WO4) 2Sm3+ [ 18 ], and Y2WO6Ln3+( Ln=Dy, Eu, and Sm) phosphors [19].Xie et al.[20] manufactured a series of Dy3+, Eu3+ codoped and Dy3+ single doped NaBi(WO) phosphors.Still, the PL emission intensity at 423K drops to 77.2% of that at 303K.Shi et al.[21] observed the characteristic emissions of Eu3+ ions in the CaGdSbWO8: Eu3: + phosphor under the excitation of 225 and 500 nm.The obtained security ink can be used for anti-counterfeiting labels as well as for encrypting information.

ained security ink can be used for anti-counterfeiting labels as well as for encrypting information.To the best of our knowledge, Dy3+ ions doped CaGdSbWO8 tungstate phosphors have not been investigated to this day.Herein, Dy3+-doped tungstate CaGdSbWO8 (CGSW) phosphors were synthesized successfully.Besides, the phase purity, surface morphology, photoluminescence properties, thermal stability, and CIE chromaticity coordinates of the CGSW: Dy3- phosphors were systematically investigated.The manufactured w-LED based on a UV-InGaN chip (=365 nm) shows excellent potential in applications. 2.Experimental section 2.1.Synthesis of CGSW:Dy3+ phosphors The dysprosium-doped CGSW phosphors were synthesized via a conventional high-temperature reaction.CaCO3 (99.99%), Gd2O3 (99.99%), Dy2O3 (99.99%), Sb2O3 (analyticalgrade), and WO3 (analyticalgrade) obtained from commercial sources were used as starting materials.The stoichiometric reactants, when x=5 mol%, 0.1291 g CaCO3, 0.2221 g Gd2O3, 0.0120 g Dy2O3, 0.1880 g Sb2O3, and 0.2290 g WO3 were weighed by the electronic balance, then thoroughly mixed and ground in an agate mortar for 15 min.Afterward, the homogeneous mixture was placed into the crucible and heated in the muffle furnace for 5 h in air at 1300 C..The ultimate samples were completed after cooling to the room temperature and re-grounding for 15 min.The chemical reaction formula is as follows: Fig.1.The XRD patterns of CGSW: x Dy3+( x=1-35 mol%) phosphors.employed to obtain the temperature-dependent PL spectra of the samples.The relevant photoluminescence characteristics of the manufactured LED can be determined by a USB4000 fiber optic spectrometer (OceanOptics). 2.3.Fabricate of w-LEDAw-LED can be fabricated by employing prepared phosphors on the basic of 365 nm InGaN chip.

A novel yellow whitish Dy3+ activated NaZr2 (PO4) 3 phosphor: Structural, spectral and optical investigations Vishav Deep Sharma a, Pooja Khajuria a, Sandeep Kumar b, Ram Prakash a,*, R.J.Choudhary ca School of Physics, Shri Mata Vaishno Devi University, Katra 182320, J&K, India b Department of Chemistry, Mokpo National University, Muan-gun, South Korea c UGCDAEConsortium for Scientific Research, Indore 452001, India ARTICLEINFOKeywords: XRDFESEMPLFTIRXPSABSTRACTThis study details the effective solution combustion synthesis of novel Na (1-x) Zr2Dyx (PO4) 3 (x=0.05 −0.5) (hereby abbreviated as NaZrPO: Dy3+) phosphor.The structural investigation of synthesized phosphor employing X-ray diffraction and FTIR spectroscopy reveals the formation of single-phase phosphor and the presence of (PO4) 3-group.The lattice parameters turned out to be a=b=8.798A, c=22.794A..The morphological and chemical analysis is characterized by FE-SEM and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, respectively.According to PL spectrum, three traditional emission bands of Dy3+ ions (482 nm, 574 nm, and 663 nm) are observed, and the concentration quenching of the Dy3+ ions in the phosphor occurred at 3 mol.% as a result of the dipole-dipole interaction.Photometric results reveal the emission of the synthesized phosphor in the yellow-whitish region with a color purity of 80%.The optical parameters obtained from diffuse-reflectance spectroscopy, such as refractive index, metallization criterion, and bandgap, for the optimal molar concentration (3 mol.%) are 2.109, 0.46, and 4.3 eV, respectively.

REVIEWAReview of the Eficiency of White Light (orOther) Emissions in Singly and Co-Doped Dy3+Ions in Diferent Host (Phosphate, Silicate, Aluminate) Materials Leelakrishna Reddy 1 Received: 25February 2023 / Accepted: 18April 2023 © The Author(s) 2023 Abstract In this review we will present several research papers pertaining to white colour (orother) emission from Dy3+ doped and undoped phosphor materials.The search for a single component phosphor material that could deliver high quality white light under UV or near UV excitation is an area of active research for commercial purposes.Amongst all rare earth ele ments Dy3+ is the only ion that could deliver simultaneously blue and yellow light under UV excitation.In optimizing the Yellow/Blue emission intensity ratios, white light emission can be realized.Dy3+(4f9) displays approximately 4 emission peaks at around 480 nm, 575 nm, 670 and 758 nm corresponding to transitions from the metastable 4F9/2 state to various lower states, such as 6H15/2 (blue), 6H13/2 (yellow), 6H11/2 (red) and 6H9/2 (brownishred), respectively.In general, the hypersensitive transition at 6H13/2 (yellow) is electric dipole in nature and becomes prominent only when Dy3+ ions are positioned at low symmetric sites with no inversion symmetry in the host matrix.On the other hand, the blue magneti dipole transition at 6H15/2 becomes prominent only when Dy3+ ions are positioned at highly symmetric sites in the host material with inversion symmetry.Despite the white colour emission from the Dy3+ ions, these transitions are mainly associated with parity forbidden 4f -4f transitions, the white light produced maybe diminished at times, hence the need to include a sensitizer to bolster the forbidden transitions experienced by Dy3+ ions.

hence the need to include a sensitizer to bolster the forbidden transitions experienced by Dy3+ ions.In this review we will focus on the vari ability of the Yellow/Blue emission intensities in diferent host materials (phosphates, silicates, and aluminates) from Dy3+ ions (dopedorundoped) by studying their photoluminescent properties (PL), their CIE chromaticity coordinates and cor related colour temperature (CCT) values for white colour emissions that is adaptable to diferent environmental conditions.Keywords Luminescence · Phosphor · Dy3+ ion · Transitions · Doped materials Introduction White light-emitting diodes (WLED) is the next generation of solid-state lighting (presentdayuse) that has replaced the traditional incandescent and fluorescent lamps of bygone days [1, 2].The reason for its use is because of its superior brightness, long lifetimes, absence of toxic mercury and cost saving energy properties [1, 2].There are essentially three ways to fabricate WLEDs: (i) a combination of a blend of red, blue, and green phosphor materials, (ii) a dual combination of a blue emitting light diode with a yellow emitting phosphor material, where the most famous Ce3+ doped yttrium aluminum garnet ( YAG; Ce3+) commercial phosphor material comes to mind, and finally (iii) fabrication of single phased all inclusive phosphor material doped with specific rare-earth ions for colour tuning [1, 3].From case (ii) above, a similar combination of colours to obtain white light can be achieved by doping Dy3+ ion in a single phased host material, because the characteristic emission colour for this Dy3+ ion lies in the blue and yellow colour regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.Trivalent dysprosium Dy3+(4f9) generally possesses 2 intense characteristic emission peaks at 485 nm, which corresponds to a blue magnetic dipole 4F9/26H13/2 transition and usually, a hypersensitive yellow electric dipole 4F9/26H15/2 transition at 575 nm, respectively.The optimal yellow to blue (Y/B) intensity peak emission ratios yields white light.

nm, respectively.The optimal yellow to blue (Y/B) intensity peak emission ratios yields white light.The position of the Dy3+ ions in the host environment is of crucial importance for eficient white light emissions.When Dy3+ ions are positioned at low symmetric sites in the environment of the host material with no inversion center, yellow emissions at 485 nm are of relatively higher intensity compared to blue light emissions at 575 nm wavelength are observed.On the other hand, when Dy3+ ions are positioned at highly symmetric sites in the environment of the host without inversion symmetry, then blue light colour emissions are relatively higher than the yellow light colour emissions.A host on its own by its very nature is unable to emit white light, thus the necessity for the embedding of dopant ions, which in this case is Dy3+ ions [1].The search for a single phased phosphor material for white light emission for LED application when doped with Dy3+ ions or co-doped with other rare-earth ions (othercolourssuchasblueandgreen) for persistent luminescence under UV excitation is an area of active research.There is potential need to fabricate materials with unconventional emission properties, where previously the existence of defects was found to suppress the photoluminescence properties of materials, but now defects are found to be a storage or a trapping site for charges in the generation of persistence luminescence that was observed with specific host materials [3].Potential host materials that could fit this criterion could be phosphates, silicates, aluminates, borates, etc.However, white light emissions from Dy3+ doped host materials sufer some drawbacks due its parity forbidden nature of its 4f – 4f transitions of the Dy3+ ions.In the later part of this review, an attempt is made to ameliorate this situation by co-doping it with other rare –earth ion to bolster the parity forbidden nature of the Dy3+ ions.

n by co-doping it with other rare –earth ion to bolster the parity forbidden nature of the Dy3+ ions.However, this process may lead to diferent colour emissions (besideswhitecolourlight), depending on whether the dopant (Dy3+) is a sensitizer or an activator, but the result is for prolonged luminescence emissions long after the UV excitation source is removed.In this review, we will focus on research papers, firstly for enhancing white light emissions through Dy3+ doping, and in the second part, a look at persistent luminescence when Dy3+ is co-doped with other rare-earth ions in diferent host materials, as well as the mechanism for persistence luminescence will be discussed.Factors for Consideration for White Light Eficiency and Persistent Luminescence in Singly doped Dy3+ and Co-Doped Host Materials Researchers in this review have published many papers using Dy3+ ions for white light emissions or co-doped it for persistent luminescence, but have not reached the desired standards for commercialization, due to degradation of the light or lack of consistency for prolonged luminescence (ortheineficiencyofthemechanism).Some, if not all these factors need to be factored in producing optimal emission characteristics (white light eficiency in the first instance and consistency of its illumination in the second instance) [4, 5]: (a) Low preparation costs.(b) High CRI and low CCT values.(c) High chemical and thermal stabilities.(d) Appropriate choice of host compounds and dopants.(e) Nature of Y/B intensity ratios in producing electric dipole or magnetic dipole transitions.(f) Emission lifetimes: fluorescence or phosphorescence emissions.(g) Influence of concentration on the Y/B ratio in Dy3+ doped materials.(h) Mechanism of white light colour emission from Dy3+ doped host materials. High CRI and Low CCTValues According to Wikipedia [November 2022], the colour rendering index (CRI) is “a quantitative measure of the ability of a light source to reveal the colours of various objects faithfully in comparison with a natural or standard light source”.This means that a light source must depict the natural colour of an object [4].CRI values range from 0 to 100, thus a value of 100 implies that a light source is identical to the spectrum of daylight.In general, light sources should have CRI values greater than 80 for it to be commercially acceptable.The other factor for consideration is the correlated colour temperature (CCT) appearance.This is defined as the temperature appearance of a white LED light source (lamp).It is measured in kelvins and is determined using McCamy’s empirical formula: CCT=- 449 n3+ 3525 n2 -6823n + 5520.33, where n represents the inverse slope line and is given by n=(x-0.332) / (y-0.186).In general, CCT values fall in 4 categories: (2700 – 3000K) is regarded as warm white light, (3000 – 4500K) is regarded as bright white light and (4500 – 6500K) is regarded as natural daylight and colour colours beyond these values are regarded as coolish bluish white light [Wikipedia, November 2022]. materials, offering insights that bridge fundamental physics and practical applica tions [1].Thermoluminescence, a luminescence phenomenon arising from the release of stored energy in the form of light upon heating, provides a unique means to probe the trapping and detrapping processes of charge carriers in a material.The interaction between the dopant ions and the host lattice, coupled with the influence of defects and crystal structure, produces distinct TL responses.

attice, coupled with the influence of defects and crystal structure, produces distinct TL responses.TL studies have garnered substantial attention in the realm of boratebased phosphor (BBPs) materials, with a particular focus on compounds like GAB.This category of materials holds remarkable potential for luminescence applications owing to their unique energy storage and release mechanisms [2–5].Extensive investigations into TL properties have been conducted on various borate materials, aiming to unravel the intricate interplay between lattice defects, charge carriers, and luminescence centers.These studies have not only contributed to the fundamental understanding of borate materials’ behaviour but also paved the way for their diverse practical applications.Previous research on BBPs materials, including GAB, has demonstrated the immense potential of TL studies in shedding light on the underlying physical mechanisms governing their luminescence behaviour.These investigations have not only enriched our understanding of the complex interactions within these materials but have also unlocked novel avenues for exploiting their luminescent properties across diverse fields.Before delving into investigations on GAB materials, it is significant to provide a comprehensive overview of these aspects, accentuating the intriguing nature of borate materials.Highlighted here is a collection of doped and non-doped phosphors that have undergone investigation within the realm of this scientific domain: A3(BO3)2 (A=Na,K):Eu3+, Tb3+ [6], YAl3 (BO3) 4 Eu3+[7], SrAlBO4zEu3+[ 8 ] BaznBO3F: Bi2+[9], Li4Ca (BO3) 2: Dy3+[ 10 ] LiBa2B5O10:: RE3+ ( RE=Dy, Tb and Tm) [11], NaSr4 (BO3) 3Eu2+, Dy3+[12], Zn (BO2) 2Tb3+ [ 13 ] KMgBO3: Eu3+, Tm3+[ 14 ].Our luminescence research group is well-equipped with an extensive repository of knowledge and expertise in the domain of crafting BBPs samples and delving into their TL properties.

knowledge and expertise in the domain of crafting BBPs samples and delving into their TL properties.Specializing in the creation of BBPs, our team possesses refined expertise in generating specimens suitable for exploring TL properties.We have devised diverse methodologies to produce phosphor samples, each endowed with a range of TL attributes, enabling us to analyse the effects of various parameters on their TL behaviour.In the context of RE-doped phosphor specimens scrutinized here, the following candidates emerge: GdAl3 (BO3) 4 [4], both non-doped and YAl3 (BO3) 4; Eu3+[15], YAl3 (BO3) 4: Tb3+[16], ZnB2O4: Gd3+ [ 17 ], and ZnB2O4: Eu3+[18], LaB3O6: Tb3+[ 19 ] Recently, Sinclair (2022) made a significant contribution to the field by authoring a comprehensive review that covers BBP synthesi methods, conducts a detailed analysis of their TL properties, and ex plores the growing landscape of phosphor materials with new potential in dosimetry.Furthermore, this article explores the challenges and constraints associated with BBPs, providing a direction for future research in this area [20].While the landscape boasts a plethora of RE-doped and non-doped, meticulously tailored for dosimetric pursuit with attendant TL properties and BBPs samples kinetic attributes, a gap remains to be filled—a TL study of a RE incorporated GAB phospho specimen is conspicuously absent from the literature.The first entry into this realm originated from Alajlani et al.(2023), who examined the TL properties and kinetic parameters of non-doped GAB synthesised via the gel-combustion (GelC) approach [4].The investigation’s findings un veiled TL glow peak temperatures of 106 ◦C and 277C for the generated GAB sample, accompanied by activation energy values spanning 0.84–1.63 eV.The researchers concluded that the GelC method repre sents a potent avenue for producing non-doped GAB with desirable TL attributes and kinetic traits.

Fig.1.Response of the TL glow curve of the GAB sample doped with 3 wt% Dy3+ to different filter combinations.The phenomenon of IRSL-TL wideband blue filter yielding a signifi cantly more intense peak in TL response can be attributed to several underlying physical factors.One of the key factors is the selective sensitivity of the filter to certain wavelength ranges that are particularly relevant to the TL emission process.TL involves the release of stored energy in the form of light when previously trapped charge carriers are thermally activated and move from their excited energy states to lower energy states.During this process, various luminescent centers contribute to the emission of light at different wavelengths.The IRSL-TL wideband blue filter is specifically designed to capture light within a range of wavelengths that align with the emission characteristics of the luminescent centers involved in the TL of the studied material.

capability of Dy3+-based vanadate garnet phosphors for solid-state lighting and temperature sensing. 1Introduction Over the years, light-emitting devices based on solid-state technology have made profound advancements in lighting due to their benefits, such as energy eficiency, an extended lifetime, low energy consumption, environmental friendliness, and so on.1–4 Nevertheless, the commercially available devices based on a blue LED and yellow phosphor, YAG: Ce3+, are limited by their low color rendering index due to the lack of the red emission component.As a solution to this problem, the combination of red-green-blue phosphors with the NUV chip is introduced.However, color rendering is limited owing to the cyan gap in the 480–520 nm region.5 Thus, it is high time to bridge the cyan gap to realize full spectrum emission with better color rendering.As a result, researchers have paid significant attention to developing cyan-based phosphors.Lanthanide ions are an attractive choice in designing phosphors with better emission properties for multifunctional applications.6,7 Among various lanthanide-based activators, Eu2+, Ce3+ and Bi3+ optical centers are widely studied for cyan phosphors in various host structures.5,8–10 Recently, Dang et al.reported better luminescence of vanadate-based cyan phosphors, Rb3RV2O8 ( R=Y,.Lu).11 Vanadates are known for their self-activated emission in the blue-green region, which can be tuned towards the cyan region via structural modifications and the energy transfer strategy more easily.12,13 In various vanadate-based phosphor systems, the garnet structure ofers more freedom to tune the emission owing to the unique structural framework, flexibility in cation substitution, and compositional diversity.1,4,14 The general stoichiometry of the garnet structure is A3B2C3O12 where A, B, and C correspond to dodecahedral, octahedral, and tetrahedral sites.

KEYWORDS: EPR, TSL, SrB4O7, Dy, photoluminescence 1.INTRODUCTION There has been a plethora of reports on rare earth (RE) activated borate matrices being proposed as inorganic phosphor materials for radiation dosimetry and luminescence application.1−3 On one hand with relatively lower efective atomic number, borate based systems can mimic human tissue for dosimetry applications.On the other hand, due to their non-centrosymmetric structure, the materials show higher radiative yield for application in light industries.Additionally, the relatively lower cost associated with borate based materials and their easy availability tilt the balance in their favor.The alkaline earth borate SrB4O7 (SBO) has been of particular interest to scientists worldwide where the material has been incorporated with all sorts of rare earth ions for targeted applications.4−10 Because of the favorable properties, such as higher lumen output, color-rendering index, energy eficiency, and greater radiation stability, the material has shown promising results in a wide range of applications in solid state lighting, display devices, lamp phosphors, white light generation, dating and dosimetry, etc.It is well-known that solid state luminescence dosimetry is based on the radiation energy storage in a material in the form of charge carriers (holesorelectrons) that subsequently get trapped at vacancies and interstitials.The release of these trapped charge carriers by heating (thermoluminescence, TSL process) or by photon energy (optically stimulated lumines cence, OSL process) is what gives the information about the past events.

content: pounds were crystallized in the tetragonal scheelite type structure with space group (I41/a, No.88).The morphology and functional group were confirmed by the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and Fourier transform infrared(FTIR)spectroscopy.Upon near-Ultraviolet (n-UV) excitation, the PL spectra exhibit the two characteristic emissions of Dy3+ ions, blue (4F9/26H15/2) at 487 nm and yellow (4F9/26H13/2) at 574nm respectively.The optimum concentration of Dy3+ ionis 3 mol% and then quenching occurred due to multipolar interaction.Further, enhanced the emission intensity by codoping with monovalent (Li+), divalent (Ca2+) and trivalent (Bi3+) ions.Among them, Li+ ion codoped samples are shown maximum intensity (50times) more than Dy3+ doped phosphors as relaxation ofparity restriction ofelectric dipole transition because oflocal distortion ofcrystal field around the Dy3+ ions.In addition, by incorporation of Eu3+ ions into NaLa (MoO4) 2: Dy3+ system, tuned the emission color from white to red, owing to energy transfer from Dy3+ to Eu3+ ions.The intensity parameters ( 2, 4 ) and radiative properties such as transition probabilities (AT), radiative lifetime (rad), and branching ratio were calculated using the Judd-Ofelt theory.CIE color coordinates CCT values indicates that these phosphors exhibit an excellent white emission.The determined radiative properties, CIE and CCT results revealed that the Dy3+-activated NaLa (MoO4) 4 phosphors are potential materials for developing white LEDs, and optoelectronic device fabrications. 1.Introduction In the past decades, researchers have shown a greater interest in the development of the white light-emitted diodes (WLEDs) as a new generation of the light source [1–4].Due to their several advantages like it is environmental friendly, low energy consumption, long lifetimes, high luminescence efficiency and high performance efficiency [5–7].

rgy consumption, long lifetimes, high luminescence efficiency and high performance efficiency [5–7].The two tradition ways to achieve WLEDs are: first method involves combining green LEDs with yellow YAG:Ce3+ phosphors, which generally emit white light, while the second involves combining near UV-LEDs with blue, green, and red spectral region phosphors, which are more expensive and have lower luminescence efficiency [8].Moreover, they have a low color rendering index (CRI) and high correlated color temperature, which limits their use as general lighting or medical lighting [9].In order to solve above mention problem researcher started taking interest in developing of stable single-phased white light phosphors by doping single activator in the host matrix which can be match well with UV-LEDs chips [10].To meet the requirement of these, the selection of appropriate host matrix also play an important role.Nowadays, molyb date have been widely used because of their excellent optical properties as well as their potential applications in phosphors and laser [11–13].Among these, double molybdate compound possess a tetragonal symmetry with the scheelite type structure to be a good luminescent host materials [14–18].Furthermore, the MoO42- group has a broad absorption band in the ultraviolet (UV) region and have strong charge transfer band from MoO42- group to rare-Earth(RE) ions.Hence, strong PL emission are obtained in RE activated NaLa (MoO4) 2 phosphors under UV-light excitation.Therefore, it is well known that Dy3+ ions produce yellow emission at 575 nm (4F9/26H13/2) and blue emission around 480 nm (4F9/26H15/2) leads to the near-white emission i.e.yellowish white when Y / B is larger, or bluish white when Y / B is smaller [9].But unfortunately due to lack of red emission, Dy3+ singledoped generates white emission with poor performance qualities, such it emits cold white light [19–23].To overcome with this problem, we need to add red emitting activator in Dy3+ doped phosphors.

[19–23].To overcome with this problem, we need to add red emitting activator in Dy3+ doped phosphors.As europium ion (Eu3+) can emit the strong red emission at 615nm (5D07F2), which is used as red-orange luminescent centre [23].In general, the trivalent Eu3+ ion exhibits four emission peaks due to transition 5D07F J ( J=1, 2, 3, 4).Hence, it is possible to obtained the single-phased whit emitting phosphor by co-doping Eu3+/ Dy3+ ions into the same host lattice, which resulting in a tunable white to red emission because Dy3+ ions efficiently transfer its energy to Eu3+ ion in host matrix, which producing both the emission band ofDy3+ and Eu3+ ions which emit warm light [24, 25].Dy3+ doped SrWO phosphor was reported by Gopal et al [26], but their luminous properties are not good enough for making WLEDs devices.There are so many ways to enhance the luminescence intensity ofwhite emission has been reported such as annealing at higher temperature and substitution of appropriate sensitizer ions [27].Literature survey reveal that, an enhancement of emission intensity was observed on rare Earth ions activated phosphors along with small amount of co-dopant ions as a sensitizer [28] due totheir ionic size and charge of the cations are different than the host (La3+) lattice.As a result, distortion is produced in crystal lattice which leads to break the local site symmetry and enhance the emission intensity [29].Based on the literature survey, till now there is no detailed report on structural and optical properties on monovalent, divalent, and trivalent ions co-doped with Dy3+ activated NaLa (MoO4) 2 phosphors.Therefore, the present studyaims in the improving the emission intensity by co-doping with monovalent (Li+), divalent (Ca2+) and trivalent (Bi3+) ions in the ng concentration of Dy3+ and Eu3+ ions in the NaLa (MoO4) 2 host lattice. 2.Experimental 2.1.Chemicals Molybdenum oxide (MoO3), sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), Lanthanum oxide (La2O3) were used for the preparation of host material.While, Dysprosium oxide (Dy2O3) was used as dopant and Lithium Carbonate (Li2CO3) Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3);, Bismuth Oxide (Bi2O3) and Europium oxide (Eu2O3) were used as co-dopant ions in the preparation ofthese phosphors. 2.2.Synthesis A series of NaLa1-xDyx (MoO4) 2 ( 0.00 x0.11 ) were synthesized by the conventional solid-state reaction method.In a typical synthesis ofNa a0.95Dy0.05 (MoO4) 2 compound, stoichiometric amount of analytical grade sodium carbonate (0.2649g), lanthanum oxide (0.7738 g; pre calcined at 800C ), dysprosium oxide (0.0466g) and molybdenum oxide (1.4394g)were weighted and grinded thoroughly for 30 min in an agate mortar to achieve uniformity.The mixture was transferred into the porcelain crucible and calcined at 750C for 4h.in a muffle furnace, finally the furnace was cooled down to room temperature.Similarly, stoichiometric amount of lithium carbonate, calcium carbonate, and bismuth oxide were taken as a co-dopant ion for the preparation of NaLa0.97-AyDy0.03 (MoO4) 2 ( A=Li+, Ca2+ and Bi3+ up to 5 mol%) phosphors.Also, europium oxide was used to prepare double substitution of Dy3+/ Eu3+ in La3+ site in the NaLa (MoO4) host matrix.All the prepared compounds were subjected to characterization. 2.3.Characterization All the synthesized compoundsweresubjected to powder x-ray studies using PANalytical Empyrean powder diffractometer.Rietveld refinement method was used to determine the structural parameters for all the samples using FullProf Suite-2000 program.The surface morphologies ofthe samples were examined using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM).

Highly-doped lanthanide nanomaterials for eficient photothermal conversion – selection of the most promising ions and matrices Agnieszka Paściak, Małgorzata Misiak, Karolina Trejgis, Karolina Elżbieciak-Piecka, Oleksii Bezkrovnyi, Łukasz Marciniak, Artur Bednarkiewicz ⁎, Institute of Low Temperature and Structure Research, Polish Academy of Sciences, Okólna 2, 50–422Wroclaw, Poland articleinfo Article history: Received 2August 2022Received in revised form 1November 2022Accepted 2November 2022Available online 3November 2022Keywords: Photothermal conversion eficiency Nanoheaters Lanthanide-doped nanomaterials Neodymium abstract Materials doped with rare earth ions are widely used in luminescence applications.However, alternative uses of these materials, such as photothermal conversion, have not yet been systematically investigated.In this work, we systematically and quantitatively compare internal and external photothermal conversion eficiency of materials doped with neodymium, thulium and ytterbium ions, and co-doped with samarium and dysprosium ions.Furthermore, we investigate influence of various matrix materials on photothermal conversion eficiency.These include fluoride, oxide, vanadate and perovskite materials.This was done to determine if photothermal conversion eficiency is dependent on dopant and matrix selection.Our research indicates that the highest internal and external photothermal conversion eficiency is achieved with neodymium ions.Moreover, NdVO was found to be the most promising host for future applications.Although the internal photothermal conversion eficiency was relatively low (19%), NdVO exhibited significant external photothermal conversion eficiency of 0.08L/g·cm at 806 nm, which is ca.14 times higher than that of NaNdF at the same wavelength.

Fig.1.Schematic diagram of gel-combustion process used for the synthesis of considered nanomaterial.In mercury-free lighting, luminous devices, field emission displays, and optical thermometry, Dy3+ ions may be used.Dy3+ emits in the visible light spectrum in its 4 f9 electronic state as a consequence of 4f electronic transitions.The effect of the surrounding environment allows the shielding of the 5d and 6s electrons to emit in a direct and potent way.Trivalent dysprosium photoluminescence properties are examined when excited by UV and NUV region.The transitions; 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 are accountable for the blue band at 480 nm and the yellow band at 575 nm, respectively [28,29].The ratio of the blue to yellow emission bands influences the phosphor’s overall emission colour since different hosts produce yellow hypersensitivity to different extents.Hence, white-light may be produced via adjusting yellow to blue bands ratio according to changes in the host environment.The hypersensitive electric dipole transition of Dy3+ ions makes them a useful probe for studying the symmetry of the host lattice [30].There are several methods for synthesizing rare earth (RE) doped nanoscaled phosphors with appropriate particle sizes.In the current investigation, we employed a urea-assisted gel-combustion methodology to produce GdSr2AlO5: Dy3+( x=1-6 mol %) nanophosphors because of the benefits of straight forward preparation using a lowtemperature and one-step procedure.Urea functions as reductant and supplies energy for redox-reaction between fuel and oxidants in combustion process [31].The fabrication and optical research of Dy3+ doped GdSr2AlO5 nanophosphors for the production of white light emission have not been reported.

3+ doped GdSr2AlO5 nanophosphors for the production of white light emission have not been reported.To the best of our knowledge, no literature is accessible on the effect of trivalent dysprosium ions concentration in crystallinity and luminous performance of GdSr2AlO5 host.From the structural aspect, we need a GdSr2AlO5 host which is flexible and reliable and that allows us to replace the inner cation with the suitable dopant metal with on wide network changes in the host.According to the findings of the current study, a host system may be simply replaced by a low concentration of are earth (RE) ions, providing the ideal energy transfer mechanism.Moreover, complete structural, optical and luminescence properties were investigated in detailed manner.This exploratory study on Dy3+ doped GdSr2Al05 offers a chance to develop an economically viable white light emitting diode material. 2.Experimenta 2.1.Chemicals used and synthesis High purity chemicals of Sigma Aldrich viz.gadolinium nitrate hexahydrate, dysprosium nitrate pentahydrate, aluminium nitrate nonahydrate, Strontium nitrate and urea were procured and used without any further purification.Deionized water (DI) was used as solvent in the synthesis.Nano powdered samples of host GdSr2AlO5 and different Dy3+ content (1–6 mol %) doped GdSrAlO phosphors were synthesized using gel-combustion method, as displayed in Fig.1.Firstly, an aqueous solution was prepared by dissolving gadolinium, strontium and dysprosium nitrate in distilled water in a stoichiometric ratio and stirred on magnetic hot plate continuously a t80C for approximately 20 mints [32].Later, urea was added to the resulting aqueous mixture and mixed solution was stirred continuously at about 80C till a viscous gel was obtained.Now, transparent gel was kept in preheated muffle furnace at 600C for combustion.Consequently, self-sustained exothermic reactions take place resulting into formation of porous and fluffy white materials.

Abstract Dy3+-doped CaY2Al4SiO12 phosphors were prepared using the sol–gel method.Xray diffraction (XRD), field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy analyses (EDS) were used to analyse the crystal structure, morphology, and elemental composition of the prepared samples.The luminescence behaviour of the sample was investigated using photoluminescence (PL) and thermoluminescence (TL) techniques.The prepared CaY2Al4SiO12: XDy3+ phosphor showed a characteristic blue and yellow emission at 480 and 583 nm, respectively, with an excitation wavelength of 350 nm.The most intense PL emission was found for a4 mol% doping concentration of Dy3+ ions.The CIE diagram of the phosphor showed bluish-white colour emission.For TL studies, the prepared phosphors were irradiated with a60Co γ (gamma) source and the TL glow curve of the CaY2Al4SiO12: 0.04Dy3+ phosphor showed three overlapped peaks.

ource and the TL glow curve of the CaY2Al4SiO12: 0.04Dy3+ phosphor showed three overlapped peaks.For the Gaussian peaks, Chen's peak shape method was applied to determine the kinetic parameters of the samples. KEYWORDS phosphor, photoluminescence, sol–gel method, thermoluminescence, XRD1 | INTRODUCTIONIn recent decades a marked evolution has been noticed in the field of optical and luminescence applications using phosphor materials [1, 2].Garnet-based phosphor materials show superb luminescence characteristics, high thermal stability, good chemical, and physical stability, and other energy-efficient properties.Garnet acquires a cubic crystal structure with complicated positioning of different cations in the unit cell.The affability of the garnet structure allows the substitution of ions at the dodecahedral, octahedral, and tetrahedral sites.Garnet phosphor material can be used in different fields such as laser and white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs).For example, the yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) host with lanthanide ions is a broadly used phosphor material for solid-state lighting applications [1–3] Garnet-based phosphors have been explored by many research groups.Singh et al.and Katelnikovas et al.investigated the luminescence behaviour of the CaY2Al4SiO12: Pb2+ and yellowemitting CaY2Al4SiO12Ce3+ garnet phosphors respectively [4, 5].Similarly YAG:Dy [6, 7], Lu1Gd2Ga2Al3O12: Dy [8], CaY2Al4SiO12: Eu0.03 (CYASG:Eu) [9], Nd-doped YAG nano-powders [10], and Pr3+- Cr3+ and Tb3+- Cr3+ co-doped Y3Al2Ga3O12 (YAGG) phosphors [11] have been studied by other research groups.Trivalent dysprosium is the most preferred rare earth ion for producing white light-emitting luminescence materials.To explore specific luminescence host materials with better enhancement in intensity, trivalent dysprosium ions play a vital role [12].In the present study, we synthesized CaY2Al4SiO12xDy3+ phosphors using the sol–gel reaction method.

the present study, we synthesized CaY2Al4SiO12xDy3+ phosphors using the sol–gel reaction method.The luminescence behaviour of the CaY2Al4SiO12xDy3+ phosphors was studied in detail via the combined techniques of XRD, FESEM, EDS, photoluminescence excitation/photoluminescence (PLE/PL) spectroscopy, and thermoluminescence (TL) spectroscopy.A survey of the literature showed that CaY2Al4SiO12: XDy3+ phosphors prepared via the sol–gel synthesis method had not been studied before.In the present work, the PL and TL properties of the CaY2Al4SiO12: x Dy3+ phosphors are also reported for the first time as per our knowledge. 2 | EXPERIMENTAL2.1 | Sample synthesis In the present work the CaY2Al4SiO12xDy3+(where x=0.01–0.06) phosphors were prepared using the sol–gel method.Initially, all the starting materials, such as r Ca (NO3) 24H2O, Y (NO3) 36H2O, Al (NO3) 3.9H2O, SiO2, Dy (NO3) 3, and citric acid (citric acid/metal ion 2:1, molar ratio), were taken in stoichiometric ratio and dissolved in 10 ml of de-ionized water in a borosil beaker on a magnetic stirrer rotating at 500 rpm.After stirring it for 1 h, a transparent hydrated solution was obtained and this solution was kept at 110C for 1.5 h in a furnace until an homogeneous dried gel was obtained.To get a fine powder, the dried gel was ground with a mortar and pestle for 10 min and sintered at 400C for 2 h.The brown-coloured sample then obtained was ground and annealed at 1000C for 5 h to produce the final sample powder [4, 13].The sample synthesis process is shown in Figure 1. 2.2 | Characterization The XRD pattern was recorded using a Bruker D8Advanced diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 1.54 Å at a scanning rate of 0.04/s.To investigate the PL characteristics at room temperature, an RF-5301PC spectrofluorophotometer (Shimadzu) was used.A xenon lamp of 150W, provided with this setup, worked as an excitation source.

r (Shimadzu) was used.A xenon lamp of 150W, provided with this setup, worked as an excitation source.To study the morphology and elemental composition, field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy analyses (EDS; Carl Zeiss UHRFESEMModel Gemini SEM500KMAT) were used.Thermoluminescence characteristics were studied using a Nucleonix 1009I TL reader. 3 | RESULTSANDDISCUSSION3.1 | Structural and morphological studies Powder X-ray diffraction patterns (XRD) of the CaY2Al4SiO12xDy3+(where x=0.01 to 0.06) phosphors are displayed in Figure 2.The XRD diffractograms show that all the peaks were very similar to the standard JCPDS card no.33–0040.The phase structure of the synthesized phosphor had a cubic phase with a Ia3d space group.A few extra impurity peaks of Ca2Al2SiO7 indicated by ‘*’ can be observed in the XRD patterns.These impurity peaks are similar to the peaks reported by Katelnikovas et al.[5].No peaks due to the addition of dopant ions were observed in the XRD pattern of the CaY2Al4SiO12: x Dy3- phosphors, showing that Dy3+ ions had been appropriately incorporated into the garnet host.
