Microscopic and luminescence characteristics of Dy3+ doped KSrVO nanophosphors as energy eficient photoluminescent material with potential application in white light‐emitting diodes Neha Lalotra 1 · Priya Kaith 2 · Kamni Pathania 1 Received: 20June 2023 / Accepted: 14September 2023 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2023 Abstract Nanotechnology has drawn an enormous amount of attention by providing various measures to reduce energy consumption.Phosphor-converted white-light emitting diodes (pc-w-LEDs), which are used in lighting applications, are gaining popularity.These materials are afordable, efective, and safe for the environment.Therefore, the main objective of the current study is to synthesize an economical phosphor which consumes low energy and is less harmful to the environment.In thi study, Dysprosium (Dy3+) doped Potassium Strontium Vanadate (KSrVO4) nanopowders synthesized via the combustion process and using X-ray difraction, FESEM, EDAX, HRTEM, UV-Vis spectroscopy, and photoluminescence spectroscopy techniques, we have examined its various structural, spectroscopic, optical, and morphological characteristics.The crystallite size was estimated using the XRD patterns and was found to be 25.724 nm.The functional groups contained in synthesized phosphor were identified using FTIR spectrum measurements.Using HRTEM, a particle size of 36.33 nm was predicted, which is consistent with the XRD results.The Kubelka-Munk approximation is used to determine the band gap energy of the produced nanophosphors.Three major peaks that correspond to the transitions of 4F9/2→6H J ( J=15/2, 13/2, and 11/2) were discovered at 476 nm, 578 nm, and 669 nm, respectively, under the excitation of 390 nm near UV light.

e discovered at 476 nm, 578 nm, and 669 nm, respectively, under the excitation of 390 nm near UV light.We investi gated the impact of Dy3+ doping, the enhancement of emission intensity and the mechanism of concentration quenching on the photoluminescence spectra of the KSrVO4 host.K SrVO4: Dy3+ also demonstrated a suitable CCT (3745K), enhanced color purity and high quantum yield in this work, indicating that this phosphor has potential applications in w-LED devices.Keywords Combustion synthesis · Orthovanadate · XRD · TEM · SEM · UV-Vis Introduction Phosphor-converted white-light emitting diodes (pc-w-LEDs), a novel source for the forthcoming generation of solid-state lighting, have drawn interest from all across the world.They have various unique advantages such as the low energy consumption as well as low environmental impact, the absence of mercury, excellent chemical and physical stability, longevity and luminous eficiency, and the availability of finished products in a wide variety of sizes (Panse et al.2016; Zheng et al.2012; Lougdali et al.2022).A large number of researches have been conducted to investigate various luminous materials to aid in the development of acceptable phosphors.When these phosphors are stimulated by near-ultraviolet radiation, they generate white light.For generating phosphors with highly eficient emissions, it is extremely important to choose the right materials and guarantee their superior physical and chemical stability.These materials have been recombined with greater light capitulation, constructive emission wavelength, faster fluorescence breakdown, and temperature endurance making them suitable for application in detectors for high energy physics and even medical imaging (Sun et al.2012; Yerpude and Dhoble 2012).At present, the production of white light-emitting diodes follows a typical method in which blue InGaN (indiumgalliumnitride) chips are combined with commercially available phosphors (Zeng et al.2008).

(indiumgalliumnitride) chips are combined with commercially available phosphors (Zeng et al.2008).Nevertheless, this approach used for the fabrication of white-light emitting diodes (w-LEDs) had some drawbacks, including a poor color rendering index and a high correlated color tem perature.In order to address these issues, an alternative approach for the production of white-light emitting diodes (w-LEDs) entails combining ultraviolet/near-ultraviolet (UV/NUV) chips, which emit light in the range of approximately 350–420 nm, with red-blue-green (RGB) phosphors in the appropriate proportions.However, this particular step poses practical challenges and a significant drawback of this method is the variability in the color of the RGB nanophosphors.Therefore, the use of single-phased nanophosphors efectively addresses these issues (Chahar et al.2018; Sehrawat et al.2019).Through careful examination of these empirical observations, it becomes evident that the introduction of rare earth ions into an appropriate host lattice is a very efective approach for achieving the production of single-phased phosphors that produce white light.The selection of an appropriate rare earth ion and host matrix is a crucial challenge in order to achieve improved luminous outputs.Due to their wide range of applications, the nanophosphors doped with trivalent rare earth (RE) have attracted a lot of interest lately in electrical devices, white-LEDs, thermal detectors, medical appliances, and other areas (Zhou et al.2020).Therefore, significant advancements have been achieved in the field of rare earth doped phosphors and nanoparticles with the aim of optimizing and enhancing their luminescence qualities.In the construction of phosphors, the role of the host is vital which is doped with RE (rareearth) ions to display amazing features.Due to their superior physical and chemical characteristics, compounds based on vanadate oxide have many advantages.

erior physical and chemical characteristics, compounds based on vanadate oxide have many advantages.These include excellent chemical stabil ity, thermal stability, exceptional luminescence performance, and a variety of crystal shapes that produce a very rich crystal field environment.Klement and Kresse were the first to explain how KSrVO4 was created by a solid-state reaction at a high temperature.Later, other scientists used KVO3 and SrO as starting materials to manufacture this chemical in sealed gold tubes (Azrour et al.2000; Olazcuaga et al.1987).The structural, spectroscopic, and spectral characteristics of the title compound after it has been doped with additional dopants have been the subject of various studies.In relation to the literature review, the spectroscopic characteristics of KSrVO4 doped with Sm3+ were examined by Biswas et al.(2015).Additionally, he also studied the optical characteristics of Tb3+ doped KSrVO4 (BiswasandKumar2023).Cao et al.(2016) described the structural as well as energy transfer of the KSrVO4: Eu3+ for LEDs.A paper has been published by Sharma and Singh (2022) on the doping of Mn2+ in KSrVO4 regarding the application in optical devices.The photoluminescence properties of KSrVO4 doped with Nd3+ have been previously studied by Sharma and Singh (2021).However, there is currently no existing research on the nanophosphor KSrVO4 doped with Dy3++.This report serves as the first comprehensive study on the impact of Dy3+ doping on various properties of KSrVO4 including bandgap measurements, cell parameters, structural characteristics, vibrational behavior, optical, and photoluminescence properties.The novelty of this research work is evident in its detailed examination of these properties.Dysprosium is possibly one of the most significant rare earth ions that were of interest for this study.This is as a result of the excellent optical and electrical characteristics of its constituents.

udy.This is as a result of the excellent optical and electrical characteristics of its constituents.Due to the 4F9/26H15/2 transition in the 470–500 nm range and the 4F9/26H13/2 transition in the 570–600 nm range, Dy3+ emits luminescence lines.The color of the luminescence created is very near to white if the emission intensities of the two transitions are identical (Shoaib et al.2019).As a result, by altering the ratio of yellow to blue emission in Dy3+ ions, we selected these dopants for use in the direct manufacture of white-light emitting diodes (w-LEDs) (Dalal et al.2023 ).More study on this topic is encouraged by the lack of a report on the Dy3+ doped KSrVO4In the present work for the synthesis of KSr (1-x) VO4: x Dy3+( x=0-3 mol % ) low-cost combustion technique is used and their structural, optical, and spectral characteristics have been examined to assess their potential for display and solid-state lighting (SSL) applications.The orthorhombic phase nanoparticle synthesis was proven by PXRD patterning.The particle size and properties were investigated using TEM and SEM techniques.Virtuous white luminescence was visible by PL spectroscopy, and this was later confirmed through CIE and CCT research.The synthesized nanophosphor is useful for advanced solid-state lighting systems like white-light emitting diodes (w-LEDs) because of its crystalline and optical properties.They also demonstrated great color purity and efective emission intensity as compared to previous works, making them suitable for commercial usage.The produced nanophosphor series may be used in a wide range of real-world applications based on various photoluminescent parameters such as in lasers, fabrication of white-light emitting diodes (w-LEDs), solar cells, bioimaging, latent fingerprinting, formation of luminescent security ink, thermal and electrochemical sensors, plasma display panels, photocatalysts, hydrogen storage materials, and other advanced solid-state lighting technologies.

Optical thermometry based on fluorescence intensity ratio of Dy3+-Doped oxysilicate apatite warm white phosphor Qiyun Liu 1, Meihua Wu1, Boli Chen, Ximing Huang, Mingyong Liu, Yifei Liu, KeSu, Xin Min, Ruiyu Mi, Zhaohui Huang Beijing Key Laboratory of Materials Utilization of Nonmetallic Minerals and Solid Wastes, National Laboratory of Mineral Materials, School of Materials Science and Technology, China University of Geosciences (Beijing), Beijing, 100083, PRChina ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Optical thermometer Oxysilicate apatite Fluorescence intensity ratio Dy3+ ABSTRACTThe development of non-contact thermometers is one of the important applications of phosphors.In this work, a photoluminescence strategy by introducing Dy3+ for application in fluorescence intensity ratio thermometry (FIR) was investigated in detail.The FIR approach employs the fluorescence intensity ratios of 4I15/26H15/2 and 4F9/2-6H13/2, due to the Boltzmann variant distribution between two excited states at specific temperatures.The crystal structure, morphology, and luminescence behaviors of CaLa4 (SiO4) 3O Dy3+ were studied.When the excitation wavelength is 348 nm, two strong emission peaks of CaLa4-x (SiO4) 3O x Dy3+ at 478 and 573 nm respectively, as well as two small emission peaks located at 456 nm and 661 nm.The optical temperature measurement performance of the phosphors at different temperatures (298K–548K) was achieved because of the different thermal quenching transitions of 4F9/2-6H15/2 and 4F9/2-6H13/2.The maximum relative sensitivity and absolute sensitivity of the as-prepared phosphors as optical thermometers could reach as high as 0.1673% K-1 at 298K and 0.007087% K− 1 at 548K, respectively.

content: enhanced with an increase in doping concentration up to 3 wt %, followed by concentration quenching.The confinement effects of localized resonant energy transfer might cause higher concentration quenching.PL emission spectra were affected by the temperature range from 10K to 300K.PL emission anomalies at 270K in SrSnO3:Dy3+ have been reported to be consistent with a structural phase transition at this temperature.This work confirms Singh et al.’s observation, revealing that SrSnO3 has a phase transition at 270K. 1.Introduction Long-lasting phosphors (LLP) are a type of energy-storing material that absorbs and stores energy when exposed to sunlight or artificial light, and then gradually releases the energy by using visible light after the excitation source has been removed at room temperature for a period of several hours.A huge amount of interest has been attracted in LLPs over the past few years due to their potential applications in afterglow lights, such as road signs, information security, and anti-counterfeiting technologies [1,2].Additionally, perovskites-type oxides are a large class of materials with interesting physiochemical properties, including superconductivity, multiferroics, and electro-optics [3–5].A broad range of applications in science and technology have drawn attention to SrSnO because of its fascinating photophysical behaviour and electronic band structure.It can be used for capacitive applications at low temperatures, as a dielectric material in quantum circuits, lithium-ion batteries, and humidity sensors at high temperatures [6–9].Because of octahedral tilting caused by Sn ions, orthorhombic perovskite SrSnO typically experiences a structural distortion.Additionally, cation substitutions, synthesis techniques, and calcination temperatures alter the structure from an orthorhombic phase to a tetragonal or cubic phase [8–10].

n temperatures alter the structure from an orthorhombic phase to a tetragonal or cubic phase [8–10].Due to their attractive luminescence as well as stable physicochem ical characteristics, rare earth doped alkaline earth stannates associated with the perovskite structure have received significant interest.For instance, Goto et al.(2008) reported luminescence mechanism of Pr and Tb–Mg incorporated SrSnO3 phosphor materials synthesized through high temperature solid-state reaction technique.They suggested that after the energy has been absorbed by the host material, energy is transferred from the host lattice to rare-earth ions [11].Lei et al.(2007) examined the possible mechanism for the LLP of the Sm doped CaSnO3 phosphors prepared by two-step approach.In CaSnO3: Sm3+ reddish-orange LLP emission is clearly seen following UV light excitation [12].Kotan et al.(2013) presented luminescence properties of Tb doped SrSnO3 prepared by a solid-state reaction method, which exhibits a green-yellow and orange-red emissions in the range of 400–700 nm [13].Wang et al.(2015) published a paper in which they discussed a potential afterglow mechanism of Sm doped SrSnO3 phosphor sample prepared using high temperature solid state method [14].Canimoglu et al.(2015) reported cathodoluminescence (CL) properties of Eu3+Tb3+ and Dy3+ activated CaSnO3 under electron beam excitation.Their findings suggested that this type of material may possess various potential research and application opportunities due to its excellent luminescence properties [15].Zhao et (2017) reported the afterglow mechanism of Gd3+ doped CaSnO3 phosphors.Because of the triplet-to-singlet (T1S0) transitions of the Sn2+ ions, CaSnO3Gd3+ phosphors produce blue light [16].Hu et al.(2020) studied luminescence properties Pr doped CaSnO3 samples.Due to its greenish-blue chromaticity coordinates, it can be used in LEDs with low color temperatures and high color rendering indexes.

KEYWORDS photoluminescence, rare-earth ions, thermoluminescence, zirconia 1 | INTRODUCTIONRare-earth ions are often used as luminescent centres due to their internal electronic structure and abundant energy levels [1].Photoluminescence (PL) spectra of rare-earth ions show three types of transitions: charge-transfer transitions, 4f–4f transitions, and 4f–5d transitions [2, 3].Rare-earth-doped luminescent materials have the advantages of low quenching temperature, narrow emission band, long fluorescence lifetime, high quantum efficiency and good optical stability [4, 5].For this reason, they are widely used in many fields such as infrared induction, information display, solar cells, light storage, disease treatment and biological detection [6–8].Zirconium oxide ( ZrrO2, zirconia) is a high technological ceramic material with a wide variety of advanced applications due to outstanding mechanical, electrical, and optical properties.Moreover, ZrO2 is considered an excellent host material in PL and thermoluminescence (TL) applications because of its wide band gap (5–7 eV) [1, 9], good transparency, high refractive index, excellent photochemical stability, low phonon frequency (470cm-1) and good corrosion resistance [10].However, the TL properties of ZrO2 are determined by its polymorphic structure and chemical composition [4, 5].Solution-based ZrrrO2 or doped- ZrO2 powders synthesis routes include methods based on coprecipitation [11], hydrothermal synthesis [12] and sol–gel [13].

routes include methods based on coprecipitation [11], hydrothermal synthesis [12] and sol–gel [13].The Pechini method is another widely used solution.In a Pechini method, common metal salts are dissolved in a solution using citric acid as a chelating agents of metal ions, then ethylene glycol or a polyethylene glycol.The preparation of homogeneous precursors forms a polymeric resin on a molecular level thus segregation of particular metal ions is reduced, and compositional homogeneity is guaranteed [14–17].Due to its cheapness, handiness and insensitivity to water existence, this method has been used rather extensively in the synthesis of ferroelectric [18], capacitor [19], superconducting [20], photocatalytic [21], optical [22] and electrolytic materials for solid oxide fuel cells [23].Recently, the TL properties of ZrO2 have been subjected to many research papers.Lokesha et al.[24] reported that pure monoclinic ZrrrO2 has natural TL emissions that disappear when annealed [25].Several glow peaks for different crystal forms [26–28] and irradiations [24, 29–32] have been reported.The position and parameters of peaks depend strongly on the type of irradiation, such as gamma [33–36], beta [24], X-ray [37, 38], electron [39] and ultraviolet (UV) [33] radiation.The dose–response of some of the peaks was reported to be linear [24, 32].Lokesha et al.[24] reported that the position of some peaks shifted when the irradiation dose was increased, while some of the peaks remained stable.It was also reported that the saturation level varies depending on the material [40, 41].The effect of dopants on the glow curve was investigated, and impressive results were reported.The glow curve of pure monoclinic ZrO2 exposed to beta irradiation shows six glow peaks [31].However, the peak temperatures and parameters change slightly with the Sm3+ dopant [31].Lai and Su [37] reported that the peak at 200C ( 21.

meters change slightly with the Sm3+ dopant [31].Lai and Su [37] reported that the peak at 200C ( 21.5C / s ) in pure monoclinic ZrrrO2 emerged at about 220C in the zinc (Zn)-doped samples and the peak intensities were around 1.3 times more intense than that of the undoped ones.Lai and Su [38] suggest that Er2O3 doping in ZrrrO2 creates new trapping centres.In addition, many others reported that erbium (Er) [42] and ytterbium (Yb) [42] doping also cause new trapping levels, but gadolinium (Gd) [43], samarium (Sm) [42, 43] and dysprosium (Dy) [42–44] do not create new trapping levels.The TL emission of ZrO2 in the monoclinic phase decreased rapidly in the first 48 h after irradiation [26, 31].In general, the peaks at low temperatures have been reported to entirely disappeared in the first 24 h [24, 45], while the others at higher temperatures are very stable over a long period [24, 32, 45–47].The TL glow curves of ZrrrO2 consist of two broad, prominent peaks and several weaker peaks at higher and lower temperatures [48].The number and position of the peaks are influenced by the irradiation dose [24], the grain size [26, 32, 39, 44, 49], the annealing temperature [24, 44, 50], the excitation wavelength or type of radiation [33, 35, 49], the composition of the impurities [26, 39, 44, 51] and the heating rate [39, 52].So far, many studies have been reported on the TL properties of ZrO2 prepared by different synthesis methods, such as burning in solution and sol–gel.However, no sufficient number of studies could be found examining ZrrrO2 synthesized by the Pechini method.It is known that the crystal structure of ZrrrO2 is directly influenced by the synthesis method utilized, and the TL properties change accordingly.The present study aims to investigate the PL and TL properties of pure and rare-earth-doped ZrO2 synthesized by Pechini-type sol–gel process.

and TL properties of pure and rare-earth-doped ZrO2 synthesized by Pechini-type sol–gel process. 2 | MATERIALSANDMETHODS2.1 | Experimental methods The ZrO2, ZrO2: Dy3+ZrO2: Dy3+- Gd3+ZrO2: Dy3+- Yb3+ZrO2; Dy3+- Er3+ and ZrO2: Dy3+- Sm3+ powders were synthesized via Pechini method.ZrCl (99.5%), Sm (NO3) 36H2O (99.9%), Dy (NO3) 3.5H2O (99.99%), Gd (NO3) 36H2O (99.9%), Er (NO3) 35H2O (99.99%) and Yb(NO) 5H O (99.9%) powders were used as the starting materials.These powders were weighed in stoichiometric ratios and dissolved in distilled water.Then, citric acid and ethylene glycol were added to the mixture.The obtained solution was stirred at 80C until gel formation.The gels formed were dried in an oven at 120C for 24 h.The gels were preheat treated at 900C for 12 h in an alumina crucible.Then, heat treatments were applied at 1100 and 1200C for 12 h, respectively.X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD; Philips Panalytical, Empyrean, 45 kV, 40 mA, Cu-Kα, 0.02/2θ) measurements were made to determine the phases.The thermal behaviour of the synthesized compounds was investigated by differential thermal analysis/ thermogravimetric analysis (DTA/TGA; Perkin Elmer Diamond) analysis.Measurements were made in a nitrogen gas atmosphere at a temperature range of 50-900C, a flow rate of 200 mL/min, and a heating rate of 10C/min.Surface and particle size determination was analysed with scanning electron microscopy (SEM, LEO440).PL properties were examined by a photoluminescence spectrophotometer (PTI, Quanta Master TM30) operating at 200–900 nm with a xenon lamp.Phosphors were spread on aluminium pans, cold-pressed under 100 kg / c m2 for 5 s and weighed to 80.1 mg.The phosphor was then annealed at 600C for 60 min to remove any residual radiation effects.The irradiations were performed at room temperature with beta-rays from a calibrated 90Sr - 90Y source.The current dose rate was calculated to be 6.07Gy/min based on the geometry of the irradiator (Type9022A) [53].

ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Solid-state synthesis Luminescence LiYGeO4Dysprosium ABSTRACTLiYGeO samples were synthesized using the solid-state method, and the XRD analysis showed that the best phase purity was obtained at a sintering temperature of around 1080C..Additionally, the inclusion of additional lithium carbonate during synthesis improved both phase purity and photoluminescence in dysprosium-doped samples.The photoluminescence measurements indicated that LiYGeO4: Dy is a yellow phosphor ( max=576.5 nm).In this study, we also conducted investigations into emission lifetimes and quantum yields, which are discussed in detail.Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of LiYGeO4: Dy as a promising luminescent material with tunable emission properties. 1.Introduction Rare-earth doped oxides have been widely studied as luminescent materials, while germanates have received less attention than other oxides.
section: Solid-state synthesis of Li Y Ge O4 and luminescence properties of Dy-doped samples ![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-08-11/8ced6eae-68d9-4def-92c4-172a2f39e140/5959292d05ef6c741c9d95a14c83f5e767cf009bfb4ed4d479dff82d7e3fe579.jpg) Martynas Misevicius <sup>a,b,*</sup>, Evelina Griniuk <sup>b</sup>, Rimantas Ramanauskas <sup>a</sup> <sup>a</sup> State Research Institute Center for Physical Sciences and Technology, Sauletekio avenue3, LT-02300, Vilnius, Lithuania <sup>b</sup> Institute of Chemistry, Faculty of Chemistry and Geosciences, Vilnius University, Naugarduko street24, LT-03225, Vilnius, Lithuania ## H I G H L I G H T S • Pristine and Dy-doped LiYGeO<sub>4</sub> samples were prepared by solid-state synthesis.• Using additional Li2C O3 in starting mixture improves phase purity and PL intensity.• Dy-doped samples exhibited yellow emission with highest peak at576 nm.## A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Solid-state synthesis Luminescence LiYGeO4Dysprosium ## A B S T R A C T LiYGeO samples were synthesized using the solid-state method, and the XRD analysis showed that the best phase purity was obtained at a sintering temperature of around1080C ..Additionally, the inclusion of additional lithium carbonate during synthesis improved both phase purity and photoluminescence in dysprosium-doped samples.The photoluminescence measurements indicated that Li Y Ge O4 : Dy is a yellow phosphor ( m a x = 576 .5 nm).In this study, we also conducted investigations into emission lifetimes and quantum yields, which are discussed in detail.Overall, our findings demonstrate the potential of Li Y Ge O4 : Dy as a promising luminescent material with tunable emission properties.## 1.Introduction Rare-earth doped oxides have been widely studied as luminescent materials, while germanates have received less attention than other oxides.

content: y studied as luminescent materials, while germanates have received less attention than other oxides.However, recent reports of super-long persistent luminescence in LiYGeO4: Bi3+[1] have generated interest in this material as a host matrix.Table 1 provides a comprehensive comparison of different germanates doped with various activators.Lithium yttrium germanate LiYGeO4 belongs to the orthorhombic crystal system with the space group Pnma (62), and its structure is composed of [ LiO6 ], [YO6], and [ GeO4 ] polyhedra [2,3].Yttrium(III) is one of the rare-earth elements (REEs) and is easily exchangeable with other REEs.Li YGeO4: Eu3+ is a red-emitting phosphor exhibiting persistent luminescence [4] and first-principles on the mechanism of such phenomenon has been studied [5], while the use of Tb3+ as an activator in this germanate results in green persistent luminescent phosphor [ 6, 7 ].Furthermore, LiYGeO4 is a suitable host for upconverting phosphors when doped with Er3+/ Yb3+[8].Moreover, mechanoluminescence has been detected in LiYGeO4: Bi3+[9] and it can be enhanced via Bi3+→Tb3+ energy transfer [10].Also Mn2+-doped lithium yttrium germanate has biological window emission and has been suggested for in vivo bioimaging [11].All of this demonstrates that LiYGeO4 is a suitable host for various luminescent materials, making it an excellent choice for investigation as a matrix.Dysprosium(III) is a rare-earth element that has shown great potential as an activator for luminescent materials.One of the reasons for its popularity is its ability to emit light in the blue, yellow, and red regions of the visible spectrum, which makes it possible to use dysprosium as a singly-doped white-emitting phosphor [12,13].To date, several different crystal hosts have been explored as matrices for Dy3+ doping, including oxides, fluorides, and borates.Some examples of these include Ca3Al2O6 [14], SrAl2O4 [15], CaAl12O19 [16], LaAlO3 [17], GdAlO3 [18], and Gd3Ga3Al2O12 [19].

Ca3Al2O6 [14], SrAl2O4 [15], CaAl12O19 [16], LaAlO3 [17], GdAlO3 [18], and Gd3Ga3Al2O12 [19].Additionally, dysprosium-doped glasses have also been studied, with promising results for potential application in white LED lighting [12,20,21].The luminescence properties of dysprosium are still being investigated, but the research thus far suggests that it is a promising activator for the development of new phosphors, especially those intended for use in white LED applications.Table 1Comparison of different germanates doped with various activators.

up> – synthesis methods: SS – solid-state synthesis; SC – single-crystal growth; GC – glass-ceramic.The current study presents an investigation on dysprosium-doped lithium yttrium germanate ( LiYGeO4: Dy ) phosphors.As demonstrated in Table 1, the research on dysprosium-doped germanates is scarce [22, 23] compared to the overall publications on luminescent germanates.To the best of our knowledge, there are no existing reports on LiYGeO4: Dy3+ phosphors.The synthesis process was optimized to enhance the phase purity of the samples.Subsequently, the luminescent properties of the prepared LiYGeO4:Dy samples were thoroughly examined and analyzed. 2.Experimental Synthesis.All samples were synthesized using the conventional solidstate synthesis method.Stoichiometric amounts of analytical grade starting materials ( Li2CO3, GeO2, Dy2O3, Y2O3 ) were mixed and ground in an agate mortar.The obtained mixtures were transferred to a crucible and heated.Li YGeO4 samples were synthesized by firing them for the first time at 800C for 5 h.The resulting products were re-ground and sintered at higher temperatures for 5 h.A temperature range from 960C to 1160C was used for synthesis optimization, and subsequently, a temperature of 1080 ◦C was used for Dy-doped samples.The obtained products were once again re-ground using an agate mortar and used for further analysis.Characterization.The purity of the synthesized compounds was evaluated by X-ray powder diffraction using a MiniFlex II (Rigaku) diffractometer with CuK radiation (=1.5406 ) and a D-Tex Ultra detector.The measurements were conducted in a Bragg-Brentano geometry at a rate of 10◦/min (step size 0.01◦).Photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra were recorded using Edinburgh Instruments FLS980 spectrometer equipped with a450W Xe arc discharge lamp, a photomultiplier (HamamatsuR928P) and mirror optics for powder analysis.Excitation spectra were corrected with a reference detector.

) and mirror optics for powder analysis.Excitation spectra were corrected with a reference detector.The luminescence decay measurements were performed using excitation at a wavelength of 347 nm and emission monitored at 576.5 nm.The excitation source used was a Xe μ-flash lamp.The measurement time window was set to 8 ms, and a total of 4000 channels were utilized for the measurements.Quantum efficiencies were calculated by measuring emission spectra of the samples in Teflon coated integration sphere.Ba SO4 was used as a reference. 3.Results and discussion A series of LiYGeO4 samples using different sintering temperatures in the range of 960-1160C were prepared by the conventional solid-state synthesis method.XRD patterns of the samples are depicted in Fig.1 (left).The diffractograms of all samples are in good agreement with the standard data of LiYGeO4 (PDF04-002-3479), although small amounts of additional phases can be identified.At lower temperatures, peaks attributable to Y2O3 (PDF00-041-1105), 2Ge O5 ( PDF01.078 – 7780 ) Li2GeO3 (PDF04-008-3006), and YGeO (PDF04-014-3368) can be identified but gradually diminish with increasing temperatures up to 1040C..Sintering temperatures from 1040C to 1100C give the best phase purity with only trace amounts of additional Y2Ge2O7.Higher temperatures again result in the formation of an additional Li2GeO3 phase.XRD analysis reveals that the least amount of additional phases was obtained when the sample was sintered at 1080 ◦C (Fig.1 (right)).The obtained results are in good agreement with data reported in previous studies [ 1, 4, 7 ].A closer inspection of published X-ray diffractograms reveals that additional peaks can be seen in the region around 292-theta in most of the samples.In summary, the best phase purity was obtained in the sample prepared at 1080C, although the additional phase Y2Ge2O7 suggests that breaking of stoichiometry might be occurring during sintering due to the evaporation of lithium.

hat breaking of stoichiometry might be occurring during sintering due to the evaporation of lithium.In order to amend loss of lithium during sintering, a set of samples were prepared by adding extra Li2CO3 to the starting mixtures.XRD patterns of these samples were recorded and analyzed, as shown in Fig.2.It can be observed that the additional lithium ions have a positive effect on the phase purity of the synthesized samples.Doping LiYGeO4 with Dy3+ might also influence phase formation, thus samples with various dysprosium doping concentrations were synthesized, and their XRD patterns are depicted in Fig.3.It was determined that within our tested range (doping up to 8% Dy), dysprosium does not affect phase purity, and the obtained X-ray diffraction results are very similar to those of undoped samples.The ionic radius of dysprosium (0.912 Å) is similar to that of yttrium (0.9 Å).Therefore, it is highly likely that dysprosium incorporates into the crystal structure of LiYGeO4.This is supported by the fact that the XRD patterns of the doped samples are not significantly altered, indicating that dysprosium ions replace yttrium ions in the crystal lattice.The previously described strategy of using excess Li2CO3 in the starting mixture was employed to prepare two series of samples doped with 1% and 2% dysprosium.XRD patterns of the samples, as shown in Fig.4, indicate that the desired LiYGeO4 phase is present in all of the samples. Photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra were recorded for LiYGeO4 samples doped with different concentrations of Dy, and are presented in Fig.5.The excitation spectra were measured in the range of 250–500 nm with the emission wavelength fixed at 576.5 nm, and consisted of sharp peaks resulting from f-f transitions from the ground state of the Dy(III) ion (6H15/2) to various excited states (as marked in Fig.5).

hypersensitive transition, which is strongly influenced by the symmetry of the Dy3+ surrounding environment.When Dy3+ is located at a low-symmetry site (withnoinversioncenter), the former transition Fig.2.XRD patterns of pristine LiYGeO4 samples prepared using different amounts of additional Li+ ions in starting mixtures.Black bars represent standard diffraction peaks of LiYGeO4 (PDF04-002-3479).The color coordinates of all samples were derived from their respective emission spectra and are presented in Fig.8.The yellow luminescence observed in all phosphors corresponds to the dominant peak observed in the PL emission spectra, namely the 4F9/26H13/2 transition at 576.5 nm.Notably, all samples exhibit nearly identical color coordinates, and no discernible trends are observed in our series.The luminescence decay kinetics of all samples were measured, and the results are presented in Fig.9.

Fig.8.CIE1931 chromaticity diagram for various Dy-doped LiYGeO4 samples.Samples with different dopant concentration are marked by squares, samples prepared with different amounts of additional lithium in starting mixtures and doped with 1% and 2% of dysprosium are marked by triangles and circles, respectively. 4.Conclusions decay components in dysprosium luminescence decay is related to the concentration of dysprosium ions in the host material.As the concentration of dysprosium increases, the relative amplitude of the fast decay component increases, while the relative amplitude of the slow decay component decreases.This behavior is due to the interaction between dysprosium ions, which leads to energy transfer between them and affects the luminescence decay kinetics.

osium ions, which leads to energy transfer between them and affects the luminescence decay kinetics.At low dopant concentrations, the dominant decay component is the slow one, corresponding to radiative decay from isolated dopant ions.However, at high dopant concentrations, the fast decay component becomes dominant due to energy transfer between the closely spaced dopant ions, leading to nonradiative decay.The quantum yields of the samples were measured, and the results are listed in Table 3.The quantum yields of the samples with different dysprosium concentrations coincide with the PL emission intensities (depicted in Fig.5 ).The highest quantum yield is in the 2% Dy-doped sample, while higher doping levels result in a decrease in luminescence efficiency.Adding additional lithium during the synthesis of 1% Dy-doped samples improves quantum yields.Similar to the XRD and PL measurements

Full Length Article Spectroscopic and energy transfer properties of NaTb (WO4) 2 phosphor and crystal sensitized by Dy3+ Jiaqi Zhang a,b, Yidong Huang b, Xinghong Gong b, Jianhua Huang b, Yanfu Lin b, Yujin Chen b,* a College of Chemistry, Fuzhou University, Fuzhou, Fujian 350116, China b Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Materials Chemistry and Physics, Fujian Institute of Research on the Structure of Matter, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Fuzhou, Fujian 350002, China ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Dy3+:NaTb(WO4)2 phosphor Dy3+:NaTb(WO) crystal Dy3+ sensitizing ions Spectroscopic property Dy3+Tb3+ energy transfer ABSTRACTTwo series of Dy3-+:NaTb(WO) and Ḋ y Ḍ 3 +:NaGd(WO) phosphors doped with different Dy3+ concentrations were prepared by the solid-state reaction method.Dy3 +→Tb3+ energy transfer and fluorescence properties of Dy3+: NaTb (WO4) 2 phosphors doped with different Dy3+ concentrations were firstly investigated by exciting at 455 nm.Strong Tb3+ green fluorescence around 545 nm was observed in the Dy3++:Nab (WO4) 2 phosphors due to the efficient Dy3+Tb3+ energy transfer.Excited at 455 nm, polarized spectroscopic properties of a (9.28 at.%) Dy3+: NaTb (WO4) 2 crystal grown by the Czochralski method were studied at room temperature.The peak absorption cross-sections of the crystal at 454.6 nm, corresponding to the 6H15/24I15/2 transition of Dy3+, are 2.7410-21 and 3.9310-21 c m2 for σ and π polarizations, respectively.The peak emission cross-sections of the crystal, corresponding to the 5D47F5 transition o Tb3+, are 5.610-21 at 545 nm and 11.

ctions of the crystal, corresponding to the 5D47F5 transition o Tb3+, are 5.610-21 at 545 nm and 11.510-21 cm 2 at 548.6 nm for σ and π polarizations, respectively.Tb3+ green fluorescence around 545 nm was obviously enhanced in the crystal excited at 455 nm due to the Dy3+Tb3+ energy transfer.The results show that Dy3+ can be used as sensitizing ions to enhance the visible fluorescence of Tb3+ in the NaTb(WO) phosphor and crystal excited at 455 nm. 1.Introduction Based on its 5D47F5 5 transition emitting around 540 nm, Tb3+ has been widely studied as an activating ion of green luminescent and laser materials, which can be used in many fields, such as lighting, display, biomedicine and visible light communication [1–4].Up to now, many Tb3+ doped phosphors, such as Tb3+Ca2Ga2SiO7, Tb3+LaBMoO6, Tb3+BiOCl, and Tb3+: CsAlSi2O6, have been investigated and used in white light-emitting diodes (w-LEDs) [5–8].Tb3+ doped fluoride crystals have also been demonstrated as promising gain media for green laser.For example, pumped by a diode laser at 488 nm, a542 nm green continuous-wave (CW) laser with an output power of 43.8 mW and a slope efficiency of 52% has been obtained in a.Tb3+: LiLuF4 crystal [9].At present, the developed 450 nm blue diode has been widely used as the excitation light source of w-LEDs [10–12].However, Tb doped materials have no absorption band around 450 nm, and are usually excited by ultraviolet or 486 nm light [13,14].Dy3+ can effectively absorb blue light around 450 nm due to its 6H15/24I15/2 transition [15].Furthermore, the 4F9/2 multiplet of Dy3+, which is located below the 4I15/2 multiplet, is only about 700 cm - 1 higher than the 5D4 multiplet of Tb3+.Therefore, the efficient energy transfer from Dy3+ to Tb3+ may be occurred in the Tb3+/ Dy3+ co-doped materials.Then, the green emission of Tb3+ can be enhanced due to the sensitization of Dy3+ under excitation at 450 nm.

the green emission of Tb3+ can be enhanced due to the sensitization of Dy3+ under excitation at 450 nm.Up to now, some investigations have shown that an efficient energy transfer between Dy3+ and Tb3+ can be occurred in Tb3+/ Dy3+ co-doped materials excited by ultraviolet light [16–18].Under the excitation at 368 nm, the emission intensities at 543 and 584 nm of Tb3+ in Dy3+/ Tb3+: Ca1.5Sr1.5 (PO4) 2 phosphors increase with the slight increment of Dy3+ concentration, due to the energy transfer from Dy3+ to Tb3+[19].Under the excitation at 350 and 377 nm absorbed both by Tb3+ and Dy3+, as well as 485 nm absorbed by Tb3+, visible fluorescence bands peaked at 541 and 620 nm of Tb3+ can be enhanced obviously by the sensitization of Dy3+ in Tb3+/ Dy3+ co-doped phosphate glasses [20].However, to the best of our knowledge, energy transfer between Dy3+ and Tb3+ as well as the emission characteristic of Tb3+ in Tb3+/ Dy3+ co-doped materials, especially for the crystal, excited at 450 nm have not been investigated in detail.In addition, because of the weak cross-relaxations between the upper multiplet 5D4 and lower multiplets 7F J ( J=0-6 ), concentrationdependent fluorescence quenching of the 5D4 multiplet is weak in the Tb3+ doped luminescent material [21].Therefore, it is meaningful to develop a high concentration Tb3+ doped luminescent material that can be excited by light source around 450 nm.Tungstate forms a variety of inorganic compounds with monoclinic and tetragonal structures, which is an interesting luminescent material host.NaTb (WO4) 2 (NTW) crystal has a tetragonal structure with a space group of I41 / a and can be grown easily by the Czochralski method.Polarized spectroscopic properties of the NTW crystal have been studied at room temperature, and the crystal has large absorption and emission cross-sections [22].Up to now, studies about luminescence properties of Dy3+:NTW phosphors and crystal have not yet been reported.

studies about luminescence properties of Dy3+:NTW phosphors and crystal have not yet been reported.In this work, energy transfer between Dy3+ and Tb3+ in the Dy3+: NTW phosphors with different Dy3+ doping concentrations excited at 455 nm was investigated firstly.Then, a Dy3+: NTW crystal was grown and the polarized spectroscopic properties of the crystal excited at 455 nm were analyzed. 2.Synthesis and spectroscopic properties of Ḋ y Ḍ 3 - þ:NTW phosphors 2.1.Synthesis and characterization Two series of x Dy3-+:NTW ( x=0, 1, 5, 10, 15 and 20 at.%) and rx Dy3+: NaGd (WO4) 2 ( Dy3+: NGW, x=1, 5, 10, 15 and 20 at.%) phos phors were prepared by the solid-state reaction method.The starting materials of Tb4O7 ( 99.99 % ) Dy2O3 (99.99%), Gd2O3 (99.99%), Na2CO3 ( A.R.), and WO (A.R.) were weighted according to the desired stoichiometric ratio.The raw materials were fully mixed in an agate mortar and then had been sintered in air at 1000 ◦C for 25 h.XRD measurements of all the phosphors were carried out on a MiniFlex 600 powder diffractometer with a Cu-Kα radiation (=1.5406 ) For brevity, only the XRD patterns of the x Dy3+: NTW ( x=0, 10.and 20 at.%) and x Dy3-+:NGW (x=10 and 20 at.%) phosphors are shown in Fig.1(a).All the diffraction peaks are indexed to the tetragonal phase of the NGW (JCPDS25–0829).No secondary phase is observed in the XRD pattern, which indicates that the Dy3+ doping concentration as high as 20 at.% could not cause the change in the crystal structure.The magnified XRD curves in a range of 28.0–29.5◦ for different phosphors are shown in Fig.1(b).It can be seen that the peak position has an obvious shift towards a larger 2θ angle, which may be caused by the smaller ion radius of Tb3+( 0.92: A ) and Dy3+(0.91 Å) than that of Gd3+(0.94 Å). 2.2.Spectroscopic properties Excitation spectra, fluorescence spectra, and fluorescence decay curves of the phosphors were recorded at room temperature by a spectrometer (FLS1000, Edinburgh).

ay curves of the phosphors were recorded at room temperature by a spectrometer (FLS1000, Edinburgh).By monitoring the fluorescence at 545 nm corresponding to the 5D4→7F5 transition of Tb3+, the excitation spectra of the Dy3+NGW, Dy3+:NTW and NTW phosphors were recorded.No excitation band appeared in the excitation spectrum of the Dy3+NGW phosphor, and the excitation spectra in 420–520 nm of the (10 at. % ) Dy3+: NTW and NTW phosphors are shown in Fig.2.Energy level diagrams of Dy3+ and Tb3+ are shown in Fig.3.Only a strong excitation band around 488 nm appeared in the excitation spectrum of the NTW phosphor, which corresponds to the 7F65D4 transition of Tb3+Compared with the excitation spectrum of the NTW, there are three additional excitation bands of 424–435, 445–461 and 466–483 nm observed in the excitation spectrum of the Dy3+: NTW phosphor, which correspond to the transitions from 6H15/2 to 4G11/2, 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 multiplets of Dy3+, respectively.The stronger excitation intensity around 488 nm observed in the NTW phosphor than that in the Dy3+: NTW phosphor is caused by the higher Tb3+ concentration in the NTW phosphor.By comparing the excitation spectra of the Dy3+NGW, Dy3+NTW and NTW phosphors, it is confirmed that the Dy3+Tb3+ energy transfer process can be occurred, and the Tb3+ emission at 545 nm can be realized by pumping the Dy3+ at 455 nm in the Tb3+/ Dy3+ co-doped material. content: e the excited Dy3+ after influenced by 60 kGy gamma doses. 1.Introduction In recent years rare earth (RE)-doped glasses have been extensively investigated due to their gifted luminescence properties [1].These kinds of glasses have high emission eficiencies in the range from ultraviolet to the infrared region.This emission is corresponding to 4f–4f electronic transitions owing to the shielding effects of the outer 5 s and 5p orbital on the 4f electrons [2].Such important optoelectronic properties give these materials good chance to be used as solid-state lasers, optical amplifiers, sensors, color displays and solid-state lighting (LEDs) devices [3–5].To fulfill the requirements to get the best optoelectronic devices, attention should be given for the kind of the doped glass.Borate glass is generally known to have good solubility of rare earth ions, due to its different coordination numbers besides to its other important properties such as high thermal stability and low melting point [6].Though, borate glass is sensitive to its surrounding atmosphere and hygroscopic.This problem was found to be solved by the addition of another glass forming material such as silicon oxide.The soda-lime- borosilicate glass has been found to be a suitable optical material because of its optical transparency at the excitation and lasing wavelength [7].However, the spectroscopic characterizations changed according to the kind of the added rare earth ion.To enhance the optical characteristics, the doping RE ions should be chosen to have high luminescence properties [8–10].Dysprosium is considered as one of the most suitable rare earth ions with excellent luminescence eficiency and useful for high density optical storage.It is also well-thought-out to be one of the most RE ions competitor for telecommunication amplifiers, mid-IR lasers (4.4and2.98nm) and Q-switching devices [11].It is known that emission of Dy ions in the visible region depends mainly on its non-hypersensitive and hypersensitive transitions.

ions in the visible region depends mainly on its non-hypersensitive and hypersensitive transitions.The first transition is (4F9/26H15/2) in Dy3+ ion which is the non-hypersensitive one and is considered as a magnetic dipole transition, it is insensitive to the host environment [12,13].On the other hand, the other transition in Dy3+ ion is (4F9/26H13/2) which is hypersensitive transition, that considered to be an electric dipole transition; it is greatly sensitive to the host environment [14,15].Though, the intensities are strongly sensitive for both transitions to the coordination environment of the host glass system Main objective of this work is to carry out a study of the reducing effect of gamma irradiation on optical properties in the UV- NIR absorption range, luminescence properties using PL spectroscopy, Physical, structural properties of Dy3+ ions using ESR as a candidate for optoelectronic glasses.For this purpose, two concentrations of Dy ions doped in borosilicate glass containing sodium were used.The physical properties of the prepared glass are also investigated. 2.Methodology 2.1.Materials and methods Glass samples containing 25% Si2O-30 % Na2O-45 % B2O3 doped x Dy2O3, where x=0, 2, 4 mol% were carefully weighed and mixed.The glass samples were labelled as BSN, BSNDy and BSNDy4; respectively.The used chemicals are Sigma Aldrich high pure (99.99%) sodium carbonate (Na2CO3), Boric acid (H3BO3), dysprosium oxide (Dy2O3) and silicon oxide (SiO2)..The samples were melted using porcelain crucible in electrical furnace.at 1100 °C for 1/2 h then the molten poured and pressed between two preheated stainless-steel sheets and then moved to annealing oven at 450C and left till it reaches 25C 2.2.Techniques The polished glass samples with dimensions of 12 cm in area and 20.1 mm thickness were measured at room temperature, by UV–Visible/NIR spectrophotometer (model V-770-Japan) supported by PMT detector.

room temperature, by UV–Visible/NIR spectrophotometer (model V-770-Japan) supported by PMT detector.Photoluminescence spectra of the glassy samples has been detected using fluorescence spectrometer of model (Jasco FP-6500-Japan) supported with Xenon lamp that act as the excitation light source with fixed parameters as scan speed=0.1 s and step lengt 1=0.25 nm in addition to slit width 0.2 nm.ESR studies of the crushed glassy samples were recorded by ESR spectrometer of model (Bruker ER4102, Germany) with fixed parameters: Gauss Amplitude 9 and microwave power 2.553 mW under conversion time 20.48 ms and time constant 81.92 ms.Canadian 60Co gamma cell with dose rate 0.966 kGy/h established at Egyptian Atomic Energy Authority has been used to irradiate the glassy samples by 30 and 60 kGy at room temperature. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.XRD analysis X-ray diffraction analysis is recorded for all prepared samples BSN, BSNDy2 and BSNDy4 after prepared and the results according to Fig.1a show amorphous phase for all samples that prove the glassy structure of the samples.After irradiation by 60 kGy gamma dose the samples measured again and it is found that all samples still retain the amorphous characters that prove the stability of glass network after exposed to gamma ray up to 60 kGy as given by Fig.1b. 3.2.Absorption spectral analysis The absorption spectra of all glasses have been recorded in the range 270 -1900 nm.Fig.2 shows the absorption spectra of all the Dy3+ ions doped glasses.The spectrum reveals that in the presence of Dy six bands in the UV visible range at 347, 362, 386,423, 452 and 470 nm, corresponding to the ground state 6H15/2 to the transition states 6P7/2, 6P5/2, 4I13/2, 4G11/2, 4I15/2 and 4F9/2.While another five bands are observed in NIR region at 792, 887, 1084,1253 and 1662 nm corresponding to the transitions, 6F5/26F7/2,: 6F9/2,: 6F11/2 and 6H11/2 respectively.The absorption band at 1253 nm (6F11/2) is strong; this transition is a hypersensitive transition [16,17].

orption band at 1253 nm (6F11/2) is strong; this transition is a hypersensitive transition [16,17].From the figure it can be noticed that no new peaks were formed nor a change in their positions is observed, but the only change is in their intensity.This can be referred to the conversion of the s p2 planar triangle BO3 units to Sp3 planar tetrahedra BO4 units, which is more stable.At the same time more non bridging oxygens are formed.This observed increase in the intensity of the absorption bands with the increase of Dy ion concentration in the NIR range can be also, an indication of the uniformly distribution of Dy ions in the glass matrix.As according to beers Lambert law [18] the increase in the absorbance intensity at a certain wavelength is an indication of the increase in concentration. Fig.1.X-Ray Diffraction analysis of all prepared samples (a) before and (b) after exposed to 60 kGy of gamma ray.Figure 3a,b,c viewing that the base glass (BSN) has no significant peaks before or after irradiation.On the other hand, glass containing 2% Dy (BSNDy2) showed a slight shift to a higher wavelength for all peaks upon irradiated by a dose of 30kGy, while its absorbance is highly reduced.It can be also noticed that the peaks returned to its initial wave-length position when the irradiation dose is 60 k Gy, with more reduction in its intensity.The observed red shift of the bands at 30kGy can be referred to the excitation of the electrons occurred by this irradiation dose causing increasing in the number of NBOs while the decrease in the absorption can be an indication of the less freedom of the electrons to transit between sites in the same orbital [19].

RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYStructural, morphological, and optical characteristics of Gd2Si2O7: Dy3+ nanophosphors for WLEDsIsha Gupta 1 | Devender Singh 1 | Pawan Kumar 1 | Sitender Singh 1 | Shri Bhagwan 2 | Vinod Kumar 3 1Department of Chemistry, Maharshi Dayanand University, Rohtak, Haryana, India 2Department of Chemistry, Government College Satnali, Mahendergarh, Haryana, India 3Department of Physics, Netaji Subash University of Technology, Delhi, India Correspondence Devender Singh, Department of Chemistry, Maharshi Dayanand University, Rohtak 124001, Haryana, India.Email: devjakhar@gmail.com Funding information Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, India.Grant/Award Number: 09/382 (0247)/2019-EMR-IAbstract Yellowish-white light-emitting Gd2-Si2O7: Dy3+ ( x=1-5.mol%) nanophosphors were prepared using a solution combustion synthesis method.Fluorescence spectrophotometry and X-ray diffraction measurements were performed to scrutinize the optical performances and phase recognition of the designated nanophosphors.The outcomes specified that the prepared phosphors were crystallized into a triclinic phase with a P-1 space group.As the concentration of Dy3+ ions was increased, the unit-cell volume decrease proportionally due to the replacement of large-sized Gd3+ by small-sized Dy3+ ions.Under ultraviolet excitation at 349 nm, emission spectra consisted of two pronounced emission lines at 482 nm (blueline), 578 nm (yellowline), and a relatively weaker emission at 670 nm (redline) due to 4F9/26H15/2, 4F9/26H13/2, and 4F9/2→6H11/2 intraconfigurational transitions of Dy3+ ions, respectively.The evidence about the site symmetry around Dy3+ ions was examined by considering the ratio of yellow-to-blue emission intensity.The observed critical distance (R) value was 20.

ing the ratio of yellow-to-blue emission intensity.The observed critical distance (R) value was 20.56A (5A), which signified that energy transfer primarily occurred due to multipolar interaction.The obtained coordinates were close to the white region of the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage chromaticity - diagram, which marked a significant milestone in the development of white lightemitting diodes. KEYWORDS critical distance, Gd2Si2O7, triclinic, WLEDs, yellow-to-blue (Y/B) 1 | INTRODUCTIONIn recent years, material scientists have made marked efforts to replace traditional lighting tools with advanced lighting resources to meet the intensified demand for global energy consumption [1, 2].Therefore, energy saving is a significant challenge that entices the widespread attention of material innovators.This issue is overwhelmed by the development of light-emitting single-phase nanophosphors, which might be the future of solid-state lighting (SSL) devices.The characteristic luminescence of phosphors primarily depends on the types of host lattice, synthesis method, nature, and concentration of dopant ions.Several rare-earth-doped aluminates [3, 4], vanadates [5], oxides [6], phosphates [7, 8], and silicates [9] have been identified in the published literature.Three crystalline structures of silicates, i.e.oxy orthosilicates Gd2SiO5 (GSO), pyrosilicates Gd2Si2O7 (GPS), and apatite-like silicates Gd4.67 (SiO4) 3O (GSAP), occur in the Gd2O3 – SiO2 pseudobinary system [10].Among them, gadolinium disilicate (Gd2Si2O7) phosphors classify themselves as a significant class of light-harvesting nanomaterials because of their peculiar characteristics, viz., their nonhygroscopic nature, excellent thermal and chemical stability, wide band gap, and high density, which cast them as the best performers in disparate fields such as medical imaging, high-energy physics, scintillators, fuel cells, white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), etc.[11, 12].Gd2Si2O7 exhibits two different polymorphic forms, i.e.

light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), etc.[11, 12].Gd2Si2O7 exhibits two different polymorphic forms, i.e.polymorph - Gd2Si2O7 consists of isolated chainlike Si3O10 groups plus additional SiO4 tetrahedra, while the - Gd2Si2O7 structure contains all Si atoms arranged in Si2O7 double tetrahedral groups [13].Rare-earth-doped x - Gd2Si2O7 silicates reveal excellent luminescence properties desired for the design and architecture of SSL devices [14].Trivalent rare-earth ions are preferred as dopant ions, as their ionic radii match the radii of the host matrix [15].The luminescence behaviour of Ce3+-doped Gd2Si2O7 phosphors has been studied broadly [10], although to the author's knowledge, the elucidations of the optical and structural characteristics of Gd2Si2O7 doped with other rare-earth ions (Eu, Sm, Tb, and Dy) are very limited [16].Gd2Si2O7 is an inert matrix in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum and has the well known ability of Gd3+ ions to efficiently absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation and transfer it to some active rareearth ions such as Dy3+, Tb3+, and Er3+[17].Based on the known capacity of Dy3+ ions to emit in white regions in the matrix, - Gd2Si2O7 was used to fabricate single-phase light-emitting Dy3+.doped phosphors.Characteristically, synthetic routes play a vital role in deciding morphological and optical characteristics [18].However, despite the high chemical and thermal stability shown by rare-earth silicates, only a few reports have been found in the published literature about phosphors based on these matrices [19].The solution combustion synthesis (SCS) method has the benefits of homogeneity, a short heating period, and requires low temperature during the preparation of phase pure Gd2Si2O7 compound [20–22].The traditional chemical route, viz., the solid-state method, would alternatively need a higher synthesis temperature and a longer heating time.Here, authors have explored the possibility to synthesize Gd2-xSi2O7: x Dy3+(x=1–5 mol%) using a SCS method.

RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYStructural, morphological, and photoluminescence properties of RE ( RE=Dy3+, Eu3+, Sm3+) -doped CaAlBO phosphor synthesized by combustion method Roshana T.Maske 1 | Atul N.Yerpude 1 | Rupesh S.Wandhare 2 | Sanjay J.Dhoble 3 1Department of Physics, N.H.College, Bramhapuri, India 2Department of Physics, ACSCollege, Maregaon, India 3Department of Physics, RTMNagpur University, Nagpur, India Abstract Correspondence Atul N.Yerpude, Department of Physics, N.H.College, Bramhapuri, Chandrapur District 441206, India.Email: atulyerpude@gmail.com The CaAlBO4.R E ( RE=Dy3+, Eu3+, 5 m3+) phosphor were prepared via combustion synthesis and studied by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) analysis, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), photoluminescence (PL) spectra and CIE coordinates.The phase formation of the obtained phosphor was analyzed by XRD and the result was confirmed by standard PDFCard No.1539083.XRD data successfully indicated pure phase of CaAlBO4 phosphor.The crystal structure of CaAlBO4 phosphor is orthorhombic with space group Ccc 2 (37).The SEM image of CaAlBO4 phosphor reveals an agglomerated morphology and non-uniform particle size.The EDS image provides evidence of the elements present and the chemical makeup of the materials.Under the 350 nm excitation, the emission spectrum of Dy3+ activated CaAlBO4 phosphor consists of two main groups of characteristic peaks located at 484 and 577 nm which are ascribed to 4F9/2→6H15/2 and 4F9/2→6H13/2 transition of Dy3+ respectively.The PL emission spectra of CaAlBO4: Eu3+ phosphor shows characteristics bands observed around 591 and 613 nm, which corresponds to 5D0→7F1 and 5D0→7F2 transition of Eu3+ respectively, upon 395 nm excitation wavelength.

rresponds to 5D0→7F1 and 5D0→7F2 transition of Eu3+ respectively, upon 395 nm excitation wavelength.The emission spectra of Sm3+ activated CaAlBO4 phosphor shows three characteristic bands observed at 565, 601 and 648 nm which emits yellow, orange and red color.The prominent emission peak at the wavelength 601 nm, which is attributed to 4G5/2→6H7/2 transition, displays an orange emission.The CIE color coordinates of CaAlBO4RE ( RE=Dy3+, Eu3+, Sm3+) phosphor are calculated to be (0.631, 0.368), ( 0.674, 0.325) and (0.073, 0.185).As per the obtained results, CaAlBO4: RE ( RE=Dy3+, Eu3+, Sm3+) phosphor may be applicable in eco-friendly lightning technology. KEYWORDS borate, combustion synthesis, phosphor, photoluminescence, SEM, X-ray diffraction 1 | INTRODUCTIONIn the past decades, research and the scientific community have been more interested in the development of lanthanide-activated phosphor because of its large applications in areas such as plasma display, solar cells, laser, white light, bio-imaging and phototherapy [1–4].In the current investigation, there are a number of research papers on the development of inorganic phosphors and on trying to improve the luminescence properties of the phosphors.The new solid light source, such as white light-emitting diode (IED) has tremendous advantages over lamps, such as high efficiency, long life, environmental protection, good color rendering and energy savings.Because of their high efficiency, long life, energy savings, and environmental protection, the demands on solid-state lighting devices increases day-by-day and creates interest in research.There are so many inorganic compounds used to study luminescence properties, such as silicate, aluminate, borate and phosphates.The borates have tremendous properties like stable chemical properties, high luminous efficiency and are simply synthesized.Owing to their advantages, the borate material is used in non-linear optical devices, high-efficiency florescent lamp, laser mate rial and plasma display panels [5–8].

RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYStructural, optical, and luminescence properties of Dy3+-activated potassium calcium silicate phosphor for white light-emitting diodes Vibha Sharma 1 | Shreya Maurya 1 | Anu 1 | Aman Prasad 2 | Allam Srinivasa Rao 1 1Department of Applied Physics, Delhi Technological University, New Delhi, India 2Department of Physics and Computer Science, Dayalbagh Educational Institute (DEI), Deemed University, Agra, India Correspondence Allam Srinivasa Rao, Department of Applied Physics, Delhi Technological University, Bawana Road, New Delhi 110042, India.Email: drsrallam@gmail.com Funding information Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-University Grants Commission (CSIR-UGC), Government of India, Grant/Award Number: UGCRef, 1352CSIR-UGCNETDFC.2018 Abstract A dysprosium (Dy3+)-activated potassium calcium silicate (K4CaSi3O9) phosphor was prepared using a solid-state synthesis route.The phosphor had a cubic structure with the space group Pa3 as confirmed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements.Details of surface morphology and elemental composition of the as-synthesized undoped KCS phosphor was obtained using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy.The chemical structure as well as the vibrational modes present in the as-prepared KCS phosphor was analyzed using Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy.Diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) were used to determine the optical bandgap of the phosphors and were found to be in the optical range 3.52–3.71 eV.Photoluminescence (PL) spectra showed intense yellow emission corresponding to the 4F9/2→6H13/2 transition under 350 nm excitation.Commission International de l0Eclairage colour chromaticity coordinates were evaluated using the PL spectral data lie within the white region.

lour chromaticity coordinates were evaluated using the PL spectral data lie within the white region.Dexter theory and the Inokuti–Hirayama (I–H) model were applied to study the nature of the energy transfer mechanism in the as-prepared phosphors.The relatively high activation energy of the phosphors was evaluated using temperature-dependent PL (TDPL) data and confirmed the high thermal stability of the titled phosphor.The abovementioned results indicated that the as-prepared KCS: Dy3+ phosphor was a promising candidate for n-UV-based white light-emitting diodes. KEYWORDS activation energy, I–H model, luminescence, phosphor, w-LEDs1 | INTRODUCTIONIn this modern era of digitization, in many areas affecting social and economic development, energy is crucial.The constant demand for energy results in permanent changes to our environment.A significant portion of the total energy generated across industries is used for both indoor and outdoor lighting.Typical incandescent and fluorescence lighting uses either gas discharge or heat.Due to the high temperatures involved, both phenomena are linked to significant energy losses [1, 2].Along with energy efficiency, it is crucial to guarantee that the lighting technology is environmental friendly.There is no prominent option compared with solid-state lighting if all of these requirements must be met.It is based on light-emitting diodes, which are essentially semiconductor chips with p–n junctions that are forward biased to emit light.Luminous efficacy, low power dissipation, persistence, environmental friendliness, and a lasting operative lifetime are just a few of the wonderful advantages that phosphor converted light-emitting diodes (pc-LEDs) have over other traditiona sources of lighting [3].Most currently available white LEDs (w-LEDs) use a blue-emitting (450–470 nm) diode, which activates a Y3Al5O12: Ce3+ (YAG:Ce) phosphor and causes it to generate yellow light.

ich activates a Y3Al5O12: Ce3+ (YAG:Ce) phosphor and causes it to generate yellow light.How ever, the lack of the red component in this method results in a low and high colour rendering index (CRI) and colour-correlated tempera ture (CCT) values, respectively, in the light that is produced [4].A common technique for producing white light is to coat an n-UVLED chip with red, green, and blue (RGB) phosphors.But it is not an easy task to maintain the proper ratio of RGB colour-emitting phosphors to obtain resultant white emission and the use of three phosphors requires a greater number of dopants that increases the cost of LEDs.Therefore, it is necessary to dope a single rare earth ion to lower the costs.Owing to at least two preeminent emission bands in the blue and yellow regions, Dy3+ is the most suitable rare earth ion for the production of white light [5].White light produced by Dy3-+ ion-doped phosphors has high quantum efficiency, thermal stability, cost– effectiveness and the desired values of the Commission Internationa de l0Eclairage (CIE) and CCT [6].Moreover, the selection of appropriate host material is required to obtain qualitative luminescence [6].Various materials such as oxides, nitrates, silicates, vanadates and molybdates are used as the host, but silicates are preferred as they possess high chemical and physical stabilities.Silicates have hightemperature strength and chemical inertness that makes them strong candidates for many practical applications [7].Recently, various reports have used Dy3+ ion as a dopant and silicates as the host mate rial to reinforce the luminescence properties of phosphors [8–12].To the best of our knowledge, no reports are accessible on the lumines cence studies of Dy3+-doped KCS phosphors.

f our knowledge, no reports are accessible on the lumines cence studies of Dy3+-doped KCS phosphors.Therefore, in the cur rent work Dy3+-activated KCS phosphors were synthesized using a conventional solid-state synthesis approach and investigated for thei structural, morphological, and luminescence behaviours in detail using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectros copy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), photoluminescence (PL), PL decay, and temperature-dependent (TD)-PL characterizations.The results obtained in the present study show that the KCS: Dy3+ phos phor could be a favourable candidate for the application of w-LEDs. 2 | EXPERIMENTAL2.1 | Phosphor preparation KCS: x Dy3+ ( 0.5 ss 1.5, x=0.25 ), represented by KCSDy0.50, KCSDy0.75, KCSDy1.00, KCSDy1.25 and KCSDy1.50, was prepared using traditional solid-state synthesis route.The starting materials were potassium carbonate ( 1, CO3, 99.9 % ), calcium carbonate ( CaCO399.9%), silicon oxide ( SiO299.99%) and dysprosium oxide ( Dy2O399.9%).The raw ingredients were first weighed in accordance with the nominal composition of phosphor and then completely mixed and ground for 2 h using an agate mortar and pestle.The ground samples were kept in alumina crucibles and then heated at 800-C for 5 h in an electric furnace.After cooling down, the final products were ground once again for further characterization [13, 14].The complete procedure for the synthesis process is represented by the flowchart in Figure 1. Structural-suppressing concentration quenching in dysprosium single-phase white emission and their application in optical thermometric and white light-emitting devices Fuhua Gao a, Wasim Ullah Khan a,*, Waheed Ullah Khan b, Zhiqi Yea, Yueli Zhang a,** a State Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Materials and Technologies, School of materials science and Engineering, Sun Yat-Sen University, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510275, China b Institute for Advanced Study, Shenzhen University and School of Physics and Optoelectronics Engineering, Shenzhen 518060, PRChina ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Suppressed concentration quenching Energy migration Thermometric Light-emitting diodes ABSTRACTSingle Dy3+ doped material is indispensable to establish single-phase white emission.However, concentration quenching (CQ) and poor stability limit its wider application.Herein, Dy3+-doped Ca3LuAl3B4O15 ( CLAB; Dy3+) is reported to be an advanced dual-emitting micro phosphor with promising optical properties making it a promising applicant with potential applications in thermometric and n-WLEDs.The host has a highly disordered crystal structure, suppressing the CQ phenomena of Dy3+, and attains a high doping level.Using the Kubelka–Munk equation, the optical bandgap Calculated for the matrix is 66 e V, which is ideal for n-WLEDs.Under 350 nm UV light, the prepared CLAB: Dy3+ displayed emissions at 476 nm and 569 nm with a CIE diagram of (0.382, 0.402) and IQE up to 18.3%.The Blass and Dexter model analyzed the energy migration (EM) mechanism.The dual emissions in CLAB: Dy3+ have distinct thermal reactions caused by thermal quenching.

Structural and luminescent behaviour of Dy(III) activated Gd3Al5O12 nanophosphors for white-LEDs applications Pawan Kumar a, Sitender Singh a, Isha Gupta a, Kapeesha Nehra a, Vinod Kumar b, Devender Singh a,* a Department of Chemistry, Maharshi Dayanand University, Rohtak, 124001, India b Department of Physics, Netaji Subash University of Technology, Sector 3, Dwarka, Delhi, 110078, India HIGHLIGHTS • Urea based gel-combustion method has been utilized for the synthesis of Gd3- xAl5O12:xDy3+ (x=0.01 to 0.07) nanophosphors.• XRD data based Rietveld refinement technique confirms the formation of cubic crystal phase.• The crystallite size and lattice microstrain were calculated by Debye-Scherrer’s and Williamson-Hall method.• Dipole-quadrupole interactions are accountable for the phenomenon of concentration quenching.• Combination of blue and yellow bands in the emission spectra is responsible for the white emission of the considered nanomaterials. content: ed the development of a single cubic phase of all the prepared samples with space group Ia-3d (230).Furthermore, the crystallite size was calculated through Debye-Scherrer’s formula and the Williamson-Hall method.In the EDX spectrum, the nonappearance of peaks analogous to the foreign elements affirms the pure synthesis of the considered phosphors.TEM observation reveals agglomerated porous crystalline material with non-uniform shapes and varying particle size in 2080 nm range.Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy has been applied for the examination of chemical bonding with other vibrational characteristics.The luminescence study confirms the intense blue and yellow emission of synthesized phosphors at 482 nm and 576 nm respectively owing to 4F9/26H J ( J=15/2, 13/2) transitions.Moreover, the detailed evaluation of the concentration quenching process established that dipole-quadruple interaction is answerable for the decrease in luminescence intensity after optimum dopant ion concentration.The chromatic analyses recommend that emission from the optimized nanophosphors lies in the region of cool white light.The outcomes of the present investigation propose that Gd3Al5O12: Dy3+ phosphors might be a potential candidate for white-LEDs applications. 1.Introduction Energy is a driving force for the economy of a country because it is a major aspect certifying the growth of the material civilization of modern society.The speedily expanding market in the lighting area has increased the demand for the production of a light-emitting material.The synthesis of phosphors has widely fascinated the enormous consideration because of their remarkable characteristics including brilliant thermal durability, high intensity and environmentally friendly behaviour [1–3].However, significant upgrading is needed to fabricate the nanophosphors having minor current saturation, superior efficiency and better color coordinates [ 4, 5 ].

sphors having minor current saturation, superior efficiency and better color coordinates [ 4, 5 ].Inorganic phosphors based on rare earth metal ions find a wide array of applications in the photonic field such as display devices (field emission display, vacuum fluorescent displays, plasma display panels and flat panels display) [6–8], magnetic resonance imaging, cathode rays tubes, infra radiation detectors, fluorescent lamps, biological labels, scintillators, solar cells, lasers, optical fibers, electroluminescent and solid-state lighting [9–12].Among the various host materials, aluminate garnet (due to their exceptional radiation conversion efficacy, high chemical and radiative durability and wide band-gap) as a host matrix shows superior characteristics like resistance properties, high melting point and high strength at high temperature [13–15].Additionally, it demonstrates a few more significant characteristics like humidity sensors and transparent materials.The garnet (Gd3Al5O12) has a body-centered cubical (BCC) structure with space group Ia-3d [16].Rare earth aluminate garnet crystal has BCC structure formed of Al–O tetrahedron and Al–O octahedron, in which Al–O polyhedra are associated with each other through the common angles.In this skeleton, each tetrahedron is linked to four octahedrons and each octahedron is associated with the six tetrahedra [17].Trivalent dysprosium ion-doped gadolinium aluminate garnet shows both yellow and blue emission which is utilized in the develop ment of the optical display devices and white light-emitting diodes.In addition, Gd3+ may sensitize the 4F9/26H15/2 (blue) and 4F9/26H13/2 (yellow) emissions of trivalent dysprosium ion, through an effective energy-transfer between Gd3+ and Dy3+ ions, further improving the Dy3+ emission [18].Also, Dy3+ containing compounds utilized as thermographic phosphors are widely considered for the measurement of surface temperature by applying a thin coating of the phosphors to the substrate.

aerosol furnace method, co-precipitation method, gel-combustion technique, sol-gel process, spray-pyrolysis process etc.have been employed for the synthesis of the nanophosphors [19–24].This study aims to report the synthesis, structural and luminescence analysis of Gd3Al5O12: Dy3+ phosphors.From the literature survey, no report is available for the present phosphors synthesized by the gel-combustion technique.The elemental and detailed structural analysis was done by EDX, TEM, XRD and FT-IR spectroscopy.The optical nature of the processed nanomaterial was inspected via photoluminescence spectroscopy. 1.1.Exploratory 1.1.1.Materials and synthesis The powdered samples of Gd3-xAl5O12: x Dy3+ ( x=0.01 to 0.07) nanophosphors were synthesized through self-propagating gel-combustion method (Fig.1).The high purity chemicals i.e., rare earth nitrates including Gadolinium nitrate hexahydrate [ Gd (NO3) 3.6H2O399.9% pure], Dysprosium nitrate hexahydrate [ Dy (NO3) 3.6H2O3, 99.9% pure], Aluminium nitrate nonahydrate [ Al (NO3) 3.9H2O, 99% pure] and Urea [ NH2CONH2, 99% pure] were purchased from Sigma Aldrich.Ni trates of metals have been preferred as raw materials due to their easy dissolution in water and low decomposition temperature [25].The weighed quantity of precursors in their stoichiometric composition were dissolved in a little amount of deionized (DI) water and the solution was allowed for thermal treatment (about 80 ◦C) on the magnetic hot plate with rigorously stirring for about 15–20 min.A viscous framework mixture was obtained on heating and then the calculated amount of urea was added with a small amount of water in the solution.A transparent gel-type solution was prepared for the further heating process.In this process, a self-sustained exothermic redox reaction takes place between urea as reducer and metal nitrates as an oxidizer.

ned exothermic redox reaction takes place between urea as reducer and metal nitrates as an oxidizer.Now, this viscous blend was placed into the preheated (600C) furnace for 12 min to carry out proper combustion.During the combustion, emission of gases such as N2, CO, CO2, NO2 and NH3 takes place which results in a fluffy white porous product.The deliverance of massive energy throughout the redox combustion reaction was liable to the crystallinity and low-temperature treatment, answerable for the smaller particle size of the powdered samples [26].The obtained product was ground and sintered at 1100, 1200 and 1350C temperature for 4 h.After calcination, the crystalline product was ready for carrying out different analyses. 1.2.Instrumentation The investigation of structural and spectroscopic characteristics of selected materials was examined by exploiting diverse techniques at room temperature.The phase excellence of Gd3Al5O12 and Dy3+ activated Gd3Al5O12 nanomaterials were investigated through X-ray diffractogram, recorded in the wide range of Bragg angles (2θ) in between 10 and 80 with Cu-Kα (=1.5416 Å) radiation source by using a Rigaku Ultima-IVX-ray diffractometer (workingatavoltageof40kVand40mAcurrent).The instrument operates at a scanning rate of two degree per minute and a step interval of 0.02◦.Rietveld refinement was achieved by utilizing the FullProf program to evaluate basic lattice parameters and for the quantification of crystalline phases.The investigation of the particle’s shape, size and morphological information of the processed materials was carried out via Transmission Electron Microscopy (TECNAIelectronmicroscope) operating at a voltage of 200 kV.The nature of vibrations of metallic bonds in the molecules of present nanophosphors was recorded by using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (NicoletiS50FTIRspectrophotometer).The elemental assimilation and element analysis mapping was carried out on Elemental Ametek EDX spectrometer.
