content: O stretching and B-O-B bending modes as well as Al-O and Gd-0 bonds in the phosphor samples.Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis reveals that Sm, Eu, Dy, and Tb have been successfully doped into GdAl3 (BO3) 4..The observed broad intrinsic luminescence band can be caused by oxygen-induced luminescence defects in the GAB host with hydrous precursors.The luminescence properties of rare earth ion-doped GdAl3 (BO3) 4 samples are analysed by photoluminescence spectra, showing their optimal doping concentrations and critical distances of Dy3, Eu3, Sm3 and Tb3+ are 2 wt% − 25.8 Å, 7 wt% − 17 Å, 1W1 % - 32.59 A, and 7 w t0/0-17.03A.Additionally, the energy transfer mechanism for luminescence quenching was determined as dipole-dipole (for Dy3+, Eu3+, and Tb3+) or dipole-quadrupole (forSm3+) ) and the cross-relaxation process.Gd Al3 (BO3) 4 samples obtained by doping with different RE3+ ions exhibit intense light emissions with different colors originating from different RE3+ ions under 349 nm excitation.When doped with different concentrations of RE3+ ions, the luminescence properties of the samples changed.The synthesized luminescence materials have potential applications in lighting and display technologies. 1.Introduction A high luminescence efficiency phosphor material is currently in great demand for various applications in photonics due to its energysaving and environmental friendliness.These are well studied and documented in the literature.Rare earth elements (REE) either singly or co-doped into these phosphor materials play a very central role in photonic applications such as solid-state lasers, displays, solar panels, and sensors [1–6].Phosphors obtained through the synthesis of novel, single-phase REEs through various chemical processes exhibit high quantum efficiencies and are therefore essential for a variety of photonic applications [7,8].

high quantum efficiencies and are therefore essential for a variety of photonic applications [7,8].Recently, borate-based phosphors have sparked interest in the luminescent community due to their excellent properties, including lowtemperature synthesis, good optical properties, large nonlinear optical coefficients, high thermal and chemical stability, and environmental friendliness [9–11].It is a very active and burgeoning area of research.Similarly, due to their high luminescence efficiency, wide excitation wavelength range, a high quenching temperature, and stable thermal properties, RE ion activated aluminates have been key topics of study in the literature for many years [12–14].The luminescence performance of doped ions is highly dependent on the choice of matrix.Efficient inorganic boro-aluminate-based phosphors such as the compound GdAl3 (BO3) 4 (GAB), which possesses a huntite structure [ CaMg3 (CO3) 4 ] with trigonal crystal structures associated with the space group R32 [15], can therefore be a suitable host for lanthanide ions to emit luminescence.Combined with the excellent properties of both boric oxide and alumina, GAB becomes a low-cost and environmentally friendly host material [16].Compared to other materials, GAB can accommodate various dopant ions and has a weaker quenching of luminescence combined with excellent thermal stability, high luminescence efficiency, favorable nonlinear optics, and excellent physical and chemical properties.As a phosphor host, it is suitable for a wide range of photonic applications.By understanding the properties of the GAB phosphors and their interactions with the RE ions, the authors hope to gain insight into the ways in which they can be used in lighting and displays, such as their potential for high efficiency.A general review of the studies in the literature on GAB host material and the results obtained is given below.Yang et al.

1%; 2%; 2%; 3%; 5% and 7%) as high purity and RE additives.As a first step, 10 ml of distilled water solution was dissolved in a quartz beaker, followed by the addition of boric acid.This solution was mixed with urea and glycine as fuels and stirred continuously at a constant temperature ( i.e., 80C ) for an hour on a magnetic stirrer.Following the opening of the beaker lid, the water immediately evaporated, gel formed, and the heating and stirring process continued.Then, the gel-like solution was placed in a preheated muffle furnace at 650C for combustion, and gray porous nanostructures were formed by a rapid combustion reaction.It is completely calcined in a muffle furnace at 1100C for 2 h to complete the process and remove impurities.Rare earth doped nanophosphors are now ready for characterization after cooling GAB nanomaterials in the form of white fly ash for 24 h.

Gd3+/ Sm3+), ( Al3+/ Eu3+; Gd3+/ Eu3+), and ( Al3+/ Tb3+; Gd3+/ Tb3+) are (71.69%; 2.15%), (81.13%; 3.22%), (77.35%; 1.07%), and (73.58%; 1.88%), respectively.To indicate that a dopant ion can be substituted by an ion in the host structure, this ratio must be less than 15% [28].According to the results, we suggest that Gd3+ sites in the GAB host can be effectively replaced by any RE dopant ion, such as Dy3+3+Eu3+ and Tb3+ due to comparable ionic radii and similar valence of those ions.By introducing Dy3+ and Tb3+ ions, the main diffraction peaks shift slightly towards higher degrees compared to undoped GAB.Nevertheless, when Eu3+ and Sm3+ ions are doped, the main peaks are slightly shifted to a lower degree [29].This is due to Gd3+ ions having a larger ionic radius than Dy3+ and Tb3+ but a smaller ionic radius than Eu3++and Sm3+.In conclusion, the results indicate that all RE ions used in this study are undoubtedly incorporated into the lattices of the GAB host without altering the crystalline structure of the samples.This suggestion is consistent with previous literature examples of GAB samples [ 16, 18, 30 ].Yang et al.(2022) reported the luminescence properties of Dy3+ single-doped and Eu3+ co-doped GAB phosphors [16].Because the ionic radius and charge valence of RE3+ ions are close enough to that of Gd3+, authors conclude that the Dy3+ and Eu3+ site can be substituted for Gd3+Therefore, they can occupy the same site without disrupting the crystal lattice structure.The parameters from Rietveld refinement confirm this, as they indicate that Eu3+ and Dy3+ actually occupy the Gd3+ site.Zhang et al.(2016) investigated energy transfer processes of Ce3+/ Tb3+ doped GAB samples [30].It was found that both Ce3+ and Tb3+ ions were easily replaced by Gd3+ ions inside the GAB host structure.Note that although the ionic radius of Ce3+( 1.

replaced by Gd3+ ions inside the GAB host structure.Note that although the ionic radius of Ce3+(1.01nm) is larger than that of 3+Eu3+, and Dy3+ ions used in our study, Ce3+ ions would easily substitute Gd3+ sites.The substitution results in a reduction in the volume of the cell as well as a variation in the coordinates of the atom’s position in the cell [16].Clearly, the synthesized crystals exhibit lattice distortion.The reduced symmetry of the crystal field is beneficial for the luminescence properties of the doped ions.This is because of the lattice distortion that occurs due to the substitution of the lattice atoms.The distortion changes the local environment of the ion and leads to a shift in the electronic energy levels, which in turn affects the optical properties of the material.Gd3+ substitution for other RE3+ is conductive to the regulating the luminescence properties of GAB hosted phosphors.This can be beneficial for applications such as phosphors and scintillators [31].Furthermore, each of the REs incorporated replaces a few of the Gd3+ ions without altering the rhombohedral structure of the GAB.Notably, since the ionic radius of Gd in the host sample is very close to the ionic radius of the doped REs, GAB allows higher concentrations of REs to be doped into the host material.While the radius change represents a very small change in the bulk lattice parameter, the volume change at luminescence sites may be very large.This is because of the close coupling between traps and recombination sites.The average crystalline sizes of undoped GAB as well as Dy3+, Sm3+, Eu3+, and Tb3+ singly doped GAB phosphors were estimated using Scherrer’s equation [32].All samples were obtained with an average crystalline size of 45 nm.Fig.2 shows the FTIR spectra of different as-synthesized GAB nanomaterials in the range of 450-4000 cm - 1.The recorded infrared spectra mostly reflect vibrations related to the B−O group vibrations, as illustrated in Fig.2.

reenish-yellow light situated at (0.425, 0.472) in CIE coordinates with a color temperature of 3652K.All the measured luminescence lifetime curves exhibited a single-exponential nature.Excellent thermal stability was found for this tungstate phosphor (the activation energy is 0.3520.01 e V ).The measured absolute photoluminescence quantum yield was around 10.5%.The results presented in this work show that Li3Ba2Gd3 (WO4) 8Dy3+ phosphors with strong yellow emission are promising candidates for white-light emitting LED (wLED) applications.Received 15th April 2023Accepted 27th June 2023DOI: rsc.li/rsc-advances 1.Introduction In recent years, white light-emitting diodes (wLEDs) in the eld of solid-state lighting have gained growing attention due to their outstanding advantages, such as high reliability, high luminous eficiency, good material stability and environmental sustainability.1–5 Presently, one of the most common approaches to achieve white light is to blend commercial blue LED chips with yellow phosphors such as the well-known Ce3+ doped yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG:Ce3+).6,7 It shows high stability and performance (high PhotoLuminescence Quantum Yield, PLQY), absorbing blue light and emitting yellow persistent luminescence, as well as combining eficiently those blue and yellow photons to yield white light in a compact wLED.8 However, the YAG material has a high melting point (1970C9) which makes the industrial exploitation of this material expensive.It is therefore relevant to search for new efective luminescent materials that radiate yellow light with cheaper industrial fabrication cost (e.g.lower melting temperature).The performance of such wLEDs highly depends on the luminescence performance of the phosphors which are doped with diferent rare-earth ions (RE).10,11 The host matrix and activator ions are two factors that inuence the luminescence properties of the phosphor.

activator ions are two factors that inuence the luminescence properties of the phosphor.Among the activator ions (RE), dysprosium ions (Dy3+) are of interest to produce yellow emission.The 4F9/26F15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions in Dy3+ ions are located in the blue and yellow spectral regions, respectively.It is known that the 4F9/2 rl & 6H13/2 transition is hypersensitive to the crystal eld (according to the selection rules L=2, J=2 ).12-14Therefore, the relative intensity of the yellow emission is responsive to the surrounding local environment of the Dy3+ ions and it is possible to change the ratio of yellow to blue (Y/B) emission intensities and produce white light using Dy3 doped luminophores.15,16 The Y/B ratio depends on the level of Dy3+ doping and the structure of the host matrix (i.e., the symmetry of the point group for the Dy3+ ion sites).17 The emission intensity of the 4F9/26F13/2 transition is greater than that of the 4F9/26H15/2 transition (resultinginyellowluminescence) for the case where Dy3+ ions localize to the low-symmetry sites, and vice versa.Among the many crystals that have been reported, tungstate crystals exhibit a much higher Y/B intensity ratio compared to other crystals, due to the high level of covalency of the metal–ligand binding.18–20 Tungstate crystals are an important class of oxide host matrix for doping with RE ions.These crystals have received much interest due to their stable chemical properties, rich crystal chemistry, and potential applications in areas such as laser systems, electrochemistry, and photonics.21–23 Asa member of the tungstate family of materials, the quaternary compound Li3Ba2RE3 (WO4) 8 ( RE=La-Lu, Y ), which is isostructural with Li3Ba2RE3 (MoO4) 8, has been explored as a host for solid-state lasers, and its crystal structure has been solved by Pan et al.24, 25It shows a monoclinic system with C2/c space group symmetry.

Study on the thermoluminescence and optically stimulated luminescence of LiMgPO4: Dy phosphors synthesized by different methods Zilong Yin, Henglei Chen *, Guangwen Feng, Qun Jing, Mieradilijiang Muhetaier School of Physics and Technology, Xinjiang University, 830017, Urumqi, China ARTICLEINFOKeywords: LiMgPO4:DyTLOSLSol-gel method High-temperature solid-state method ABSTRACTLiMgPO4:Dy phosphors were synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method and sol-gel method.The effects of different synthesis methods on crystal structure, morphology, thermoluminescence (TL) properties, and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) properties of LiMgPO4:Dy were studied using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), TL glow curve and continuous wave OSL (CW-OSL) curves.XRD patterns showed that the crystal phase of the samples synthesized by the two methods is LiMgPO.The morphology of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was better than that synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method.The TL sensitivity of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was higher than that synthesized by hightemperature solid-state method.The TL strongest glow peak of the LiMgPO4: Dy sample synthesized by hightemperature solid-state method was 363K, while that the LiMgPO4: Dy sample synthesized by sol-gel method was 380K.The OSL sensitivity of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was significantly higher than that synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method.The synthesis method had no effect on the OSL decay of the sample.LiMgPO:Dy phosphor synthesized by sol-gel method may be a suitable candidate material for radiation dosimetry. 1.Introduction Thermoluminescence (TL) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) are widely used in the field of radiation dose measurement (Kumar et al., 2011).
section: Study on the thermoluminescence and optically stimulated luminescence of Li Mg P O4 : Dy phosphors synthesized by different methods Zilong Yin , Henglei Chen <sup>*</sup>, Guangwen Feng , Qun Jing , Mieradilijiang Muhetaier School of Physics and Technology, Xinjiang University, 830017, Urumqi, China ## A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: LiMgPO<sub>4</sub>:Dy TL OSL Sol-gel method High-temperature solid-state method ## A B S T R A C T LiMgPO<sub>4</sub>:Dy phosphors were synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method and sol-gel method.The effects of different synthesis methods on crystal structure, morphology, thermoluminescence (TL) properties, and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) properties of LiMgPO<sub>4</sub>:Dy were studied using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), TL glow curve and continuous wave OSL (CW-OSL) curves.XRD patterns showed that the crystal phase of the samples synthesized by the two methods is LiMgPO .The morphology of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was better than that synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method.The TL sensitivity of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was higher than that synthesized by hightemperature solid-state method.The TL strongest glow peak of the Li Mg P O4 : Dy sample synthesized by hightemperature solid-state method was363K, while that the Li Mg P O4 : Dy sample synthesized by sol-gel method was380K.The OSL sensitivity of the samples synthesized by sol-gel method was significantly higher than that synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method.The synthesis method had no effect on the OSL decay of the sample.LiMgPO :Dy phosphor synthesized by sol-gel method may be a suitable candidate material for radiation dosimetry.## 1.Introduction Thermoluminescence (TL) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) are widely used in the field of radiation dose measurement (Kumar et al., 2011).

content: luminescence (OSL) are widely used in the field of radiation dose measurement (Kumar et al., 2011).The luminescence mechanism of TL and OSL is basically the same, only after the material absorbs the radiation energy, the excitation mode is different.TL stimulates the material to emit light by heating, while OSL stimulates the material to emit light by irradiation of light source (Malthez et al., 2018).Compared with TL, OSL has many advantages, such as high sensitivity, wide measuring range, easy to use, real-time online measurement, etc., so OSL is more popular in the field of radiation dose measurement (Singh et al., 2012).To date, many materials have been studied in order to develop phosphors with excellent OSL properties, such as Y3Al5O12(Kulkarni et al., 2008), NaLi2PO4(Sahare et al., 2016), MgAlO (Pan et al., 2021) and MgBO (Kitagawa et al., 2021; Ozdemir et al., 2021).In recent years, LiMgPO4 doped with rare earth elements has become a promising radiation dose material due to its good chemical and thermal stability and optical properties (Thomas and Sebastian, 2012).Dhabekar et al.(2011) first tested the OSL properties of LiMgPO4: Tb, B phosphors with OSL sensitivity 1.3 times that of commercial Al2O3:C.Afterwards, Gai et al.(2015), Kulig et al.(2016), Guo et al.(2017), Gieszczyk et al.(2018) and Kellerman et al.(2020) have studied LiMgPO4 doped with rare earth elements.The research found that LiMgP04 doped with different types of rare earth elements not only exhibited excellent TL performance but also had significant OSL performance, which can be used as TL dosimeters or OSL dosimeters (Bajaj et al., 2016).The synthesis methods of LiMgPO4 doped with rare earth elements mainly include high-temperature solid-state method and sol-gel method.Goni et al.(1996) first synthesized LiMgPO4 by high-temperature solid-state method in 1996, which has been widely used due to its advantages of simple operation, high yield and high repeatability.

h has been widely used due to its advantages of simple operation, high yield and high repeatability.The sol-gel method has the advantages of low synthesis temperature, good mixing effect of precursor and high purity of synthesized material.In2020, Keskin et al.(2020) et al.have synthesized LiMgPO4, LiMgPO:Tb and LiMgPO4: Dy phosphors by sol-gel method, and conducted radioluminescence, photoluminescence, cathodeluminescence and thermoluminescence studies.The TL curve of LiMgPO4; Tb showed two temperature peaks at 471K and 556K.Palan et al.(2016) et al.have synthesized LiMgPO4; Tb using the high-temperature solid-state method.The TL curve showed four temperature peaks at 423K, 511K, 564K and 629K, respectively.The variety of trap types and trap depths in crystals synthesized from different methods lead to differences in the number and position of peak temperatures, thereby affecting the TL and OSL properties of the materials.It is crucial to explore the TL and OSL properties of rare-earth doped LiMgPO4 synthesized by different methods in order to synthesize high-performance TL and OSL materials.Rare earth elements are mainly used as dopants and play an important role in the manufacture of highly sensitive TL and OSL phosphors.In this work, the rare earth element Dy is used as a dopant because Dy-doped LiMgPO4 may be a suitable candidate for radiation dosimetry.In order to synthesize LiMgPO4: Dy luminescent materials with better properties, LiMgPO4: Dy phosphors were synthesized by high temperature solid phase method and sol-gel method.TL and OSL properties of the samples synthesized by the two methods were compared.To our knowledge, OSL properties of LiMgPO4: Dy phosphors under β irradiation have not been reported. 2.Materials and methods 2.1.High-temperature solid-state method LiMgPO4: Dy was synthesized by high-temperature solid-state method.The doping level of Dy3+ is 0.7 mol.% of Li+.The mixtures of LiOH (A.R.), MgO (A.R.), NH4H2PO4 ( A.R.) and Dy2O3 (A.R.) in molar ratio were ground in an agate mortar.

MgO (A.R.), NH4H2PO4 ( A.R.) and Dy2O3 (A.R.) in molar ratio were ground in an agate mortar.The resulting mixture was placed in a corundum crucible and insulated in a resistance furnace at 600K for 1 h and then at 900K for 1 h.Then it was heated to 1173K and kept warm for 10 h, and then cooled to room temperature naturally.After the sample was taken out and ground again, it was kept at 1173K for 10 h and cooled to room temperature naturally to obtain the final product. 2.2.Sol-gel method LiMgPO:Dy was synthesized by sol-gel method.The doping level of Dy3+ is 0.7 mol.% of Li+NH4H2PO4 (A.R.) and C6H8O7 ( A.R.) as chelating agents were added into 50 mL ultrapure water to form solution 1, then LiNO3 ( A.R.) and C4H6O4Mg+H2O ( A.R.) were added into 50 mL ultrapure water to form solution 2, and dopant Dy (NO3) 35H2O ( A.R.) was dissolved into 5 mL ultrapure water to form solution 3.To add slowly solution 2 to solution 1 and stir to form the mixture, then transfer the mixture to a large beaker and add solution 3 and stir at room temperature for 2 h.Then the large beaker was put into a drying oven and dried at 353K for 8 h to get clear gel, followed by drying at 373K for 20 h and 473K for 30 min to get dry gel.Once the dry gel has cooled to room temperature, remove the dry gel from the large beaker and grind it into a powder in an agate mortar.Finally, the dry gel was heat treated and calcined in a corundum crucible for 3 h at 1123K in a resistance furnace. 2.3.Methods of characterization The BRUKERD8 advance X-ray diffractometer (XRD) was used to test the crystal structure of the sample.The scanning rate was 4◦/min and the scanning range was 580◦.The morphology of LiMgPO4: Dy was observed by HITACHSU8010 field emission high-power scanning electron microscopy (SEM).The 0.1 g powder samples was pressed into a disc with a diameter of 9 mm, and the TL glow curve of LiMgPO4: Dy was measured through the LTTL-3DS multifunctional defect fluorescence spectrometer.

LiMgPO4: Dy was measured through the LTTL-3DS multifunctional defect fluorescence spectrometer.The sample was irradiated with X-ray, the tube voltage was 50 k V, the tube current was 80A, and the cumulative dose was 5Gy.The temperature range was 300K–700K, and the heating rate was 3 K / s The 0.1 g powder samples was pressed into a disc with a diameter of 9 mm, and the OSL glow curve of LiMgPO4: Dy was measured through the TL/OSL-DA-15 spectrometer.The sample was irradiated with 90Sr - source, the dose rate was 0.073Gy / s, and the cumulative dose was 1Gy.The excitation light source uses a blue light-emitting diodes with a wavelength of 470 nm and a power of 80 m W / c m2..The detection filter used U-340 filter.The OSL signal was measured at room temperature for 300 s in CW-BOSL mode, and the time for each data point was 0.5 s. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.XRD analysis Fig.1 shows the XRD pattern of LiMgPO4:Dy synthesized by hightemperature solid-state method and sol-gel method.Compared with PDF84–0342 standard card, it was found that the crystal phase of all samples was LiMgPO4, indicating that the required samples were successfully synthesized by the two synthesis methods.The doping of rare earth elements has little effect on the crystal structure of LiMgPO4, indicating that the dopants are all doped in the lattice. 3.2.SEM analysis Fig.2(a) shows the SEM image of LiMgPO4: Dy synthesized by high temperature solid-state method.The microstructure of samples synthesized by high temperature solid phase method was composed of irregular particles, including flake and fine particles.The particle size distribution was uneven, and the particle size ranged from 1 to 10 μm.The SEM image of LiMgPO4: Dy synthesized by sol-gel method is shown in Fig.2(b).The polygonal grains of the sample synthesized by sol-gel method were obvious, the particle surface was smooth and the grain boundary was clear.The sample particles were agglomerated together, and the size of the particles was about 710 μm.Fig.

nfirms the presence of Zr-O and O-H stretching, along with HO bending modes in the phosphor sample.The wide luminescence band seen at 460 nm is attributed to luminescence defects in the ZrO2 induced by oxygen, and the presence of water molecules.Photoluminescence (PL) spectra analysis reveals pronounced emission peaks at 491 and 578 nm, corresponding to 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions, respectively, upon excitation at 349 nm.Optimizing the Dy3+ doping concentration to 0.4 wt% and achieving a critical distance of 31.82 Å resulted in efficient energy transfer.Notably, co-doping K+ as a charge compensator significantly enhances the luminescence intensity.Moreover, at lower temperatures, direct excitation of Dy3+ ions through our pump wavelength, coupled with exciton-mediated energy transfer, leads to a remarkable increase in PL intensity.Tailoring the doping concentrations effectively shifts the emission spectrum of the phosphor mixture, aligning with the standard white light illumination co ordinates (0.333, 0.333).This property positions the material as a promising candidate for applications in white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs) and various high-quality lighting applications.The enhanced photoluminescence and temperature dependence observed in ZrO2: Dy3+ phosphors upon the incorporation of K++ ions pave the way for their potential utilization in advanced luminescent devices. 1.Introduction The properties of zirconia (ZrO2);, such as its high thermal and chemical stability, mechanical strength, and biocompatibility, make it a desirable matrix material for luminescent materials [1].Furthermore, its wide band gap and high refractive index provide it with transparency in the visible spectral region.The unique properties of the material make it an ideal choice for a wide range of applications such as LED lighting, optical displays, and bio-imaging.It can also be used for sensing applications due to its ability to detect chemical and physical changes [2,3].

o be used for sensing applications due to its ability to detect chemical and physical changes [2,3].It is well known that ZrO2 can take three different forms - monoclinic, tetragonal and cubic - each is a distinct polymorph which is thermally stable in varying temperature ranges [4].The size of the crystallites is a determining factor in which of the three crystalline phases of nanostructured ZrO2 will be stabilized [5].Although it is known that different temperatures can stabilize different polymorphs of ZrO2, the exact critical crystallite size needed to stabilize the three distinct crystal phases is not well understood.Additionally, larger crystallites require more energy to form and are therefore more thermodynamically unstable than smaller ones.This means that, when the size of the crystallites is small enough, the more stable amorphous phase will be formed.Recent studies have investigated the role of oxygen vacancy in stabilizing the tetragonal polymorph of ZrO2 at room temperature, because of the distinct preparation process of nanomaterials based on ZrO2 [ 6-8 ].At room temperature, ZrO2 takes on a monoclinic crystal shape; however, this can be stabilized by introducing rare earth ions such as Eu3+, Tb3+, Sm3+ to create oxygen vacancies.As the temperature increases, this material transitions into a tetragonal and cubic structure, which is unstable in bulk at ambient conditions [9].Over the past few years, ZrO2 structures have been enhanced by incorporating several rare earth elements.By introducing dopant ions to the host material generates additional energy levels in the band structure, modifying the band gap energy.This can lead to new properties of the host material such as an increase in conductivity or optical absorption.Additionally, this process has the potential to generate a whole new range of materials with different uses.This has opened up exciting possibilities for the development of a wide range of new materials for use in various applications.

7 wt) phosphor materials were synthesized using the hydrothermal route.To synthesize the ZrO2: 0.004Dy3+: x K+ phosphor material, ZrOCl28H2O (250mg) was dissolved in distilled water (25ml) using a magnetic stirrer at 1200 rpm for 10 min.Subsequently, Dy (NO3) 3 x H2O and KNO3 were added to the solution in the required stoichiometric ratios and stirring was continued for an additional 30 min.Afterwards, CH4N2O (1000mg) was integrated into the mixture.After the urea had been completely dissolved, the pH of the solution was adjusted to 12 with the addition of ammonia water.The pH value at which this phenomenon occurs is documented as optimal for attaining maximal luminescent emission.Additionally, it is well-established that the crystallization kinetics of zirconium oxide exhibit enhancement under conditions of pronounced acidity or alkalinity.Upon reaching the targeted pH level in the precursor solution, the emergence of a white precipitate serves as a tangible indication that the process of ZrO2 formation has been initiated [20].The mixture was stirred for an additional 2 h before being transferred to a45 ml Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave and hydrothermally treated at 140C for 24 h.The mixture was gradually cooled to the room temperature at a rate of 5C / s.Following cooling down to room temperature, the white precipitate was collected, washed (threetimesthroughDIandacetone) and dried in an oven at 60C for 3 h.Finally, the samples were calcined in a muffle furnace at 500C for 3 h to remove impurities and complete the process.The same procedure was used for the synthesis of the ZrO2: x Dy3+ and undoped samples. ch element is depicted with its atomic and weight percentage in the insets of the experimental data.XRD analysis confirmed the existence of a close correlation between the concentrations of the ions and their nominal values.Zr O2 was success fully incorporated with Dy and K, as demonstrated by this finding.The order of luminescence enhancement impact by various alkali metal cations (M+) is arranged in the order of IK > INa > ILi.This hierarchy likely stems from the distinctive ionic radii associated with each alkali metal, resulting in varying degrees of influence on the surrounding crystal field environment encompassing the luminescent center.Among these, K+ ions, boasting the most substantial ionic radii, manifest the most pronounced enhancement in luminescence efficiency.Upon the introduction of Dy3+(trivalentdysprosium) into the ZrO crystal structure, its role as a dopant—substituting Zr4+—introduces the potential for charge imbalances.The selection of K+ ions holds promise as a superior candidate for integration into the ZrO2 framework.This selection hinges on their larger ionic dimensions, which have the propensity to induce a reduced lattice distortion.Moreover, the K+ ions exhibit a heightened potential to effectively counterbalance the positive charge associated with the Dy3+ ions, accentuating their suitability for this role. PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: RSCAdv., 2023, 13, 13423 Synthesis, photoluminescence, Judd–Ofelt analysis, and thermal stability studies of Dy3+ doped BaL a2Zn O5 phosphors for solid-state lighting applications Irfan Ayoub ab and Vijay Kumar *ab Received 21st April 2023Accepted 26th April 2023Here, we report a series of white-emitting Bia (La2-xDyx) ZnO5 ( x=0-7 mol%) phosphors synthesized via a high-temperature solid-state reaction.The synthesized phosphor's phase purity and tetragonal crystal structure were confirmed by an X-ray powder difraction (XRPD) pattern.The wide bandgap characteristic feature was assessed through reflectance spectra, and the estimated bandgap was found to be 4.70 eV.Besides analyzing the efect of doping on the surface morphology, the distribution of ions on the surface was observed through the secondary ion mass spectroscopy technique.The synthesized phosphor was found to display bluish (486nm) and yellowish (576nm) bands in the emission spectra under the excitation of 325 nm and 352 nm, which together are responsible for producing the white luminescence.The analysis of Judd–Ofelt parameters indicates the symmetric nature of Dy3+ substitution in the present host.The thermal stability of the phosphor was assessed by varying the temperature up to 403K, and it was found that the synthesized phosphor possesses improved thermal stability with an activation energy of 0.29 eV.The photometric evaluations of the present phosphor revealed the CIE coordinates around the near-white regime (0.3448, 0.3836), along with the colorcorrelated temperature value of 5102K.All research on this luminescent material's unique features points to the possibility of using it to fabricate white-light-emitting devices for solid-state lighting applications.

Materials synthesis and characterization A series of Ba (La2-xDyx) ZnO5 ( x=0-7.mol%) phosphor material was synthesized by using the solid-state reaction method.All the precursors employed, i.e., BaCO (99.9%), La2O3 (99.9%), ZnO (99.9%), and Dy2O3 (99.9%), were procured from Sigma Aldrich.Following the stoichiometric calculations, the required amount of all the precursors was thoroughly mixed in an agate mortar for several hours.During mixing, ethyl alcohol was added at regular intervals for proper homogenization.The mixture was then transferred to an alumina crucible and kept in a mufle furnace at 900 °C for 2 h with a heating and cooling rate of 5 min - 1,.The mixture was removed from the furnace for further grinding and then calcinated at 1200 °C for 6 h with a heating and cooling rate of 5 * min - 1.Aer calcination, the mixture was ground into a powder form of the desired nanomaterial.

RESEARCHARTICLELUMINESCENCEWILEYThermoluminescence dosimeter (TLD) studies of Ca10K (PO4) 7Dy phosphor for applications in radiation dosimetry Sansar Chand 1 | Rohit Mehra 1 | Vibha Chopra 2 1Department of Physics, Dr.B RAmbedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar, Jalandhar, India 2P.G.Department of Physics and Electronics, DAVCollege Amritsar, Amritsar, India Correspondence Rohit Mehra, Department of Physics, BRAmbedkar National Institute of Technology Jalandhar, Jalandhar, Punjab, India.Email: mehrar@nitj.ac.in Abstract This study reports the thermoluminescence (TL) aspects of Ca10K (PO4) 7Dy phosphor synthesized using a wet chemical method for the first time.The X-ray diffraction (XRD) results confirm the formation of the desired crystalline phase.Surface morphological studies reveal the formation of polyhedrons and agglomerations having an average diameter of 200 nm, while energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) data show the presence and composition of the elements in appropriate amounts.The effect of Dy doping concentration has been studied on the TL properties with exposure to gamma radiations from the Co-60 source.The best TL response has been observed for 5 mol% Dy doping concentration.The glow curve is simple and consists of a single peak at 130C..The effect of the heating rate has been studied on the TL glow curve, and the heating rate of 5C / s shows the best TL response.The various TL properties such as annealing conditions, dose–response, TL linearity, fading, and reusability of the prepared phosphor have been studied to check its suitability as a good TL dosimeter (TLD).TL characterization of the phosphor reports that the TL response is linear from 5- to 2000Gy.The results show that this phosphor can be a good TLD for the dosimetry of gamma radiations from Co-60.

KEYWORDS dosimetry, gamma irradiation, phosphates, phosphor, thermoluminescence 1 | INTRODUCTIONPhosphate phosphors are getting attention as they are good luminescent hosts and show efficient photoluminescence (PL) and thermoluminescence (TL) properties [1].Recent studies have reported their remarkable applications in light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and radiation dosimetry [2].Phosphate phosphors doped with rare earth elements are being explored in radiation dosimetry because of their important features such as nontoxicity, chemical and thermal stability, low effective atomic number, and low-cost synthesis [3–6], as well as their noticeable fluorescent properties [7, 8].The development of a new TL dosimeter (TLD) with enhanced properties requires a thorough understanding of the role of the defects in producing luminescence.In this study, a small attempt has been made to explore the TL characteristics of new Ca10K (PO4) 7Dy phosphor.TL is exhibited by any material when it has been previously exposed to some ionizing radiation, and subsequent heating releases the energy absorbed in the form of light signal [9].In TL dosimetry, a linear relationship between the absorbed dose and TL intensity emitted by the TLD is utilized for its use in radiation dosimetry.The other applications of TL include archeological dating, medical dosimetry, personnel dosimetry, space dosimetry, etc.TL is very sensitive to defects, so it is also utilized to study defects present in the material [10].The properties exhibited by a phosphor for its practical applications, such as radiation dosimetry or LEDs, depend on the nature of the dopant.Highly sensitive TL and PL phosphors are developed using rare earth elements as dopants [2].Here Ca10K (PO4) 7 (CKP) has been doped with Dy due to its good luminescence properties.It has been used as a dopant in various solid-state lighting (SSL) phosphors for making white LEDs [11–13].

its TL glow curve using a TLD reader. 4.1 | Annealing conditions Proper annealing conditions are required to use a phosphor as a TLD material.TL properties exhibited by a phosphor strongly depend on the annealing procedure before irradiation, and it stabilizes the trap structure as well [23].To obtain the maximum TL sensitivity of this phosphor, proper annealing conditions were optimized.Pre-annealing is done to stabilize the trap structure and erase the previous irradiation memory, if any, and make it a fresh TLD.For this purpose, Ca10K (PO4) 7: Dy samples were annealed at different temperatures, i.e., 100C, 200C, 300C, and 400C for 30 min and 1 h.All the samples were irradiated by a test dose of 25Gy, and the TL response was recorded.It was found that 200C for 30 min is the optimum preannealing temperature (Figure5).Post-annealing is done to remove any previous residual irradiation effect, which is supposed to remain after the TL readout.This thermal treatment aims to bring back the trap/recombination center structures to the previous original state so that the TLD can be reused.Post-annealing releases the charge carriers (i.e., the trap occupancy decreases) [24] trapped in the trapping sites due to which TL decreases.For the determination of post-annealing temperature, the sample was given a test dose of 30Gy and then annealed at 300C for 15, 30, 45, 75, and 120 min.It was observed that the TL signal was completely erased, and only the background was left after 45 min of post-anneal, so 300C for 45 min is the post-annealing temperature. from 5- to 2000-Gy gamma dose.The TL glow curve starts saturating after this dose (seeFigure9).This can be explained based on the track interaction model.This model emphasizes the role of localized trapping/ recombination entities for linear dose–response.According to this model, during irradiation, the number of traps generated along the track of the ionizing radiation depends on the length and cross-section of the track.Along the track in the matrix, the dose level is not uniform, and this results in the nonhomogeneous spatial distribution of dose, which causes inhomogeneous occupational probabilities of trapping centers.At lower doses, the recombination completely occurs within the interior of the track, and linear response is observed as the TL intensity is simply proportional to the number of tracks, i.e., to the dose and the electrons coming out of the traps that are captured by the recombination centers.Due to the competitive centers, the recombination occurs within TC/LC Thermoluminescent glow curve of Gd1-xRExAlO3 (RE=Dy or Pr) beta irradiated phosphors Alejandro Alonso Sotolongo a, Teodoro RIvera Montalvo b, Daniel Nolasco Altamirano b, Tzarara Lopez-Luke a, María Eugenia Contreras García a, Juan Z arate Medina a,* a Instituto de Investigaci on en Metalurgia y Materiales, Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolas de Hidalgo, Edif.“U”, C.U., Morelia, 58060, Michoacan, Mexico b Instituto Polit ecnico Nacional, CICATA-Legaria, Legaria 694, Mexico City, 11500, Mexico City, Mexico ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Thermoluminescence Order kinetic Sensitization GdREAlOABSTRACTPhosphors composed of Gd1-xRExAlO3 ( 0 x5 RE=Dy or Pr) stoichiometries were synthesized using the reverse coprecipitation pathway.The thermoluminescent responses of all phosphors were studied under beta radiation exposure.Doping the gadolinium aluminate host improved the thermoluminescent response of the phosphors, with the phosphors composed of Gd0.99Dy0.01Al O3 and Gd0.95Pr0.05Al O3 being the most sensitive.The Dy3+ ions produced a higher improvement of the thermoluminescent signal than the Pr3+ ions.Additionally, a proportional relationship between the similarity of the atomic numbers of the dopant and replaced ions and the sensitivity to thermoluminescence was confirmed.Besides, a slight shift of the thermoluminescent peaks toward lower temperatures was detected for doped phosphors.In the repeatability tests applied to the phosphor composed of Gd0.99Dy0.01Al O3, an anomalous increase in sensitization was observed.The observed sensitization was associated with the formation of electron trap clusters resulting from the continuous exposure to beta radiation.Furthermore, another sensitization phenomenon was detected in the phosphor with Gd0.95Pr0.05Al O3 stoichiometry when it was heated at low temperatures.

efficiency of the thermoluminescent mechanisms due to the incorporation of activators. 1.Introduction Protection radiology fields as personal dosimetry, environment dosimetry and retrospective dosimetry require materials endowed of the physic property known as stimulated luminescence.The mentioned phenomenon is associated to how capable are the crystal lattice defects of trapping the free charge carriers produced by ionizing radiation.The charge carriers leave trapped into metastable energy states placed in the band gap, whose existence is connected to the imperfections of the crystal lattice.Once a charge carrier is trapped, it could be released by an energy external stimulus.The charge carriers commonly are electron, then, the crystal defects capable to trap electron are called electron traps.The ionization also produces holes, which like the electrons are trapped into crystal defects that give rise to recombination centers.The released electron moves into the conduction band, after this, the elec tron can be trapped by another electron trap, or recombining into a recombination center, producing a photon emission, or returning to the valence band by nonradiative recombination.The stimulated luminescence classification depends on the nature of the stimulus applied to the electron traps.If the stimulus is composed of photons, the phenomenon is known as optically stimulated luminescence.

f the stimulus is composed of photons, the phenomenon is known as optically stimulated luminescence.On the contrary, when the material is heated to release the trapped electrons, the phenomenon is called thermoluminescence (TL) (Bøtter-Jensen et al., 2003; C.M.C.M.Sunta, 2014).The TL process has been simulated by electron energy transition phenomena.The formulation takes in count several approaches to simplify the differential equations, enough for they can be solved by numerical or analytical way.Among the approaches there is one proposed by Randall and Wilkins (1945) that dismisses the retrapping phenomenon, which is classified as first order kinetic (FOK) (Randall and Wilkins, 1945).Furter, there is another model, proposed by Garlick and Gibson (1948) that considers the retrapping as the dominant pro cesses, and it is assigned to a second order kinetic (SOK) (Garlick and Gibson, 1948).The kinetic order is a parameter defined to describe how determinant the retrapping is.It is associated to a quantitative value, which is close to 1 when the retrapping is weak, and closer to 2 or even it goes beyond 2 in conditions where the retrapping is really important (C.M.Sunta, 2014).Additionally, an intermedium model placed between the FOK and the SOK was proposed by May C.E.and Partridge J.A.(1964), which is recognized as general order kinetic (GOK) (May and Partridge, 1964).The defect concentration increases by doping the material.It is logic to figure a proportional relationship between the intensity of the TL signal and the lattice defect concentration.However, it has been proved that there is a suitable dopant amount for each material to maximize its response (Bilski et al., 1996; Kumar et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2021).An excessive dopant concentration leads to a reduction in the average dis tance between defects.As the lattice defects come closer together, they begin to interact with each other.The interactions produce electron traps endowed of less long localized metastable energy levels.

1.The maximum temperature was kept for 5 h.Achieved the said period, the powders came back to room temperature trough heat exchange with the environment.The powders were reground and sieved with a number 100 sieve. 2.2.X ray diffraction (XRD) The XRD patterns was recorded with a Bruker D8Advance X ray diffractometer, which uses CuKα with a1.541 Å wavelength.The measurements were recorded into a range between 20◦ and 70◦.Additionally, it was applied a time step equal to 0.66 s and a2θ step of 0.02◦.The patterns were indexed with the DIFFRAC.EVA V4.2.1 software. 2.2.1.Calculation of crystallite size The average crystallite size D of powders was estimated by the Scherrer formula named: D=K1 where λ is the incident wavelength, β is the full-width at half maximum (FWHM), θ is the Bragg angle and K is a constant.The Scherrer formula was relied on assuming both gaussian profiles for the diffraction peaks and small size cubes for crystallite shapes.The aforementioned considerations lead to a value of K=0.94 (Klug and Alexander, 1974).The values of β were calculated applying a gaussian adjustment to the most intense diffraction peak, which was located at 2θ⁓34◦. 2.3.TL measurements Before to record the glow curves, it was weighed 10 mg for each sample of the phosphors.

ter energy eficiency and a longer working life which result in a greater environmental friendliness.These advantages result from the spontaneous light emission in semiconductors caused by the radiative recombination of excess electrons and holes created in the presence of an electric current which resolves many constraining factors in other light sources.The nearly monochromatic emission of classic LEDs can be used to excite other phosphors which in return are able to emit white light.The combination of these two elements is the basis for "solid-state illumination" using white LEDs (WLEDs).The first commercial solid-state lighting WLED was produced in 1996 based on InGaN semiconductors and the inorganic phosphor (YAG:Ce).It opened the door for the further development of WLEDs1.Rare earth (RE) ion-doped materials are widely used in photonic devices and other lighting applications because of their superior optical performance and a long and stable lifetime.WLEDs can be produced by using RE phosphors to generate blue or near-UV light and balancing it with a yellow emission or a complementary package of red, green, and blue emissions.RE ion emission characteristics significantly depend on the electronic structure of the RE ion, the host matrix, the network modifiers and the doping concentration 2–4.Among the RE ions in glass hosts, Dy3+ has a broad emission spectrum and a high luminescence eficiency.This is caused by two main emission bands in the blue and yellow regions of the visible spectrum, which correspond to the transitions 4F9/26H15/2 (magneticdipole) and 4F9/2→6H13/2 (electricdipole).Due to a hypersensitivity of the yellow transition, its emission intensity is greatly impacted by the local field environment 5, whereas the blue transition is less sensitive to the host.These emission bands enable to adjust the stimulation of white light by tuning the yellow to blue emission intensity ratio by changing the host composition.

www.acsami.org Research Article First Achievement of Yellow Laser Operation in Dy3+.-Doped Borate Crystals Yisheng Huang, Xiaoru Gong, Lizhen Zhang, Zhoubin Lin, GeZhang, Bing Teng, Bingxuan Li, * and Shijia Sun* Cite This: ACSAppl.Mater.Interfaces 2024, 16, 49556−49562 Read Online ACCESSMetrics & More Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: Continuous-wave (CW) yellow lasers have been demonstrated successfully by using a GaN laser-diode (LD) pumping in borate crystals for the first time.The Dy3+: GdMgB5O10 (Dy:GMB) crystal with dimensions up to 331915 m m3 is grown by the top-seeded solution growth method, and the polarized spectroscopic properties are investigated systematically at room temperature.The line strengths, Judd−Ofelt (J−O) intensity, spontaneous transition rates, fluorescence branching ratios, and radiative lifetimes are calculated in detail by the Judd−Ofelt theory.Under direct pumping of 452 nm LD, a compact continuous-wave yellow laser with a maximum output power of 628 mW and laser wavelength of 581 nm is generated based on a Y-cut Dy: GMB crystal.To our knowledge, it is not only the highest output power for yellow laser obtained in Dy3-+-doped crystals but also the first yellow laser operation achieved by borate crystals under direct LD pumping.The results reveal that the Dy:GMB crystal is an optical material with important application prospects in yellow laser.

KEYWORDS: yellow laser, Dy3+ ion, borate crystal, optical material, phonon energy 1.INTRODUCTION The yellow laser (570−590 nm) has significant applications in biomedicine for retinal vascular diseases, laser source for ytterbium (Yb) optical lattice clock, astronomy for guide star laser, and so on.1−4 Taking a laser near 577 nm as an example, it corresponds to the maximum absorption peak of hemoglobin and oxygenated hemoglobin, but the absorption of both lens nucleus and macular pigment is negligible, which is very beneficial for retinal photocoagulation.5,6 Ytterbium (Yb) lattice clock is one of the three optical clocks (aluminum, strontium), and the clock laser source is the most important factor limiting its development.At present, a578.2 nm laser source is required to probe the 1S03P0 clock transition of Yb atoms confined in an optical lattice.7,8 Despite numerous important demands, the corresponding materials and technologies for achieving yellow laser emission are indeed very limited and can be roughly divided into three categories: the self-frequency-doubling (SFD) of infrared lasers, through the sum of two laser frequencies in a self-frequency laser crystal (SFG+SHG), and stimulated Raman scattering in crystals.9 −13However, the above methods all involve frequency conversion technology, which can easily lead to drawbacks, such as complex optical systems, poor beam quality, unstable laser power, and expensive equipment and facilities in practical applications.

eam quality, unstable laser power, and expensive equipment and facilities in practical applications.Recently, with the rapid development of blue laser diodes (LD), yellow laser emission has become a new hotspot by directly pumping rare-earth ion Dy3+ based on the 4F9/2 6H13/2 transition.14 Because not only in terms of commercial application of lasers but also in terms of their wider promotion, they have a series of advantages, such as simple optical systems, compact structures, low costs, and low signal-to-noise ratio.However, despite numerous reports of yellow fluorescence emission under blue LD pumping by doping Dy3+ ions in various host crystals, the situation of achieving yellow laser operation is not optimistic.15−20 At present, only three representative crystals doped with Dy3 ions exhibit good yellow laser performances: The 583 nm Dy3:YAG self-pulsed laser with an output power of 150 mW and slope eficiency of 12%, the 575 nm Dy3+: ZnWO4 continuous-wave (CW) laser with an output power of 110 mW and slope eficiency of 13%, and the 573.9 nm Dy3+/ Tb3+: LiLuF4CW laser with an output power of 351 mW and slope eficiency of 15 %.21-23Obviously, the above results are far from our expectations in the field of yellow laser.In this paper, we successfully prepared a high-quality Dy3+.ions-doped borate crystal GdMgB5O10 and achieved CW laser operation under GaN-LD pumping with center wavelengths of 579 and 581 nm, respectively.The maximum laser output power reached 628 mW, which is currently the highest output power for a yellow laser obtained in Dy3+-doped crystals to our knowledge.Moreover, it is not only the first time that yellow laser operation has been achieved in Dy3+ ion-doped borate crystals with high phonon energy but also the laser emission wavelength efectively fills the gap in the current yellow laser band. 2.EXPERIMENTAL SECTION2.1.Crystal Growth.

EDGEARTICLEView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: Chem.Sci., 2024, 15, 8019 Tuning white light emission using singlecomponent tetrachroic Dy3+ metallacrowns: the role of chromophoric building blocks† All publication charges for this article have been paid for by the Royal Society of Chemistry Elvin V.Salerno,‡a Svetlana V.Eliseeva, ‡*b Stephane Petoud *b and Vincent L.Pecoraro *a White light production is of major importance for ambient lighting and technological displays.White light can be obtained by several types of materials and their combinations, but single component emitters remain rare and desirable towards thinner devices that are, therefore, easier to control and that require fewer manufacturing steps.We have designed a series of dysprosium(III)-based luminescent metallacrowns (MCs) to achieve this goal.The synthesized MCs possess three main structural types LnGa4 (L) 4 (L) 4 (typeA), Ln2Ga8 (L) 8 (L) 4 (typeB) and LnGa8 (L) 8 (OH) 4 (typeC) (HL0, HL00 and HL000 derivatives of salicylhydroxamic, benzoic and isophthalic acids, respectively).The advantage of these MCs is that, within each structural type, the nature of the organic building blocks does not afect the symmetry around Dy3+.By detailed studies of the photophysical properties of these Dy3+- based MCs, we have demonstrated that CIE coordinates can be tuned from warm to neutral to cold white by (i) defining the symmetry about Dy3+, and (ii) choosing appropriate chromophoric building blocks.These organic building blocks, without altering the coordination geometry around Dy3+, influence the total emission profile through changing the probability of diferent energy transfer processes including the 3T1Dy3+ energy back transfer and/or by generating ligand-centered fluorescence in the blue range.

the 3T1Dy3+ energy back transfer and/or by generating ligand-centered fluorescence in the blue range.This work opens new perspectives for the creation of white light emitting devices using single component tetrachroic molecular compounds Received 17th January 2024Accepted 19th April 2024DOI: rsc.li/chemical-science Introduction White light production is important in a modern society and has applications in ambient lighting and/or screen backlighting in liquid crystalline displays.Presently, light emitting diodes (LEDs) are becoming the state of the art in light production as they can be highly eficient and tunable.To obtain white light emission (WLE), multiple colours need to be combined on a single device since LEDs are usually monochromatic emitters.1 Hence, dichroic, trichroic and tetrachroic approaches have been used that combine blue/yellow, red/green/blue (RGB) or RGB/cyano emitters, respectively.2 The use of multiple colour components implies a signicant diference in comparison to broadband emitters, such as the sun.Generally, the broader the emission prole, and the more colour components, the better is the colour rendition.3 The CIE (Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage) colour space is commonly used to standardize how the average human eye will perceive the colour of an object.4 The CIE chromaticity coordinates are dened by three numbers ( x, y, z )..The chromaticity of an object can be plotted in a two-dimensional CIE diagram, since it implies a normalization condition: z=1 xy.The white light region lies in the centre of the diagram, with the neutral white light having coordinates (0.33, 0.33).White light can also be described by its Correlated Colour Temperature (CCT), where its quality is dened by the blackbody equivalent temperature.

r Temperature (CCT), where its quality is dened by the blackbody equivalent temperature.Modern white light emitting devices include sources such as uorescent lamps,5 high-pressure sodium–mercury lamps,6 solid state light emitting diodes,7 organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs).8,9 Single component white light emitters are desirable because they allow for thinner materials with greater manufacturing reproducibility and enhanced stability over time.10,11 Several lanthanide(III) ions (Ln3+) emitting in the visible range, namely, Sm3+, Eu3+, Tb3+, Dy3+, Tm3+, have the potential to emit compatible lights.Typically, the creation of individual materials that display WLE involves various Ln3+ ions, each with diferent properties, either independently or in combination with the light emitted by organic chromophoric ligands or an inorganic matrix.Several compounds possessing WLE capabilities have been created with a combination of diferent visible-emitting Ln3+The variation of the concentrations of the individual Ln3+ allows one to tune the corresponding relative emission intensities and, thus, to control the CIE coordinates.The pertinence of this strategy has been demonstrated for molecular materials,12,13 Ln3++-based polymers,14–21 metal–organic frameworks (MOFs),22–26 inorganic materials,27–29 and hybrid organic/ inorganic 30–33 materials.Alternatively, to produce WLE, the combination of emission signals arising from a single visible-emitting Ln3+ and organic ligands or inorganic matrix can be used.34,35 The validity of this approach has been demonstrated for molecular Eu3+ compounds,36 as well as for Dy3+ compounds.

RESEARCHARTICLEView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: IChFt, 2024, 11, 5924 Exploring structural and optical properties of CLSO:Dy for ultra-sensitive luminescent thermometers and high-bright screen printing† Xinyao Zhang,a Zhen Sun, *a Ruiying Lu,a Jiarui Xu,a Hongyu XUa and Wei XubHerein, a novel scheme is employed to develop ultra-sensitive luminescent thermometers and highbright luminescent inks for screen printing.We synthesize CaLa4Si3O13 (ClSO): Dy3+ by a traditional hightemperature solid-phase method and accurately predict its radiation properties using Judd–Ofelt (J–O) theory.On this basis, Eu3+ or Tb3+ ions with diferent radii are introduced into ClSO: Dy3+ to modify the crystal structure rigidity.The activation energies of ClSO: Dy3+, Dy3+/ Eu3+, and Dy3+/ Tb3+ samples are calculated to be 0.256 eV, 0.315 eV and 0.289 eV, respectively, which demonstrate that Eu3+ or Tb3+ enhances the structural stifness, and thus, improves the thermal stability of materials.Simultaneously, the Debye temperature and thermal expansion coeficients as valuable parameters for structural stifness also confirm the above-mentioned results.Furthermore, we propose a strategy in which the multiplication of LIRs based on multiple emission peaks with opposite thermal quenching properties follow a Boltzmanntype distribution, resulting in a dramatically increased relative sensitivity of ClSO: Dy3+, Dy3+/ Eu3+, and Dy3+/ Tb3+ thermometers to 2.92 % K-1, 3.32 % K-1 and 3.19 % K-1, respectively.This work not only provides valuable insights into the development of superior temperature sensitive materials but also develops optical anti-counterfeiting technology based on screen printing.Received 18th May 2024, Accepted 15th July 2024DOI: rsc.li/frontiers-inorganic 1.

.Received 18th May 2024, Accepted 15th July 2024DOI: rsc.li/frontiers-inorganic 1.Introduction Optical thermometers based on luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) possess distinct advantages in temperature measurement, including non-contact operation, rapid response time, high sensitivity and spatial resolution.As a result, it finds wide-ranging applications in industrial manufacturing, biomedical research, and scientific investigations.1–4 The thermal-coupled level (TCL) thermometer ofers several prominent advantages, including a well-defined temperature measurement principle and a straightforward process without any reference requirements.5 According to the current frontier reports, the exploration of the LIR optical temperature measurement of rare earth-doped materials is relatively deep; however, there are still some shortcomings in improving the sensitivity of ratiometric thermometers.Other approaches have also been taken to design LIR thermometers possessing better sensitivity, for example, Hu et al.proposed a potential method for modifying the host phonon energy to enhance the temperature sensing performance 6 and verified that hosts with a lower phonon energy have a better temperature sensitivity.Yang et al.posited that materials with stronger crystal field strengths were considered to be better for luminescent thermometers with larger LIR values and sensitivities.7 Subsequently, Liu et al.used LIR technology to study the role of hosts in the luminescence characteristics of rare earth-doped materials and the influence of bond covalency in crystals on the thermal sensitivity of diferent hosts.8 Obtaining optical thermometers with better sensitivities has always been a challenge; therefore, new attempts are needed to study thermosensitive materials.Luminous ink is a type of ink with high brightness, high saturation, and strong color efects.

erials.Luminous ink is a type of ink with high brightness, high saturation, and strong color efects.The printing process is straightforward, with accurate overprinting, and the printed efect is comparable to that of ordinary inks; however, when under ultraviolet light, the printed matter exhibits abnormal brightness.Consequently, the luminous ink is widely employed in decorative printing, security identification, and information anti-counterfeiting.9 In terms of anti-counterfeiting printing, rare earth-doped luminescent inks have unique chemical and physical characteristics, making it dificult to copy the luminescent efect of their printing, which efectively improves the anti-counterfeiting ability of the product and reduces the probability of counterfeit and shoddy goods.Additionally, rare earth-doped luminescent inks usually have certain chemical stability, good resistance to high temperatures and good wear resistance.It can maintain a stable luminescent efect under various environmental conditions, which ensures the long-term efectiveness of the luminescent ink anti-counterfeiting label.10,11 Rare earth-doped phosphors play a vital role in anti-counterfeiting printing due to their long fluorescent lifetimes, unique multicolor luminescence, and safety advantages making them the best choice to meet high quality and safe ink requirements.Judd–Ofelt (J–O) theory, as one of the crucial theoretical methods for investigating the optical properties of rare earth ion-doped materials, has been widely employed by numerous researchers since its inception.12–15 The experimental results have consistently demonstrated excellent agreement with this theory.Nisar Hussain et al.investigated the luminescence of Dy3+ in Ba2La8 (SiO4) 6O2 phosphors and described the ligand environment around Dy3+ using the J–O parameters calculated by the photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectra.16 Mustafa İlhan et al.

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Achieving high sensing sensitivity in a Dy3+ doped garnet phosphor toward optical thermometry† Cite this: J.Mater.Chem.C, 2024, 12, 19536Shichang Long,ab Minfeng Tian,a Dan Zhang,b Xixian Luo,b Wen Xu,b Ying Tian *a and Shuangyu Xin*b Optical thermometers have garnered significant attention.and there has been a rapid development of high-performance optical thermometers.However, achieving high sensing sensitivity phosphor materials is still a significant challenge.In this study, a Dy3+ doped garnet Ca2.5Hf2.5Ga3O12 (CHGO) phosphor with high sensing sensitivity is reported.Characteristic blue emissions originating from the thermally coupled energy levels of 4 | 15/2 and 4F9/2 to the 6H15/2 ground level of Dy3+ ions were investigated, observing opposite temperature dependent emission behavior.The fluorescence intensity ratio (FIR) approach was utilized to investigate the optical temperature sensing properties of CHGO: Dy3+ phosphors based on the diferent thermal quenching transitions of the thermally coupled energy levels ( 4 | 15/2 6 | H15/2 and 4F9/2→6H15/2 ).Under 352 nm light excitation, CHGO: Dy3+ exhibits the maximum absolute and relative sensitivities of 0.13 % K-1 at 523K and 2.12 % K-1 at 298K, respectively, demonstrating high performance temperature sensing, high sensitivity, excellent repeatability and reusability.Finally, a simple optical temperature sensing strategy was proposed to investigate the optical thermometry performance of CHGO: Dy3+ phosphors, indicating their great optical thermometry behavior for optical thermometric applications.This study focusing on the optical temperature sensing of CHGO: Dy3+ phosphors lays a robust foundation and constitutes a valuable resource for future investigations delving into the realm of temperature sensing capabilities of Dy3+-doped phosphors.

e investigations delving into the realm of temperature sensing capabilities of Dy3+-doped phosphors.Received 6th August 2024, Accepted 10th October 2024DOI: rsc.li/materials-c 1.Introduction Accurate temperature monitoring is crucial for scientific and industrial applications.Optical thermometers have caught much attention due to their advantages of precise temperature measurements, fast detection, and resistance to harsh environments.1–4 Additionally, conventional contact temperature sensors, such as liquid, pressure, and thermocouple sensors, have made a significant advancement over the past few decades.5–7 While contact temperature measurement, such as thermometry, is an ideal method to study phenomena that change with temperature, it also exhibits considerable limitations, including low response rates, low resolution, and inability to accurately measure in harsh environments that involve high temperatures, extreme pressures, and corrosive conditions.8–10 In contrast, contactless optical temperature sensing has garnered significant attention and interest due to its noninvasive nature, higher accuracy, and high sensitivity, overcoming the limitations of conventional contact thermometry.This method indicates temperature changes by monitoring optical signals such as wavelength, bandwidth, lifetime of the excited states and the fluorescence intensity ratio (FIR).11 Among these methods, the FIR approach utilizing thermally coupled energy levels (TCLs) has sparked significant research attention owing to the appropriate energy gap of TCLs from 200 to 2000 cm-1, and using this approach outstanding temperature sensing performance can be achieved.

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: J.Mater.Chem.C, 2024, 12, 12854 Deconstructing excitation transitions in Dy3+.doped CaWO4 to develop a new ratiometric luminescent thermometry for achieving ultra-high sensing sensitivity† Qianrui Liu,ab Baosheng Cao, *b Miao Gao,b Lulu Qiu,b Yujie Weng,b Yangyang He,b Xiaoguang Han*a and Bin Dong b Investigating excitation transition behavior is crucial for elucidating the photoluminescence (PL) characteristics of lanthanide ion-doped phosphors.This investigation provides a basis for developing new ratiometric luminescent thermometry methods based on thermally influenced excitation processes.In this study, the excitation transition lines of trivalent dysprosium (Dy3+) and charger-transfer band (CTB) in Dy3+- doped CaWO4 ( CaWO4; Dy ) phosphors were efectively deconstructed using the Dy3+ concentration- and temperature-dependent PL excitation (PLE) spectra in the ultraviolet range of 280–340 nm.The phosphors exhibited a thermal-quenched PLE intensity for Dy3+ and a thermalenhanced PLE intensity for CTB owing to energy transfer between the CaWO4 host and Dy3+.A new ratiometric thermometry strategy was introduced using the opposite thermal-dependent PLE intensity of CTB as the temperature probe and Dy3+ as the reference signal.This method was based on the excitedstate absorption intensity ratio between CTB and Dy3+.This new thermometry method exhibited ultrahigh performance, reaching maximum absolute and relative sensitivities of 1.72K - 1 at 575K and 4.66% K-1 at 300K, respectively.This study presents a novel approach for developing highly sensitive and stable optical thermometric Dy3+-based materials and provides guidance for constructing an effective ratiometric thermometry strategy based on the deconstructed PLE properties.

onstructing an effective ratiometric thermometry strategy based on the deconstructed PLE properties.Received 12th June 2024, Accepted 15th July 2024DOI: rsc.li/materials-c Introduction Trivalent dysprosium (Dy3+) ion-doped phosphors have received significant attention owing to their diverse electronic energy levels and unique photoluminescence (PL) properties.1–3 Upon excitation with ultraviolet light or an infrared laser, the Dy3+-doped phosphors exhibit characteristic blue and yellow emissions, making them highly applicable across numerous fields, including imaging technology, new light sources, and luminescent sensors.4–9 Particularly, Dy3+-doped phosphors are used as highly effective optical ratiometric thermometers owing to their good thermometric characteristics.These properties mainly depend on the temperature-dependent luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) derived from the electronic transitions of thermally coupled energy levels (TCLs) of 4I15/2 / 4F9/2.10-14However, the thermometric performance of Dy3+ is often limited by thermal-quenched luminescence and the narrow energy gap of 4I15/2 / 4F9/2TC S15Moreover, the LIR strategy, which incorporates dual emitting centers based on the temperature-dependent energy transfer between Dy3+ and other lanthanide (Ln3+) emitters or the matrix, has been implemented.This approach has led to various temperature-dependent changes in PL properties to improve the thermal sensitivity of phosphors.16,17 Calcium tungstate (CaWO4)., with high optical and chemical stability, exhibits superior ultraviolet light absorption, unique optical properties, and eficient energy transfer to Ln3+.

erior ultraviolet light absorption, unique optical properties, and eficient energy transfer to Ln3+.Additionally, CaWO4 serves as an excellent host material for Dy3+ doping to generate eficient PL properties.18,19 InDy3-doped CaWO4 ( CaWO4; Dy ) phosphors, the distinct blue and yellow PL emissions can be produced through two methods: direct excitation of Dy3+ with ultraviolet A-band (UVA) light (around350nm) 1 and the matrix-mediated sensitization from the charger transfer band (CTB) of the CaWO4 host to Dy3+ under ultraviolet C-band (UVC) excitation (around260nm) 20,21Furthermore, a thermometry strategy based on LIR of Dy3+ and WO42- (Fig.1a) exhibited high thermometric sensitivity owing to the inverse temperature-dependent PL evolution between Dy3+ and CTB.22However, the limited thermal-enhanced PL intensity and fewer PL bands of Dy3+ resulted in minimal improvements in LIR-based thermometric properties. more easily distinguishable PL excitation (PLE) transitions of Ln3+ compared with its PL transitions.5, 15A versatile strategy has been implemented for developing EIR-based thermometry methods for CaWO4: Dy phosphors; moreover, these devices mainly utilize multiple excitation transition pathways of Dy3+ within the UVA range.9,23,24 However, most temperaturedependent excitation transitions of Dy3+ are prone to thermal quenching, leading to reduced thermometric sensitivity.25Conversely, thermally enhanced excitation transitions often depend on the excitation transition of 4I15/2 / 4F9/2TCLs.26 Therefore, exploring diverse temperature-dependent excitation pathways independent of TCLs of Dy3+ is crucial for designing novel EIR thermometry methods based on the luminescent properties of Dy3+-doped phosphors.Due to the rich ladder-like arranged energy levels with a moderate energy gap (7000cm-1between4F9/2and6F1/2) Dy3+ possesses grouped excitation transitions from each low energy levels to various high energy levels, which exhibits unique temperature-dependent excitation transition behaviors and diverse EIR-based thermometric behaviors compared with other lanthanide ion such as Er, Tm, Ho, Eu, Tb, and so on.23 However, the excitation bands of Dy3+ often overlap, posing dificulties in diferentiation owing to its numerous excitation transition branches.27 Moreover, the broad PLE bands of the CaWO4 matrix, which widens and redshifts at higher temperatures, worsen the overlapping with PLE branches of Dy3+ particularly in the ultraviolet B-band range (UVB) (280– 315 nm).28 Therefore, deconstructing the PLE spectra from CaWO4: Dy phosphors and accurately assigning their PLE transition lines are crucial.This process is fundamental for designing novel Dy3+-based luminescent thermometry methods and exploring their novel applications.

r designing novel Dy3+-based luminescent thermometry methods and exploring their novel applications.Herein, we extensively investigated the distinct excited transition lines of Dy3+ and CTB within CaWO4: Dy phosphors in the UVB region to develop a highly sensitive Dy3-based luminescent ratiometric thermometry method.The PLE spectra of CaWO4: Dy phosphors with various Dy3+ concentrations were deconstructed to identify each CTB branch resulting from Dy3+ doping in the CaWO4 host.By analyzing temperature-dependent PLE spectra, we identified the specific PLE transition lines of Dy3+ in the UVB region.Additionally, a new ratiometric thermometry strategy was implemented based on the EIR of CTB and Dy3.This method utilized the inverse temperature-dependent PLE intensities of the well-resolved CTB and Dy3+ excitation transition branches (Fig.1b).The proposed EIR-based thermometry strategy exhibited ultra-high sensitivity and reliability in sensing, indicating the excellence and significant potential of CaWO4: Iy phosphors for temperature sensing applications. Experimental A simple coprecipitation method was used to prepare CaWO4: Dy phosphors, as described in a previous study.29The raw materials included Na2WO42H2O (4N, Aladdin), CaCl22H2O (4N, Aladdin), and Dy2O3 (4N, Aladdin).First, 10 mmol of Na2WO42H2O and CaCl22H2O were added to deionized water to produce 0.5 mol L-1 solutions of Na2WO4 and CaCl2, respectively.Dy2O3 powder in appropriate proportions was dissolved in excess nitric acid, heated, and stirred.The excess solvent was evaporated to produce 0.01 mol L-1Dy (NO3) 3 solutions.Subsequently, 1.98 mL of CaCl2, 2 mL of Na2WO4, and 1 mL of Dy (NO3) 3 were thoroughly mixed and stirred.The resulting white precipitate was collected via centrifugation and washed with deionized water.After drying for 24 h, the products were heated at 1523K for 6 h and then cooled to room temperature (RT) in the furnace.The 1 mol% Dy3-doped CaWO4 phosphors ( CaWO4: 1Dy ) were obtained after thorough grinding of the material.

RESEARCHCombustion Synthesis and Influence of Dy3+ ions on Structural and Photometric Attributes of Olivine-type LiMgPONanophosphors for Illumination Applications Neha Lalotra 1 · Kamni Pathania 1 Received: 20September 2024 / Accepted: 12November 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024 Abstract The low-cost technique of combustion synthesis was used to synthesize the trivalent Dysprosium (Dy3+) doped olivine type Lithium Magnesium Phosphate (LiMgPO4).X-ray difraction (XRD) analysis verified the orthorhombic phase, corresponding to the space group Pnma.The crystallite size of 50.83 nm was calculated using Debye-Scherre formula.FESEM technique was used to study the morphology of the sample which depicts its porous nature.High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy (HRTEM) analysis provided an average particle size measurement of 652.04 nm.The phosphor’s photoluminescence (PL) excitation spectrum revealed distinct peaks in the ultraviolet (UV) and near-ultraviolet (nearUV) regions, aligning with the characteristics of Dy3+ ions.Four emission peaks were observed in the PL spectra at various wavelengths: 4F9/26H15/2 (482nm), 4F9/2 6H13/2 (578nm), 4F9/2→6H11/2 (663nm) and 4F9/26H9/2 (700nm).Near-white light emission was observed at the Commission International de l’Eclairage (CIE) coordinates of Dy3+ activated LiMgPO4 [LMP] phosphor, which were ( x=0.41, y=0.42 ) with color purity of 49.20%.The band gap of the prepared phosphor was calculated using difuse reflectance spectra, yielding a value of 4.47, 0.02: e V.The results indicated that the synthesized phosphor had potential for various illumination applications when combined with other phosphors under near-UV stimulation.

of phosphor-converted light-emitting diodes (PC-LEDs) represents the next generation in solid-state lighting, gaining attraction in the illumination industry due to their extended lifespan, high
