Dysprosium-Doped Glass-Ceramics From the System Na2O-Al2O3-SiO2-B2O3-Dy2O3I.Koseva 1 | P.Tzvetkov 1 | P.Ivanov 2 | M.Gancheva 1 | V.Nikolov 3 1Institute of General and Inorganic Chemistry, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria | 2Institute of Optical Materials and Technologies, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria | 3Institute of Mineralogy and Crystallography, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria Correspondence: I.Koseva (ikosseva@svr.igic.bas.bg) Received: 22April 2024 | Revised: 11September 2024 | Accepted: 3November 2024Funding: This research is supported by the project BG05M2OP001-1.001-0008 “NATIONALCENTEROFMECHATRONICSANDCLEANTECHNOLOGIES,” funded by the Operational Programme Science and Education for Smart Growth 2014–2020, co-financed by the European Union through the European Regional Development Fund.Keywords: nano glass-ceramic | photoluminescence | rare-earth ions | silicate phosphor | X-ray ABSTRACTGlasses from the system Na2O-Al2O3-SiO2-B2O3-Dy2O3 are prepared with three different concentrations of the Dy3+ ion—0.5, 1, and 2 at%.Glass-ceramics are obtained after thermal treatment of the parent glass at 580C and 630C during 2, 5, and 24 h.The crystallizing phases, the crystallinity degree, and the nano crystalline size are determined.The crystallizing phases after thermal treatment are NaAlSiO4 in two different modifications and Na3B3O6.XRD analyses show the presence of third unknown phase in some samples.Emission and excitation spectra of the glass-ceramics show the characteristic peaks of Dy3+( 4F9/2→6H15/2, 4F9/2→6H13/2 and 4F9/2→6H11/2 at 483, 575, and 668 nm, respectively).The yellow peak is dominating in all samples.
section: Dysprosium-Doped Glass-Ceramics From the System Na<sub>2</sub>O-Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>-SiO<sub>2</sub>-B<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>-Dy<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> I.Koseva<sup>1</sup> | P.Tzvetkov<sup>1</sup> | P.Ivanov<sup>2</sup> | M.Gancheva<sup>1</sup> | V.Nikolov<sup>3</sup> <sup>1</sup>Institute of General and Inorganic Chemistry, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria | <sup>2</sup>Institute of Optical Materials and Technologies, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria | <sup>3</sup>Institute of Mineralogy and Crystallography, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Sofia, Bulgaria Correspondence: I.Koseva (ikosseva@svr.igic.bas.bg) Received: 22April2024 | Revised: 11September2024 | Accepted: 3November2024Funding: This research is supported by the project BG05M2OP001-1.001-0008 “NATIONAL CENTER OF MECHATRONICS AND CLEAN TECHNOLOGIES,” funded by the Operational Programme Science and Education for Smart Growth2014–2020, co-financed by the European Union through the European Regional Development Fund.Keywords: nano glass-ceramic | photoluminescence | rare-earth ions | silicate phosphor | X-ray ## ABSTRACT Glasses from the system Na2O - Al2O3 - Si O2 - B2O3 - Dy2O3 are prepared with three different concentrations of the Dy3+ion—0.5, 1, and2 at%.Glass-ceramics are obtained after thermal treatment of the parent glass at580C and630C during2, 5, and24 h.The crystallizing phases, the crystallinity degree, and the nano crystalline size are determined.The crystallizing phases after thermal treatment are Na Al Si O4 in two different modifications and Na3B3O6 .XRD analyses show the presence of third unknown phase in some samples.Emission and excitation spectra of the glass-ceramics show the characteristic peaks of Dy3+( 4F9/2 → 6H15/2 , 4F9/2 → 6H13/2 and4F9/2 → 6H11/2 at483, 575, and668 nm, respectively).The yellow peak is dominating in all samples.

time of the thermal treatment.This result suggests that the emission color can be controlled by these three factors. 1 | Introduction Light emitting diodes as an energy and environment saving devises are of special interest and become more and more popular in the modern life [1, 2].Different colors can be received by mixing of multicolor phosphors.White light emitting diodes can be realized by combining of blue and yellow light or by mixing of blue, green, and red lights [1, 3].The luminescence of the rare earth ions strongly depends on the concentration of the activator, composition, and crystal structure of the host and preparative method [3].Silicates are one of the most suitable materials because of their high chemical and mechanical stability and various crystal structures [2].Silicate, silicate glasses, and glass-ceramics doped by rare earth ions are among the most popular materials for optical fibers, LEDs, wave guides for optoelectronic communication, and color display devices.Compared with conventional phosphors and glasses, rare earth-doped glass ceramics are a good alternative because they are cheaper than single crystals, with higher quantum efficiency than rare earth doped glasses, with higher transmittance, and free from halo effect than solid state synthesized ceramics.Mechanical, thermal, electrical, and optical properties of the material could be improved by controlled heat treatment of the parent glass [4–6].Dysprosium ion is a typical white light emitting ion possessing two dominant emission bands in the blue (460–500 nm) and the yellow (560–600 nm) regions.The first is assigned to the 4F9/2→6H15/2 magnetic dipole transition, which is slightly dependent on the local symmetry.The latter one is assigned to the hypersensitive electric dipole transition 4F9/26H13/2, which intensity is strongly influenced by the Dy3+ environment.

tric dipole transition 4F9/26H13/2, which intensity is strongly influenced by the Dy3+ environment.So, the intensity ratio of yellow-to-blue (Y/B) emissions in Dy3+-doped phosphors is mainly influenced by the interaction between Dy3+ ion and the surrounding ions from the matrix [7].Investigations on the Dy3+-doped silicates prepared by conventional solidstate synthesis are published: Li2SiO3 [8, 9], NaAlSiO [10], Sr2SiO4 [ 11, 12 ], BaSiO [12], Mg2SiO4 [ 12 ], Ca2SiO4 [ 13, 14], and Dy3+: Ca2MgSi2O7 [15].Investigations are conducted also on glasses Na2O-BaO-Bi2O3-SiO2 [ 16 ], Na2O-SiO2-CaO [ 17], and glass-ceramics containing SiO2 – Al2O3 – NaF [18], SiO2 – Al2O3 – Na2O-YF3-B2O3 [ 19 ] The crystal structure of natural nepheline is hexagonal with space group P63.It consists of AlO4 and SiO4 tetrahedra, connected with oxygen bridges.It can be described as a derivative of the hightridymite structure, where half of the silicon ions are replaced by aluminum.Sodium cations are incorporated in the cavities of the structure [20, 21].Nepheline compound exists at room temperature also in different polymorphic modifications, depending on the method of preparation [22, 23].These modifications transform to hexagonal one at 160C C-200C.Phase transition in structure similar to high tridymite occurs at 870C NaAlSiO4 compound is with nepheline like structure.No pure sodium nephelines are observed in the nature.The NaAlSiO4 single crystals are stable up to 1350C and then transform to low carnegeite [24].In this paper, we present our investigations on phase formation, particle size, and luminescence properties of doped by Dy3+ glass-ceramics prepared from the system Na2OAl2O3SiO2 – B2O3 and the influence of dopant concentration and thermal treatment conditions on their luminescent properties.To our knowledge, this kind of investigations are not published yet. 2 | Experimental Na2CO3 ( p.a.), Al2O3 ( p.a.), SiO2 ( p.a.), H3BO3 ( p.a.), H2O3 ( p.a.), H3BO3 ( p.a.), O3 ( p.a.

2O3 ( p.a.), SiO2 ( p.a.), H3BO3 ( p.a.), H2O3 ( p.a.), H3BO3 ( p.a.), O3 ( p.a.), and Dy2O3 (p.a.) were used as row materials.Glass composition is Na2OAl2O3 – SiO2 – B2O3 in a ratio 29:14:27:30 mol%, doped by 0.5 -, 1, and 2at% Dy3+.Glass synthesis were carried out in a resistive furnace with Kantal heating wire permitted maximum working temperature of 1200C and in a chamber furnace with MoSi2 heating elements permitted maximum working temperature of 1550C.Glasses were melted in platinum crucibles.First, the mixture was heated at 700C for decomposition of the sodium carbonate and boric acid, and then the melt was heated at 1300C during 3 h for homogenization.As obtained, glass was cooled to the room temperature by quick removing from the furnace.Thermal analyses of the obtained glasses were done by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on a Netzsch 404F3Pegasus instrument, Selb, Germany.The samples were investigated at a heating rate of 10C / min in an argon atmosphere.The infrared spectra were recorded on a Nicolet iS5Fourier transform interferometer (resolution < 2 cm - 1 ) at ambient temperatures using KBr discs as matrices.No ion exchange or other reactions with KBr have been observed.The prepared glasses were thermally treated at 580C and 630°C during 2, 5, and 24 h for establishing of the crystallizing phases.Structural characterization was carried out by powder X-ray diffraction using a Bruker D8Advance powder diffractometer with CuKa radiation and SolX detector.X-ray diffractograms were recorded at room temperature.Data were collected in the 2θ range from 10 to 80° with a step 0.04 and 1 second per step−1 counting time.X-ray diffractograms were identified using the Diffractplus EVA program [25].The average crystallite size was calculated from the integral breadth of all peaks using Scherrer equation and the TOPAS3 program—General profile and structure analysis software for powder diffraction data, 2005, Bruker AXS, Karlsruhe, Germany [26].

structure analysis software for powder diffraction data, 2005, Bruker AXS, Karlsruhe, Germany [26].The area of the amorphous phase was determined by using a straight line for description of the background and single line for fitting the amorphous component.The emission and excitation spectra were measured on Horiba Fluorolog 3-22TCS spectrophotometer equipped with a450-WXenon Lamp as the excitation source.All spectra were measured at room temperature.The luminescence decay time curves were measured on the same equipment with excitation source NanoLed pulsed laser diode (375nm) and monitoring emission 575 nm. 3 | Results and Discussion XRD patterns of the synthesized glasses from the system Na2OAl2O3 – SiO2 – B2O2 in a ratio 29:14:27:30 mol%, doped by 0.5, 1, and 2 at% Dy3+, are presented in Figure 1.No distinct phase peaks are observed in the range of 225-40 confirming the amorphous nature of the samples.The DSC curves and the obtained results for the glass transition temperature (Tg), the crystallization onset temperature (Tx), the glass stability parameter (Tx-Tg), and the crystallization temperature of the phase in the glass (Tc) are presented in Figure 2 and in Table 1.The resulting curves show a transition temperature of the glasses between 480C and 515C.The onset temperature of crystallization varies between 560C and 575C.The Tx-Tg parameter varies between 60C and 70C..There is a slight tendency for rising the temperatures, but the glass stability parameter slightly decreases with increasing of the dysprosium concentration (Table1).More than one maximum is observed in the crystallization peak; therefore, more than one phase crystallizes during heat treatment of glasses.

FIGURE1 | XRD patterns of the synthesized glasses from the system Na2O-Al2O3-SiO2-B2O3 in a ratio 29:14:27:30 mol%, doped by 0.5, 1, and 2 at% Dy3+The IR spectra of the dysprosium-doped glasses in the region of 1600-400 cm - 1 are presented in Figure 3.In the obtained infrared spectra, mainly four broad intense lines are visi-ble - in the high-frequency region (1200-1600cm-1) around 1400 cm - 1, in the medium-frequency region (700-1200cm-1) around 1020 cm - 1, and in the low-frequency region (400– 700 cm - 1 ) around 700 cm - 1 and around 450 cm - 1.According to the literature, the absorption lines in the interval 1400– 1200 cm - 1 are typical for the vibrations of the BO3 groups [27], and the lines between 1170 and 930 cm - 1 are due to the BO4 groups [28].The lines are identified as follows: 1470, 1404, and 1195 cm - 1 for BO3 stretching vibrations; 1387 cm - 1 for BO3 asymmetric vibrations; 1287 cm - 1 for vibration of boroxol rings; 1107 cm - 1 for BO4 symmetric vibration; 1021 and 960 cm - 1 for BO4 stretching vibration.The line around 1020 cm - 1 also contains the vibrations of the SiO4 and AlO4 groups [29].The line at 722 cm - 1 is due to the vibration of isolated SiO4 and AlO4 groups.The vibrations of the NaO4 tetrahedra are seen as a line at 456 cm−1 [30, 31].The vibrational lines of the Si-O-Al bridge bonds are also located in the same place [32].As the concentration of dysprosium increases, no particular difference is observed in the infrared spectra; therefore, the influence of dysprosium on the glass structure up to a concentration of 2 at% is insignificant.

RESEARCHInvestigation on Luminescence Properties of Dy3+Ions Doped NaBaB9O15Phosphors for Optoelectronic Applications V.Parthibaraj 1 · R.Vijayakumar 2 · Ranjib Kumar Padhi 3 · K.Ramachandran 4 · K.Maheshvaran Received: 26June 2024 / Accepted: 19July 2024 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024 Abstract A series of Dy3+ ions doped NaBaB9O15 phosphors with diferent dopant concentration was synthesized by solid state reaction.The phase purity was checked by X-ray difraction analysis and the functional groups present in as prepared phosphors was investigated with the help of FTIR spectral analysis.Under 386 nm excitation, the photoluminescence spectra exhibit three emission bands around 482 nm, 574 nm and 664 nm due to 4F9/26H J / 2 ( J=15, 13, 11 ) transions respectively.The optimum doping concentration of Dy3+ ions was found to be 5 mol%.The color coordinates are estimated from the emission spectra to check the dominant emission color and the color coordinates of the studied phosphors are fall on white region of CIE1931 diagram.The decay curve analysis was made to determine the lifetime of excited state of Dy3+ ions and the decay curves are exhibited bi-exponential behavior irrespective of Dy3+ ion concentration.All these measurents are done in room temperature and the results obtained from these studies are discussed in detail to claim their usage in light emitting devices.

obtained from these studies are discussed in detail to claim their usage in light emitting devices.Keywords Phosphors: Rare Earth · Luminescence Studies · Lifetime Introduction In many crucial scientific applications involving the creation of artificial light, rare earth ions (RE) activated in the inorganic luminescent materials are appropriate because they have advantages of high eficiency, good thermal stability and durability, etc.They find application in phosphor-converted white light emitting diodes (WLEDs), solid-state illumination, display technology and active laser materials etc.[1–7].In recent years, incandescent and fluorescent lights account for 20–30% of total electrical energy usage have been replaced with WLEDs.Furthermore, WLEDs have a higher luminous eficiency than traditional lighting, and are more reliable, all of which contribute to considerable energy savings in solid state lighting [8].The primary method that generates white light is mixing a blue InGaN chip with a (YAG: Ce3+) yellow phosphor.The color rendering index (Ra) and CCT are excessively high due to deficiency of red light components [9].To solve these issues, near-UV or blue LED chip is combined with multicolor (blue, green, and red) phosphors in a novel way to produce white light.Red phosphor design for high-quality w-LEDs are crucial, where as blue and green phosphors have already seen commercial success [10].The disadvantage of these approaches is that over a prolonged period of operation, the phosphors’ individual degradation rates lead to poor chromatic aberration and poor performance [11].Therefore, it is crucial to create a single phased phosphor that can release white light when illuminated by UVLEDs in order to replace YAG: Ce3+ yellow phosphor.Therefore, Conclusion In the present work, the structural and optical properties of NBB: x Dy3+ phosphors are studied as a function of Dy3+ ion concentration.The XRD patterns confirmed the formation of single phase NaBaB9O15; Dy3+ phosphor.FTIR studies revealed the existence of several functional groups in the studied phosphor.The studied NaBaB9O15; Dy3+ phosphor gave two strong emission bands in blue and yellow regions and also shows feeble red emission under the excitation of 386 nm.The doping concentration of Dy3+ ions was optimized to be 5 mol%.The concentration quenching occurred in PL spectra is due to dipole-quadrupole interactions.The color coordinates of studied phosphor pass through the white region of CIE diagram confirmed the ability to produce white light emission and it can be used for domestic lighting.The lifetime studies revealed that the decay time of studied phosphors are comparable to the previous reports.Among all Dy3+ concentration, 5 mol% of Dy3+ ions doped NBB phosphor can be suggested as potential material to fabricate phosphor coverted single phase white LEDs and display devices.Author Contributions V.Parthibaraj: Conceptualization, Writing-Original draft preparation, R.Vijayakumar: PL characterizations and analysis.Ranjib Kumar Padhi: Methodology, Validation.K.Ramachandran: Data curation, Funding acquisition.K.Maheshvaran: Writing-Reviewing and Editing, Supervision.Funding The authors declare that no funds, grants, or any other support was received during the work and preparation of this manuscript.Data Availability No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study. pubs.acs.org/JPCCLuminescence of Triple Perovskite Ba3MgTa2O9: Dy3+Up to 1100 °CMarcos R.Imer, Amos Afugu, Zhen-Fei Liu, and Federico A.Rabufetti* Cite This: J.Phys.Chem.C2024, 128, 16628−16639 Read Online ACCESSMetrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: The luminescence response of Dy3++-doped Ba3MgTa2O9 (BMTO:Dy) between room temperature and 1100C was studied in the context of hightemperature thermosensitive phosphors.Single-phase BMTO:Dy was synthesized via solid-state reaction.Powder X-ray difraction, difuse reflectance spectroscopy, and density-functional theory calculations were used to probe its crystal and electronic structure.Variable-temperature time-resolved decays of the 4I15/26H15/2 transition of Dy3+ (457nm) were collected and the temperature dependence of the excited-state average lifetime was quantitatively analyzed with two objectives: establish mechanisms driving luminescence thermal quenching and assess the potential of BMTO:Dy as a high-temperature luminescent thermometer.Quenching was observed above 450C and appeared to be driven by thermal ionization of the 4I15/2 excited state to the host’s conduction band, with a temperature-dependent activation barrier in the 1.1−1.5 eV range.The occurrence of high-order (≈21) multiphonon relaxation to lower-lying 4f levels as an additional or alternative quenching pathway at high temperatures could not be ruled out.

evels as an additional or alternative quenching pathway at high temperatures could not be ruled out.As a luminescent thermometer, the operational temperature range of BMTO:Dy was between 450 and 1100C and temperature sensitivities ranged between≈2.1% C-1 at 538C and 0.9 % C-1 at 1100 °C.Findings presented herein expand the library of high-temperature thermosensitive phosphors to group Vd0 refractory metalates, a class of materials that ofers the opportunity to tailor luminescence response through rational tuning of crystal, vibrational, and electronic structure. ■ INTRODUCTIONThermosensitive phosphors are ideal temperature sensors for combustion applications, where temperatures typically exceed 500C.Their unique suitability is predicated on their ability to operate in environments where contact thermometry and pyrometry are problematic to implement and do not aford adequate performance in terms of temperature accuracy and spatial resolution.1−4 The ability of thermosensitive phosphors to serve as thermal markers in combustion systems is illustrated by a number of examples that encompass both basic and applied materials research problems.Included in that list are understanding failure mechanisms and predicting lifetimes of thermal barrier coatings in gas turbine engines, surface temperature mapping and establishing the dynamics of heat flow in combustors,8−21 mapping temperature fields in hot gas flows,22,23 and in-service monitoring of rotating compo nents in turbomachinery.18 Thermosensitive phosphors typically consist of a host matrix doped with an activator.Temperature sensing may be approached from a lifetime or a ratiometric standpoint, with the former being preferred for high-temperature combustion applications.In this approach, the lifetime of the activator’s emissive state (τ) serves as the thermometric parameter to convert optical signals to temperature values.

ive state (τ) serves as the thermometric parameter to convert optical signals to temperature values.Lifetime depends on the rates of radiative and nonradiative relaxation processes, with the latter being strongly temperature-dependent and driving luminescence thermal quenching.The rate of change in lifetime with temperature determines the performance of the phosphor as a thermometer.It directly impacts figures-of-merit such as operational temperature range, temperature sensitivity and resolution, and spatial resolution, among others.For example, enhancing thermal quenching leads to a steeper decrease in lifetime, thereby improving temperature sensitivity.From a chemist’s perspective, it follows that achieving synthetic control over nonradiative relaxation processes governing thermal quenching is critical to design thermosensitive phosphors with targeted performance.Exercising synthetic control over thermal quenching path ways requires materials platforms in which structural (topologyofcationicsubstructure), vibrational (phononfrequencies), and electronic features (bandgap) of the host may be compositionally tuned, as these are directly relevant to the luminescence response of the activator.The library of high temperature thermosensitive phosphors for which experimental luminescence data above 500 °C are avail- abl e8-10, 15-21, 23-57 is largely dominated by Dy3+ as the activator of choice (see Supporting Information, Tables S1 and S2).A Dieke diagram of the 4f levels of Dy3+ is depicted in Figure 1, along with relevant radiative and nonradiative Figure 1.Dieke diagram of Dy3+.Blue emission from excited state 4I15/2-is indicated with a solid arrow.

ure 1.Dieke diagram of Dy3+.Blue emission from excited state 4I15/2-is indicated with a solid arrow.Nonradiative processes multiphonon relaxation (MPR) and ionization to the conduction band (CB) via charge transfer (CT) are depicted with dotted arrows.The double arrow denotes thermal coupling between states 4I15/2 and 4F9/2.processes.The lifetime of the 4I15/2 excited state extracted from its decay to the 6H15/2 ground state is used as the thermometric parameter.The fact that it occurs in the blue region of the spectrum (≈455 nm) afords minimal interference from blackbody radiation.High-temperature thermosensitive phosphors have been realized by incorporating Dy3+ into a number of wide bandgap hosts ( Eg > 6 e V ) includinrl, & yttria - stabiliizedzirconiarl ( YSZ &=YxZr1-xO2-x / 2 ), 10,35,38,44,45,47,50 aluminates (YAlO, GdAlO, rlr YAG=& Y3Al5O12 ), & silicates ( Y2SiO5, Y2Si2O7 ), 35, 48, 50 and aluminosilicates ( Ca2Al2SiO7,.( Ba, Sr ) Al2Si2O8 ).35, 50In these hosts, luminescence quenching at high temperatures occurs via high-order multiphonon relaxation (MPR), a process driven by low efective frequency phonons that bridge the gap between the lanthanide’s emissive level and lower-lying levels.37,56,58,59 This process has been invoked to rationalize quenching in YSZ:Dy above 450C (order18), 10 and YAG:Dy above 900C (order20) 52 and 1200C (order23).10 A remarkable absence in the list of hightemperature phosphors is that of group V and VI d0 oxides featuring MOnm- oxoanions as building blocks, specifically niobates, tantalates, molybdates, and tungstates.These metal ates ofer a high degree of structural, vibrational, and electronic tunability via chemical substitutions, which is highly desirable from the standpoint of manipulating nonradiative processes governing luminescence thermal quenching.

from the standpoint of manipulating nonradiative processes governing luminescence thermal quenching.Triple perovskite Ba3MgTa2O9 (BMTO) serves to illustrate their potential as host materials for high-temperature phosphors on account of its thermal stability and compositional tunability.It has a melting point of 3100C and has been examined as a candidate for thermal coatings.60−62 crystal structure is shown in Figure 2 and is amenable to a wide range of chemical substitutions.BMTO crystallizes in the P3m1 trigonal space group and exhibits the archetypical perovskite arrangement (Figure2a).63 Barium sits in cuboctahedral holes in the A site, while corner-sharing MgO6 and TaO6 octahedra are located in the B site.Ba2+ ions occupy two distinct holes, which difer from each other in the second coordination shell of barium, specifically in the number of neighboring Mg2+ and Ta5+ ions (Figure2b).Aliovalent substitutions include lanthanide doping in the A site of the perovskite lattice 64 and may be performed to impart luminescence response.Isovalent substitutions in the A and B sites 63,65,66 may be conducted to tune metal connectivity, vibrational frequencies, and bandgap.BMTO features an indirect bandgap of≈4.3 e V, 67 significantly narrower than that of hosts typically used in high-temperature phosphors (videsupra).This feature is noteworthy because it may open an alternative luminescence quenching pathway via thermally activated charge transfer (CT) from the activator’s excited state to the host conduction band (CB).68Thermal ionization of excited Dy3+ to the conduction band has been proposed as the primary quenching mechanism for group V metalate phosphors GdVO4: Dy65 ( Eg=3.9: e V ) 70 and LiNbO3: Dy71 ( Eg.=3.7 e V ).72In spite of their potential, lanthanide-doped BMTO and substituted derivatives have not been studied as high-temperature thermosensitive phosphors.

l spinel and involves a specic arrangement of metal cations (AandB) and oxygen anions.These materials have been widely used in ceramic pigments, magnetic materials, printing technologies, and catalysts.1–3 Cobalt aluminate (CoAl2O4), commonly known as Thenard blue, is a spinel-type oxide known for its intense blue color and various applications.It is known for its bright blue color, which results from the electronic transitions of Co2+ ions in the tetrahedral crystal eld.4 In the visible light region, the optical properties of CoAl2O4 are primarily inuenced by the d–d transitions of Co2+ (3d7) electrons in the tetrahedral (Td) structure.Hybridization between the O-2p and Co-3d orbitals permits dipole-forbidden d– d transitions.5 The optical, electromagnetic, and color properties of the CoAl2O4 material can be efectively changed by adjusting the p–d hybridization.The simplest way to change the p–d hybridization in the CoAl2O4 compound is to dope it with a transition metal or rare earth ions.Doping transition metals and rare earth ions into the CoAl2O4 host can change its color and optical and magnetic properties.3,5 Pradhan et al.fabricated and studied the spectroscopic and magnetic properties of spin-frustrated Mn-doped CoAl2O4 spinel.5 Research shows that the absorption spectra associated with d–d transitions are altered by Mn doping at the Co site.Random substitution of Mn introduces various magnetic exchange pathways of difering magnitudes, which enhance the interactions between the magnetic ions.Competitive magnetic exchange interactions between Co2+ and Mn2+ ions give rise to the magnetic properties of the material.Wang and colleagues suggested that the luminescence properties of CoAl2O4 are enhanced when doped with Ce and Mn ions.6 The blue color diminishes as the number of doped ions increases.

content: ed with Ce and Mn ions.6 The blue color diminishes as the number of doped ions increases.The photoluminescence enhancement in Ce and Mn co-doped CoAl2O4 is attributed not to the energy transfer between Ce4+ and Mn4+ but to surface or impurity defects.Tong et al.suggested that when the doping amount is less than 10%, A3+ can be partially replaced by trivalent rare earth ions (RE3+), forming spinel CoAl2-xRExO4 complex oxides.7 Replacing A3+ with RE3+ in CoAl2O4 enhances the blueness of the pigments.Er3+ ions can enhance the upconversion luminescence intensity of the CoAl2O4 pigment.The luminescence appeared blue, and variations in the luminescence intensity were observed with diferent Er doping concentrations.8 The degradation of colored and colorless organic dyes under natural sunlight was investigated using CoAl2O4 and Ni-doped CoAl2O4.The Ni-doped CoAl2O4 demonstrated higher photocatalytic activity compared to the undoped CoAl2O4, achieving photodegradation rates of 92.7% for crystal violet, 88.77% for methylene blue, and 63.34% for benzoic acid.9 Trivalent dysprosium (Dy3+) is a rare earth ion that has many important applications in optical devices and materials.Its applications include lighting, telecommunications, spectroscopy, and solar energy, making it a crucial element in the development of next-generation optical devices and materials.10, 11Dy3+ ions are capable of generating white light because of their unique luminescence properties.This was achieved through a combination of intense blue (484 nm, 4F9/26H15/2 and yellow (575 nm, 4F9/26H13/2 emissions when doped into various crystals, glasses, and glass-ceramic materials.12, 13Dy3+, doped solid-state systems can be eficiently excited by commercial ultraviolet (UV) or blue light-emitting diodes (LEDs), because there is a spectral overlap between the excitation spectra of Dy3+ ions and the emission spectra of these LEDs.13This makes them practical for use in modern lighting technology.

emission spectra of these LEDs.13This makes them practical for use in modern lighting technology.Dy3+ ions have been extensively studied in crystals, glasses, and glass-ceramic materials owing to their wellestablished optical properties and simple energy structures.13,14 These materials serve as efective hosts for Dy3+ ions to exhibit luminescence properties.Beyond their practical applications, Dy3+ ions are used as spectroscopic probes to study the local symmetry and bonding features of other RE3+ ions within diferent host matrices.15 The yellow-to-blue emission ratio of Dy3+ can vary depending on factors such as the nature of the host material and the concentration of Dy3+ ions.Dy3+-doped phosphors have been used for light-emitting diodes, especially white light-emitting diodes by adjusting the yellow-to-blue ratio of Dy3+ ions.Dy3+ ions stand out not only for their ability to generate white light but also for their role in advancing optical technologies through their use in various luminescent materials.16,17 Judd–Ofelt (JO) theory is a powerful tool for analyzing the local environment around RE3+ ions and predicting their optical properties.Traditional JO analysis relies on absorption spectra to determine the Judd–Ofelt parameters ( ).However, this approach can be challenging for powder materials.To solve this problem, recent studies have proposed alternative methods for calculating the parameters, using diferent spectral types such as difuse-reection spectrum, uorescence decay curve, and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectrum.In the above spectra, the PLE spectrum is particularly versatile as it can be obtained for various material morphologies, including lms, nanocrystalline structures, bulk crystals, and glasses.In this study, the PLE spectra of Dy3+ ions were utilized to calculate the parameters of CoAl2O4: x Dy3+NCs.

Check for updates PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Cite this: RSCAdv., 2024, 14, 22642 Optimizing white light emission in Dy(III) complexes: impact of energy transfer from mono and bidentate ligands on luminescence† Sofia Malik,a Komal Jakhar,‡*a Devender Singh, ‡*a Anjli Hooda,a Sonia Redhu,a Swati Dalal,a Vandana Aggarwal,a Sumit Kumar,b Rajender Singh Malikb and Parvin Kumarc Received 27th May 2024Accepted 11th July 2024Complexes of dysprosium(III) ions with 1,1,1,5,5,5-hexafluoro-2,4-pentanedione featuring various mono and bi-dentate neutral ligands have been prepared and thoroughly investigated.The synthesized complexes exhibit an octa-coordinated environment, achieved by stoichiometrically combining organic ligands and Dy(III) ions.This octa-coordination environment of Dy(III) ion was confirmed by FT-IR spectroscopy, thermogravimetry and elemental analysis.Near-white light (NWL) is emitted when complexes were exposed to UV radiation, indicating a significant flow of energy from the sensitizing moieties towards the Dy(III) ion.This NWL emission might have resulted due to a balance between the intensities corresponding to emission peaks at 480 nm (blue) and 575 nm (yellow) in Dy1–Dy3.Emission spectra recorded at diferent excitation wavelength were utilized to study the tunability of CIE color coordinates.In addition to their high thermal stability, the complexes display bipolar paramagnetic shifts in their NMR spectra.The 4F9/2→6H13/2 transition, contributing 62% of the total emission, stands out as a promising candidate for laser amplification due to its dominance in the emission spectra.Additionally, NWL emission observed in a solid Dy( ) complex opens intriguing possibilities for its application in next-generation white-light emitting devices.

opens intriguing possibilities for its application in next-generation white-light emitting devices.DOI: rsc.li/rsc-advances 1Introduction There has been a strong push towards the development and wide spread use of energy eficient SSL (solidstatelighting) technologies and smart devices in response to increased global demand for energy.Solid-state white-light-emitting materials ofer remarkable benets, like energy conservation and extended lifespan, leading to their widespread adoption across various applications, ranging from large-panel displays to lasers.1–4 It is important to note that SSL sources can be classi-ed based on the material used in their fabrication.For instance, LEDs employ inorganic phosphors, while OLEDs make use of organic semiconductors.Furthermore, SSLs can be categorized based on the method by which they emit light, with LEDs utilizing UV excitation and OLEDs relying on electrical excitation.5,6 Considerable interest surrounds the realm of white light emission (WLE) which can be obtained using two diferent approaches: dual color emitters [blue either with red (B/R) or with yellow (B/Y)] or simply employing three-colour emitters that mix primary colors (RGB).7–9 To generate white light, a variety of methods are employed, including the incorporation of diferent dopants or multiple phase matrices.These matrices can be composed of various materials like nanomaterials, organic compounds, hybrid organic–inorganic substances, metal complexes or inorganic phosphors.These materials have unique properties for achieving white light emission and sometimes combining these diferent materials is necessary to reach the desired outcome.

content: emission and sometimes combining these diferent materials is necessary to reach the desired outcome.Additionally, WLE from single molecules is also attainable, covering entire visible spectrum.10–12 Such systems comprises of a single-phase-single-emitter which eases the manufacturing process, resulting in materials which are light weight and thin, making them particularly well-suited for use in optical devices.13 WLE from single molecules can be generated by utilizing trivalent lanthanide (Ln) complexes.The fascinating aspect of lanthanide luminescence is that it relies on indirect excitation of lanthanide ions, unlike other conventional photoexcitation methods.This is on account of parity restricted behavior of their f–f transitions which results in low absorptivity (0.5–3 dm 3 mol 1 cm 1).14,15 To overcome this limitation, researchers have turned to suitable sensitizers, which possess the unique ability to indirectly transfer energy to lanthanide ions and function as antennas.16,17 They absorb incident light and sensitize metal ion by eficiently transferring this energy to their excited states.Subsequently, excited Ln(III) ion engages in radiative relaxations to the lower electronic states.Narrow peaks are obtained in the emission spectra of these complexes due to the well-shielded 4f electrons of the lanthanide ions, which result in sharp and well-dened electronic transitions that are relatively unafected by the ligand eld and surrounding environment.However, it is essential to highlight that selection of chromophoric sensitizer should be done carefully so that it functions as antenna along with producing its own emission in blue region which is basic necessity to produce white light.18–20 This dual functionality is crucial for the production of white light when it is coordinated with the yellow light-emitting Dy3+ ion.

GRAPHICALABSTRACTUrban ecological lighting W-LED with low disturbance to plant ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Anti-thermal-quenching Dy3+-activated phosphors Urban ecological lighting ABSTRACTWhite light-emitting diode (LED) for night lighting disrupts photoperiod in plants, which affects the plant’s photosynthesis.Therefore, it is necessary to find a new type of white LED with little effect on plant photosynthesis.In this study, a series of phosphate phosphors Ca9NaY2/3 (PO4) 7: Dy3+ ( CNYP: Dy3+) were synthesized.Cation Li+ substitute Na+ were used to improve the luminescence properties of CNYP:Dy3+ phosphor.The CNYP: Dy3+ phosphor exhibits visible white light emission with emission peaks at 480 nm (bluelight) and 570 nm (yellowlight) excited by the near ultraviolet light 350 nm.The optimal concentration of Dy3++ was 0.10 mol, and the mechanism of concentration quenching was evaluated as energy migration among the nearest or next-nearest Dy3+.The substitution of Na+ by Li+ of CNYP: 0.10Dy3+ improves the internal quantum efficiency from 30.24% to 59.05 %, and presents good near-zero thermal quenching performance at 423K.To assess the suitability of this phosphor for urban ecological lighting, the spectrum resemblance (SR) index between the electroluminescence spectrum of the prepared pc-LED and the absorption spectra of chlorophyll a and b was evaluated as 6.63% and 18.61%, respectively.This work exhibits a feasible scheme for the development of urban ecological lighting. 1.

content: ectively.This work exhibits a feasible scheme for the development of urban ecological lighting. 1.Introduction Artificial lighting is a universal feature of human society.For the animal and plant world, however, artificial lighting creates a new type of environmental stress that disrupts the natural light–dark cycle [1–3].Light condition is a crucial factor in the photosynthesis process of plants [4,5].Adequate light promotes plant growth, while excessive light can hinder it, disrupting photosynthesis and ultimately leading to the death of plants [6,7].Therefore, it is necessary to develop a kind of urban ecological lighting source that can meet the needs of urban lighting and only make a slight impact on the light environment of animals and plants.Phosphor-converted light emitting diode (pc-LED) is an outstanding lighting source, which has the advantages of adjustable spectrum, energy saving and environmental protection, have being widely used in urban lighting [8,9].Pc-WLED, known for its closest resemblance to natural light, is commonly utilized for urban lighting purposes [10,11].However, during the night lighting period, they will affect the photoperiod of plants, so that plants cannot carry out photosynthesis normally [12].This is mainly due to the large overlap between the emission spectrum of conventional white LED and the absorption spectrum of plant pigments, thus affecting plant photosynthesis during night lighting.At present, the acquisition of white pc-LED is mainly through the following schemes [8]: (1) blue LED chip combining yellow light emitting phosphor [13,14]; (2) n-UVLED chip combining red/green/ blue light-emitting phosphors [15]; (3) n-UVLED chip combining blue/ yellow-emitting phosphors [12].Among these, only the third scheme results in a sufficiently small overlap between the emission spectra and the absorption spectra of the plant pigments.

ciently small overlap between the emission spectra and the absorption spectra of the plant pigments.The rare earth ion activator Dy3+ in the 4F9 configuration has abundant energy levels, typically exhibits two main emissions include blue emission at 480 nm (4F9/26H15/2) and yellow emission at 570 nm (4F9/26H13/2) [16,34].In addition, the optimal excitation region is usually around 350 nm and 390 nm, which can be effectively excited by n-UVLED chip.In this way, the pc-LED combined by Dy3+-activated phosphors and n-UV chips will present an eco-friendly white light emission.The - Ca3 (PO4) 2 type structure is an excellent matrix structure in phosphate compounds [17–19].There are five Ca2+ sites available for occupation (Ca1-Ca2latticesite) and can be occupied by mono, bivalent or trivalent ions without disrupting structural stability [20,21].For instance, M8MgSc (PO4) 7.x Dy3+( M=Ca / Sr ), Ca9La (PO4) 7: Dy3+, Eu3+ and Ca8ZnY (PO4) 7Dy3+[ 16, 22, 23 ] ].In general, Dy3+ ion activated - Ca3 (PO4) 2 structure phosphor is the star candidate for the develop ment of urban ecological lighting pc-LED with high thermal stability and high luminous efficiency.Herein, the CagNaY2/3 (PO4) 7 (CNYP) matrix was selected in the - Ca3 (PO4) 2 structural family and activated with trivalent dysprosium ions.The structural and optical properties of CNYP: Dy3+ were analyzed.It can be efficiently excited by n-UV light (350nm) and emits both blue (480nm) and yellow (570nm) light.The effects and mechanism cation substitution (Li+insteadofNa+) strategies on the photoluminescence properties and thermal stability of phosphors were studied.The change of thermal quenching behavior is discussed in detail.Finally, the spectrum resemblance (SR) index between the electro-luminescent (EL) spectra of prepared pc-LED devices and the absorption spectrum of plant chlorophyll is evaluated.All the results suggest that the CNYP: Dy3+ phosphor has a good application prospect in urban ecological lighting. 2.Experiment section 2.1.

escence properties analysis The PLE and PL spectra of CNYP: x Dy3+ phosphor are shown in Fig.3ab.In the PLE spectra range of 280–480 nm, it can be intuitively observed that seven main excitation peaks at 325, 350, 365, 388, 426, 450, and 472 nm, corresponding to the 6H15/26P3/2, 6H15/26P7/2, 6H15/26P5/2, 6H15/24I13/2, 6H15/24G11/2, 6H15/24I15/2 and 6H15/24F9/2 electronic transition in Dy3+ 4f-4f, respectively.The PLE spectrum reveals that CNYP: x Dy3+ has two excitation peaks (365, 472 nm) suitable for commercial near-ultraviolet and blue chips respectively.Under the optimal excitation peak at 350 nm, the PL spectrum predominantly exhibits two distinct emission peaks, located at 480 nm and 570 nm, respectively.The emission peak in the short wavelength blue region (480nm) is generated by the 4F9/26H15/2 transition, which is mainly magnetically allowed and almost unaffected by the crystal field strength around Dy3-+.The latter yellow peak at 570 nm corresponds to the 4F9/26H13/2 transition.This transition is a spin-forbidden forced electric dipole transition that is very sensitive to the crystal field strength around Dy3+.And this 4F9/26H13/2 transition only occurs when Dy3+ in a low symmetric position at the non-inverted symmetry center of the crystal lattice.The strongly 4F9/26H13/2 radiative transition indicates that Dy3+ is at a symmetric site in the lattice in the CNYP matrix.Fig.3c shows the concentration of Dy3+ dependence PL spectra integrated intensity of CNYP: x Dy3+.With the increase in Dy3+ concentration, the integral intensity exhibits a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing, reaching its peak atx=0.10 mol.In general, this concentration quenching of emission intensity involves non-radiative energy transfer between activator ions.This process mainly includes exchange interaction, radiation reabsorption and electric multipole interaction.

Figure S5a-f shows the temperature (K) dependent-emission spectrum of CN1-yLyYP: 0.10Dy3+.It is an interesting anti-thermal quenching property that the emission intensity shows a trend of first increase and then decrease with increasing temperature (can see in Fig.5e).Generally, the anti-thermal quenching property can be attributed to two possible mechanisms: excellent structural rigidity and defect level.The former high structural rigidity can be empirically analyzed by Debye temperature.For the latter, defects are unavoidable in the materials synthesis process.The anti-thermal quenching phenomenon is attributed to the compensation of emission losses at high temperatures by thermally activated defect levels.As reported, - Ca3 (PO4) 2 structure have five Ca sites, among this sites Ca4 sites are not completely filled, so this special crystal structure can form a large number of vacancies.In the matrix CagNaY (PO4) 7, Y3+ is introduced by replace the Ca2+ site, and to accommodate the charge balance, the following reaction (1) will occur: 3Ca2+→2Y3+ + V (1) where VCa represents the Ca vacancy, which indicates that the three calcium sites are replaced by two Y sites to satisfy the charge balance, leaving one Ca vacancy.Therefore, this special crystal structure can form a large number of cationic vacancies.These calcium vacancy defects and other inherent defects in the matrix can form defect level below the conduction band.It can be observed from Fig.5e and Figure S5 that the anti-thermal quenching gradually weakens with the substitution of Na+ by Li+.The integral emission intensity at 423K relative to 298K decreasing with the increasing of yLi+.For CNYP and CLYP, the defect energy levels must be different.In the structural evolution from CNYP to CLYP, the cell volume shrinks, and the structure is optimized.The weakening anti-thermal quenching may be caused by the introduction of Li+ to reduce the defects in the matrix and adjust the defects level.

Abstract This study describes the luminous properties of Pb5 (PO4) 3Br doped with RE3+( RE=Dy3+, Eu3+ and Tb3+) synthesised using the solid-state method.The synthesised phosphor was characterised using Fourier-transform infrared, X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy and photoluminescence measurements.Dy3 - +-doped Pb5 (PO4) 3Br phosphor exhibited blue and yellow emissions at 480 and 573 nm, respectively, on excitation at 388 nm.Eu3+-doped Pb5 (PO4) 3Br phosphor exhibited orange and red emissions at 591 and 614 nm, respectively, on excitation at ex=396 nm.Pb5 (PO4) 3Br; Tb3+ phosphor exhibited the strongest green emission at 547 nm on excitation at ex=380 nm.Additionally, the effect of the concentration of rare-earth ions on the emission intensity of Pb5 (PO4) 3Br: RE3+( RE3+=Dy3+, Eu3+ and Tb3+) phosphors was investigated. ARTICLEINFOGRAPHICALABSTRACTKeywords: Boro-phosphate glass Urbah energy Decay profile CIE chromaticity Thermoluminescence ABSTRACTA novel Fluro boro-phosphate host matrix doped with the 1 mol% of Dy3+ ions ( 50B2O3+ 20P2O5+ 10Ti O2+10Sr CO3+ 4Ba F2+ 5Ba CO3+ 1Dy2O3 ) was prepared using a conventional melt-quenching mechanism, and its structural characteristics were explored through the Powder-XRD, FT-IR, FT-Raman, EDAX and SEM spectro scopic analysis.The XRD spectrum of the glass confirmed its non-crystalline or amorphous structure.FT-IR and FT-Raman spectrum studies revealed that various borate and phosphate groups present with a variety of stretching and bending vibrations.Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and Energy Dispersive X-ray analysi (EDAX) analysis have been used to examine the surface morphology and the presence of elements, respectively in the prepared glass.The optical absorption spectrum was used to explore the electronic band structure through the measurements of optical band-gap energy and Urbach energy.The luminescence spectrum reveals the emission characteristics of Dy3+ ions due to the electric-dipole and magnetic-dipole transitions.It is found that the decay time of the 4F9/2 excited level at a concentration of 1 mol% Dy3+ in the glass matrix is tri-fit non exponential.The CIE chromaticity coordinates and the concentration influence on Y/B intensity ratios were computed for the creation of white light from the luminescence spectrum.The present work also discusses the findings after figuring out the correlated color temperature associated (CCT) with the color purity (Pe).The Thermoluminescence (TL) characteristics and the kinetic parameters of the glass were studied after the γ-irradiation with a dose of 2 kGy.

structure of Dy3++ ions and the electron-hole pair formation upon irradiation in the glass matrix. 1.Introduction Glasses made of pure borate and phosphates are not as chemically/ thermally stable as other host glass matrix.Superior thermal and chemical properties of silicate glasses necessitate very high temperatures for synthesis and short viscosity retention times [1].Phosphate glasses are particularly improved in terms of chemical durability by the inclusion of trivalent metal oxides and mixed-alkali oxides.The synthesis of boro-phosphate glasses is less temperature-intensive than that of silicates, and they exhibit greater chemical and thermal stability than borate and phosphate glasses.The increased glass formation is caused by more structural disorders brought on by various cation forms.Borophosphate glasses make attractive hosts for rare earths because of their low glass transition temperature, outstanding optical properties, high transparency, and cost.Boron phosphate substances with water in their constitution and a B: P ratio lower than 1 are produced by combining BO4 and PO4 groups in different structures [2].In the Boro-phosphate glasses, the PO4 tetrahedra that make up the phosphate glass network are joined by covalent phosphorous-oxygen bonds, allowing them to form a polymerized structure whose level of bonding is determined by the glass composition.The proportions of trigonal BO3 and tetragonal BO4 units in the borate glass also impact the composition of the glass.The result of adding B2O3 to the phosphate network depends significantly on the B/P ratio and the overall quantity of network formers.Additionally, B2O3 has a higher mass absorption coefficient for γ-radiation and thermal neutron absorption capacity than P2O5, indicating that boro-phosphate glass would be a better option for immobilizing radioactive waste [3].

ture suggests they can produce electron trapping states in the intra-band-gap of the host substance.In the luminescent feature, different rare earth ions emit colors of their own.Glasses with Dy3+ doping are potential materials for w-LEDs and other solid-state lightning devices [10,11].The Dy3+ doped glasses often emit light in the blue (4F9/26H15/2) and yellow (4F9/26H13/2) zones due to the electric and magnetic dipole interactions, respectively.Since the 4f level shift, the chosen Dy3+ ion has played a significant role in producing the white emission.The Dy3+ ion is also recognized as an flocalised trap-creating ion and is discovered to prolong the afterglow.Dy3+ ions become excited as a result of radiation exposure, and direct electron transfer from these excited states to trap centers results in thermo-luminescence (TL) emission.The emission spectra for boro-phosphate glass with 1 mol% Dy3+ ions exhibit concentration quenching in most of the reports [ 12, 13, 8 ] which can be attributed to Dy3+ ion dipole–dipole interactions (Dextertheory).The non-radiative energy transfer process that occurs between adjacent Dy3+Dy3+ ions causes concentration quenching in glass matrix systems with higher RE dopant concentrations [14].The present study focuses on the structural and optical characteristics of Fluro Borophosphate glass doped with 1 mol% of Dy3+ ions for applications as w-LEDs and laser sources.Additionally, research on TL kinetic factors and TL-EPR correlation was conducted to comprehend the TL mecha nism of this glass system upon irradiation. 2.Experimental procedure 2.1.Materials synthesis Dy3+ doped fluroboro-phohphate (DFBP) glass in a composition of 50B2O3+ 20P2O5+ 10Ti O2+ 10Sr CO3+ 4Ba F2+ 5Ba CO3+ 1Dy2O3 was synthesized by the typical melt-quench technique.

content: ited two strong emission peaks at 480 nm and 580 nm, which are characteristic transitions of Dy3+ ions.However, the relative intensity between these peaks varies considerably due to the variation of the co-dopant/compensator (Li+, Na+, K+) concentration, representing the variation of the crystal field.Effects of different charge compensators (A+) and their concentration on the structural and luminescence properties of ZrO2: (0.01) Dy3+: x A-+ phosphors were thoroughly investigated.Further, Judd-Ofelt parameters were calculated.Total emission colour (TEC) concentration of ZrO2: (0.01) Dy3-+ phosphors were improved remarkably with the addition of charge compensators (A+), which would promote their applications in solid state lighting.The effective blue emission of the phosphors was changing with different co-dopant incor poration.Implying possible use of this material as a blue emitting phosphor as a blue emitting component in three-component white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs). 1.Introduction Recently zirconia has gained the attention of the research because of their applications in different fields such as UV protective coating, gas sensors, solid-oxide fuel cells, thermal barrier coatings, self-lubricating bearings, and luminescence.It possesses important chemical and physical properties like high melting point, low thermal conductivity, high thermal expansion coefficient etc., [1,2].Zirconia could form three different phases namely cubic, tetragonal, and monoclinic.At low temperatures it forms monoclinic phase, when heated to 1150 ◦C zirconia forms tetragonal phase and finally at temperature 2300 ◦C it forms cubic phase.When the temperature is reversed the phases also will be reversed.In our previous work the high temperature cubic phase of the zirconia was made stable at room temperature because of the mesoporous structure and oxygen defects [3].

onia was made stable at room temperature because of the mesoporous structure and oxygen defects [3].Numerous methods are reported for synthesizing zirconia, including solution combustion, sol-gel, solid-state reaction, and hydrothermal, to name a few.Solution combustion has gained recent popularity due to its distinct advantages: ease of use, rapid reaction times, and the formation of mesoporous final products.When trivalent rare earth metal ions are substituted in a metal oxide matrix, they exhibit characteristic photoluminescence, however their emission intensity and emission colour could be altered by modi fying the crystal symmetry surrounding the rare earth ion [4].Luminescent efficiency can be altered by varying composition and/or phase of the phosphors.Some reports suggest that even 1 mol % of co-dopant can lead to a great improvement of phosphor’s luminescent efficiency.Recently, significant research is devoted to increase the emission efficiency of rare earth doped phosphors by co-doping with alkaline metals.The goal of co-dopants is generally related to the process of cross relaxation, charge compensation, and up conversion.Subsequently, lot of efforts are made to increase the luminescent efficiency by co-doping the host with metal ions.Monovalent alkali elements like, Li+Na+ and K+ were widely used as co-dopants owing to their proven effect in enhancement of luminescence [5].As their electron affinity, charge state and ionic radius are quite different from host, their substitution may alter the crystal lattice and thus affecting the site symmetry around the rare earth ion.This distortion in turn could modify the emission in tensity and emission colour to a considerable amount [6].Difference in the Pauling’s electro negativity and atomic/ionic size between the host, dopants and co-dopants has a prominent role in the photoluminescent characteristics of phosphors [7].In our previous work, we reported enhancement of PL emission intensity in Dy3+ doped ZrO2 by co-doping with Li+ ions [8].

we reported enhancement of PL emission intensity in Dy3+ doped ZrO2 by co-doping with Li+ ions [8].Dhananjaya et al., reported, emission intensity enhancement due to lithium-ion co-doping in Gd2O3: Eu3+ phosphors [9].Several studies highlight the influence of co-doping on luminescence properties in various materials.Dai et al.[10], found that adding 3% Dy3+ to CaSr2 (PO4) 2 yielded maximum photoluminescence (PL) intensity.Further co-doping with 3 mol% alkali metal ions ( Li+, Na+, K+ ) revealed superior brightness in Li+ doped samples compared to Na+ and K+ co-doping.Yu et al.[11], observed similar luminescence enhancement in SrZnO2: Eu3+ co-doped with Li+, Na+, and K+, attributing it to their low oxidation states and compatible ionic radii.Li et al.[12], demonstrated a significant increase in PL intensity in CaMoO4: Tb3+ co-doped with these alkali metal ions using a solid-state method (SSM).Notably, the emission intensity grew proportionally with co-dopant concentration up to the equal concen tration of Tb3+.Kuang et al.[13], reported similar effect in CdSiO3.The ionic radii of the dopant and co-dopant play a significant role in the emission intensity.Co-dopants play various roles as a flux, sensitizer or as a charge compensator [14–16].It may enter into the host lattice, producing oxygen defects or could alter the crystal field surrounding the activator (REions), thus influencing the emission property of the phosphor [17].It is imperative to probe the properties of the co-dopants to understand the precise mechanism of luminescence enhancement, and to look for other effective ions for co-doping.While elements like Na+; K+ and Li+ are widely available and known for their diverse properties, a comparative study on their impact on PL remains less explored.This work is devoted to providing a comparative study on doping with monovalent alkali metal ions in different concentrations ranging from 1 mol% to 9 mol% and to identify the best suitable ion and concentration for ZrO2: Dy3+ phosphors.

glycine (NH2CH2COOH); zirconyl nitrate ( ZrO (NO3) 2; lithium nitrate ( Li (NO3); sodium nitrate (NaNO3), and potassium nitrate (KNO3).Stoichiometric ratios of the reactants were taken to obtain the preferred products.Preparation was carried out in a twostep process: in the first step, Dy2O3 was added to 1:1 diluted nitric acid and the resulting suspension was gently heated to form a transparent dysprosium nitrate residue.In step 2: zirconyl nitrate, dysprosium nitrate (preparedinstep1), glycine and lithium nitrate was dissolved in 100 ml double distilled water to form a clear solution and then introduced into a muffle furnace preheated to 500C..Glycine was used as fuel, maintaining the fuel to oxidizer ratio at unity.White fluffy mesoporous ZrO2: (0.01) Dy3+ x Li+ ( x=0.0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.07 and 0.09) nanopowder were formed.Similar process was followed to synthesize another two series of samples with varying concentration of Na+ and K+ as co-dopants.Sodium nitrate was used as the source of sodium and potassium nitrate was used as the source of potassium.These samples were further calcined at 750C for 2hr. 3.Results and discussion 3.1.Powder XRD analysis It is well known that photoluminescence emission spectra mainly depend on the crystalline phase, crystallinity, particle size and surface morphology of phosphor materials.In this regard PXRD studies become imperative in identification of the phase and crystallite size of the particle.PXRD patterns of ZrO2: (0.01) Dy3+: 0.07Li +, 0.07Na + and 0.05K + nanophosphors are presented in Fig.1 (A)..

rphology of the nanophosphors plays crucial role in photoluminescence and other physical properties.The SEM spectrographs were recorded in-order to study the morphology of the samples and presented in Fig.3.Lithium-ion doped samples reveal a smoother texture while samples doped with sodium and potassium reveal a coarse structure.EDAX of the samples are provided in the right side of corresponding SEM images.In Fig.3(A), the peak corresponding to lithium is absent in this spectrum.However, the peaks corresponding to sodium and potassium could be seen in Fig.3(B-C) respectively.Hence, the presence of lithium in the samples has to be confirmed by other possible method. 3.4.XPS studies EDAX spectra could not identify the presence of lithium ions in the prepared samples, (because the device used to study the EDAX spectra cannot detect first three elements in the periodic table) therefore in-order to confirm the presence of lithium ions and to study the charge compensation XPS study for the Li+ co-doped sample was taken and as shown in Fig.4.The complete survey scan of the ZrO2: Dy3+: Li+ sample in the range 1350 to 0 e V, as shown in Fig.4(a).The spectra confirm the presence of zirconium, oxygen, dysprosium, and lithium ( Zr3d, O1s, Dy3d and Li1s) in the lattice.The binding energy of C1s peak was taken as the reference to analyze the charging effects.The high-resolution scan of Zr3d, O1s, Dy3d and Li1s of the samples are presented in Fig.4 (b-e) These high-resolution scans are further de-convoluted to identify the elemental bonding of each species.The binding energy, FWHM, atomic weight % and the corresponding assignment for the individual peaks are represented in Table 2.The Zr3d spectra in Fig.4(b) have doublet peaks (3d5/2and3d3/2) at 181.72 eV and 184.33 eV.This peak could have appeared due to the presence of bonded zirconium - ors are presented in Fig.6(a–b) respectively.The excitation spectra composed of several sharp peaks.These excitation peaks at 325 nm, 350 nm, 368 nm, 385 nm, and 425 nm can be attributed to the 6H15/24M17/2, 6P7/2, 6P5/2, 4K17/2, and 4G11/2 electron transitions of Dy3+ respectively.The emission spectra reveal two broad spectra centred at 480 nm and 580 nm corresponding to 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 respectively.The peak between 375 nm and 475 nm can be assigned defect related luminescence, like F-centers and oxygen vacancies [29].PL emission intensity increased up to 7 mol% of sodium concentration and the emission intensity decreases for further increase in the sodium ion concentration.Photoluminescence excitation and emission spectra of the K+ co-doped samples as shown in Fig.7(a–b) respectively.PL emission intensity increased up to 5 mol% of potassium concentration and the emission intensity decreases for further increase in the potassium ion concentration.This can be assigned to the cumulative effects of charge compensation; lattice distortion and phase of the resultant samples causes by the incorporation of potassium ion [30].Emission intensity of the samples increases with the alkali metal ion concentration.For Na+ and Li+ co-doped samples the maximum emission intensity was observed for samples with 7 mol%.Whereas for the K+ ion doped samples the intensity reached its maximum for the 5 mol% and the PL emission intensity decrease thereon

content: 11 nm for Eu3+ in the red spectrum, and a notable green emission for Tb3+ due to specific transitions.The photoluminescence (PL) analysis indicates that luminescence is optimized through precise doping, leveraging dipole interactions, and localized resonant energy transfer, which are influenced by dopant concentration and spatial configuration.Temperature studies show emission intensity variations, particularly noticeable below 100K for Tb3+ doped samples, demonstrating the nuanced balance between thermal quenching and luminescence efficiency.This temperature dependency, alongside the identified optimal doping conditions, underscores the potential of these materials for advanced photonic applications, offering insights into their thermal behavior and emission mechanisms under different conditions. 1.Introduction Borates, compounds containing boron-oxygen bonds, exhibit an intricate and diverse structural chemistry, attracting significant interest from both the scientific community and for practical applications.Their remarkable versatility is attributed to the unique ability of boron atoms to form varied polymerization clusters through coordination with oxygen, leading to the formation of structures such as triangular boron trioxide (BO3) or tetrahedral boron tetroxide (BO4) clusters, among others.These processes give rise to a variety of polymerization clusters such as B2O5, B2O7, B3O9, and B5O10, each with distinct properties and unique applications (Mutailipu et al., 2021).Historically, the synthesis of metal borates has primarily relied on methods such as high-temperature solid-state reactions or boric acid flux techniques, facilitating the creation of a broad spectrum of compounds.The exploration of borates has unfolded over the last nine decades, with research efforts concentrated in three key areas: the study of alkali and alkaline-earth-metal borates; investigations into main group and tran sition metal borates; and exploration of alkaline-earth-metal borates doped with rare-earth ions.

an sition metal borates; and exploration of alkaline-earth-metal borates doped with rare-earth ions.The systematic study of borate crystal structures initiated in the 1930s through the groundbreaking work of Zachariasen, Goldschmidt, Hauptmann, and others led to the identification of over 2500 crystal structures of borates, both hydrous and anhydrous, as recorded in the ICSDDatabase (ICSD-2016) (Bubnova et al., 2017).This extensive research has not only clarified crystal structure terminology but has also categorized borates into various families, including those related to huntite structures, thus enriching our understanding of borate chemistry (Filatov and SBubnova, 2000; Becker, 2001; Belokoneva, 2008; Parth e, 2004; Xue et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2020).This extensive exploration underscores the continuous relevance and potential of borates in various scientific underscores the continuous relevance and potential of borates in various scientific and technological domains.The growing interest in borates is driven by the development of novel borate phosphors, which stand out for their superior phosphorescent properties.These properties, coupled with exceptional nonlinear optical capabilities, chemical stability, thermal resistance, and straightforward synthesis, underscore the potential of borates in optoelectronics and other technological applications.Their capacity to form complex polyanions paves the way for the creation of technologically promising borate structures, further amplified by the incorporation of rare-earth elements into borate matrices, thus expanding their functional capabilities (Verma et al., 2018; Kishor Tawalare, 2022).This advancement has opened new avenues for the development of cutting-edge technologies, particularly in energy-efficient lighting and high-precision optical instruments.

edge technologies, particularly in energy-efficient lighting and high-precision optical instruments.In the realm of research, the 1990s saw the successful of new rare-earth (R) calcium borates, such as RCa4O (BO3) 3, R2CaO (BO3) 2, and RCaB7O13, within the R2O3-CaO-B2O3 ternary system (Khamaganova et al., 1991; Norrestam et al., 1992; Chen et al., 1988).Among these, LaCOB, part of the ReCOB family ( Re=La, Gd, Lu, and Y), distinguished itself through its application potential in lighting displays, nonlinear optics, and scintillation devices, thanks to its unique lumi nescent properties and structural versatility (Ayvacikli et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2013; Mishra et al., 2022).These developments highlight the importance of interdisciplinary approaches, combining materials science, chemistry, and physics, to explore and optimize the properties of borates for advanced applications.Referred to as LACOB phosphors, these materials’ unique luminescent properties and structural diversity make them prime candidates for advanced photonic applications.The body of research on various LACOB phosphors, synthesized using different chemical methods and activated with rare-earth elements such as Sm3+, Nd3+Yb3+, is extensive.For instance, Zhang et al.(2014) demonstrated that Sm3+-doped La2CaB10O19 (Sm:LACOB) crystal, grown using the top-seeded solution growth (TSSG) method, exhibited strong 599 nm orange fluorescence under 410 nm excitation, suggesting potential applications in medical imaging and diagnostics (Zhang et al., 2014).Shan et al.(2015) studied the spectroscopic properties of Tb3++-doped La2CaB10O19 (Tb:LACOB) crystal, also grown using TSSG, finding that its unpolarized absorption and emission spectra provided valuable insights into its optical behavior (Shan et al., 2015).Srinivas (2016) demonstrated structural and optical properties of Ca3La2 (BO3) 4 doped with Tb prepared using a high-temperature solid-state reaction method (Srinivas, 2016).

vices.Received 5th December 2023, Accepted 29th February 2024DOI: rsc.li/dalton 1.Introduction As the hotspot in the solid-state lighting area, the development of highly power eficient, sustainably devised solid-state lighting devices is a key concern for materials scientists and researchers globally as the world is now experiencing an energy crisis.1–3 Solid-state lighting technology, especially white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs), has completely revolutionized the field of luminescence owing to its exceptional properties, which include low power consumption, high energy eficacy, long lifetime, excellent lumen performance, and environmental stewardship.1,3–5 Trivalent lanthanide (Ln3+) -activated inorganic phosphors have attracted considerable attention as next-generation lighting sources due to their superior physicochemical features such as long-lived luminescence, narrow emission bands, appropriate color rendering index (CRI) and correlated color temperature (CCT) and low toxicity.3,5–7 The intricate luminescence properties of Ln3+ ions arise from their unique electronic structure that enables Ln3+ ions in solids to eficiently emit photons in the ultraviolet to visible or infrared (IR) spectral regions.3,7 Among the various down-shifting lanthanidebased activators, Dy3+ ions are a potential candidate for producing white light owing to their inner-shell 4f–4f transitions, especially 4F9/26H15/2, magnetic and 4F9/26H13/2, electric dipole transitions, resulting in blue and yellow emission, respectively.

ldrich).Zn O: x Dy3+ nanoparticles with varying concentrations of Dy3+( x.=0, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, and 0.20 at%) were synthesized by the co-precipitation method assisted by ultrasound radiation.This method contains two steps.In the first step, zinc nitrate hexahydrate and 0.04 at% Dy (NO3) 3 x H2O were separately dissolved in 20 mL and 5 mL of deionized water by using a conventional ultrasound bath for 7 minutes.Next, 1.2M of NaOH was dissolved in 20 mL of deionized water using an ultrasound bath for 10 min.In the second step, the two nitrate solutions were mixed under vigorous stirring at room temperature for 10 minutes to ensure uniform mixing, and the aqueous solution of NaOH was added slowly, yielding a white precipitate.The reaction was allowed to proceed for 10 min after the complete addition of NaOH.The resulting white suspension was exposed to ultrasonic radiation for 30 minutes.The resulting mixture was centrifuged to remove the solvent.The obtained samples were washed thrice using distilled water and ethanol to remove the by-products generated during the synthesis process.Finally, the obtained powdery substances were fully ground and then subjected to annealing in a mufle furnace at 300C for 2 h to obtain ZnO: Dy3+ nanoparticles. 2.2Characterization The structural and phase purity analysis of the Zno: Dy3+ nanophosphors were examined using an X-ray difractometer (Bruker D8ADVANCE having Cu-Kα radiation,=1.5405 ) in the angular range of 2θ from 20 to 80°.The morphology determination, X-ray dot mapping imaging, and elemental analysis were carried out using a Nova Nano SEM-450Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope equipped with an XFlash detector 6/10 (Bruker) and using the software QUANTAX200.The elemental analysis was further carried out using Inductively coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (Thermo Scientific iCAP QcICP-MS).
