content: whole visible spectrum from 400 nm to 700 nm is fulfilled, resulting in a strong white light emission.Further, the hue of the white light can finely be adjusted, via tuning the excitation wavelength.High pressure-induced luminescence enhancement has also been demonstrated.Based on the CsRbDyClI crystals, we have also fabricated a series of white light-emitting diodes, with the color coordinates of (0.33, 0.33), illustrating its great potential in the solid-state lighting applications.The dysprosium-based double perovskite studied in this work offers us a nice choice for designing HDP-based white light emitting devices. 1.Introduction Lead halide perovskites (LHPs) with the formula of ABX (A is a monovalent cation, B is a lead ion, and X is a halogen ion) have attracted wide attention owing to their excellent photoelectric properties, such as high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) and tunable bandgaps [1–6].Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) based on LHPs have demonstrated remarkable optoelectronic performance [7,8].However, the toxicity and low stability of the perovskite crystals still remain as major obstacles toward practical applications [9,10].To overcome these impediments, it is desirable to search for stable and nontoxic alternatives with compa rable optoelectronic properties [11–13].Lead-free halide double perovskites, characterized by the genera formula A2MIMIIX6, where a monovalent (MI) and a trivalent (MIII) metal are used to substitute two divalent lead (Pb) in the simple perovskite formula of ABX, have been proposed as stable and environmentally friendly alternatives to Pb-based halide perovskite [14–16].The synthesized pure undoped A2MIMIIIX6 materials usually demonstrate low PLQY due to the presence of dark self-trapped excitons (STEs), resulting in poor luminescent performance [17–19].

he presence of dark self-trapped excitons (STEs), resulting in poor luminescent performance [17–19].Trivalent rare earth ions with a unique configuration of f-electrons and abundant energy levels have marvelous photoluminescence (PL) properties, where up conversion (UC) and down conversion (DC) PL usually can be achieved by energy-level transition of single or multiple rare earth ions [20–26].For example, Wang et al.reported that the phosphor of YO:10%Er3+7%K+ exhibited a strong UC emission [27].Jia et al.designed a transparent composite film using Gd2O3: Eu3+ phosphor particles with efficient DC luminescence, which served as an effective spectral converter for the conversion of broadband solar-blind UV light to visible light [28].Trivalent rare earth ions can also promote the light absorption and tailor the band gap of host materials.Due to the unique features, rare earth doped perovskite crystals and devices for optical and electrical controls have been widely reported [ 29, 30 ].For instance, Eu3+ doped CaF2 films generated pure blue, white, and red luminescence [31].Tb3+ doped oxyfluoride glass exhibited a large ab sorption cross section, high stability, high PLQY, and sensitive spectral conversion characteristics under UV excitation [32].Besides, Hou et al.reported that Dy3+ and Sb3+ doped Cs2NaYCl6 perovskite materials realized white light emission with a high PLQY [33].Yang et al.showed that Er3+ doped Cs2Ag0.9Na0.4In0.9Bi0.1Cl6 (CANIBC) nanocrystals (NCs) displayed both a strong STE emission and an efficient characteristic emission of Er3+, and they also successfully fabricated white LEDs based on the Er3+ doped CANIBC phosphors [34].Wang et al.presented that Ce3+ was co-doped with Bi3+ into lead-free double perovskite Cs2A gInCl NCs, which prevented the STE migration and the emission quenching of the co-doped perovskite [35].Among the lanthanides, Dy ions have been used as dopants in perovskites to modify the properties.For instance, Kubicki et al.

ions have been used as dopants in perovskites to modify the properties.For instance, Kubicki et al.showed that Dy ions could be incorporated into the perovskite structure of CsPbCl3 characterized by solid-state NMR [36].Liu et al.reported that the lattice doping of Dy ions could enable phase transition and tunable photoluminescence of Cs2ZrCl6 nanocrystals [37].Zhou et al.demonstrated that Dy3+ was used as nucleating agents to enhanced the luminescent performance of CsPbI3 quantum dot-embedded borosilicate glass [38].In previous works Dy ions have been utilized as dopants, while very few studies have been focused on Dy as the host ion.From this perspective, this work investigates on the optical properties of novel perovskites using Dy as the host ion, and reports on their white light emissions.In this study, we innovatively designed and synthesized white luminescent materials with the structure of CsxRb3-xDyCl6-xIx. Dy3-+ was used as the host ion in HDPs by a hydrothermal method, realizing a white light emission and great hue adjustability within the visible light range.Based on Dy-HDPs, we also achieved white LED devices using the CsxRb3-xDyCl6-xIx crystals, showing a white light emission with the CIE coordinates of (0.33, 0.33), correlated color temperature (CCT) of 5809K, and relatively high color rendering index (CRI) of 92.6.Our results show a promising alternative approach to broadening the halide double perovskite family. 2.Results and discussion The CsxRb3-xDyCl6-xIx crystals were synthesized by the hydrothermal method, which possess cubic crystal structure and belong to the Fm3m space group [39].As shown in Fig.1a.In this structure, Rb+ and Dy3+ ions are coordinated with Cl- and I− ions, forming an octahedral structure.These octahedra are connected by shared corners alternately, creating a three-dimensional architecture with Cs+ located on the interstitial spaces to maintain charge equilibrium.

imensional architecture with Cs+ located on the interstitial spaces to maintain charge equilibrium.The Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns of CsxRb3-xDyCl6-xIx crystals are shown in (a) (b) Fig.1b.The patterns of the three samples are similar, and the diffraction peaks are observed without impurity peaks, indicating the pure phase nature of three samples and high crystallinity.Besides, the patterns appear to match with the theoretical calculation data of the Fm3m cubic space point group structure from the Materials Project crystal structure of other lanthanide-based family Cs2NaLnX6 (Ln represents lanthanide ions, and X is Cl, Br, or I) perovskites, which was addressed in Ref.[40].The doping of Rb+ into CsxRb3-xDyCl6-xIx crystals tends to replace Cs+ due to their same valence states.By careful examination of the region between 26.5◦ and 28.5 ( Fig.1c).The diffraction angles for Cs1.3Rb1.7Dy Cl4.7I1.3 and Cs1.6Rb1.4Dy Cl4.4I1.6 are greater than that of Cs2.0Rb1.0Dy Cl4.0I2.0.indicating the contraction of the crystal lattice.This trend is mainly due to the fact that Rb+ ions are smaller than Cs+ ions, and Cl- ions are smaller than I− ions.It is speculated that they both contribute to the lattice variation, since the impacts caused by both factors are similar by comparing previous works [41,42].In addition, the diffraction peaks for Cs1.3Rb1.7Dy Cl4.7I1.3 and Cs1.6Rb1.4Dy Cl4.4I1.6 are sharper than Cs2.0Rb1.0Dy Cl4.0I2.0, and this conclusion further indicates that the better crystallinity of the former two samples [43].Note that a series of samples with a variety of Cs/Rb ratios were synthesized, and the PL spectra are shown in Fig.S1 in the Supporting Information.According to the PL spectra, three representative samples of CsxRb3xDyCl6-xIx ( x=1.3, 1.6,., and 2.0) were discussed in the paper.

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: Nanoscale, 2025, 17, 7128 Multilevel, solar-blind, and thermostable physical unclonable functions based on host-sensitized luminescence of Ga2O3Dy3+Dong Zhu,a,b Chunfeng Wang, *a Fuhang Jiao,a Jiujun Xu,a Haoran Xu,a Shun Han,a Peijiang Cao,a Yuxiang Zeng,a Ming Fang, a Wenjun Liu,a Deliang Zhu*a and Youming Lu*a,b Optical physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are powerful tools to combat counterfeiting, owing to their unpredictable preparation processes and unique, identifiable information content.Achieving high entropy and robustness in optical PUFs is essential for practical applications but remains challenging.This study demonstrates a multilevel, solar-blind, and thermostable PUF based on host-sensitized luminescence of trivalent dysprosium (Dy3+) in β-phase gallium oxide (-Ga2O3).The controllable occupation of Dy3+ in both tetrahedral and octahedral Ga3+ sites o - Ga2O3 results in heterochromatic optical emission, which afords the resulting PUFs with a multilevel encoding capacity of 44096 at 6464 pixels.The wide bandgap (∼4.6 eV) of β- - Ga2O3: Dy3+ confines the PUF response to solar-blind irradiation, encompassing a light spectrum in the range 230–270 nm, which does not overlap with ambient light, ensuring interference-free stimulation and therefore achieving 100% recognition accuracy.Additionally, the high thermal quenching activation energy (0.386eV) of Ga2O3: Dy3+ provides thermal stability, enabling the PUFs to operate from room temperature up to 125C With near-ideal uniformity, uniqueness, and reproducibility, these PUFs hold considerable promise for practical applications in anticounterfeiting and encryption.

hese PUFs hold considerable promise for practical applications in anticounterfeiting and encryption.Received 12th December 2024, Accepted 16th February 2025DOI: rsc.li/nanoscale Introduction Counterfeit consumer products have led to economic losses at a billion-dollar scale.In particular, counterfeit medical devices and medicines have been threatening human safety and public health.In the digital age, private information including communication, military, finance, and personal data, are often vul nerable to abuse by mercenary actors for purposes including cyber terrorism across all areas of modern society.A myriad of security strategies including fluorescent holograms, graphical barcodes, watermarks, security inks, and software-based cryptogra phy have been developed to deter counterfeiting and unauthorized access.1–5 However, these conventional security strategies rely on deterministic production processes, which become susceptible to duplication over time owing to their weak construction and advancements in precision processing technology.Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) are devices that create unique cryptographic “fingerprints” by exploiting the inherent randomness of physical features introduced during manufacturing or material synthesis.6,7 These features are impossible to replicate, making PUFs an attractive alternative to conventional security strategies.Since the introduction of PUF concepts, various types of PUFs, including optical,8–11 magnetic,12–15 and electronic,16–19 have been reported.Optical PUFs derive their encoded information from the optical properties of materials, ofering distinct advantages, which include material versatility, ease of processing, output complexity, non-contact characteristics, and immunity to electro-magnetic interference.

sing, output complexity, non-contact characteristics, and immunity to electro-magnetic interference.Additionally, they enable quick and straightforward verification using portable image capture tools and well-established image processing techniques.20–23 Thus, optical PUFs utilizing various materials and manufacturing routes have emerged since the pioneering work by Pappu et al.24For example, Gu et al.developed Raman-based PUF labels composed of diferent types of core– shell nanoparticles with various mapping resolutions for anticounterfeiting.25 Kayaci et al.presented the design and facile fabrication of organic light-emitting PUFs under ambient conditions using green-emissive oligo(p-phenyleneethynylene) molecules.26 Kim et al.demonstrated a lens-free optical PUF based on stochastically manifested difraction using native silk fibers.27 Jung et al.proposed a scalable approach for creating optical PUFs utilizing the kinetics of oxide particles in polymer solutions.28 Im et al.reported a four-dimensional PUF by forming time-varying chaotic phosphorescent patterns on MoS atomic seeds.29 Huang et al.demonstrated near-infrared circularly polarized PUFs by incorporating Yb-doped metal halide perovskite nanocrystals into chiral imprinted photonic films.30 While great progress has been made, it should be noted that the stimulation light wavelength of many existing optical PUFs falls within the UVA (320–400 nm) or visible (400–780 nm) spectral ranges, which will be afected or overshadowed by the ambient light, perturbating the generation of PUF patterns and thus diminishing the recognition accuracy.And these luminescent materials are prone to be sensitive to the fluctuation of thermal excitation, which may alter their original luminescence properties, resulting in the distortion or invalidation of PUF labels.

www.small-journal.com Interfacial Interaction Modulated Radiation Defects for Self-Charging Persistent Mechanoluminescence Yingjuan Yan, BoZhou,* Ziyi Guo, Xiao He, Wanyuan Wei, Shaofan Fang, Lei Zhao, and Zhaofeng Wang* Self-charging persistent mechanoluminescence (SC-PML) is ofparticular interest for stress sensing/visualization applications, as it not only notably extends the time window available for stress observation, but also avoids the pre-charging with great convenience.However, the intrinsic physical principles ofthe SC-PML are still unclear.Herein, a phosphor Sr9LiMg (PO4) 7Dy3+ with an initially clean trap structure is reported to exhibit repeatable SC-PML up to 30 s when incorporated into a flexible polydimethylsiloxane.The observed divergence between the SC-PML and the transient photoluminescence provides a unique insight in terms ofthe mechanics-induced trap creation for delving into the fundamental mechanisms.The muti-mode stimuli/ irradiation tests further suggest the presence ofa high-energy process at interface associated with the mechanoluminescence.This process is capable ofproducing efects analogous to those ofX-ray irradiation, and suficient to facilitate the generation oftrapping centers within Sr9LiMg (PO4) 7Dy3+ lattice.The above findings provide a clear insight for SC-PML, and the as-developed SC-PML material is further applied for the multi-mode anticounterfeiting and stress-sensing devices as representatives.

further applied for the multi-mode anticounterfeiting and stress-sensing devices as representatives.present, most of the reported ML materials have a short lifetime in a range from nanoseconds to microseconds, involving a transient mechanics-optics conversion process.[7–11] Apparently, the fast mechanical responsiveness and short lifetime endow the ML materials with unique advantages on the non-contact and distributed stress sensing and monitoring for continuous applications.[12–18] However, for the applications of visualized mechanics displaying and imaging, the short lifetime ML is inconvenient to be captured and recorded by naked eyes or conventional devices, and therefore the persistent ML (PML), which can display afterglow after mechanical stimuli, is highly required.[19,20] Initially, the PML materials are always accompanied with the energy pre-stored ML, which requires a pre-irradiation step to pre-store energy in the material structures.[19] Then, the pre-stored energy can be gradually released after mechanics stimulation to exhibit PML.The typical 1.Introduction Mechanoluminescence (ML) is a light emission phenomenon from a solid material in response to mechanical forces, such as friction, stretching, compression, impacting, and twisting.[1–6] AtPML materials with the above physical processes are BaSi2O2N2: Eu2+, Sr2P2O7: Eu, Y, and LiGa5O8.[ 21-23 ] For practical applications, such pre-charging-based PML is hard to meet the practical demands as the pre-irradiation would increase the dificulty for operation with lacked self-recoverability.

s as the pre-irradiation would increase the dificulty for operation with lacked self-recoverability.During recent years, a class of materials have been reported that they do not have ML properties on their own, but exhibit repeatable and self-activated ML when incorporated with appropriate elastomer matrices, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS).[24–27] This kind of ML is called resultant ML, whose energy source is pointed to the interface interactions between the material grain and elastomer.[25–27] The rising resultant ML brings great opportunities to break through the existing PML performance, as the composites ofthe phosphors and matrices yield abundant interfacial interactions [ 25-27 ] Based on the concept of resultant ML, the self-charging persistent mechanoluminescence (SC-PML) was developed, which was first reported by our group in 2022 in the composites of Sr3Al2O5Cl2: Dy3+/ PDMS.[ 25 ] The Sr3Al2O5Cl2: Dy3+ itself cannot exhibit ML and PML, which are able to appear in the PDMS-based composites.Under mechanical stimuli, the composite material can convert the mechanical energy into light directly, with no need for pre-irradiation.Simultaneously, part of the mechanical energy can be stored in the material structure which is the so-called self-charging process.The self-charged energy can be gradually released after mechanics stimuli, and thus the PML is produced.Obviously, the SC-PML is an efective solution to address the conventional issues of the pre-charging-based PML, showing great convenience for the long-term stress observation, tracking, recording, imaging and displaying.Although the overall process of the SC-PML has been elucidated, the specific physics in terms of how the mechanical energy is converted and self-stored in the composite structure are still unclear, which basically hinder the development of high-performance SC-PML materials.The persistent luminescence has been well recognized to come from the shallow metastable levels or traps.

ersistent luminescence has been well recognized to come from the shallow metastable levels or traps.Therefore, the trap structure as well as its evolution is inevitable to be involved in the physical processes of SC-PML.[19,28,29] To clearly disclose the physics in terms of the self-charging process with no interference, a material with initially clean/simple trap structure is preferential.For luminescent centers, Dy3+ is preferred because of its unique 4f9 electronic configuration with energy levels primarily governed by 4f inner-shell electron transition and abundant metastable states.[30] Herein, Sr9LiMg (PO4) 7Dy3+(SLMPD) phosphor with an initially clean trap structure was employed, and its resultant ML was investigated after compositing with the flexible PDMS matrix.The employment ofPDMS is because of its transparency, softness, flexibility, and abundant interfacial interactions with the embedded phosphors (e.g., hydrogen bonds, electrostatic interactions).[31] The results suggest that the as-fabricated SLMPD/PDMS composite elastomer exhibit repeatable SC-PML up to 30 s.The divergence between the SC-PML and the transient photoluminescence (PL), as well as the multi-mode stimuli/irradiation tests suggest the presence of a high-energy process at interface, based on which the energy selfcharging mechanisms involving the radiation defects are clarified.The SLMPD/PDMS composite with attractive SC-PML performance was further applied for the multi-mode anticounterfeiting and stress-sensing devices as representatives. 2.Results and Discussion 2.1.Resultant ML and SC-PML in an Initially Clean Trap Structure-Based Composite As illustrated in Figure 1a, the crystal structure ofthe phosphate Sr9LiMg (PO4) 7 belongs to the R-3m space group of the trigonal system, with cell parameters a=b=1.06079 nm, and c=1.96779 nm.[ 32 ] Sr2+ cations occupy three sites in the structure, with coordination numbers of 11, 9 and 7, respectively.

warm lighting systems and noncontact optical thermometry measurements, in the light of every experimental finding. 1 | Introduction Material science is a fascinating field dealing with the designing, development, and manipulation of materials for day-to-day life applications in the current scenario.The development of new luminous materials has always been crucial because of the wide range of applications they have in industry, energy, and medicine [1].Phosphors are one such material that exhibits luminescence when doped with different rare earth ions.There are multiple applications for them in various disciplines like display, W-LED, dosimetry, anticounterfeiting, and optical temperature sensors [2].Temperature is a basic metric that is significant in many domains, from industry to science.The field of noncontact temperature sensing has seen significant advancements in recent years [3].Luminescence-based measurement has garnered significant attention among these methods.Due to their temperature fluctuations, temperature-dependent luminous features, such as emission spectra, decay lifetime, and rising time of emission, may generally be used to measure temperature [4].To attain good luminescence efficiency from phosphors, there should be two important components host matrix which acts as a sensitizer in many cases and a dopant which will be an activator.Having good host systems enhances their structural and optical stability in the luminescence process.

years due to their extraordinary properties like wide excitation which can be controlled, intense emission, and favorable thermal stability.The silicate family is a stunning class of inorganic phosphors that is employed in many different applications because of its characteristics, which include transparency to visible light, chemical resistance, and water resistance [1].Different kinds of silicate were recently explored by the researchers such as NaAlSiO4 [ 5 ], Ba9Lu2Si6O24 [ 6 ], Y2SiO5 [ 7 ], and RbNa3 (Li3SiO4) 4 [8].Along with the sensitizer, activators also play a major role in presenting optical properties.Rare earth (RE)-doped luminescent materials are an interesting domain for many researchers around the world due to exceptional optical properties such as sharp emission, color tunability, and long decay lifetimes which are due to the 4f-4f transitions [9–11].Specifically, REdoped alkaline earth silicates (Ba2ZnSi2O7) phosphors have to be explored in detail for noncontact optical thermometry applications.In this present work, Ba2ZnSi2O7: Dy3+ phosphors were synthesized via a high-temperature solid-state reaction method.The primary aim of the work is to study the material's structural, optical, and thermal properties in detail and to explore the sensitivities at different temperatures for noncontact thermometry applications. 2 | Experimental Details 2.1 | PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: Dalton Trans., 2025, 54, 683 A highly sensitive ratiometric optical thermometer based on a Sr2MgWO6 double perovskite doped with Dy3+ exploiting thermally coupled and uncoupled levels† Thi Hong Quan Vu, * Bartosz Bondzior, Dagmara Stefańska, Shovan Dan and Przemysław Jacek Dereń The increasing demand for highly sensitive optical thermometers operating within a wide temperature range necessitates the development of new phosphors.In this work, the potential temperature sensing performance of a novel yellow-emitting phosphor, Sr2MgWO6 double perovskite, doped with varying concentrations of Dy3+ was investigated for the first time.Increasing the concentration of Dy3+ from 0% to 7% shifted the color of luminescence from blue to yellowish-orange within the CIE1931 color space.The energy transfer eficiency from (WO6) 6-to Dy3+ also increased significantly to 98.4%.Moreover, the sample doped with 3% Dy3+ showed the highest emission intensity, with a concentration beyond this threshold inducing concentration quenching.This phenomenon was primarily governed by dipole–dipole interactions.The highest quantum yield was found to be 30.7% for the sample doped with 3% Dy3+.Upon 266 nm wavelength excitation, the temperature sensing ability of the samples doped with 3%, 5%, and 7% Dy3+ was examined based on the fluorescence intensity ratio between the thermally coupled and uncoupled levels.It showed that the relative thermal sensitivity of Sr can be tuned by changing the Dy3+ concentration.Sr - max=3.24 % 1-1 was obtained for the sample doped with 3 % Dy3+ at 193K within the 80–273K operating range for thermally uncoupled levels.For thermally coupled levels, the Sr-max value reached 1.35% K-1 at 333K for the sample doped with 7 % Dy3+ in the range of 293–593K.

his parameter significantly depends on the characteristics of the sample and the experimental setup.On the other hand, S enables the comparison of various optical thermometers employing varying approaches.13 In the past decade, double perovskite materials have emerged as potential candidates for thermal sensing appli cations.2,14–17 SrMgWO (SMW), a novel double perovskite, has primarily been studied for its crystal structure, phase transition,18–22 and ceramic fabrication,23 and as a host for near-infrared luminescence,24,25 while its potential for temperature sensing has been unintentionally neglected.The sig nificant diference in thermal dependency on temperature between the two given emission peaks is a crucial parameter for achieving a highly sensitive luminescent thermometer.The simultaneous emissions of the tungstate host and the dopant in the spectrum ofer a self-referencing optical thermometer with relatively high sensitivity in the low-temperature range.2,11,26,27 Indeed, the tungstate host (WO6) 6-eficiently absorbs near UV and exhibits an asymmetric broad emission band from 345 to 540 nm,11,27–29 making it highly beneficial for a promising ratiometric optical thermometer.Several tungstate optical thermometers have been investigated based on, for example, (WO6) 6-and Ho3+, 26Eu3+, 27Nd3+, 2 and Er3+ 11Therefore, Sr2MgWO6 double perovskite is a prospective host for temperature sensing applications.In this study, the trivalent dysprosium ion (Dy3+) was doped into Sr2MgWO6.Dy3+ has also been demonstrated to be a suitable dopant for thermometry operating at high temperatures.30–33 Specifically, the emissions from the thermally coupled levels of Dy3+(4I15/26H15/2and4F9/26F15/2).which are separated by approximately 1000 cm - 1, are of interest for potential use in fluorescence intensity ratio-based temperature sensing.30 The relative population of these thermally coupled levels obeys the Boltzmann distribution (cf.eqn (1) above).

A novel Sr3Ga2Ge4O14.Dy phosphor: Tapping into the potential of dual-mode applications in white LEDs and optical thermometry Ziyao Wang a,*, Liya Maa, YiShao a, Yuzhong Luo a, Ruocong Liao a, Ximing Kong a, Xinyao Yang ba Shenyang Key Laboratory of Micro-arc Oxidation Technology and Application, Institute of Innovative Science and Technology, Shenyang University, Shenyang, 110044, China b Key Lab for Eco-restoration of Regional Contaminated Environment (ShenyangUniversity), Ministry of Education, Shenyang, 110044, China ARTICLEINFOHandling Editor: DrP.Vincenzini Keywords: Phosphor Luminescence intensity ratio Optical thermometry White LEDsABSTRACTA versatile Sr3Ga2Ge4O14: Dy3+ phosphor, exhibiting a classic multi-band emission spectrum stemming from the 4F9/2 t o6H15/2, 6H13/2, and 6H11/2 transitions of Dy3+ ions under ultraviolet excitation, is reported.This phosphor emits a warm white light and possesses exceptional thermal quenching resistance coupled with temperaturedependent chromatic stability.Notably, its 4F9/26F15/2 and 4I15/2-6H15/2 transitions, forming a thermally coupled level pair, exhibit opposing intensity variations with rising temperature.Leveraging this unique behavior, an optical thermometer based on the luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) between these two emissions has been devised, achieving a commendable relative sensitivity of 0.61 % K-1 at 298K.The combination of overall luminescence thermal stability and localized thermal sensitivity renders Sr3Ga2Ge4O14; Dy3+ an ideal candidate for direct integration into white LEDs, as well as for compensating spectral deficiencies in multicomponent white LED systems.

content: o white LEDs, as well as for compensating spectral deficiencies in multicomponent white LED systems.Furthermore, its potential in constructing optical thermometers underscores its multifaceted functionality and innovative value. 1.Introduction In the field of modern lighting technology, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), as the new generation of solid-state lighting sources, are gradually replacing traditional lighting methods and becoming the mainstream in the lighting market due to their high efficiency, long lifespan, environmental friendliness, and non-toxic nature [1–4].Among them, phosphors, as a crucial component in LED lighting systems, play an indispensable role in achieving efficient white light emission, optimizing spectral distribution, and enhancing light quality [5–9].However, the currently widely used LED phosphor systems, such as yttrium aluminum garnet ( YAG: Ce3+) based phosphors, while successfully applied in commercial white LEDs, primarily emit in the yellow region, leading to issues such as high color temperature and low color rendering index (CRI) in the resulting white light, which fail to meet the growing demand for high-quality lighting [10].On the other hand, the approach of utilizing red (R), green (G), and blue (B) trichromatic phosphors to achieve white light, known as the RGB scheme, offers high color rendering and adjustment flexibility.However, this system is complex and costly, and due to the different decay characteristics among the phosphors, long-term use can lead to color imbalance, affecting the consistency of lighting effects [ 11, 12 ] Against this backdrop, the exploration of novel phosphor materials to overcome the limitations of existing technologies has become a research hotspot in the LED lighting field.Among them, Dy3+-activated phosphors have attracted significant attention due to their unique luminescence properties.

ctivated phosphors have attracted significant attention due to their unique luminescence properties.The luminescence of Dy3+ ions in suitable hosts involves multiple energy level transitions, particularly the 4F9/2→6H15/2 and 4F9/26F13/2 transitions, corresponding to blue and yellow emissions, respectively [13–16].By precisely adjusting the crystal structure or chemical composition, the 2.Experimental section 2.1.Materials and methods SrGaGeO:3xDy3+ (x=0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10) phosphors were prepared using the high-temperature solid-state reaction method.Raw materials including SrCO (A.R., Macklin), GaO (A.R., Macklin), GeO2 ( A.R..., Macklin), and Dy2O3 (99.99%, Macklin) were weighed and mixed according to the stoichiometric ratios.The mixture was then thoroughly ground in an agate mortar until homogeneity was achieved.The homogenized mixture was transferred into a corundum crucible and calcined in a muffle furnace at 300 ◦C for 2 h, followed by a second calcination at 1300 ◦C for 6 h.After each calcination, the material was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature and then ground finely for subsequent procedures. 2.2.Characterization The phase .jpg) and 4 at%) phosphors.CIE coordinates were observed at the cryostat region and room temperature.Based on temperaturedependent luminescence properties and analyzing them using the fluorescence intensity ratio technique, the relative sensitivity (S) value reached 1.42% K−1, 1.72% K-1, and 0.91% K-1 at 300K for non-thermally coupled levels.Similarly, 0.08% K-1 and 0.77% K−1 are due to transitions 4S3/24I15/2 and 4F9/26H11/2, respectively, at low temperature for thermally coupled levels.As defined, thermally and non-thermally coupled levels exhibit interesting results with the rise in temperature for optical thermometry application.Temperature-dependent photoluminescence (TDPL) analysis shows that diferent excitation wavelengths and varying temperatures result in diferent emission wavelengths, as in color tunability applications.The results of our study demonstrate the suitable application as a color-tunable device and a temperature sensor.KEYWORDS: Downconversion, FIR, Sensitivity, Color tunability, Cryogenic, SrMoO41.INTRODUCTION Phosphor materials represent a cornerstone in modern technological advancements across a spectrum of fields like encrypted storage, multicolor displays, sensors, biological applications, and wLED.They facilitate the conversion of blue light emitted by semiconductor chips into a broad spectrum of visible light in the realm of solid-state lighting and for color tunability.1−4 Color-tunable devices need suitable color-correlated temperature (CCT) and adjustable Commission Internationale de l’Elcairage (CIE) coordinates for several applications like field emission displays, multicolor threedimensional displays, full-color flat panel displays, etc.5 Beyond lighting, phosphors find applications in forensic science, aiding in the analysis of lip prints (cheiloscopy), optical thermometry, and latent fingerprints.

e, aiding in the analysis of lip prints (cheiloscopy), optical thermometry, and latent fingerprints.Phosphor materials enhance the visualization of intricate lip patterns and latent fingerprints, thereby assisting law enforcement agencies in criminal investigations and identification processes.6 Additionally, phosphor-based optical thermometry ofers noncontact tem perature measurement capabilities, leveraging the temperaturedependent luminescent properties of certain phosphors.This technique provides noncontact, fast, accurate, and versatile temperature-sensing solutions, making it invaluable for industrial, medical, and nanolevel applications, including diagnostics.7 Thus, phosphors emerge as multifunctional materials with profound implications across a diverse set of scientific and technological domains.Lanthanide (Ln)-doped phosphors have attracted consid erable interest for their versatile applications, thanks to their ease of synthesis, high emission eficiency, and excellent thermal and chemical stability.8 The optical transitions in Ln3+ ions occur due to the 4f orbitals, which are well shielded from the local environment by the fully occupied 5s and 5p outer orbitals.However, direct excitation into the 4f levels often results in a low luminescence eficiency because of the low absorption cross-section of lanthanide ions.This eficiency can be enhanced through sensitization processes, typically involving charge transfer band (CTB) excitation or energy transfer (ET) mechanisms.9 In this realm, the selection of a host material is very crucial for the desired properties.Several hosts like vanadates, fluorides, tungstates, silicates, molybdates, and germinate are present, but due to distinctive advantages, like the need for reduced atmosphere to synthesize some of these, they limit the application and large-scale production.

duced atmosphere to synthesize some of these, they limit the application and large-scale production.Among host matrices, molybdates, specifically strontium molybdate (SrMoO4), have garnered attention because of their broad-spectrum tunability, optimal combination of crystal structures, ionic size compatibility, and chemical stability.Ln3+ ions facilitate transfer of energy from the ligand (O2-inMoO42-anion) to metal-charge (Mo6+) transfer referred to as LMCT bands of the molybdate matrix to the energy levels of the Ln3+ ions, thereby enhancing their characteristic emission.10 Unlike vanadates and tungstates, SrMoO4 minimizes reabsorption and concentration quenching while maintaining high luminescence eficiency and thermal stability.11 Compared to fluorides, which ofer low phonon energy but sufer from poor chemical durability and moisture sensitivity, SrMoO4 is more robust and easier to process.12 While germanates and silicates provide good thermal and mechanical properties, they often exhibit weaker energy transfer mechanisms and require higher synthesis temperatures.13 With advantages such as environmental friendliness, energy eficiency, high luminous eficacy, and extended lifetime, molybdates are well-suited for various applications.Their crystal phases vary depending on stoichiometric ratios, synthesis methods, and reaction system pH.14,15 Ln3+ ion-doped molybdates have been studied for several cutting-edge applications in optics, electronics, and magnetics.9,16,17 Eforts have been recently dedicated to the synthesis of both Y- and Ln (Ln=La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb, or Lu)-based molybdates with tunable phases, morphologies, and multicolor luminescence properties.

content: , or Lu)-based molybdates with tunable phases, morphologies, and multicolor luminescence properties.Among various Ln3+ ions, the Dy3+ ions are well studied for various applications owing to the two main luminescence bands located in the blue and yellow spectral domains, representing the electronic transitions 4F9/2H15/2 and 4F9/2-6H13/2, respectively.Similarly, Er3+ ions emit in the blue and red spectral regions owing to the transitions 4S3/2→4I15/2 and 4F9/24I15/2.18, 19The codoping of Er3+ can modify the local crystal field environment around the Dy3+ ions, thereby influencing its luminescent properties.20, 21Thus, using host excitation, it is feasible to obtain an adequate emission by combining the two rare-earth ions because in codoped systems reported data show the enhancement in optical properties due to mutual interaction via an energy transfer mechanism.22,23 Moreover, the energy levels of Er3+ and Dy3+ ions are very closely spaced; therefore, there is a high possibility for energy transfer between the two.Both Er3+ and Dy3+ show distinctively strong peaks in their respective spectral areas.Er3+ has spectral areas of 524 nm and 552 nm, both in the green, and 658 nm in the red due to transitions 2H11/24I15/2, 4S3/24I15/2, and 4F9/24I15/2, in that order.In the same way, Dy3+ ions exhibit two prominent bands of luminescence located in the blue and yellow spectral areas, respectively.These bands correspond to electronic transitions 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2.In this case, the magnetic dipole (MD) transition is 4F9/2 6H15/2, while the hypersensitive electric dipole (ED) transition is 4F9/2 6H13/2.The occupancy of Dy3+ at noninversion locations is shown by the dominance of ED.24-34In this work, we have doped two rare-earth ions because codoping Er3+ ions into a Dy3+-doped SrMoO4 matrix imparts several distinct advantages that are not achievable with Dy3+ alone.

3+-doped SrMoO4 matrix imparts several distinct advantages that are not achievable with Dy3+ alone.Additionally, the concentration and ratio of the codoped ions, as well as the influence of the host material, which afects the local environment of the ions and energy levels, further enable precise control over the emitted color.Thus, through these processes, the codoping of rare-earth ions facilitates the finetuning of luminescent properties to achieve the desired emission.Another application we are targeting in our work is noncontact temperature sensing below room temperature, ranging from 15 to 300K.As concluded from the literature survey at high temperature (>300K), Yurong Luo et al.reported that the magnitude of relative sensitivity (SR) is decreasing as temperature goes from 300 to 550K35Li Li et al.demonstrate the decrement in SR value as it goes from 300 to 500K having a positive slope.36 Yubin Wang et al.reported in their article that the resultant SR value first increases from 300 to 375K but after 375 to 550K values keep on decreasing continuously.37 Vaibhav et al.show the temperature uncertainty (δT) value is below 0.8K, which is better than many, but what we are observing is that the increment in temperature shows an increment in δT afecting the sensitivity parameters and will behave as a constraint in calculating sensitivity.22 In temperature-sensing devices, conventional temperature measurement techniques have limitations, includ ing heating of components, slow response times, and poor adaptability in complex environments, which also reduce measurement accuracy.38,39 Non-contact-based temperature sensors address these challenges, ofering faster response times, 40 electromagnetic passivity, and improved spatial resolution.Fluorescent intensity ratio (FIR) measurements are a significant approach for temperature-dependent spectra, traditionally dependent on thermally coupled levels (TCLs) within single rare-earth luminescent centers.

itionally dependent on thermally coupled levels (TCLs) within single rare-earth luminescent centers.However, TCL-based FIR techniques are limited by the 2000 cm - 1 separation constraint imposed by the Boltzmann distribution law, reducing sensitivity.For instance, Er3+ has two 2H11/2 and 4S3/2 energy levels as the thermally coupled levels with an energy separation of 628 cm - 1., whereas Dy3+ also has two 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 levels as TCLs with an energy separation of 1026 cm - 1..Thus, the conventional TCL approach struggles to achieve both high-temperature sensitivity and good signaldiferentiating ability.40An alternative method employs non thermally coupled levels (NTCLs) across multiple rare-earth ions, which overcomes TCL limitations, achieving greater sensitivity and signal diferentiation.Applications in fields such as aerospace, metallurgy, basic sciences, and engineering often require fast, precise temper-41 ature measurements, especially at cryogenic temperatures.Many FIR-based temperature sensors benefit from the noncontact nature of thermometry, high sensitivity, rapid response, and adaptability to harsh environments.42, 43By employing non-thermally coupled levels of Er3+ and Dy3+ ions, our work achieves higher relative sensitivity values in comparison to thermally coupled levels at high temperature.44 Moreover, the chemical stability of the SrMoO4 phosphor at cryogenic and high temperatures makes it a versatile phosphor material for optical thermometry over a vast temperature range. exhibit promising capabilities in scintillation-based neutron detection [4] and lamp phosphors [5].In recent years, lanthanide-activated phosphors supported by inorganic compounds have gained significant recognition due to their extensive applications in various fields, including color display devices, white light–emitting diodes (WLEDs), medical diagnostics, solar energy harvesting, and thermoluminescence dosimetry [6–8].Rare earth–doped fluoride-based materials are particularly attractive for optical applications and because they combine high quantum efficiency with favorable mechanical as well as chemical stability [9].The growing demand for WLEDs is driving the innovation of novel phosphor materials for commercial lighting solutions.These advancements have the potential to significantly lower energy consumption in the lighting industry.White light generation in LEDs can be achieved through three primary approaches: using yellow-emitting phosphors excited by blue LEDs, combining red–green–blue phosphors with the nearultraviolet LEDs.These developments pave the way for more efficient, cost-effective, and environmentally sustainable lighting technologies [10–14].Phosphate-based luminescent materials doped with rare earth (RE) elements have attracted significant attention due to the diverse optical transitions of these dopants, enabling emissions ranging from the ultraviolet to the far-infrared spectrum [15, 16].These materials function by absorbing energy typically from cathode rays or ultraviolet light and reemitting it as visible light [17].A key technological challenge has been to replace traditional fluorescent lamps, and in this context, LEDs have gained increasing popularity for use in solid-state lighting systems in recent years [18].There is considerable interest in developing improved luminescent materials that provide excellent brightness and efficiency for fluorescent lamps, LEDs, and different display systems.

nd similar species may incorporate into the product, negatively impacting the luminescence behavior.Fluorides, in particular, are highly prone to hydrolytic degradation [27].Conventionally, RE-doped phosphate phosphors with general formulas like MREP2O7 [ 28 ], M3RE (PO4) 2 [29], and MRE (PO3) 4 [30] (whereMrepresentsalkalimetalsandREsignifiesrareearthelements) have been manufactured through solid-state techniques, which necessitate long reaction durations and elevated annealing temperatures.Currently, alternative low-temperature synthetic approaches such as hydrothermal microwave methods [31], the method of coprecipitation [32, 33], sol–gel processes [34, 35], and combustion techniques [36] are being utilized for phosphor production.Among them, one-step wet chemical synthesis is gaining popularity due to its simplicity, safety, energy efficiency, and rapidity.This method has proven highly effective for fabricating a variety of materials with improved optical properties.It offers a costeffective, quick, and scalable route for producing phosphors with superior luminescent features [13, 37, 38].Despite these advances, synthesizing complex fluoride compounds that contain multiple fluoride components remains a challenging task.These constituents often have widely varying melting points, and the loss of certain elements during crystal growth is a common issue.In recent years, progress has been made with wet chemical methods specifically designed for producing fluoride materials free from OH− contamination [39–44].This study further explores the synthesis of complex fluoride systems incorporating three different components.We have reported here the synthesis and dosimetry characteristics of phosphor prepared via combustion synthesis; its formation of the desired phases of material was confirmed by an X-ray diffraction (XRD) technique.Detailed investigations on its photoluminescence (PL) properties have also been discussed.

content: nd crystalline structure using XRD carried out on a PANalytical diffractometer with Cu-Kα radiation.Scans were conducted with a step size of 0.01 and a dwell time of 20 s, across a2θ range of 10 to 60°.PL studies, including excitation and emission spectra, were performed using a Shimadzu RF5301PCSpectrofluorophotometer equipped with a sensitive photomultiplier tube.This instrument provided corrected spectra in the ranges of 220–400 nm for excitation and 300–700 nm for emission at ambient temperature.Each PL measurement utilized 2 g of the sample, and both excitation and emission spectra were recorded with a slit width of 1.5 nm. 3 | Results and Discussion 3.1 | X-Ray Diffraction Pattern of Li2Sr2Al2PO4F9Host Lattice The structural purity and degree of crystallinity of synthesized phosphor were analyzed using XRD patterns.As a compound belonging to the orthophosphate family, the monoclinic crystal structure of Na2Sr.2Al2P O4F9 (boggildite) has been documented by Hawthorne [45], with reference to JCPDS card no.01-084-0497.In this study, the Na+ ions in the lattice were substituted with Li+ ions, resulting in the formation of prepared Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9..Notably, to date, no research has been reported on the luminescent properties of RE ions doped into the Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9 host lattice.The XRD pattern of the synthesized Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9 sample is depicted in Figure 1.The diffraction pattern showed no peaks corresponding to the starting materials such as Li (NO3) 24H2O, Sr.(NO3) 24H2O, Al (NO3) 3, NH4H2PO4, or NH4F, nor any other unexpected phases, confirming the successful formation of target compounds.These findings demonstrate that the final product is both homogeneous and well crystallized.All prominent and sharp diffraction peaks correspond accurately to those expected for a pure and crystalline phase of Li2Sr.

iffraction peaks correspond accurately to those expected for a pure and crystalline phase of Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9FIGURE1 | XRD of Li2Sr2Al2PO4F9 host lattice. 3.2 | SEM of Li2Sr2Al2PO4F9Phosphor Figure 2 shows a typical morphological image of the prepared Li2Sr2Al2PO4F9 phosphor.The particles exhibit a foam-like structure composed of densely packed crystallites.The mean crystallite size lies within the submicron range.The particles exhibit nonuniform shapes and their sizes are approximately in the range of 2 to 5 μm. 3.3 | Ḋ y Ḍ 3+Photoluminescence in Li2Sr2Al2PO4F9Phosphor Figure 3 displays the excitation spectrum of Dy3+-doped Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9 phosphor.When monitoring the yellow emission from Dy3+, multiple excitation bands are evident.Within the 250- to 400-nm region, excitation bands corresponding to the f–f transitions of Dy3+ ions are detected.Figure 4 presents the PL emission spectrum of Dy3+-activated Li2Sr.2Al2P O4F9 phosphor.Under 348nm excitation, two prominent emission peaks appear at 478nm (indicativeofblueemission) and 571nm (indicativeofyellowemission), arising from the transition 4F9/26H15/2 magnetic–dipole transition and the 4F9/26H13/2 electric–dipole transition, respectively.These emissions are consistent with the behavior of Dy3+ ions.The luminescence behavior of the phosphor is significantly affected by the host lattice structure and the method of synthesis.In this case, the rapid combustion technique likely introduces structural defects due to incomplete crystallization.Additionally, the cationic disorder within the spinel framework is substantial, resulting in numerous defect sites that can function as traps for electrons and holes.Typically, low doping concentrations yield weak emission, whereas high dopant levels may lead to concentration quenching.The highest luminescence intensity for Dy3+ is achieved at a doping concentration of 1 mol%.

Effect of excitation energy on the optical temperature sensing behavior of Dy3+ doped YSZ and YAG phosphors Qiuyang Yin a,b,c,d, Yongkai Quan a,b,c, Fengyue Luo a,d, Wenran Gong e, Jichen Liu a,b,c, Jieming Chai a,b,c, Lina Zhang a,b,c, Jianyu Liu a,b,c,* a National Key Laboratory of Science and Technology on Aero-Engine Aero-thermodynamics, Research Institute of Aero-engine, Beihang University, Beijing 100191, China b Hangzhou International Innovation Institute, Beihang University, Hangzhou 311115, China c Tianmushan Laboratory, Hangzhou 311115, China d Taihang Laboratory, Chengdu 610000, China e Beijing Institute of Structure and Environment Engineering, Beijing 100076, China ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Phosphor thermometry Fluorescence intensity ratio Thermally coupled energy levels Excitation energy Sensitivity ABSTRACTFluorescence intensity ratio based on laser-induced fluorescence effect is a promising non-contact thermometry method for high-speed rotating components.However, excitation energy control is difficult to achieve a balance between enhancing signal-to-noise ratio and minimizing the heating effect.Therefore, this paper experimentally investigated the effect of excitation energy on the luminescence spectra and thermometric performance of YSZ: Dy and YAG:Dy synthesized by co-precipitation method.Based on results, the increasing excitation energy enhances fluorescence intensity without altering spectra shape and peak positions of 457 nm and 483 nm which correspond to transitions from thermally coupled energy levels of 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 to 4H15/2 level.At the excitation energy density of 84.20 mJ/cm 2, the temperature measurement errors are both less than 0.71% for YSZ: Dy (540-1036K) and YAG:Dy (540-1440K).

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: Nanoscale Adv., 2025, 7, 3038 Enhanced photoluminescence and photocatalytic properties in Dy-doped sodium zinc molybdate synthesized via a green microwave-assisted method† Sourabh Gouraha, a Khalid Bin Masood,b Sadaf Jamal Gilani,c Apoorva Rai,a H.S.Tewaria and Jai Singh*a This study focuses on the structural, photoluminescence and photocatalytic properties of a Dy3+-doped sodium zinc molybdate phosphor.The samples were synthesized using a green microwave-assisted method owing to its eficiency in time and energy consumption.The powder X-ray difraction (P-XRD) analysis confirmed the monoclinic structure of as-synthesized Dy3+-doped sodium zinc molybdate with space group C2/m.The most prominent excitation band appeared at 348 nm under 590 nm, and the emission spectra for all samples exhibited a sharp peak at around 590 nm, which is attributed to the 4F9/26H13/2 electric dipole transition of Dy3+ ions.The emission intensity increases with higher Dy3+ doping levels, reaching maximum intensity at a concentration of 6 mol% of Dy3+ in sodium zinc molybdate.Additionally, the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) chromaticity coordinates of the Dy3+ sodium zinc molybdate phosphor places it within the orangish region.Dy3+ is also found to play a great role in enhancing the photocatalytic activity of sodium zinc molybdate under UV light.These findings indicate that the as-synthesized phosphor holds promise for white LED and water purification applications.Received 13th January 2025Accepted 18th March 2025DOI: rsc.li/nanoscale-advances 1.

eceived 13th January 2025Accepted 18th March 2025DOI: rsc.li/nanoscale-advances 1.Introduction Phosphor materials are essential components in various light emitting display technologies, such as in eld emission displays, plasma display panels (PDPs), and lighting applications.1–3 White light-emitting diodes (W-LEDs) have emerged as a next-generation light source, ofering an alternative to traditional uorescent lamps due to their benets, including energy eficiency, quick response time, absence of mercury, low voltage requirements, and environmental friendliness.Currently, conversion-type white LEDs dominate largescale commercial production worldwide.4,5 Fluorescent nanophosphors activated by lanthanides have gained signicant attention in diverse applications across areas such as data storage through optical means, eld emission display technology, solar energy devices, LED illumination systems, and night vision equipment.6–8 These materials exhibit a wide range of photoluminescence (PL) emissions, inuenced by transitions such as 4f–4f and 4f–5d.Lanthanide ions (Ln3+) are particularly notable for their useful properties, including good biocompatibility, resistance to photo-bleaching, and enhanced photo-stability, making them promising for applications such as cancer cell detection, drug delivery and multimode imaging.9,10 However, for eficient PL emission, Ln3+ ions require a suitable host matrix that can transfer energy to the ions, enabling the otherwise parity-forbidden 4f–4f transitions through the crystal eld efect.11 Numerous host materials such as NaLuF4, NaYbF4, LaF3, NaGdF4, KGdF4, NaScF4, and NaYF4 have been explored for their potential in bio-imaging applications.12–14 These hosts are stable at room temperature under ambient conditions, yet oxides ofer additional advantages.

osts are stable at room temperature under ambient conditions, yet oxides ofer additional advantages.Oxide-based hosts, owing to their robust chemical and thermal stability, coupled with their environmentally friendly characteristics, overcome the limitations associated with uoride hosts.15,16 Various oxide hosts, such as molybdates, tungstates, phosphates, gallates, and aluminates, have been explored.In recent years, oxide hosts have garnered particular interest for biomedical applications such as drug delivery, bioimaging, and diagnosis, owing to their biocompatibility.17,18 Red uorescence, in particular, is highly suited for bio-imaging purposes due to its low scattering and deeper tissue penetration.13 The Dy3+ ion, with an electron conguration of 4 f9, exhibits distinctive optical properties.19 The transitions of Dy3+, speci- cally 4F9/2→6H15/2, 4F9/2→6H13/2, and 4F9/26F11/2, correspond to emissions in the blue, yellow, and red regions of the spectrum, making these transitions signicant in the study of white luminescent materials.20,21 For instance, Chengaiah and colleagues synthesized ZnMoO4 phosphors activated with varying concentrations of Dy3+ using a solid-state reaction at 900C..Their research revealed a quenching efect of the excited state 4F9/2 due to energy transfer at higher Dy3+ concentrations.3 In another study, Yang and team developed Ca9Gd (PO4) 7 phosphors, undoped and Dy3+-doped.Under ultraviolet excitation at 350 nm, they observed a prominent blue emission, indicating that Dy3+ ions were situated in positions with high symmetry and an inversion center.22 Similarly, Jamalaiah and colleagues prepared strontium aluminate phosphors with varying Dy3+ concentrations.

ly, Jamalaiah and colleagues prepared strontium aluminate phosphors with varying Dy3+ concentrations.When the Dy3+ concentration exceeded 1.0%, electron transitions driven by d–d interactions produced white light, though the phosphor's color rendering index remained low.23 As of now, there are very few known reports on Dy3-doped ZnMoO4 nanophosphors.The ZnMoO4 host matrix exhibits a crystal structure analogous to that of MgMoO4, where the (MoO4) 2-oxyanion complex serves as the fundamental building block.24,25 In this triclinic symmetry wolframite-type structure, molybdenum (Mo) ions are coordinated tetrahedrally by four oxygen (O2-) ions.Interestingly, Mo ions occupy three distinct crystallographic sites, which may contribute to the material's unique optical and catalytic properties.26,27 ZnMoO4 has garnered attention for its versatility in applications such as phosphors, laser crystals, and catalysts due to its robust chemical and thermal stability.The substitution of Zn2+ with Dy3+ ions introduces additional emission characteristics, making it particularly valuable for luminescent materials.For instance, the combination of yellow and blue emissions from Dy3+-doped ZnMoO4 results in chromaticity coordinates (x, y) that fall within the white light region on the CIE diagram.This feature enhances its applicability in white light-emitting devices.In the absence of direct charge compensation, the host matrix compensates by capturing O2- from the air.In the case of ZnMoO4; Dy3+ phosphors, two Dy3+ ions replace three Zn2+ ions, and the resulting charge compensation is provided by a zinc vacancy.28 In addition to their luminescence properties, rare-earthdoped luminescent materials have shown signicant promise in photocatalytic applications.Dy3+-doped metal oxides, such as ZnWO4, 29 exhibit excellent photocatalytic properties due to their enhanced light absorption and eficient charge carrier separation.

PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: RSCAdv., 2025, 15, 19623 Investigation of luminescence properties and ratiometric thermometry through yellow-to-blue Dy3+ emission in Ca3La7 (SiO4) 5 (PO4) O2 apatite Abir Douzi,ab Sami Slimi, ac Eduard Madirov,d Josep Maria Serres,ac Rosa Maria Sole, a Ezzedine Ben Salem,b Andrey Turshatov, d Bryce S.Richards d and Xavier Mateos *ae Dy3+-doped CaLa (SiO) (PO)O (CLSPO) phosphors were synthesized via a solid-state reaction method and characterized for their structural, optical, and thermometric properties.X-ray difraction (XRD) and Rietveld refinement confirmed a hexagonal apatite-type structure (P63/m) with refined lattice parameters of a=b=9.604 (3), c=7.103 (1) First-principles calculations for the undoped crystal revealed a direct bandgap of 4.08 eV, confirming CLSPO as a suitable host material for luminescent applications.Photoluminescence spectra exhibited characteristic Dy3+ emissions, with two blue bands ( B1468 nm, B2479 nm) and two yellow bands ( Y1; 543 nm, Y2: 575 nm).The yellow-to-blue (Y/B) intensity ratio displayed a strong temperature dependence, establishing ClSPO: Dy3+ as a promising candidate for luminescence-based thermometry.The optimal Dy3+ doping concentration was determined to be 3 at%, beyond which concentration quenching efects were observed.Photoluminescence studies further demonstrated that electric dipole–dipole interactions govern the dominant energy transfer mechanism, as evidenced by concentration-dependent quenching behavior.The absolute photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) was 5.7%, and Arrhenius analysis determined an activation energy of 0.11 eV.The decay time decreases with increasing Dy3+ concentration (from 658S at 0.5 at% Dy3+ to 252S at 10 at%).

The decay time decreases with increasing Dy3+ concentration (from 658S at 0.5 at% Dy3+ to 252S at 10 at%).The fluorescence intensity ratio (FIR) method for optical thermometry revealed an absolute sensitivity (S) of 3.2710-4K - 1 at 298K, while the repeatability (R) of the Y/B ratio exhibited a reproducibility of 95.88% at 298K, ensuring consistent and reliable temperature sensing performance.Furthermore, the luminescence remained stable over three hours of multiple heating–cooling cycles (298–523K), confirming excellent photostability and reversibility.These results establish ClSPO: Dy3+ phosphors as highly eficient, thermally stable, and optically robust materials for next-generation temperature sensors, solid-state lighting, and advanced photonic applications.Received 17th March 2025Accepted 21st May 2025DOI: rsc.li/rsc-advances 1.Introduction Over the past few decades, trivalent lanthanide ions (Ln3+) doped into phosphors have attracted considerable attention due to their extraordinary photoluminescence properties.These ions exhibit unique phenomena such as upconversion luminescence and large Stokes-shied emissions, which are highly benecial for a wide range of optoelectronic applications, including lasers, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), ber-optic ampliers, color displays, and various types of sensors.The versatility and eficiency of Ln31+-doped phosphors have rmly established them as foundational components in the advancement of modern photonic technologies.1–4 Among the various trivalent lanthanide ions (Ln3+), dysprosium (Dy3+) stands out as an exceptional activator due to its ability to emit light across a broad spectrum, ranging from visible to near-infrared wavelengths.This emission results from electronic transitions between the excited energy level 4F9/2 and a series of intermediate states within the manifold 6Hn (where n=15/2, 13/2, 11/2, 9/2, and 7/2).

nd a series of intermediate states within the manifold 6Hn (where n=15/2, 13/2, 11/2, 9/2, and 7/2).These transitions occur at distinct wavelengths, making Dy3+ particularly valuable for applications that require diverse emission proles, such as advanced optical devices and luminescent materials.5,6 The visible emission of the Dy3+ ion is primarily dened by two distinct emission bands in the blue and yellow regions of the spectrum.The blue emission, which corresponds to the transition from the 4F9/2 energy level to 6H15/2, is a magnetic dipole transition.This type of transition is largely insensitive to the local crystal eld, meaning that it remains relatively insensitive to changes in the surrounding medium.In contrast, the yellow emission, which occurs during the transition from 4F9/2: to: 6H13/2, is an electric dipole transition.This transition is highly sensitive to the local crystal eld, meaning that even subtle changes in the eld environment around Dy3+ ions can signicantly inuence the intensity and characteristics of the yellow emission.This sensitivity makes yellow emission particularly useful for studying the local environment in various luminescent materials and applications.7–10 By combining the blue and yellow emissions of Dy3+, white light emission can be achieved in singly Dy3-doped phosphors.11–16 Moreover, the relative intensities of these two emissions provide valuable insights into key aspects of the material, including energy transfer processes, local symmetry, and the coordination environment of Dy3+ ions.However, singly Dy3+-doped phosphors oen exhibit relatively low photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) due to the absence of eficient sensitization pathways.

ly low photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) due to the absence of eficient sensitization pathways.For instance, Dy3+-doped nanoglass-ceramics have been reported to exhibit a PLQY of approximately 15.2%,17 while Dy2O3-doped alkaline-earth borate glasses have demonstrated a PLQY of 23.74% under 453 nm laser excitation.18 Understanding these factors is essential for optimizing the phosphor's eficiency and expand ing its applicability in optical devices.9,11,15,19 In addition to factors such as host material, pump wavelengths and Dy3+ ion concentration, temperature plays a key role in tuning the blue-to-yellow intensity ratio of Dy3+-activated luminescent materials.Temperature changes can inuence emission properties, enabling ne-tuning of the output color, which is essential for optimizing the performance of these materials in various applications.9,20–22 Dy3+-doped phosphors are well established in the eld of thermometry, especially through the use of the luminescence intensity ratio method.This technique typically relies on the variation between two blue emission lines, which arise from transitions involving the thermally coupled energy levels 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 in the ground state 6H15/24,9,20,22–24Due to the presence of numerous intermediate energy levels within the Dy3+ ion, the thermally coupled energy states 4I15/2 and 4F9/2 govern several temperature-dependent emission processes.The Boltzmann distribution can be applied to describe the population dynamics between these two levels, which inuences the intensity ratio of the two blue emission lines, corresponding to the 4I15/26H15/2 and 4F9/26F15/2 transitions.This population distribution also afects the two yellow emission lines, corresponding to the 4I15/26F13/2 and 4F9/26F13/2 transitions.By considering both blue and yellow emissions, the Boltzmann distribution provides a more complete description of the temperature dependence of the emission intensity ratios.

provides a more complete description of the temperature dependence of the emission intensity ratios.Therefore, in contrast to room temperature, the yellow-to-blue intensity ratio of Dy3+-doped phosphors is expected to show signicant variations at elevated temperatures.These variations may lead to observable color changes in the phosphors.In addition, the relationship between the yellow-blue intensity ratio and temperature can be dened quantitatively, enabling this relationship to be used for accurate temperature measurements in thermometry applications.The optical properties of phosphors doped with Ln3+ ions are influenced both by the specific type of Ln3+ ions used and by the choice of host material.Once Dy3+ ions are incorporated into various inorganic crystalline materials such as apatite-type materials, they can generate a wide range of attractive luminescence properties.As an apatite compound, Ca8La2 (PO4) 6O2 (CLPO) has been used as a phosphorescent host in various studies.25–27 Zhu et al.synthesized and studied a series of Ce3+.doped CLPO phosphors, whose emission can be modulated to f 27 Ce3++ and Eu2+.activated CLPO phosphors, emitting in the blue region of the spectrum, and explored the mechanisms of luminescence as well as the associated energy transfer processes.26 Fang et al.conducted a systematic study of the photoluminescence properties of Eu3+ doped CLPO-based phosphors.25 In an efort to identify and develop more eficient luminescent materials, and with the aim of optimizing their photoluminescent properties and discovering materials with superior performance, the researchers carried out an in-depth exploration of cation and anion substitutions within the apatite compound.They synthesized and analyzed a series of modied compounds, including Ca2+ x La8-x (SiO4) 6-x (PO4) x O2 (CLSPO) doped with Eu2+ ions (where x=0, 2, 4, 6 ) 28 and Eu3+ ions (where x=0, 3, 6 ).

content: x O2 (CLSPO) doped with Eu2+ ions (where x=0, 2, 4, 6 ) 28 and Eu3+ ions (where x=0, 3, 6 ).29Additionally, a related study investigated apatites doped with 2% Eu and a wider range of x values ( x=0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ), focusing on the emission properties of both Eu2+ and Eu3+ ions.30 These studies collectively demonstrate the versatility of apatite-based phosphors in hosting lanthanide ions at various doping levels and oxidation states, providing a foundation for exploring the photoluminescence behavior of new dopant systems such as Dy3+.In this context, Cheng et al.synthesized a series of Eu3+-doped CLSPO phosphors and investigated in detail their photoluminescence properties, Judd–Ofelt analysis, and temperature sensing characteristics via absolute emission intensity.31 In this study, we successfully synthesized CLSPO: Dy3+ phosphors and evaluated their structural, optical, and thermometric properties.The study focuses on the (Y/B) emission ratio, leveraging its sensitivity to both doping concentration and temperature for optical sensing applications. 2.Experimental 2.1.Synthesis CLSPO:xDy3+ phosphors, with x=0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 10 at% in the raw materials mixture, were synthesized using the solidstate method in an open atmosphere.High-purity raw materials were utilized: CaCO3 (99.99%, chemPUR), La2O3 (99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich), SiO ( 99%, Sigma-Aldrich), (NH4) 2H PO4 (99.0%, Alfa Aesar), and Dy2O3 (99.9%, chemPUR).The materials were rst weighed in stoichiometric proportions, then transferred to an agate mortar in ethanolic medium.They were then carefully ground to obtain a dry, homogeneous mixture.In the next step, the prepared mixture was calcined in a covered alumina crucible at 900C for 6 hours.The calcined powder was then reground and compressed into pellets under pressure.These pellets were sintered at 1350C for 10 hours in air and nally cooled to room temperature.

e pellets were sintered at 1350C for 10 hours in air and nally cooled to room temperature.The chemical reaction to prepare Ca3La7-xDyx (SiO4) 5 (PO4) O22 phosphors is as follows: 3CaCO3+7-x2La2O3+ 5SiO2+(NH4) 2HPO4+ x2Dy2O3→Ca3La7-xDyx (SiO4) 5 (PO4) O2+ by - products. 2.2.Characterization methods The X-ray powder difraction (XRD) patterns of the CLSPO:xDy3+ series ( x=0-10 at % ) ) were acquired at room temperature using a Shimadzu XRD-6000 difractometer congured in Bragg– Brentano geometry.The system utilized a CuX-ray source, a scintillation counter as the detector, and a Ni lter to suppress Kb radiation.The instrument operated at a tube voltage of 40 kV and a current of 40 mA.Difraction patterns were recorded over the 2q range of 5 to 80, with a scan speed of 2 min−1 and a step size of 0.02°, ensuring high-resolution data suitable for detailed analysis across all samples in the series.For Rietveld renement, data collection was performed under the same conditions, with a step size of 0.02 and a step time of 2 seconds.The samples were mounted on a Si(510) substrate, chosen for its low background contribution, to enhance signal clarity.The structural renement was conducted using Match!3 (Crystal Impact, demo version), enabling accurate determination of the lattice parameters and other structural details.The particle morphology and size were analyzed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with a JEOL1011 microscope, providing detailed insights into the structural features at the nanoscale.The elemental composition of the samples was examined through energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), conducted on a Thermo Scientic Scios 2 eld emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM).The EDX analysis was facilitated by a Thermo Scientic microanalyzer integrated with Pathnder soware, ensuring precise and comprehensive compositional characterization.

2 at the sample surface.The resulting PL emission was captured using an optical spectral analyzer (OSA, AQ6373E, Yokogawa Electric Corporation), with spectral resolution of 1 nm.To evaluate the temperaturedependent luminescent properties, the samples were mounted on a Linkam THMS600 heating stage.The temperature was varied from 298K to 523K, with a step size of 25K.This setup allowed precise control of the sample temperature during the measurements.The luminescence emission was collected using a90 geometry, which was chosen specically to reduce interference from the pump radiation in the recorded spectra.The photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) was determined using an optical system based on an integrated sphere (Labsphere, 6 diameter, model 3P-LPM-060-SL).The sample is positioned centrally within the sphere and illuminated by a continuous-wave LED emitting at 365 nm (Thorlabs, M365L3), powered by a laser diode controller (Thorlabs, ITC4001).

arises from the close ionic size match between Dy3 and La3 in comparable coordination environments.Based on Shannon's reference, the ionic radius for Dy3+ and La3+ are as follows: Dy3+ has a radius of 0.97 Å at CN=VII and 1.08 Å at CN=IX, while La3+ has a radius of 1.11 Å at CN=VII and 1.22 Å at CN=IX, where CN indicates coordination number 32 stability.Since the 4f-site in CLSPO exhibits nine-coordination (CN=IX), Dy3+ preferentially replaces La3+ at this position, as the relatively small size diference helps minimize signicant lattice distortion.Additionally, the 4f-site provides a symmetric and spacious environment, further facilitating Dy3+ incorporation while maintaining structural integrity.In the case of substituting La3+ ions with Dy3+ ions in CLSPO, a reduction in the unit cell volume is evident.This is demonstrated by the shi of the difraction peak corresponding to (hkl)=(002) in the XRD patterns of the CLSPO phosphors (Fig.1(c)).This peak progressively shis toward larger difraction angles (2q) with increasing Dy3+ concentration, indicating a decrease in lattice constants and a contraction of the unit cell volume, consistent with Bragg's law.The lattice parameters a, c, and the unit cell volume Vcalc decrease systematically with higher Dy3+ doping levels, as shown in Table 3.The replacement of La3+ ions in the lattice by Dy3+ is conrmed by the percentage diference in ionic radii (r) between activator ions (Dy3+) and host ions (La3+), determined using eqn (1) (ref.33): r=[ rh (CN) - rd (CN)rh (CN) ] 100 %,1 where, rh and rd represent the ionic radii of the host ion (La3+) and activator ion (Dy3+), respectively.The calculated diference in ionic radii, r, is approximately 12.61% for coordination number CN=VII and 11.48% for CN=IXTo gain deeper insights into the structure of CLSPO:Dy3+ and the incorporation behavior of Dy3 ions within the CLSPO host matrix, Rietveld renement was performed on a CLSPO:3 at% Dy3+ sample.Fig.

candidate for the manufacture of NUV-based WLEDs and solid-state lighting. 1 | Introduction Globally, much attention has been paid to the development of white-light-emitting diodes (LEDs) [1].Phosphor-converted WLEDs play an important and crucial role in the solid-state lighting area, including environmental friendliness, energy efficiency, low energy consumption, and the substitution of conventional high-energy-consuming incandescent lamps [2–5].To date, a wide range of techniques have been employed to produce phosphor-converted WLEDs.The combination of YAG:Ce3+ with an InGaN chip is a potential method for producing white-light emission [6].Phosphor materials, which convert high-energy radiation into visible light, have garnered significant attention because of their wide range of applications in lighting, displays, and bioimaging [7, 8].Phosphor materials that exhibit luminescence can be excited by various sources, including ultraviolet (UV) light, electron beams, and blue light [9–11].The development of new and improved phosphors is an active area of research, with ongoing efforts to enhance their efficiency, color properties, and stability for various applications [12–14].The selection of a suitable host material is very important for a phosphor to display photoluminescence.The host is a crystalline matrix that provides a structural framework for phosphors.Common host materials include oxides, sulfides, silicates, aluminates, borates, and phosphates [14–16].Barium boro-phosphate (BaBP) crystals offer several advantages as host materials for phosphor preparation, making them attractive for various applications in optoelectronic devices.

for phosphor preparation, making them attractive for various applications in optoelectronic devices.Barium boro-phosphate (BaBP) generally exhibits good transparency in the UV–visible region [13, 17–19].This wide transparency window is crucial for the efficient excitation of dopant ions and emission of visible light without significant reabsorption within the host material.The optical properties of the host material can be tailored by varying the ratios of barium, boron, and phosphorus oxides in the composition.This tunability allows the excitation and emission wavelengths of the phosphors to be fine tuned.These materials often possess good chemical durability and thermal stability, which are important for the long-term performance and reliability of phosphors in various applications [20, 21].Barium borophosphates tend to have relatively low phonon energies compared with other host materials.This is advantageous because it reduces non-radiative energy losses from excited dopant ions, leading to a higher luminescence efficiency [22–24].Dysprosium (Dy3+) ions are widely used as activators in phosphor materials because of their unique luminescence properties, particularly their ability to emit light in the blue and yellow regions of the visible spectrum [12, 25, 26].This makes them valuable for various applications, particularly in the generation of white light.Dy3+ has an electronic configuration of [Xe] 4f9.Transitions within the 4f energy levels are responsible for characteristic luminescence [27–29].Dy3+ ions typically exhibit three main emission bands in the visible region: blue emission in the 470–500 nm, due to the 4F9/2→6H13/2 transition; yellow emission in the 570–600 nm, due t o4F9/2→6H13/2 transition; and red emission in the 650–680 nm, due to 4F9/2→→6H11/2 transition [10, 30].The emission of Dy3+ ions in the visible spectrum is influenced by the surrounding host matrices [31].
