Novel non-thermoluminescent CaSO4: D: y dosimeters A.I.Castro-Campoy a,b, C.Cruz-Vazquez a, R.P erez-Salas c, V.M.Castano d, R.Bernal c,* a Departamento de Investigacion en Polímeros y Materiales, Universidad de Sonora, Apartado Postal 130, Hermosillo, Sonora, 83000, Mexico b Frascati National Laboratories, National Institute of Nuclear Physics (INFN), Via Enrico Fermi 54, 00044, Frascati, Italy c Departamento de Investigaci on en Física, Universidad de Sonora, Apartado Postal 5-088, Hermosillo, Sonora 83190, Mexico d Centro de Física Aplicada y Tecnología Avanzada de la Universidad Nacional Aut onoma de M exico.Apartado Postal 1-1010, Quer etaro, Quer etaro, 76000, Mexico ARTICLEINFOKeywords: Afterglow-based dosimetry CaSO4:DyBeta particle irradiation Long persistent phosphors ABSTRACTThe non-thermoluminescence afterglow-based dosimetry performance of self-agglomerating pellet-shaped CaSO4:Dy phosphors synthesized through a low-cost, environmentally friendly method is first reported.Thermoluminescence (TL) and afterglow (AG) were analyzed in samples exposed to beta particle irradiation in the dose range from 0.06 to 8.0Gy.Characteristic TL glow curves consist of an intense TL maximum at 134 ◦C, a shoulder at 200 ◦C, and a maximum at 447 ◦C.CaSO4:Dy exhibits a highly sensitive AG response for 24 h with linear behavior from 0.06Gy to 8.0Gy.A remarkable reproducibility of both the TL and the AG response was observed in repeated irradiation–readout cycles with no need for pre-irradiation annealing.The synthesized CaSO:Dy exhibits promising properties to be used as an AG-based dosimeter for real-time radiation detection and dosimetry.Moreover, this phosphor might be applied as a long persistent phosphor (LPP), being a cost effective alternative to other available LPPs. 1.

content: sa long persistent phosphor (LPP), being a cost effective alternative to other available LPPs. 1.Introduction Thermoluminescence (TL) is the light emission from a solid when heated after exposure to ionizing radiation.If the emitted light can be expressed as a reproducible function of the exposure dose, the TL phenomenon allows dose assessment.The TL-based dosimetric technique is known as TL dosimetry, and nowadays it remains a reliable and widely used technique (Chand et al., 2020; Duragkar et al., 2019).Afterglow (AG) or Persistent Luminescence is the prompt light emission from a phosphor after being excited by ionizing radiation exposure.Since this luminescence phenomenon was first proposed by P erez-Salas et al.(1993) as the basis for a non-TL dosimetric technique, there has been an increasing interest in synthesizing new materials with features suitable for AG dosimetry.AG-based dosimetry applications range from personnel to clinical (Hern andez-Ortiz et al., 2013).In TL dosimetry, the amount of light emitted during the heating of a phosphor previously exposed to radiation is used, as this is a defined function of the dose.This dosimetry is passive because the dose is determined after exposure (typicallyseveraldaysafterirradiation).In contrast, in AG-based dosimetry, the emitted light is measured during or immediately after exposing the phosphor to irradiation.If the amount of AG light is proportional to the dose, the measurement of AG allows for real-time and in situ dose assessment, i.e., real time and in situ dosimetry.Perhaps the most attractive feature of AG dosimetry (yetunexplored) is real-time and in situ detection, which is exceptionally advantageous for clinical applications, e.g., radiotherapy (Pal et al., 2008).Furthermore, the instrumentation for AG does not require a heating device, which is a key component of standard TL dosimeters (TLD) readers, making the procedure cheaper (P erez-Salas et al., 1993) and far simpler in terms of both experimental setup and analysis (e.g., temperature lag) (Piters and Bos, 1994; Piters et al., 1994).

experimental setup and analysis (e.g., temperature lag) (Piters and Bos, 1994; Piters et al., 1994).Phosphors that exhibit AG in intervals of minutes, hours, or days after radiation exposure are often called long persistent phosphors (LPPs).LPPs are interesting materials for various applications, including information storage, advanced displays, night-vision surveillance, latent fingermark detection, in vivo medical imaging, and microelectronics (Shanker et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020).While various inorganic persistent phosphors with different chemical compositions have been studied, such as oxides, nitrides, sulfides, and halides (Stanish et al., 2020), most research concerns aluminate-based or silicate-based materials, typically with more than one lanthanide as dopants and synthesized by complex and expensive methods.SrAl O-based LPPs are the most widely studied materials.These are typically doped with Eu2+ and Dy3+ and synthesized via solid-state reactions at temperatures of 1300C or higher for extended periods (10hormore).This high-temperature, long-duration synthesis presents challenges for large-scale production and conflicts with sustainability prin ciples (Li et al., 2016; Rojas-Hernandez et al., 2018).Dy-doped CaSO4, commonly known as TLD-900, is currently used in personnel dosimetry due to its low TL fading, high TL sensitivity, wide dose range, good thermal and physical stability, low cost, and high TL emission at low doses (Forner et al., 2020; Nuraeni et al.).Compared to other commercially available dosimeters (for instance, TLD-100), CaSO4 presents a higher energy dependence and sensitivity to photons due to its high effective atomic number ( Zeff=15.3 ) CaSO4.-based materials exhibit high sensitivity to low-energy X-rays and lower sensitivity to gamma radiation (Forner et al., 2020).Nuraeni et al., reported on the response of CaSO4: Dy when exposed to beta and gamma radiation.

Khanin et al., 2019).However, there is scarce information about TLDs that exhibit AG, most notably TLD-400, based on CaF:Mn (Danilkin et al., 2008), and TLD-900, based on CaSO4: Dy (Pradhan and Bhatt, 1981; Visocekas and Ouchene, 1983).Visocekas (Visocekas and Ouchene, 1983) observed a weak AG for many hours after the initial irradiation, which led to the first report of CaSO4: Dy as an LPP.In2011, Mori et al.(2011) reported on the AG of CaSO4: Eu,Pr up to 2 h by adding Li.Nonetheless, no reports exist on the AG-based dosimetry performance of CaSO4based phosphors.Accord ingly, in this article the AG-based dosimetry performance of pellet-shaped CaSO4: Dy phosphors synthesized using a low-cost and environmentally friendly method is first reported. 2.Materials and methods Self-agglomerating pellet-shaped CaSO4: Dy (0.25 mol %) samples were prepared following the route described by Bernal et al.(2008), where a homogeneous Na2SO4 (Merck, 99.99%) aqueous solution was slowly added to a homogeneous CaCl22H20 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%) aqueous solution in stoichiometric ratio while stirring at room temperature until the formation of the CaSO4 precipitate.For Dy-doping, the suitable quantity of DyCl3 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99%) was added to the CaCl22H20 aqueous solution.The resulting powder was then pressed in a hydraulic press and annealed in a furnace to obtain 0.060 g pellet-shaped samples.Further details of the synthesis procedure are thoroughly discussed in previous reports (Bernal et al., 2008; García-- Haro et al., 2016; Castro-Campoy et al., 2019).

hence, it qualifies as a long persistent phosphor (LPP).Further research could be very interesting since CaSO4: Dy is cheaper and simpler to synthesize than other long-lasting phosphorescent materials. 5.Conclusions As the afterglow (AG) phenomenon hampers using a phosphor as a thermoluminescent dosimeter, it opens the possibility of performing non-thermoluminescence (TL) dosimetry.In this work, CaSO4:Dy phosphors were successfully synthesized through an environmentally friendly, cost-effective method.Dy-doping enhances the TL intensity and shifts the maximum toward lower temperatures, which gives rise to intense AG interesting for real-time and in-situ AG-based dosimetry applications.The integrated AG is a linear function of the beta irradiation dose in the studied range (from 0.06 to 8.0Gy), it exhibits a remarkable reproducibility in repeated irradiation – AG readout cycles, and the lower detectable dose was determined to be 85.3 μGy, features that make the synthesized phosphors attractive for medium and low dosage AG dosimetry.Moreover, it was observed that the AG response still remains 24 h after irradiation, so these phosphors can be classified as long persistent phosphors (LPPs), representing a cheaper option compared with other known LPPs.From the experimental evidence here presented, it can be concluded that the synthesized CaSO4: Dy phosphors exhibit suitable properties as real-time and in situ AG-based radiation detectors, dosimeters, and LPPs.Of course, more research is needed on this concern.

pubs.acs.org/acsaom Article Optical Characteristics and Judd-Ofelt Analysis of Dy3+-Activated Bismuth Oxychloride Phosphors for Potential Applications in WLEDs, Optical Thermometry, and Forensic Sciences Ansu Sara Solomon, Kavia J.Albert, S.Masilla Moses Kennedy, and Prathibha Vasudevan* Cite This: ACSAppl.Opt.Mater.2025, 3, 2616−2632 Read Online ACCESSMetrics & More ABSTRACT: Designing iconic WLEDS derived from a single host has bestowed an impetus to the synthesis of Dy3+-activated bismuth oxychloride (BiOCl) phosphors via a facile solid-state method.The insights of crystal structure were confirmed using X-ray difraction analysis and the Rietveld refinement method.The investigation of the UV−vis-NIR spectra extended the characteristics of bonding structures and radiative emission of the samples.The photoluminescence spectrum reveals the feasibility of white light generation harnessing the luminescence characteristics of Dy3+ with a critical concentration of 2 mol %.The photometric characteristics of the sample at critical concentration suggested color coordinates of (0.29, 0.33), CCT of 6864K, and LER of 304 lm/W.Furthermore, the ultrahigh Internal Quantum Eficiency (IQE) of 96.39% exhibited by the optimized sample gives notable insight for future investigations in the fields of robust and sustainable optoelectronic applications.The synthesized phosphor demonstrated a better temperature sensitivity over 303−483K while utilizing temperature-dependent photoluminescence for diferent modes of analysis.

he luminescence characteristics of materials have a great impact on the design of the host material.Therefore, identifying an appropriate host material that can improve the luminescence quality and provide better white light emission is crucial.Among the diferent host matrices, metal oxyhalides are of great interest in account of their low phonon energy, which enhances photoluminescence with minimum nonradiative transitions.20 Metal oxychlorides are considered to be an appropriate host material for the preparation of phosphors with specific application.21,22 The distinct crystal structure of BiOCl, along with its enhanced ability to incorporate activator ions, positions it as an efective host for the phosphor material.The red luminescent polymers based on Eu3+ activated BiOCl have been reported for their lighting and forensic applications.23 Latha et al.observed green emitting BiOCl: Tb3+ phosphors for the applications of forensic science and security ink.24 Reeta et al.demonstrated diferent implementations of the BiOCl: Dy3+ system in medical and forensic studies.25 The codoping of Ho3+ and Yb3+ in BiOCl significantly enhances the photocatalytic activities of BiOCl: Ho3+/ Yb3+ microspheres, as demonstrated by Wu et al.26Moreover, this host material proved its potential applications in photocatalysis, superconductors, dyes, pharmaceuticals, air quality analysers, and light-driven machines.27 This approach firmly positions multifunctional materials at the forefront of research eforts.In this work, we prepared trivalent Dy3+ doped bismuth oxychloride (BiOCl) phosphors and analyzed their structure, photoluminescence, and optical thermometric characteristics.The varying concentrations of Dy3+ ions and their luminescence intensity were analyzed.The applications in wLEDs and forensic studies are carried out to ofer deep insights into their luminescent and structural behavior.

section: Optical performance and luminescence properties of Dy3+-doped LaM J B5O10 phosphors Jabir Hakami <sup>a</sup>, U.H.Kaynar <sup>b,c</sup>, M.B.Coban <sup>d</sup>, H.Aydin <sup>e,f</sup>, R.Alamri <sup>a</sup>, D.A.Jabali <sup>a</sup>, N.Can a,g,* <sup>a</sup> Jazan University, College of Science, Department of Physical Sciences, Physics Division, P.O.Box114, 45142Jazan, Saudi Arabia <sup>b</sup> Bakırcay University, Faculty of Engineering and Architecture, Department of Fundamental Sciences, Menemen, Izmir, Turkiye <sup>c</sup> Bakırçay University, Biomedical Technologies Design Application and Research Center, Menemen, Izmir, Turkiye <sup>d</sup> Balikesir University, Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Department of Physics, Balikesir, Turkiye <sup>e</sup> Central Research Laboratories, Izmir, Katip Celebi University, Turkiye <sup>f</sup> Graphene Application & Research Center, Izmir, Katip Celebi University, Turkiye <sup>g</sup> Nanotechnology Research Unit, College of Science, Jazan University, P.O.Box.114, Jazan45142, Saudi Arabia ## A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Dy<sup>3+</sup>-doped LaMgB O Photoluminescence Concentration quenching Activation energy Correlated Color temperature (CCT) ## A B S T R A C T Despite significant advancements in borate-based phosphors, improving luminescent efficiency and thermal stability, particularly at high temperatures, remains a persistent challenge.In this study, Dy3+-doped La Mg B5O10 (LMBO) phosphors were synthesized and characterized for their photoluminescent properties to address these issues.Under344 nm excitation, the Dy3+-activated LMBO phosphors exhibited strong luminescence with characteristic peaks at482 nm (blue), 578 nm (yellow), and663 nm (red), corresponding to specific Dy3+transitions.Optimal luminescence was achieved at a doping level of2 wt% Dy3+<sup>+</sup>, beyond which quenching effects reduced emission intensity.

content: a doping level of 2 wt% Dy3++, beyond which quenching effects reduced emission intensity.The critical quenching distance (Rc) was estimated at 24.66 Å, indicating predominant non-radiative energy transfer.Moreover, thermal quenching was reduced, with the activation energy for thermal quenching determined to be 0.1975 eV, demonstrating that the material can maintain reasonable luminescence efficiency at elevated temperatures.Time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy revealed multi-exponential decay behavior, indicating the presence of multiple decay processes.The average luminescence lifetimes were calculated as 632 μs for the 2 wt% Dy3+ sample and 539 μs for the 3 wt% Dy3+ sample, with a clear concentration quenching effect observed at higher dopant levels.Colorimetric analysis in the CIE1931 color space revealed a shift toward yellow with increasing Dy3+ concentration, achieving a correlated color temperature (CCT) of 6595K at 2 wt% Dy3+.This shift supports the material’s potential for photonic and lighting applications.These findings highlight a significant advancement in addressing the thermal stability issue in phosphor materials, making Dy3+-doped LMBO phosphors promising candidates for advanced photonic technologies. 1.Introduction Borate-based materials have garnered significant research interest for their unique luminescence and structural versatility, making them suitable for various photonic applications, particularly in LED technology.Among these, LaMgB5O10 (lanthanum magnesium pentaborate, LMBO) stands out as an excellent candidate for rare-earth (RE) doping due to its robust crystal structure.This structure, characterized by lanthanide chains linked by BO4 tetrahedra and BO3 triangles, creates an optimal environment for enhanced luminescence [1,2].Compounds such as RBO3, RAl3 (BO3) 4, and RMgB5O10 (where R represents Y, La–Lu) are promising phosphors for high-power emitters in the visible range under UV excitation [3–5].

–Lu) are promising phosphors for high-power emitters in the visible range under UV excitation [3–5].These materials are extensively used in LED technology, a key application for borate-based phosphors.For instance, white LEDs often employ a combination of blue, green, and red phosphors or semiconductor emitters to achieve broad-spectrum white light, with borate compounds playing a crucial role in this process.The study of LMBO as a host material began with foundational work by Eljouhari et al.(1996), who explored the photoluminescence (PL) of Ce3+, Tb3+, and Mn2+ in LMBO-based glasses.This foundational work provided essential insights into the interactions of various dopants with the borate matrix, establishing a basis for subsequent research [1].Volkova et al.(2005) further examined the luminescent properties of LMBO, particularly focusing on the behavior of Tm3+ doped samples.Their work demonstrated that TmMgB5010 crystals exhibit intense blue emission with significant thermal stability, positioning them as suitable candidates for high-temperature photonic applications [2].Subsequen research expanded to include other rare-earth (RE) dopants.Mikhailik and Kraus (2010) explored the enhancement of VUV-excited lumines cence in red-emitting pentaborate phosphors through sensitization, particularly highlighting the role of Tb3+ in enhancing Eu3+ emission in TbMgB5O10 hosts [6].Sakirzanovas et al.(2011) reported strong orangered emissions in Sm3+-doped LMBO, demonstrating its potential fo applications in fluorescent devices [7].Bajaj et al.(2017) furthe explored Ce3+-doped LMBO, which exhibited intense blue light emission suitable for UV-LED applications [8].Moreover, a study conducted by Mitina et al.(2023) investigated the luminescent properties of LMBO doped with Tb3+ and Eu3+, demonstrating strong red emission and emphasizing its potential for applications in white light generation and other photonic technologies [9].

4 f transitions, offer a unique combination of yellow and blue emissions, making them particularly suitable for generating white light, which is crucial for a wide range of lighting applications.In addition to improving lumines cence, the energy migration mechanisms in Dy3+-doped LMBO are critical for maintaining high luminescence efficiency at elevated temperatures.These mechanisms involve energy transfer through cross relaxation and dipole–dipole (d-d) interactions, which are mitigated by the relatively large critical quenching distance.As a result, non radiative energy losses are minimized, allowing the material to retain its luminescence even under thermal stress.This makes Dy3+-doped LMBOa promising candidate for high-temperature photonic applications.The incorporation of Dy3+ into the LaMgB5010 matrix enables efficient light emission and enhances the material’s performance at elevated temperatures, making it highly relevant for SSL applications The relatively high thermal stability of Dy3+-doped LMBO can be attributed to the energy migration mechanisms, where non-radiative energy losses are minimized, and energy transfer between Dy3+ ions is optimized.These mechanisms result in improved luminescent efficiency and reduced thermal quenching, which is essential for high-temperature photonic applications.A comprehensive review by Tawalare (2022) discussed the ongoing interest in LMBO, particularly its applications in solid-state lasers and light-emitting diodes (LEDs).The review covered the effects of different dopants, such as Ce3+, Tb3+, and Eu3+, on the luminescence properties of LMBO but did not specifically address Dy3+ doping, indicating a gap in the current research that this study aims to fill [10].

ally address Dy3+ doping, indicating a gap in the current research that this study aims to fill [10].Although no studies have specifically focused on Dy3+-doped LMBO to date, research on other Dy3+-doped systems, such as in gadolinium aluminate borate phosphors, has demonstrated enhanced luminescence properties through energy transfer mechanisms and tunable color emission [11].These findings underscore the potential of Dy3+ as a dopant in various host materials, highlighting the importance of exploring its effects in LMBO.This gap in the literature is significant, especially as hightemperature PL can provide critical insights into the thermal stability and potential high-temperature applications of these materials.Additionally, previous studies have primarily focused on room temperature PL measurements of Ce3+, Tb3+, Sm3+, and Eu3+ doped LMBO, without exploring their thermal stability at elevated temperatures.Our work addresses this gap by investigating the thermal quenching behaviour of Dy3++-doped LMBO, demonstrating its retention of luminescence efficiency at elevated temperatures.This makes Dy3+-activated LMBOa promising candidate for high-power LED and other SSL applications, where thermal stability is a critical factor.Borates have garnered significant attention as phosphor substrates due to their advantageous properties, including high thermal and chemical stability, low synthesis temperatures, and wide transparency ranges.These features make them well-suited for applications in SSL and luminescent displays.Additionally, borates exhibit excellent radiation resistance and can efficiently incorporate a variety of dopants, enhancing their luminescent properties.Studies by Sakirzanovas et al.(2011), Tawalare et al.(2022), Volkova et al.(2023) have highlighted the efficiency of borates in luminescent applications, particularly due to their strong crystal-field effects and energy transfer properties [7,10,12].Moreover, the work by Mu et al.

trong crystal-field effects and energy transfer properties [7,10,12].Moreover, the work by Mu et al.(2014) further supports the use of borates in luminescent displays, emphasizing their potential for high-performance phosphor applications [13].In addition, Dy3+ ions are particularly important activators in luminescent materials due to their characteristic blue (4F9/26H15/2) and yellow (4F9/26H13/2) emissions.Zheng et al.(2022) have demonstrated that Ce3+ ions can act as sensitizers, enhancing energy transfer to Dy3+ ions and improving luminescence efficiency in phosphor systems.For instance, in the Ca9ZnK (PO4) 7: Ce3+, Dy3+ phosphor system, efficient energy transfer between Ce3+ and Dy3+ ions leads to tunable photoluminescence, achieving both high thermal stability and broad-spectrum white emission, making it suitable for solid-state lighting applications [14].In this research, we explore the potential of Dy3+-activated LMBO synthesized via a microwave-assisted sol–gel method.This method, which allows for lower processing temperatures and energy efficiency, offers significant advantages over traditional solid-state synthesi methods [11].The structural and luminescent characteristics of Dy3+ doped LMBO are characterized using techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD), Rietveld refinement, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), alongside room temperature, low temperature, and high-temperature luminescence measurements.This study aims to expand the understanding of borate phosphors by exploring the incorporation of Dy3+ into LMBO, which may contribute to the development of advanced materials for photonic application 2.Experimenta 2.1.Synthesis LMBO and Dy3++-doped LMBO were synthesized using a microwaveassisted sol–gel combustion approach.Lanthanum oxide ( La2O3, 99.99% purity, Sigma Aldrich) was dissolved in nitric acid to form lanthanum nitrate.Magnesium nitrate ( Mg (NO3) 2.9H2O, 99.

as dissolved in nitric acid to form lanthanum nitrate.Magnesium nitrate ( Mg (NO3) 2.9H2O, 99.0 % purity, Sigma Aldrich) and boric acid (H3BO4) were added to the solution as aluminium and boron sources.The mixture was vigorously stirred to ensure the complete dissolution of the precursors.Dysprosium nitrate ( Dy (NO3) 3, Sigma Aldrich, 99.9% purity) was added in varying concentrations (0.5 wt%, 1 wt%, 2 wt%, 3 wt%, 5 wt%, and 7 wt%) for doping.Doping levels were precisely controlled by adjusting the amount of dysprosium nitrate added to the solution.The solution underwent a sole-gel process, gently heated to form a gel-like structure.After gel formation, the mixture was microwaved, rapidly heating the material to combust organics and form the crystalline phase.The microwaveassisted combustion process reduces processing time and enhances the homogeneity of the final product.The resulting powder was cooled to room temperature, finely ground, and annealed at 960C for 72 h to enhance crystallinity.The annealing process is consistent with the protocols established in previous studies on RE-doped borate compounds where such conditions have been shown to optimize the formation of the desired crystalline phase and enhance material properties.Similar treatments were employed by Sakirzanovas et al.(2011) who annealed LMBO doped with Sm3+ at 1020 ◦C for 8 h, and by Volkova et al.(2023), who annealed TmMgB5O10 at 900C for 72 h [7,12].These conditions were selected to ensure the successful dopant incorporation into the host lattice and stabilize the crystal structure, as achieved in this study for Dy3+-doped LMBO.The microwave-assisted sol–gel method was employed in this study due to its advantages over the traditional high-temperature solid-state method.While the solid-state method is known for producing highly crystalline materials, it typically requires significantly longer processing times and higher temperatures, which can be less energy-efficient and more time-consuming.

content: nd carriers are released in the form of mechanical or thermal excitation when refilling is complete.By constructing the traps in the phosphor during X-ray excitation and using it for repetitive imaging, the detection limit is 74.78 nGy/s, and the spatial imaging resolution is as high as 16 lp/mm.This discovery provides a new idea for the development of time-delayed X-ray scintillator.© 2025Published by Elsevier B.V.on behalf of Chinese Society of Rare Earths. 1.Introduction X-ray's non-invasive penetration capability is substantial and widely utilized, allowing its extensive application across various fields including medical imaging,1e4 security detection,5,6 industrial inspection,7,8 and scientific research.9 The scintillator, which converts high-energy radiation into visible light, is a key core component of X-ray imaging.10 Most existing X-ray scintillators perform real-time conversion of high-energy radiation for imaging, thereby enabling effective assessment of both the real-time status of equipment and the immediate condition of patients.11,12 However, the high energy of X-ray can cause damage to patients or monitored objects during real-time imaging.13 Additionally, realtime imaging requires the use of high-sensitivity, rapid imaging systems, which are relatively expensive.14 Delayed imaging scintillators can perform imaging by utilizing the residual luminescence of the material or the energy trapped in internal defects after X-ray irradiation has been completed.15,16 Therefore, developing scintillator materials capable of delayed imaging can effectively address the issues associated with real-time imaging scintillators, and hold significant research value.The key to developing X-ray time-lapse imaging scintillators is to make them have excellent sustained luminescence performance, so the scintillator should have stable energy traps.16,17 Stable energy traps are the guarantee of continuous luminescence and information storage.

6,17 Stable energy traps are the guarantee of continuous luminescence and information storage.Current researchers have developed fluoride nanocrystals 18e2 0 or metal halides as materials 21e23 for delayed imaging scintillators.Fluoride nanocrystals have excellent luminescence properties under X-ray excitation, and Liu et al.15 first reported the development of NaLuF:Tb3þ nanocrystals as X-ray time-delayed scintillators.However, the trap structures in fluoride nanocrystal materials are unstable, which can easily lead to loss of imaging information, and the imaging data can only be read once.Metal halides have stable trap structures and relatively high imaging accuracy,16 but their inherent high toxicity greatly restricts their application in the medical field.Therefore, constructing stable traps for storing X-ray energy in environmentally friendly materials is crucial for the development of practical delayed imaging scintillators, which ensures that the carriers of the scintillator will not be prematurely or less likely to be de-trapped from the trap under the influence of the environment and result in the loss of imaging information.In this work, we successfully prepared the Sr2Al6O11: Dy3+( SAO: Dy3+) phosphors with permanent energy traps under X-ray irradiation.Furthermore, a flexible scintillator film based on SAO: Dy3+ was developed, which enables prolonged delayed imaging and repeated reading of imaging data.The strategy of constructing traps while imaging fulfills the conditions for the development of X-ray delayed scintillators, provides a new idea for the development of scintillator materials. 2.Experimental 2.1.Materials and synthesis A series of SAO: x Dy3+( x=0.25 %, 0.50 %, 1.00 %, 1.50 %, 2.00 %, in mass ratio) phosphors was synthesized by high temperature solidstate reaction method.

Article Synthesis and Luminescent Properties of Dy3+ et.A ctivated Yellow Phosphors with Anomalous Thermal Quenching for w-LEDsAnlin Zhang 1,2, Huapeng Sun 3, Xiang Li1 and Bin Deng 1,2,* 1 School of Chemistry and Environmental Science, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou 423043, China Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Xiangnan Rare-Precious Metals Compounds Research and Application, Xiangnan University, Chenzhou 423043, China 3Chenjiang Laboratory, School of New Energy, Chenzhou Vocational Technical College, Chenzhou 423000, China Correspondence: dengbinxnu@163.com Abstract Thermal stability is a crucial factor in evaluating phosphors and determining whether they can be utilized in white light emitting diodes (w-LEDs).In this work, a series of Sr6LuAl (BO3) 6Dy3+(SLAB:Dy3+) phosphors was synthesized via high-temperature solidstate reaction.The synthesized SLAB: Dy3+ phosphor exhibits narrow-band emission in the range of 450–700 nm under 348 nm UV excitation.The strongest emission peak is located at 577 nm and is primarily due to 4F9/2.6H13/2 electron transitions.The optimal doping concentration of Dy3+ in the synthesized phosphor was 15 mol%.The integrated emission intensity of the synthesized phosphor at 480 k is 97.84% of that at 300 k, with excellent thermal stability.The activation energy Eg=0.62 eV.Meanwhile, the Commission International de l’Eclairage (CIE) coordinates of the prepared w-LEDs were (0.309,0.363) with a correlated color temperature (CCT) of 6497K.Preliminary experimental findings suggest that SLAB:Dy3+ phosphors hold promise for utilization in w-LEDs applications.

mon method is to excite tricolor phosphors—red, green, and blue—with near-ultraviolet chips [11,12].The w-LEDs prepared with this method offer a range of advantages, including high energy efficiency, low cost, high color rendering index, and long lifespan.Therefore, the development of new phosphors is crucial for realizing high-quality w-LEDs.At present, most commercial w-LEDs phosphors are made by doping rare earth ions into matrix materials such as borates, phosphates, and silicates.Among the many rare earth ions, Dy3+ ions have attracted attention due to their rich energy level structure.The electronic configuration of Dy3+ is 4 f95 s25 p6.Under ultraviolet (UV) or near-ultraviolet (n-UV) excitation, Dy3+-doped phosphors exhibit narrow-band emission in three different colors [13,14]: the 4F9/26H15/2 electronic transition is dominated by blue light (magneticdipoletransition), the 4F9/26H13/2 electronic transition is dominated by yellow light (electricdipoletransition), while the 4F9/26H11/2 transition is dominated by red light.The intensity of the magnetic dipole transitions and electric dipole transitions is affected by the symmetry of the environment surrounding the luminescent center.If the intensity of the electric dipole transition is strong, it indicates that the Dy3+ ion is in a higher asymmetric ligand position, and vice versa.Currently, Dy3+-doped fluorescent materials have been extensively studied and reported, such as Li3Gd3Te2O12: Dy3+ [ 15 ].Na2Ca Sn2Ge3O12: Dy3+[16], Sr3MgSi2O8: Dy3+[17], and Ca3 (PO4) 2: Dy3+[ 18 ] The matrix material is an important component of phosphors, and its performance determines the quality of the phosphors.Borates have been attracting attention in the field of luminescent materials due to their stable physicochemical properties, high optical thresholds, and low synthesis temperatures.

to their stable physicochemical properties, high optical thresholds, and low synthesis temperatures.The structural types of borates are diverse, such as BO3 (planartriangles), BO4 (tetrahedra), and the poly-borate ions B4O7 and B6O13Different types of borates correspond to different crystal field environments and exhibit different luminescent properties in luminescent materials.A large number of borate phosphors have been studied and reported.P.Liang et al.prepared Ba3Sc2 (BO3) 4: Eu2+[19] phosphors by partially substituting Sc ions with Al and Ga ions, which exhibited excellent thermal stability.The w-LEDs devices prepared with this phosphor exhibit a high color rendering index and low color temperature.M.Behera et al.synthesized Eu3+-doped Y2CaB10O19 [20] phosphors by a high-temperature solid-state method.The results show that the synthesized phosphor is suitable for the preparation of w-LEDs.Therefore, borates are ideal matrix materials for synthesizing rare earth-doped phosphors.In this work, a series of SLAB: Dy3+ phosphors were successfully synthesized by high-temperature solid-state reactions.The phase purity, surface morphology, elemental distribution, spectral properties, and concentration quenching mechanism were systematically studied.Additionally, w-LEDs devices were fabricated by SL.A B: Dy3+ phosphors, and their optical performance was tested, laying an experimental foundation for their application in the field of solid-state lighting. 2.Results and Discussion In previous studies, it has been confirmed that the SLAB host belongs to the hexagonal crystal system with R3 space group.The lattice parameters of Sr6LuAl (BO3) 6 are a=b=12.1565 Å, c=9.0853 Å, V=1162.7538 Å3 [21].Figure 1a exhibits the XRD patterns of the prepared SLAB: x Dy3+( x=1-30.mol%) phosphors.The XRD curves of phosphors doped with different concentrations of Dy3+ ions can be well indexed to the standard card of the SLAB matrix (PDF04-009-2962) [22].

Synthesis and photoluminescence properties of RE3+( RE=Eu,.Dy, and Sm)-doped BaAl2Ge2O8 phosphors Sk.Khaja Hussain 1, Weiwei Xiang 1, Jae SuYuDepartment of Electronic and Information Convergence Engineering, Institute for Wearable Convergence Electronics, Kyung Hee University, Yongin-si, Gyeonggi-do, 17104, Republic of Korea ARTICLEINFOHandling Editor: DrP.Vincenzini Keywords: BaAl2Ge2O8Rare-earth ions Phosphors Thermal stability Color purity ABSTRACTTrivalent rare-earth ( RE3+; RE=Eu, Dy, and Sm) ions doped BaAl2Ge2O8 (BAGO) phosphors were synthesized using a pechni-type sol-gel method.The phase formation of the BAGO host lattices prepared at various temperatures was characterized by X-ray diffraction, which revealed a monoclinic crystal structure with space group I12/c (No.15).The morphological characteristics of the optimized BAGO: RE3+ phosphors, characterized by using a field-emission scanning electron microscope, showed that they had aggregated structures of micrometer sized particles.The photoluminescence (PL) properties of BAGO: RE3+ phosphors under ultraviolet (UV) and near-UV excitations showed strong and characteristic emissions.The concentration quenching behaviors were systematically investigated to determine the optimal doping concentration of each phosphor.Additionally, temperature-dependent PL measurements were performed to evaluate the thermal stability of the phosphors, and Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage chromaticity coordinates for the optimized phosphors were calculated to assess their suitability for solid-state lighting applications. 1.

content: ed phosphors were calculated to assess their suitability for solid-state lighting applications. 1.Introduction The 21st century has seen a significant increase in the demand for advanced luminescent materials due to promising applications in solidstate lighting, display technology, and photonic devices [1–3].Among various types of luminescent materials, rare-earth (RE) ions doped phosphors have emerged as a cornerstone due to their excellent optical properties such as high quantum efficiency, tunable emission color, and excellent thermal stability [4,5].The trivalent RE (RE3+) ions, such as Eu3+, Sm3+, and Dy3+, exhibit characteristic electronic transitions within the 4f-4f or 5d-4f configurations, producing sharp and distinct emission lines that are highly suitable for various optoelectronic applications [6–8].Therefore, strategic design and optimization of RE-doped phosphors are essential to achieve enhanced luminescence performance.As is known, Eu3+ ions exhibit efficient red emission, which mainly comes from the 5D07F2 electric dipole transition, resulting in an intense and very pure red luminescence [9].This property makes Eu3+-doped phosphors suitable candidates for red-emitting components in white light-emitting diodes (WLEDs) and advanced display technol ogies [10].On the other hand, Dy3+ ions are widely known for their characteristic blue and yellow emissions arising from the 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions, respectively [11].This combination of blue and yellow emissions often results in an emission that is nearly white, making Dy3+-activated phosphors very attractive for white-emitting applications [12].Additionally, the Dy3+ ions are known for their long-lived emission, making them effective for sustained luminescence and anti-counterfeiting applications [13].Likewise, Sm3+ ions are distinguished by their characteristic orange-red emission, which mainly occurs from the 4G5/26H J / 2 transition [14].

their characteristic orange-red emission, which mainly occurs from the 4G5/26H J / 2 transition [14].In particular, this transition results in an intense orange-red emission, making Sm3+-doped phosphors promising candidates for red-emitting applications [15].Bi a Al2Ge2O8 (BAGO) has recently gained great attention as a promising host material for divalent or trivalent RE ion doping because of its excellent structural and optical properties [16].The BAGO matrix features a rigid framework formed by interconnected [ AlO4 ] and [ GeO4 ] tetrahedra, which provides a chemically stable and and Si, which are elements of group IV of the periodic table, BAGO is also expected to exhibit excellent luminescence properties like BaAl2Si2O8 [18,19].In addition, the wide bandgap and low phonon energy of BAGO facilitate efficient energy transfer processes, making it a versatile platform for incorporating various RE3+ ions [20].For instance, BAGO phosphors singly doped with Eu3+, Eu2+, and Mn4+ have been reported, highlighting the versatility of the host [ 16, 18, 21].However, despite this potential, systematic studies on the luminescence properties of BAGO doped with various RE3+ ions are still lacking.This gap in the literature provides an opportunity for further research to fully understand and utilize the luminescence properties of RE3+-doped BAGO materials.Classically, RE3+-activated metal oxide phosphor materials have been synthesized through solid-state reaction processes.However, this method has several limitations, such as requiring long-term grinding of raw GRAPHICALABSTRACTARTICLEINFOKeywords: Solvothermal synthesis TiO2Dysprosium Phosphor Photoluminescence ABSTRACTThe emerging nanomaterial based on titanium dioxide with a series of Dy3+-doped TiO2 nanoparticles were synthesized first time using solvothermal method.X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed an anatase-type tetragonal structure (spacegroupI41/amd) with successful incorporation of dysprosium into the TiO2 lattice.Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) characterized the morphology and particle size, while Raman spectroscopy further validated the formation of TiO2 nanoparticles and highlighted the influence of Dy3++ doping on phase stability.

RESEARCHTemplate-Assisted Synthesis of Dy3+-Doped Bi2SiO5Nanospheres with Excellent Luminescence and Thermal Stability Dongxun Chen 1 · Xulong Lv1 · Yanjie Liang 1 Received: 7January 2025 / Accepted: 28January 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025 Abstract In this work, Dy3+- doped Bi2SiO5 nanoparticles with uniform spherical morphology and narrow size distribution have been successfully synthesized using a facile template-assisted approach.The efects of sintering temperature and Dy3+ doping concentration on the phase composition, morphology, and luminescence properties of Bi2SiO5: Dy3+ nanophosphor are systematically investigated through X-ray difraction, scanning electron microscopy, and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy.X-ray difraction results confirm that the synthesized Bi2SiO5: Dy3+ nanospheres exhibit a pure tetragonal phase.Meanwhile, the phosphor particles are composed of monodisperse nanospheres with an average diameter of approximately 265 nm.Upon excitation at 388 nm, intense photoluminescence is noted in the blue (4F9/26H15/2) and yellow (4F9/26H13/2) spectral regions due to the characteristic emissions of Dy3+Dy ions.Temperature-dependent PL spectra reveal that the optimized Bi2SiO5: 2.5 % Dy3+ nanospheres maintain extraordinary luminescence thermal stability, retaining 81.0% of its emission intensity at 423K compared to 303K.The phosphor also showed remarkable color stability, with CIE chromaticity coordinates shifting minimally from (0.377, 0.413) at 303K to (0.373, 0.407) at 423K.This newly developed Bi2SiO5: Dy3+ nanospheres exhibit commendable PL properties, enabling them as promising candidates for yel low phosphors in LEDs and display applications.

Lanthanide (Ln3+) ions doped inorganic luminescent materials have garnered widespread attention in the fields of display, laser, sensing, and bio-imaging due to their unique optical characteristics, such as large anti-Stokes shifts, sharp emission spectra, long excited-state lifetimes, tunable emission colors, high photostability, low toxicity, and their excellent chemical stability [1–6].Among them, Dy3+ ions, with their 4 f9 electronic configuration, are capable of emitting a characteristic blue band (470–500 nm) corresponding to the 4F9/2→6H15/2 transition, and a yellow band (570–600 nm) related to the hypersensitive 4F9/26H13/2 ( L=2, J=2 ) transition.Importantly, environmental factors, especially the chemical surroundings of Dy3+ ions, have a more significant impact on the intensity of the yellow emission [7–12].Thus, by adjusting the crystal structure of the matrix, the relative intensities of these emission bands can be controlled, allowing for the achievement of distinct colors suitable for LED and display applications [13–19].Currently, the research on Dy3-+-doped luminescent materials is primarily focused on rare-earth-based matrix systems, such as GdAlO3 [ 7 ], Y2O3 [8], Ba2RV3O11 ( R=La, Gd, Y) [13], Sr3Gd (PO4) 3 [ 14 ], and Sr3La (PO4) 3 [20].Compared to non-rare-earth-based host systems, such as CaMoO4 [10], Dy3+ ions in rare-earth-based hosts have an ionic radius closer to that of the substituted host ions, ensuring the stability of structural and luminescence performance [12].However, the increasing demand for rareearth elements has led to supply constraints and higher costs, limiting the scalability.To reduce expenses, researchers are exploring bismuth-based matrices, as bismuth (Bi) is more cost-efective and can be purified on a large scale through zone refining techniques [21, 22].

s more cost-efective and can be purified on a large scale through zone refining techniques [21, 22].On the other hand, the electronic configuration of the bismuth element is [ Xe ] 4 f145 d106 s26 p3: [ 23 ], thus Bi3+ can be obtained after losing three valence electrons, which is the most common and stable oxidation state [24].When Bi3+ ions serve as cations in the host matrix, the resulting bismuth-based compounds facilitate doping with Ln3+ ions to achieve optical functionality, owing to their similar ionic radii and valences [25, 26].Bi2Si O5 crystal is a typical bismuth-based compound with the Aurivillius-type structure, which features a unique layered architecture composed of alternating [ Bi2O2 ] 2+ and [ SiO3 ] 2-layers.At the same time, it exhibits a relatively low phonon frequency of 480 cm - 1 [27].The unique structure and phonon properties endow Bi2SiO5 materials with excel lent stability and optoelectronic properties, making it an ideal host material for rare-earth ion doped high-eficiency luminescent materials [28–33].Nevertheless, the methods for preparing Dy3+-doped Bi2SiO5 phosphors mainly include coprecipitation, hydrothermal, and melt quenching methods, which exhibit poor performances in terms of morphology control and luminescent eficiency [27, 34, 35].Recently, a template-assisted chemical method has been reported for the controllable synthesis of monodisperse Ln3+-doped Bi2SiO5 nanophosphors [28–33].That is, the solvothermal method is used to synthesize Bi-based precursor spheres, and then coating them with a SiO2 shell layer to enhance the stability and dispersibility of the Bi-based precursor core [33].During the high-temperature sintering process, the SiO2 shell layer can undergo an in-situ reaction with the Bi-based precursor to form Bi2SiO5: Ln3+ spherical phosphors.Therefore, this method can be applied to prepare Dy3+-doped Bi2SiO5 nanophosphors, enabling precise control of morphology and luminescence properties.

Materials and Methods Materials Analytical grade Bi (NO3) 35H2O was obtained by Alfa Aesar.Dy (NO3) 36H2O (99.99%) was purchased from Aladdin Reagents.Polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP, average Mw40, 000 ) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.Nitric acid ( HNO3, 68 wt % ), ethylene glycol (EG), urea ( CO (NH2) 2 ).ethanol, ammonium hydroxide ( NH3H2O, 25–28 wt%), and tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS, 98%) were provided from Sinopharm Chemical Reagents.All the chemical reagents were directly used as starting materials without further purification. Synthesis of Dy3+-Doped Precursor Nanospheres Dy3+-doped bismuth-based precursor nanospheres were synthesized via a solvothermal process [36].Typically, Bi (NO3) 35H2O (0.39mmol) and Dy (NO3) 36H2O (0.01mmol) were dissolved in a5 mL nitric acid solution (2M).Separately, CO (NH2) 2 (2.8mmol) and PVP (0.3g) were dispersed in 25 mL of EG and then gradually added to the initial solution.The mixture was stirred for 15 min before being transferred to a50 mL Teflon-lined autoclave, sealed, and heated to 150 °C for 5 h.After cooling to room temperature, the 2.5 % Dy3+-doped precursors were collected by centrifugation, washed multiple times with water and ethanol, and dried at 60C for 12 h.

Synthesis of BiSiO5:Dy3+ Nanospheres Dy3+-doped precursor QSiO2 nanospheres (referred to here as precursor@SiO ) were synthesized using a modified Stöber method [30, 33].First, 100 mg of precursor spheres were dispersed in 40 mL ethanol and 10 mL water and sonicated for 30 min.Next, 1 mL of NH3H2O and 0.2 mL of TEOS were added to the solution, which was stirred continuously at room temperature for 4 h.The resulting products were collected by centrifugation, washed several times with water and ethanol, and dried at 60C for 12 h.Finally, the precursor (a) SiO2 spheres were calcined at 700-1000 C for 2 h in the air to produce Bi2SiO5: Dy3+ nanospheres. Thermal, structural, and optical behavior of Ba2SiO4: 2% Dy phosphor with sufficient red emission Nancy Jangra a, Bharti Mohan a, Gita Rani b, Rachna Ahlawat a,* a Mat Sci Lab, Department of Physics, Ch.Devi Lal University, Sirsa, 125055, Haryana, India b Department of Chemistry, Ch.Devi Lal University, Sirsa, 125055, Haryana, India ARTICLEINFOHandling Editor: DrP.Vincenzini Keywords: TG-DTABa2SiO4: 2% Dy phosphor.band gap CCTColorimetric Cool light Excitation Emission spectra Energy level diagram ABSTRACTThis work manifests the thermal, structural, and optical behavior of alkaline metal silicates Ba2SiO4; 2% Dy phosphor annealed at different temperatures.The desired composition of the materials was synthesized via a citric acid-assisted sol-gel route.X-ray diffraction studies revealed the highly crystalline, homogeneous, and monophasic formation of particles with nano-dimensions.TGA curves were plotted to examine proper thermal behavior.The stretching and bending vibrations in the molecular band structure of all prepared specimens were indexed by FTIR spectroscopy.TEM micrographs were used to disclose the spheroidal shape of particles at high temperatures.The absorption spectra were executed to correlate the variation in the size of the particles and the band gap energy.The PL spectra portrayed the intense emission in the blue, yellow, and red regions of spectra employing 325 nm excitation.Another 250 nm excitation wavelength exhibited emission corresponding to the charge transfer state and structural defects.Corresponding decay analysis revealed the drastic increment in average lifetime with temperature.

LEDs1.Introduction Phosphor substances are pivotal in new technologies, especially in lightning equipment and accessories.They have excellent physiochemical properties with stable crystal structural formation [1,2].This research opens up exciting possibilities in the field of phosphor materials, with potential applications in field emission displays (FEDs), plasma display panels (PDPs), sensors, traffic signals, cellular phones cathode ray tubes (CRT), security printing, X-ray imaging framework, optical fibers, and white light emitting diodes [3–5].In all these applications, white LEDs are monitored as the best choice for lightning over traditional incandescent and halogen lamp lightning systems due to their extensive characteristics such as power, efficiency, reliability, high current density, consistency, ease of fabrication, harmlessness, low-ecologically affected, long life, brightness, low energy consumption and eco-friendliness [6,7].In addition, ultraviolet (UV) irradiated, phosphor-converted w-LEDs have been proven to have a high color rendering index, color stability, and color purity.In general, there are two approaches to manufacturing w-LED: the use of yellow YAG: Ce3+ phosphorescent with blue-emitting InGaNLEDs or utilizing a blue LED chip to produce a tricolor (red, green, blue) phosphor [8–10].Numerous rare earth-doped sulfide lattice matrices have been suc cessfully explored as low-power consumption phosphors [11,12].However, these materials have a brief lifetime due to their chemical instability and debasement under the attack of electrons.Another disadvantage of sulfur phosphors is that they are not environmentally safe due to sulfur gas emissions [13,14].

e of sulfur phosphors is that they are not environmentally safe due to sulfur gas emissions [13,14].Therefore, it is challenging for researchers to fabricate a phosphor material with high luminescence performance and stability.Silicate lattice substrates are much more stable than sulfides and fluorides.Alkaline earth metal silicates possess the best luminescent center due to their strength and good chemical durability.When doped with impurity ions, silicate produces phosphor powder with outstanding luminescence in the visible range [15].Moreover, silicate host lattices are popular due to their remarkable properties like stable crystalline structure, physical and chemical steadiness, outstanding formability, long lifetime, comparatively easy production, multicolor fluorescence and water resistance, high quantum efficiency, low cost, and high transparency [16].Such fascinating properties of silicates make them applicable in photonics, optoelectronics, biomedical demonstratives, etc.[17].In recent years, silicates comprised of barium elements have attracted particular focus as the luminescent host material.They can be formed in various phases by controlling the molar ratio of BaO and SiO2.Thus, there are variou silicate-based barium silicate phases Ba2SiO4BaSiO3, Ba5Si8021Ba3Si5O13, and BasSiO5 [18].The Ba2SiO4 phase exhibits unique prop erties like high nucleation, temperature stability and electrical isolation among the multiple phases.Comprehensive research has been reported to explore the luminescent properties of barium silicate phosphor material.Singh et al.[19] prepared a nanopowder of Ba2SiO4 doped Gd3+ phosphor, and the PL emission characteristics showed UV-B emission at 314 nm.Wang et al.[12] synthesized Ba1.95Si O40.05Eu2+ phosphor using the traditional solid-state reaction method and observed the luminescence intensity in the green region was enhanced with the co-doping of Lu3+ ions, which was further confirmed by both PL and TL testing.Yang et al.

ed with the co-doping of Lu3+ ions, which was further confirmed by both PL and TL testing.Yang et al.[20] studied the result of the charge compensation mechanism on the luminescent properties of Eu-doped barium silicate.Xiao et al.[12] prepared Ba2SiO4Eu2+ red phosphor, and the results conveyed that Bi3+ and Sm3+ strongly affected the luminescence properties at the optimal concentration.Trusova et al.[5] investigated the high-power white light emission from lithium and barium disilicate glass ceramics containing the different mixtures of rare earth ions in the host.Vyas et al.[2] reported that Ba2SiO4Eu2+, Nd3+ phosphor becomes a near-infrared light-emitting source under near UV light optimization.The white light generated by the strategies mentioned above is notorious for high CCT and low CRI, which exhibit poor color quality without any red component and further limit the applications in general indoor lighting.To overcome these disadvantages, finding a single-phase white phosphor for specific applications in wLEDs is desired.Nowadays, Dy3+ doped alkaline earth metal orthosilicates have attracted much attention due to their good absorption in the UV region and excellent spectroscopical behavior [21].The Dy3+ ion is subjected to stimulate radiative transition due to the 4f-4f electronic bands.These ions usually manifest sharp emission peaks in the blue and yellow spectral regions but lack red components to sound white light emission [22].Recently, co-doping of a red emitter and charge compensator ions has been reported in Dy3+ doped Ba2SiO4 phosphor to improve the white luminosity [2,4].The research scope in Dy3+ doped inorganic phosphor is yet to be explored, especially on red luminous.Therefore, we have investigated sufficient red emission corresponding to 4F9/26H11/2 transition to contribute to single-phase LEDs.It would be interesting to see the role of structural defects in red emission induced by high-temperature annealing.

of impurities creates several new trap levels, enforcing the improvement of the luminescence in the visible region.There are several methods for preparing silicates, but no one has utilized the ing temperature range of 30–800 ◦C.This study was carried out in three distinct weight loss sections.In the first section, minor weight loss of about 10.75% of the initial value till 270C was detected, attributed to the dehydration of absorbed water and moisture, decomposition of TEOS, and organic compounds of the prepared sample [23].Subsequently, the latter connotes a significant weight loss, corresponding to a36.39% drop when the temperature reached 576C.This maximum weight loss in this region results from the degradation of metal nitrates and the expulsion of undesirable gases such as CO2 and NH [24].In the next section of weight loss, the specimen is slightly changed due to minor residual impurities, and an almost flat curve was observed at a temperature above 800C, confirming no further decomposition.These outcomes indicate the evaporation of all by-products of the reaction up to 800C and the formation of a high-purity orthorhombic crystal phase of the synthesized barium silicate compound [26].In the heat flow curve, remarkable endothermic peaks were noticed at 376C and 576C.Those minor peaks are ascribed to the evaporation of water and the decomposition of metal nitrates [29].The most prominent peak at 576C articulates the decomposition of precursors and the establishment of a pure crystalline phase.The formation of the pure phase and the appearance of distinct endothermic peaks concurred with the literature [11,12].The XRD data further corroborate all these TGA-DTA results. content: as potential in simultaneous high-resolution X-ray imaging and non-contact temperature sensing. 1.Introduction Inorganic scintillators, which can convert high-energy X-ray photons into low-energy visible light efficiently [13], are indispensable in medical imaging, radiation safety monitoring, and nondestructive detection applications [4–6].However, their performance is temperature-dependent, as thermal quenching mechanisms significantly affect their light yield and energy resolution [7,8].This temperature sensitivity becomes particularly problematic in precision applications where real-time thermal feedback could optimize operational parameters.Such limitations motivate the integration of real-time temperature sensing into scintillators, enabling active compensation for thermal ef fects in patient treatment, equipment protection, and hazard prevention [9–11].X-ray-excited temperature measurement technology emerges as viable solution because it eliminates the need for an additional UV/visible light source.Simultaneous irradiation with UV light and X-rays may induce electronic transitions through fundamentally different photophysical mechanisms, which could lead to signal interference and inaccurate detection of temperature variations.In situ temperature measurement using scintillators not only avoids unpredictable technical challenges and operational complexity but also ensures accurate detection by eliminating signal interference from dual-excitation mechanisms [12].However, conventional scintillators ( e.8., CdWO4, Bi4Ge3O12 (BGO), CsI:Tl) suffer from critical limitations, including imprecise thermal sensitivity, complex single-crystal growth processes, and high manufacturing costs [13–16].Such drawbacks highlight the urgent need for novel scintillator designs that combine efficient X-ray detection with reliable temperature-sensing functionalities.Dy3+ ions, capable of integrating scintillation and self-referenced thermometry, offer an effective solution to the absence of temperature-sensing functionality in conventional scintillators [17].

Unveiling the subtle emission transition of dysprosium in CaWO4 crystals for ultra-sensitive ratiometric thermometry and anti-counterfeiting applications Baosheng Cao a,*,1, Qianrui Liu a,b,1, Lulu Qiu a, Yujie Weng a, Yangyang Hea, Xiaoguang Han b,**, Bin Dong a,*** a Key Laboratory of Photosensitive Material and Device of Liaoning Province, Key Laboratory of New Energy and Rare Earth Resource Utilization of State Ethnic Affairs Commission & School of Physics and Materials Engineering, Dalian Minzu University, Dalian, 116600, PRChina b Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Dalian Maritime University, Dalian, 116026, PRChina ARTICLEINFOHandling Editor: DrP.Vincenzini Keywords: Dysprosium Calcium tungstate Site symmetry Spectrum deconstruction Temperature-dependent spectroscopy Ratiometric thermometry Sensitivity Anti-counterfeiting ABSTRACTDy3+-doped luminescent materials have a promising application in various optical and optoelectronic fields.The unveiling of detailed energy level distribution and subtle emission transition of Dy3+ in oxide matrices is vital for developing new optical sensors.In this study, the crystallographic site symmetry of Dy3+ in CaWO4: Dy3+ phosphors prepared via the co-precipitation method was identified by the XRD, FT-IR, and Raman spectroscopy.The spectroscopic site of the S4 symmetry of Dy3+ in CaWO4 crystals was confirmed using Eu3+ as the structural probe through high-resolution, low-temperature photoluminescence spectroscopy.The detailed crystal-filed (CF) energy level arrangement and corresponding emission transition lines o Dy3+ were revealed through the spectral well-resolving and temperature-dependent PL spectra.

lines o Dy3+ were revealed through the spectral well-resolving and temperature-dependent PL spectra.Furthermore, a new ratiometric thermometric strategy based on the two opposite thermal-dependent CF transitions exhibited excellent sensitivity to a wide temperature range from 80 to 700K.In addition, a novel barcode anti-counterfeiting applicability has been certified to realize dynamic information encryption.This study provides insight into the development of new Ḋ y3 +-based phosphors and the exploration of CaWO4: Dy3-+ phosphors in advanced luminescent thermometers and anti-counterfeiting under extreme temperature conditions. 1.Introduction Trivalent lanthanide ion (Ln3+) doped luminescent materials have widespread applications in various fields such as anti-counterfeiting, biomedicine, solar cells, and lighting owing to their various photoluminescence (PL) properties, including high color purity, long fluorescence lifetime, and strong absorption capacity for excitation energy with high conversion efficiency [1–7].Notably, the temperature-dependent PL properties make Ln3+-doped material promising materials for non-contact thermometers with exceptional sensitivity, precision, and complete non-destructiveness to components.Various thermoresponsive PL parameters, including PL intensity, fluorescence lifetime, emission bandwidth, and PL peak shift, have been used to develop effective thermometric techniques [8–14].Among them, the luminescence intensity ratio (LIR) technique based on two distinct transitions with different temperature dependences has become a research focus for Ln3+-based thermometers, especially for Ln3+ with definite Boltzmann-type populations between two thermally coupled energy levels (TCLs), such as Er3+, Tm3+, Ho3+, Sm3+, Eu3+, Pr3+, and Dy3+[15–21].Wade and other researchers [ 22, 23 ] have reported that the energy gap (ΔE) of TCLs significantly influences the performance of thermometers.

reported that the energy gap (ΔE) of TCLs significantly influences the performance of thermometers.A larger ΔE improves the relative temperature sensing sensitivity Sr ( Sr=E / k T2 ), whereas extremely large ΔE decouples the TCLs, making the emission challenging to detect from the upper level of TCLs.Conversely, a lower ΔE reduces Sr and causes a severe overlap between two emission lines from TCLs, making it challenging to accurately measure the luminescent intensity.Furthermore, the appli cable temperature range influences luminescent performance.High temperatures usually lead to significant fluorescence thermal quenching, while low temperatures may be insufficient to effectively populate the upper level of TCLs.Therefore, developing a new luminescent thermometric strategy that encompasses both high and low temperatures is crucial and urgent.Dysprosium (Dy3+) -doped luminescent materials can be effectively excited by ultraviolet to emit distinct blue and yellow PL emissions, and they are commonly used in white lighting, optical thermometers, anti counterfeiting, and other applications [24–26].The LIR of blue to yellow emissions of Dy3+ can also serve as a structural probe to investigate the crystal field symmetry of Dy3+[27].In addition, temperature significantly influences the PL properties of Dy3+-doped materials, making them promising materials for its difficulty in populating upper TCLs of 4I15/2 from lower TCLs of 4F9/2 through thermal excitation caused by large ΔE of 4I15/2 / 4F9/2TCLs [28–30].Meanwhile, the broadening of Dy3+ emission peaks and severe luminescent thermal quenching at high temperatures usually make it challenging to distinguish the two emissions from 4I15/2 / 4F9/2TCLs, resulting in inaccurate PL intensities and PAPERView Article Online View Journal | View Issue Check for updates Cite this: J.Mater.Chem.C, 2026, 14, 9104 A thermally robust Dy3+-activated SC2M0312 phosphor for sustainable WLED lighting and phase transition-enabled visual cryogenic thermometry Annu Balhara,ab Priyansu Mishra,c Sreevalsa Subhagan,de Athira Raghu,fg Ashok Kumar Yadav, h Rohit Kumar Gupta,i Giri Dhari Patra, V.B.Jayakrishnan,k Subrata Das, de Ashish Kumar Mishrai and Santosh Kumar Gupta *ab The development pt?>of phosphors exhibiting negative-thermal expansion (NTE) is urgent for achieving thermally robust luminescence performance of phosphor-converted white light-emitting diodes (pc-WLEDs).The current pc-WLEDs sufer from poor thermal stability, suboptimal color rendering index (CRI) due to blue-light exposure, and high correlated color temperature (CCT).Herein, we developed a promising Sc2Mo3O12: Dy3+ phosphor with bright yellow-white emission upon ultraviolet (UV) and near-UV light excitation.Local structure analysis using extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectroscopy confirmed the occupancy of Dy3+ ions at octahedral SC3+ sites.Temperature-dependent in situ X-ray difraction study revealed a strong NTE efect in Sc2Mo3O12.Temperature-dependent photoluminescence studies demonstrated the excellent luminescence thermal stability of the Sc2Mo3O12: Dy3+ phosphor (91.4%@480K) due to enhanced structural rigidity and reduced non-radiative decay as a result of thermally induced lattice compaction.The influence of the host’s low-temperature phase transition on Dy3+ luminescence was examined under crvogenic temperature conditions.

emperature phase transition on Dy3+ luminescence was examined under crvogenic temperature conditions.Furthermore, we demonstrated the fabrication of three prototype pc-WLEDs by coating the Sc2Mo3O12: Dy3+ phosphor onto a UV-LED chip with tunable WLED parameters, i.e., CIE, CCT, and luminous eficacy, which strengthens its suitability for commercial lighting.The optical thermal sensing based on charge transfer red-shift and phase transition-induced luminescence has been demonstrated with high relative sensitivity (S) values of 2.30 (70K) and 1.14% K-1 (300K) across diferent temperature regimes, from cryogenic to high-temperature conditions, respectively, with visual color tuning.This work highlights the potential of NTE-active hosts in designing pc-WLED phosphors with enhanced thermal stability to advance the commercialization of sustainable WLED lighting, and ofers opportunities for flexible thermal sensing in complex environments.Received 14th January 2026, Accepted 24th March 2026DOI: rsc.li/materials-c 1.Introduction Solid-state lighting technology based on phosphor-converted white light emitting diodes (pc-WLEDs) has become integral to homes, workplaces, and industries, owing to their electricity eficiency, long lifespan, low cost, luminous performance and compact size.1–6 The most common commercial WLEDs use a combination of blue light from GaxIn1-xNLED chips and yellow light emitted by Y3Al5O12: Ce3+ ( YAG: Ce3+) phosphors to produce the white light spectrum.5 However, these WLEDs with an excessive blue light component tend to have a low color rendering index (CRI) and a high correlated color temperature (CCT), and longer exposure to these lights could disrupt sleep cycles and potentially cause harm to human eyes.4,7 Therefore, a continuous effort has been underway to develop new phosphor materials as potential alternatives in order to reduce the blue light exposure.

develop new phosphor materials as potential alternatives in order to reduce the blue light exposure.The sustainable pc-WLED device should satisfy the requirements of high CRI ( Ra > 80 ), high luminous efficacy, desired CCT (3000–6000K), and excellent thermal stability at optimum operating temperatures (1500C).8-10To achieve these parameters, the luminescence properties of phosphor materials need optimization to enhance the luminous efficiency and absorption, along with a rational choice of activator ions and host matrices to minimize luminescence quenching and ensure high thermal stability.In recent years, continuous eforts have been directed towards the development of eficient rare-earth doped phosphor materials to improve the performance of modern ultraviolet (UV) or near-UV chip-based WLEDs with Eu3+, Eu2+, Ce3+, Dy3+, Tb3+Pr3+, and Sm3+ as the activator ions.11–17 Among these, NUV and blue light excitable Dysprosium (Dy3+) )-activated phosphors are a promising choice for high-quality WLEDs.18 The Dy3+ ions with rich 4 f4f transitions exhibit blue (4F9/26H15/2) and yellow (4F9/26F13/2) emissions, which can be optimized for whitelight generation.19 Different such materials for WLED applications have been explored in earlier studies, for example, Ba3 (Zn-B5O10) PO4: Dy3+, 20Ca3Al2Ge3O12: Dy3+/ Eu3+, 21Sr3La Al3B4O15: Dy3+/ Ge6: O16: O25: O6: O16: O16: O16: O16: O16: O16: Tm3+, 22Li La (MoO4) x (WO4) 2-x: Dy3+, 23Na Gd (MoO4) 2: Dy3+/ Tm3+, 24: etc.Recently, host matrices with negative thermal expansion (NTE) properties have attracted huge scientific interest, particularly for developing phosphor materials that can withstand high temperature conditions and maintain stable luminous intensity.Diferent NTE materials such as ZrW2O8, ZrMo2O8, ZrW2O7, Sc2Mo3O12, Sc2W3O12, Al2Mo3O12, etc., have been reported in earlier studies.25 Among the NTE-based hosts, A2M3O12 – type ( A=trivalent.

earlier studies.25 Among the NTE-based hosts, A2M3O12 – type ( A=trivalent.cations and M=Mo/W) materials undergo volume contraction driven by the transverse vibration of MoO4 tetrahedral units, and exhibit a promising NTE efect over a broad temperature range.26 The negative thermal quenching (NTQ) of luminescence in orthorhombic Sc2Mo3O12: Eu3+ phosphors has been widely explored in the literature 27-29Recently, Yang et al.30 reported a red-emitting Al0.3Sc1.7Mo3O12Eu3+ phosphor, which maintains 180% of the initial room temperature luminescence intensity at 483K.Fan et al.29 reported a NTE-based KxMgxSc1.95-x Mo3O12: Eu3+ phosphor with significant luminescence thermal stability.Similarly, the role of the NTE effect in the thermal enhancement of upconversion luminescence has been investigated in different materials, such as ZrSc (WO4) 2P O4; Yb / Er, 31 b2-x W3O12: x Ho332Al2W3O12: Yb / Er33Sc2-2xZrxNbxW3-1.5 x O12-3x: Yb / Er28Sc2Mo3O12: Yb/Er, 34, Sc2Mo3O12: Yb / Ho, 35 and so on.The Zou group reported a29-fold enhancement of Er3+ upconversion luminescence in Yb2W3O12 crystals which were explored for ratiometric thermometry.36 In our previous study, we investigated Sc2Mo3O12: Sm3+ phosphor WLEDs and indoor plant growth LEDs.37 The NTE effect of the Sc2Mo3O12 lattice facilitated the retention of 591% of Sm3+ intensity at room temperature, even at 433K.Besides WLED applications, the phosphor materials have potential applications in easy, precise and non-invasive temperature sensing, which holds importance in various domains, such as optoelectronics, biomedicine, aviation, the automotive industry, and so on.38,39 Lanthanide-activated phosphors, including the molybdates, tungstates, and vanadates as host materials, exhibit NTQ of charge-transfer band (CTB) intensity, while the 4f–4f transitions usually undergo positive thermal quenching (PTQ).

content: ished by Elsevier B.V.All rights are reserved, including those 1.Introduction With the merits of non-contact, fast response and high sensitivity, the phosphors for fluorescent thermometry attracted the attention of researchers.Due to their excellent physical, chemical and mechanical stability, inorganic non-metallic ceramic phosphors are more suitable for extreme service temperature range and intense fluid impact in industrial environment than the nanoparticles and the metaleorganic framework (MOF) materials.1e3 The temperature-dependent fluorescence intensity ratio (FIR) and fluorescence lifetime (FL) from fef transitions of rare earth ions (RE3+) doped phosphors,4 such as Er3+ doped phosphors, are known to be appropriate signals for the fluorescent thermometry, which have been applied in industrial scenes gradually.5e8 Compared to the upconversion luminescence excited by nearinfrared lasers, ultraviolet (UV) light excitation is typically used for downconversion fluorescence, which avoids additional thermal effects.9,10 For example, when excited by 355 nm light, electrons in Dy3+ ions can be redistributed across the thermally coupled levels (TCLs) 4I and 4F9/2 (withanenergygapDEofapproximately1150cm-1) according to a Boltzmann distribution as the temperature increases, resulting in a temperature-dependent FIR signal.11e14 This thermal excitation (TE) induced FIR of TCLs has led to the development of Dy3+-doped phosphors for downconversion fluorescent thermometry over the past decades.Hertle et al.reviewed the temperature-dependent FIR performance of TCLs in various Dy3+ doped garnet hosts, noting an impressive performance of absolute sensitivity (Sa) at 10.810-4K - 1 and relative sensitivity (S) at 1.42 % / K.

Cool White Light Emitting Dy3+ Activated Disodium Calcium Pyrophosphate Phosphor for WLEDsApplication Umashankar Bhardwaj 1,2 · Ganesh Ram Banjare 3 · Chitrkant Belodhiya 4 · D.P.Bisen 4 · N.Brahme 4 · Sanjay Kumar Baghel 5 · Vikas Kumar Jain 6 · Vineet Kumar Shukla 3 · Yugbodh Patle 7 Received: 11January 2026 / Accepted: 21April 2026 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026 Abstract A series of Na2CaP2O7: xDy3+ (x=0.01–0.06) (abbreviatedasNCPO) phosphors were synthesized using the solid-state reaction method in the present research work.X-ray difraction (XRD) was used to confirm the phase purity and crystal linity of the synthesized phosphors.Morphological and elemental analyses were carried out using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), respectively.Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy assessed the functional groups, while difuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS) was employed to estimate the optical band gap.Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy was performed at an excitation wavelength of 351 nm to investi gate the luminescence properties of the prepared phosphors.Two emission bands were subsequently observed at 485 nm and 575 nm, corresponding to 4F9/26H15/2 and 4F9/26H13/2 transitions, respectively.The critical distance (Rc) between Dy3+ ions in this host was calculated to be 17 Å, indicating that both nearest-neighbor ion interactions and dipole–dipole interactions were involved.The PL decay lifetime and internal quantum eficiency (IQE) of the synthesized phosphor are determined.

e PL decay lifetime and internal quantum eficiency (IQE) of the synthesized phosphor are determined.Photometric studies reveal that the CIE coordinates fall very close to the white light region, and the CCT value is found to be greater than 5000K, indicating that the prepared NCPO: Dy3+ phosphor is a promising candidate for cool WLEDs for outdoor lighting applications.Keywords Na2CaP2O7:Dy3+ · W-H plot · CCT · WLEDsIntroduction Nowadays, the development of novel and eficient lumi nescent materials is a key area of research.As per the lit erature survey, luminescent materials play a significant role in the solid-state lighting industry.In the solid state lighting industries, phosphor converted white light emitting diode (pc-WLED) is advanced technology for eficient conversion of electrical energy into light energy [1].The rapid growth of pc-WLEDs has made them an emerging and promising candidate in the lighting industry due to their broad chromaticity color tunability, long service life, cost-efectiveness, high eficiency, lightweight nature, and environmental friendliness [2–6].Additionally, it prevents 70% of total electricity consumption and exhibits outstanding light-emitting properties [7].Pc-WLED having excellent eficiency and thermal stability is always challenging to develop and manufacture it.Two separate approaches are commonly employed to manufacture most commercial pc-WLEDs: (1) Integrating a blue LED chip with Ce3+-activated YAG phosphor and (2) combining trichromatic phosphors—red, green, and blue—with a near-ultraviolet (n-UV) or ultraviolet (UV) LED.However, both approaches typically result in a low color rendering index (CRI) and a high correlated color temperature (CCT), leading to poor eficiency [8, 9].Another drawback of these methods are high cost, Degradation-induced phase separation among emitters and Absorption overlap–induced energy loss [10, 11].

adation-induced phase separation among emitters and Absorption overlap–induced energy loss [10, 11].These significant challenges may be addressed by designing novel white-emitting phosphors that are excitable by near-ultraviolet (n-UV) or blue light and exhibit low thermal quenching along with favorable synthesis conditions.This shows that we urgently need better white phosphors for pc-WLEDs to produce high quality white light [12].To enhance eficiency, signifi cant focus has been directed towards the development of white-emitting phosphors that exhibit strong absorption in the near-UV or UV region for white-light emitting diodes (W-LEDs).As a result, researchers have concentrated on achieving single-component NUV-based white light emission through energy transfer between rare earth ions or host to rare earths [13].Luminescent materials are usually made up of a crystalline host lattice that is infused with a small amount of activator ions, typically transition metals or rare-earth elements, which facilitate the electronic transitions of electrons to emit light in the visible spectrum [14].The luminescence properties of luminescent materials are strongly influenced by their composition, phase purity, surface morphology, particle size and crystal structure.Hence, selecting an appropriate host matrix can efectively tune the activator sites, crystal field environment, and energy transfer processes, thus impacting both the luminescence eficiency and the thermal stability of the luminescent materials [15– 17].Commercially available lanthanides activated phosphors for WLEDs based on silicates, sulphides, titanates, oxynitrides, tungstate, nitrides and fluorides have some disadvantages [18].Therefore, phosphate-based phosphors have attracted considerable attention as host materials for light-emitting applications, owing to their simple synthesis process, low cost, excellent thermal and chemical stability, and diverse structural chemistry [19–21].
